materials-ai-alloy-flight.title: First AI-agent-designed alloy flies in a rocket engine
materials-ai-alloy-flight.description: An alloy proposed by an agentic AI/ICME design loop after 2027 (materials-ht-alloy-design) flies in flight hardware (combustion chamber, preburner, turbine or nozzle, including a small thruster or kick-stage part) on a commercial launch vehicle or spacecraft. Pre-existing computationally designed alloys such as GRX-810, and alloys from pre-2027 ML-assisted searches, do not count: they owe nothing to this chain.
materials-ai-alloy-flight.status_oct2026: No AI-designed alloy has flown (general). Benchmarks: the GRCop family was developed in 1987 and its printed variant GRCop-42 flew on Relativity's Terran 1 in 2023, about eight years after AM work began (~2015); Ferrium M54 went from design to flight qualification in under six years; GRX-810 (2022) and NASA HR-1 are still maturing.
materials-ai-alloy-flight.why: With design compressed to weeks (materials-ht-alloy-design, S2 2028), the floor is physical: powder atomization lots, AM parameter development (1-3 years per machine and process, physclock), property tests sized to the duty cycle (a reusable engine spends minutes at temperature per flight, so short-time creep, cyclic fatigue, oxidation and hydrogen tests of 100-1,000 h cover it; 10,000 h creep tests matter for long-life hardware) and hot-fire campaigns, roughly 2-3 years for a risk-tolerant commercial engine maker that certifies its own hardware. Historical benchmarks are slower: GRCop-42 took about eight years from AM start to flight, Ferrium M54 under six. Material qualification compresses only 0.7-0.8x in S2 and 0.5-0.7x in S3. Chain (S2): cap-applied-math (2027) -> materials-mlip-certified-uq (2028) -> materials-ht-alloy-design (2028) -> powder lot, AM parameter development, coupon and duty-cycle property tests (2029-30) -> hot fire -> first flight in a small thruster or upper-stage hot part (2030 at the earliest; P1->P7). P7 defaults to Speculative; the 2031 band is Low in S2 and Medium in S3, where cognition is near-free from 2029 and the physical multiplier is 1.3-1.5x. Value: hotter preburners and turbines and longer-life chambers for reusable engines. By 2035: historical insertions took 6-8 years, or about 4-7 years at base-case rates, so a 2028 design flies 2032-35 and S2 is Medium; Recursive (0.5-0.7x) is High; Plateau designs the alloy about 2030 and is Low. GRX-810, designed with computational models in 2022, had not flown in an engine by Oct 2026.
materials-ai-alloy-flight.strongest_case_small: Primes stick with heritage alloys (Inconel 718, GRCop) because supply chains and data exist; NASA's AMRL framework notes high alloy maturity is not a qualified material; S3's faster cognition cannot speed up hot-fire testing.
materials-ai-alloy-flight.signpost: An AI-agent-designed alloy enters hot-fire testing at SpaceX, Relativity, Ursa Major or NASA Marshall by 2029.

materials-tps-new-material-flight.title: AI-designed heat-shield material flies
materials-tps-new-material-flight.description: An AI-designed thermal-protection material, coating or ablator flies on a reentry vehicle. 'AI-designed' means composition or microstructure selected by an AI/ML-driven design loop and so stated by the developer. Achieved at the first flight of an instrumented coupon or tile of such a material; adoption as a primary heat-shield zone is tracked in the signpost.
materials-tps-new-material-flight.status_oct2026: Varda's W-5 (Jan 2026) and W-6 (May 2026) capsules re-entered with in-house C-PICA heat shields; W-4 burned up on reentry (May 2026). W-6 already flew Sandia TPS material samples and NASA Ames instrumented eChar tiles, and Starship Flight 10 (Aug 2025) flew metallic and actively cooled tiles, so the coupon channel exists. No AI-designed TPS material has flown (general).
materials-tps-new-material-flight.why: Chain (S2): AI-selected UHTC or ablator composition (materials-uhtc-tps-design, 2029) -> coupon fabrication (6-12 months) -> arc-jet screening (~1 year; the arc-jet queue binds) -> manifest on a Varda-class capsule or a Starship reentry -> flight in 2030. Commercial capsules turn flight testing from a once-a-decade event into a quarterly one, a physical-gate compression independent of AI, and coupons need no qualification. S2 stays Medium because the material itself lands only in 2029 and developers must say it is AI-designed; S3 is High because closed-loop labs deliver candidates earlier and coupon slots are plentiful. Band: above the P7 default (Speculative) because the flight article is a coupon that needs no qualification and commercial capsules offer frequent slots (W-6 already flew material samples); S2 Medium because it cannot exceed its design prerequisite (Medium, 2029); S3 High with that prerequisite High. S1 Low. Bands are judgments.

Non-AI perovskite demonstrations continue regardless; this node is the model-qualified version.
materials-perovskite-tandem-flight.status_oct2026: Perovskite tandems in orbit since Jul 2024 (Potsdam/HZB); RIT CubeSat test; certified 27.49% AM0 tandem with balloon flight (Aug 2026). No published one-year on-orbit stability record with a predictive model found as of Oct 2026.

Chain (S2): degradation models 2028 -> composition and encapsulation build and flight acceptance -> manifest and launch 2029 -> 12 months of data 2030 -> publication; every step after 2028 is on the physical clock with no slack, and the models themselves need on-orbit data to validate. S3 cannot compress the year in orbit.

materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.title: Radiation-robust high-voltage power electronics
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.description: SiC power MOSFETs (600-1,200 V class) redesigned to run near rated voltage in space, whether by empirical hardening or with a mechanism-level model of heavy-ion single-event burnout and leakage degradation. Achieved when a vendor qualifies such a part free of single-event burnout at 80% or more of rated voltage under standard heavy-ion testing (the signpost).
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.status_oct2026: Commercial SiC MOSFETs show heavy-ion single-event burnout and leakage degradation near or below half of rated voltage (NASA NEPP), which limits practical space use to roughly 250 V-class buses. CoolCAD reports hardened-by-design-and-process SiC MOSFETs with burnout thresholds above 900 V at LET above 40 MeV-cm2/mg in Texas A&M and Brookhaven beam tests, enabling derated operation above 300 V (vendor-reported, Jul 2026, not yet qualified); lateral RESURF designs reach a burnout-to-breakdown voltage ratio of ~0.67. Lateral GaN HEMTs are essentially immune to single-event burnout, and rad-tolerant GaN parts fly at lower voltages (hundreds of volts), so GaN is voltage-limited rather than burnout-limited (general). The SiC burnout mechanism is still debated.
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.why: Not an AI-math implication: vendors are already hardening SiC empirically with TCAD and beam tests (CoolCAD's vendor-reported burnout threshold above 900 V at LET above 40, Jul 2026), so the date is set by fab cycles and heavy-ion beam time, and the P7 Speculative default does not apply. High-voltage (300-800 V class) buses cut harness mass and losses for 100 kW-class orbital compute and electric propulsion; derating 1,200 V parts to ~50% throws away much of SiC's advantage. LEO plasma arcing on high-voltage arrays also limits bus voltage (NASA-HDBK-4006, general). Explaining the burnout mechanism (impact ionization and thermal runaway along the ion track, defect physics) is a physics-theory problem that AI could speed (cap-physics-theory, P6, soft), but theory is an accelerator, not a prerequisite; each redesign takes about a year per fab cycle plus beam tests, which bind. Chain (S2): hardened-by-design parts reported 2026 -> one or two redesign, fab and beam-test cycles 2027-29 -> a part qualified free of burnout at 80% or more of rated voltage 2030. Band Medium in S2 and S3 (judgment): the empirical route is close but the mechanism is still debated and the rad-hard power market is small, so fab priority is low. S3 2029 through faster design iteration; S1 2031 and Low because a capability plateau slows design iteration and the soft theory input arrives late.
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.strongest_case_small: Vendors are already fixing it empirically (layout and process hardening guided by TCAD), so mechanism theory may arrive after the parts; the rad-hard power market is small, so fab priority is low.
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.signpost: A vendor releases a SiC MOSFET qualified free of single-event burnout at 80% or more of rated voltage under standard heavy-ion testing, by 2029.

materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.title: Commercial AI chips running in orbit at scale
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.description: Operational orbital AI compute with paying customers on commercial accelerators, rated on SpaceX's AI1: 100 kW-class satellites (150 kW peak, 120 kW average, about 2.1 t) in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, flown on SpaceX's own manifest. Outside operators (Starcloud, Google) buy launch and come later.
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.status_oct2026: Starcloud ran an H100 in orbit from Nov 2025; Starcloud-2 (first commercial mission) was planned for late 2026 (company plan, Mar 2026). Google's first Suncatcher prototype (four TPUs per press reports) launched on Transporter-18 on Oct 1 2026. Nvidia announced the Space-1 Vera Rubin module (Mar 2026) with six launch partners (Aetherflux, Axiom Space, Kepler, Planet, Sophia Space, Starcloud). SpaceX targets first Starmind launches in Q4 2027 (250 kW peak / 175 kW average) and 'significant scale' in 2028 (Musk, Aug 25 2026, who cautioned listeners to be skeptical); Starcloud-3 (~200 kW) is designed for Starship. The FT reported on Oct 6 2026 that SpaceX is seeking ~$40B of debt to buy Nvidia chips (unconfirmed by SpaceX).
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.why: Not an AI-math implication: orbital compute happens on SpaceX's and Starcloud's hardware, launch and capital schedules, so this is an exogenous anchor and the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Operators already fly commercial accelerators without triple redundancy. AI math adds confidence, not the milestone: validated fault models (materials-see-system-models) and proven fault-tolerance layers (materials-verified-fault-tolerance) right-size mitigation, roughly 5-20% more useful compute per watt (assumption), which improves unit economics. Chain (all scenarios): first 100-kW-class Starmind flight 2028 (SpaceX target Q4 2027, slipped per the tree's 1.5-3x calibration) -> commissioning and first paying workloads 2029. Launch, not capital, is the gate for the leader (SpaceX held $100.8B of cash after its 2026 IPO; Mach33 names launch the physical gate). S1 stays Medium because weaker AI demand in a plateau may defer paying service. High in S2 and S3 (judgment): the chain leaves about two years of slack before 2031 and has several independent attempts (Starmind, Starcloud-2 and -3, Google's Suncatcher line). The node rates SpaceX's AI1 on its own manifest (launch-internal). Outside operators (Starcloud, Google's Suncatcher and others) buy launch and face customer access and customer prices (launch-external), which v1.3 puts at 2031 for Starship spare capacity, so their 100 kW-class service would come later than SpaceX's. Basis (R9): AI1 as Mach33 reconstructed it (150 kW peak / 120 kW average, 2.1 t, dawn-dusk SSO); the 100 kW class matches Mach33's 'Debunking the Cooling Constraint in Space Data Centers' (17 Dec 2025). materials-perovskite-primary-power.title: Perovskite arrays power operational satellites
materials-perovskite-primary-power.description: Perovskite-based (tandem or thin-film) arrays serve as primary power on operational spacecraft, for example lightweight arrays for compute or broadband constellations.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.status_oct2026: Not operational anywhere as of Oct 2026 (general); flight experiments only.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.why: Solar is ~56% of AI1's reconstructed mass at ~127 W/kg array level (33FG, Jun 2026). A perovskite tandem at equal areal density and ~30% higher efficiency would cut satellite mass ~13% (0.56 x (1 - 1/1.3)); doubling array W/kg would cut ~28%, i.e. ~1.4x fewer launches. 33FG's often-quoted ~600 versus ~1,200 Starship launches per 100 GW/yr (thin-film ~1.7 kW/kg versus rigid ~0.8 kW/kg) is an asymptotic plateau for idealized high-Earth-orbit designs, not today's compute satellites, and covers thin film generally, not perovskites. One to two years of on-orbit lifetime evidence gate adoption; risk-tolerant constellation operators with five-year design lives adopt first. Compute satellites may be designed for chip-limited lives of ~3-5 years (33FG models 5.6 -> 3.4 years at higher power), so one to two years of orbit data covers a larger share of design life; their operators self-certify, and Chinese orbital-data-center programs (Orbital Chenguang, reported $8.4B credit lines) sit next to the perovskite supply base.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.strongest_case_small: Thin-film CIGS, thinned III-V cells and better array structures may deliver the specific-power gain without perovskites, and falling launch costs reduce the value of mass savings.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.signpost: A constellation operator announces perovskite-based primary arrays on a production satellite batch, by 2030.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic: launch-saving claim corrected (the 600/1,200 figures are 33FG's idealized high-Earth-orbit plateaus, verified in its Nov 2025 post; AI1-era arrays are ~0.13 kW/kg). Advocate: short chip-limited design lives lower the evidence bar (appended; bands unchanged). Auditor: hard edge from materials-perovskite-tandem-flight (the model-qualified version) made soft, since adoption can rest on any flight heritage. Years and bands unchanged. | E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): 2035/S4 extension. earliest_year: S1 >2031 -> 2034; band_2035: S1 Speculative -> Low, S2 Low -> Medium, S3 Low -> Medium, S4 Low -> Medium. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Medium in 2034 in S2, two years after tandem flights pass 30% (2032), and 2033 in S3/S4 where yearly satellite generations adopt a generation sooner. Skeptic (no operational perovskite anywhere) vs advocate (self-certifying compute operators and Chinese programs near the supply base): Medium by 2035 kept, late in the window.

materials-in-space-mfg-product.title: Products made in orbit sold at recurring volume
materials-in-space-mfg-product.description: In-space-manufactured semiconductor substrates or crystals, or ZBLAN fiber, sold commercially at recurring volume, with quality advantages predicted by validated models.
materials-in-space-mfg-product.status_oct2026: Demonstrations only: 11.9 km of ZBLAN drawn on the ISS (2024; no published attenuation comparison yet), ForgeStar-1 plasma operations (from Dec 31, 2025; deorbit planned 2026), Varda defense and pharmaceutical reentries (W-5 and W-6 in 2026).
materials-in-space-mfg-product.why: Products sell on measured quality (fiber attenuation, defect density), not on a model's prediction, and Flawless Photonics and Varda already fly without validated models. Process models help investors and operators choose which products clear the cost of launch and return, so they accelerate this node without gating it. Recurring volume needs dedicated free-flyers, frequent return capsules and committed buyers, all physical and capital gates that AI cognition does not compress. Chain (S2): demonstrations 2024-26 -> measured quality advantage published -> multi-year offtake 2029-30 -> recurring sales 2031 (Low).
materials-in-space-mfg-product.strongest_case_small: Economics, not physics knowledge, binds, and terrestrial process improvements may close the quality gap.

materials-hot-section-reuse.title: Longer-life reusable engines from new alloys
materials-hot-section-reuse.description: Operational reusable engines whose hot-section parts (preburners, turbines, chambers) use AI-designed alloys and model-backed life prediction, extending refurbishment intervals or allowing higher chamber pressure.
materials-hot-section-reuse.status_oct2026: Not started (general); depends on the first AI-designed alloy flight.
materials-hot-section-reuse.why: Hot-section refurbishment is a major reuse cost driver (general); doubling the life of the most-replaced parts would cut turnaround cost, but proving life needs fleet hours and post-flight tear-downs, a physical clock: reuse learning took 15 months from first landing to first reflight and 3-5 years to mature life, compressing only 0.8-0.9x in S2 (physclock). Chain (S2): materials-ai-alloy-flight (2030 at the earliest, Low) + materials-creep-oxidation-life-models (2029) -> fleet-leader parts run past the prior refurbishment interval and torn down -> operator-attributed interval increase (2032 at the earliest, with 100+ heavy flights a year from 2030). Chain (S3): alloy flight (2030) -> parts flown on a subset of a high-cadence fleet (100+ heavy flights a year from 2029, physclock-heavy-cadence-100 in S3) -> attributed interval increase (2031 at the earliest, Low). The chains above take the fastest path, where the first AI alloy flies directly in a reusable main engine. The likelier first flight is a small thruster or upper-stage part, which adds a second insertion into a main engine's preburner or turbine with its own lots and hot fire (1-2 years); on that path S2 lands about 2033-34. By 2035 the node needs the alloy flight (Medium in S2), the insertion, fleet-leader teardowns and attribution, so S2 is Low and S3, where the alloy flight is High, is Medium. S1: alloy flight 2032 at the earliest -> 2034 at the earliest, Speculative by 2035.
materials-hot-section-reuse.strongest_case_small: Reuse economics are dominated by vehicle-level design and operations, and engine makers already iterate in-house alloys empirically without AI.
materials-hot-section-reuse.signpost: An operator attributes a refurbishment-interval increase to a new hot-section alloy, by 2031.

materials-qual-cycle-compression.title: New space materials reach flight in five years or less
materials-qual-cycle-compression.description: Concept-to-flight insertion of new space materials (alloys, TPS, PV) takes five years or less, shown by at least three material programs started in 2027 or later that each fly within five years of start. The first cases are most likely commercial in-house materials that skip handbook allowables; typical programs stay near 8-9 years in S3 by 2035.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.status_oct2026: Historically 10-20 years (Materials Genome Initiative), and more than 20 years and ~$400M for aerospace insertion; GE spent about two decades and over $1B on ceramic-matrix composites; Ferrium M54 (under six years) is the fast exception.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.why: Cognition is perhaps 20-30% of insertion time (Ferrium M54: under one of under six years went to design; assumption generalizing it). The rest is physical evidence: the physical-gate table compresses material qualification only 0.7-0.8x in S2 and 0.5-0.7x in S3 (5-14 years in S3), so three programs started 2027 or later flying by 2031 is at the edge even in S3. Commercial engine builders insert in-house alloys without MMPDS or NASA-STD-6030 gates (SpaceX's SX500 superalloy for Raptor, general), so handbook-accepted allowables and per-part digital-twin certification accelerate rather than gate; real-time creep, fatigue and oxidation tests still bind. Chain (S3): AI alloy design 2027-28 -> in-house allowables 2028 -> first AI-designed alloy flies 2029 -> two more programs fly 2030-31.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.strongest_case_small: Standards bodies and programs change slowly; a few fast commercial examples will not make an industry norm by 2031.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.signpost: A NASA-STD-6030 revision or MMPDS/CMH-17 policy that lets model-based evidence substitute for part of the test matrix, by 2028-29. Or an engine or spacecraft builder discloses a new material flown within five years of program start.

materials-specific-power-step.title: A step change in spacecraft power per kilogram
materials-specific-power-step.description: A fleet-level gain of 30% or more in power-system specific power (W/kg of arrays, storage and power electronics) on new spacecraft, attributable to new materials: perovskite or thin-film PV, high-voltage radiation-robust wide-bandgap electronics, higher-energy cells.
materials-specific-power-step.status_oct2026: Gains today come from array architecture (roll-out and flexible blankets) and cell-efficiency increments (general).
materials-specific-power-step.why: Power-system mass sets launch counts for orbital compute (33FG: compute satellites become power- and thermal-limited), so this is the materials outcome with the largest space-economics leverage. The array leg can deliver the step alone: arrays are about 56% of AI1's reconstructed mass at about 127 W/kg, so a 30% gain needs roughly 165-175 W/kg at array level (estimate). Thinned III-V or thin-film cells on flexible blankets can reach that without perovskites, so perovskite primary power is a soft input and light-array production at volume the hard one. Compute-fleet operators certify their own hardware for 3-5 year lives. Chain (S2): first Starmind generations 2028-30 -> a thin-film array generation flies about 2030-31 -> a year or more of flight data -> fleet adoption on new satellites in 2032. S3 equals S2 because flight evidence binds. S1 is 2035 because a plateau weakens compute-satellite demand. Bands (judgment): Medium by 2035 in S2-S4; S1 Low.
materials-specific-power-step.strongest_case_small: Array architecture and launch-cost moves dwarf material gains in this window.
materials-specific-power-step.signpost: Spec sheets of new compute or broadband buses citing new-material arrays, electronics or cells, by 2031.

physclock-flight-test-cadence.title: Monthly flight testing of a fully reusable heavy launcher
physclock-flight-test-cadence.description: A new fully reusable heavy launcher (Starship V3) flies at least 12 integrated flights in one calendar year, so flight data rather than analysis sets the pace of learning. This is the data generator that reuse, life-prediction and certification-by-analysis nodes downstream need.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.status_oct2026: Starship has flown 14 integrated flights since Apr 2023: five in 2025 (intervals 48-91 days) and three in 2026 (Flight 12 May 22, Flight 13 Jul 24, Flight 14 Sep 28; 63-66 days apart) after a ~7-month gap for the V2-to-V3 change. Flight 14 was the first orbital flight and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The FAA authorized up to 25 Starbase launches a year in 2025 (general); LC-39A's first Starship launch is targeted for around year-end in the best case (Mach33).
physclock-flight-test-cadence.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
physclock-flight-test-cadence.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor (vehicle builds and pad turnaround), so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Cadence is set by vehicle build and pad turnaround: about nine weeks per V3 loop with one active pad. A second Starbase pad, LC-39A and first reflights (expected early 2027) bring the interval to 3-4 weeks, giving 12 or more flights in 2027. AI barely changes this: Flight 12 went from Musk's 'about 6 weeks' (Jan 26 2026) to May 22, about 2.8 times the stated interval, because of V3 hardware readiness and a Starbase component failure in April, not analysis. Starship has never met a yearly flight plan: 2, 4, 5 and 3 flights (2023 to Oct 2026), 5 against 25 authorized in 2025. Twelve in 2027 needs about 3x the 2026 rate, a debut of LC-39A (not yet launched) and roughly a dozen new ships before ship reuse arrives, which makes 2027 about a coin flip, so the central year is 2028. AI-assisted mishap diagnosis (physclock-ai-mishap-analysis) shortens stand-downs whose cause is not hardware, a marginal accelerator only. Launch Keystone v1.3 (23 Sep 2026) does not date this threshold directly; its 2027 base of 3.3 flights per stack is consistent with a dozen flights in 2028.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.strongest_case_small: Two of three V3 boosters (Flights 12, 13) failed in landing burns and Flight 14 expended both stages by plan, and a pad-damaging failure (as New Glenn suffered on May 28 2026) costs 3-12 months. Only five of the 25 authorized Starbase flights flew in 2025.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.signpost: Starship flight count in 2027 (12 or more confirms); LC-39A debut by mid-2027; sustained intervals below 30 days. Flight 15 (NET Oct 19 2026 per press) would be a ~21-day interval.

physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.title: Regulators review with AI tools
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.description: The FAA's Office of Commercial Space Transportation, the FCC, NASA safety boards and ESA reviewers use AI systems to re-run and check applicants' flight-safety analyses, environmental documents and safety cases, raising reviewer throughput 2-5x without changing the rules.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.status_oct2026: The FAA proposed electronic license submissions and four burden-reducing Part 450 changes on Oct 5 2026 and on Jul 30 2026 proposed waiving requirements under 13 laws (Federal Register). The FCC voted on a 'Licensing Assembly Line' replacing Part 25 with Part 100 on Jul 22 2026, aiming to cut satellite licensing from years to months. No agency has announced AI-assisted technical review of launch licenses (general). Outside aerospace, FDA deployed a generative-AI assistant (Elsa) to its scientific reviewers agency-wide in Jun 2025, so a federal safety regulator can adopt internal AI tools within months (Axios, Jun 2025).
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.why: Reviewer hours, not statute, set most of the time between a complete application and a decision (statutory limit 180 days, general). A reviewer who can re-run a debris-risk or overpressure analysis with an AI agent in hours instead of weeks moves the queue. Reform supplies the rules regardless of AI; AI capacity decides whether the reformed process is staffed at 300+ U.S. launches a year.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.strongest_case_small: Agencies adopt slowly under procurement, FedRAMP, ITAR and liability constraints; much review time is interagency consultation, public comment and policy judgment that AI does not compress.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.signpost: FAA or FCC announcing AI-assisted review tooling; published median license evaluation times below 120 days.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.calibration_note: A3: Regulator cap: regulators changing how they review is regulator behaviour, which the same domain caps at Medium for physclock-licensing-in-weeks. S2/S3 High -> Medium.

physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.title: Tests chosen for information, not habit
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.description: AI designs development test campaigns, the tests operators control, with Bayesian optimal experimental design and sequential testing, choosing which tests, levels, sensors and replicates buy the most margin knowledge. Development test matrices shrink 10-30% (assumption) and re-tests fall. Formal qualification matrices stay set by GEVS, SMC-S-016 and ECSS-E-ST-10-03; cutting them needs customer acceptance and is modeled in physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.status_oct2026: The methods exist (Bayesian experimental design, design of experiments, sequential probability-ratio tests) but are expert-scarce; space qualification follows enveloped levels and fixed matrices (GEVS, SMC-S-016, ECSS-E-ST-10-03, general). NASA's certification-by-analysis UQ discussion group published calibration and validation challenge problems (Jul 2025). Design of experiments is not new to aerospace testing: NASA Langley has applied Modern Design of Experiments to wind-tunnel testing since the late 1990s, and DOT&E has required design of experiments in operational test plans since Oct 2010, while space qualification matrices did not shrink.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 139 is T3 but not load-bearing
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.why: A 'solved in principle, expert-scarce' problem: on-demand applied math puts an experimental-design specialist on every development campaign. Design of experiments has been available or mandated for decades, so AI removes the remaining per-campaign expert scarcity rather than inventing a method. If test campaigns are ~25-35% of the critical path and AI trims 10-30% of development test count, schedule gains are ~3-10% before any certification credit. Family 139 (subpolynomial-query log-concave sampling, T3) concerns the posterior sampling these designs use, but practical posteriors are already sampled adequately; it changes theory, not campaigns.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.strongest_case_small: Test count is driven by standards, customer requirements and workmanship screening, not information value; dropping a test that would have caught a workmanship error is a mission loss, so mission assurance will resist.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.signpost: An operator or prime reports a development test matrix cut by 15% or more through information-optimal design, by 2028.

physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.title: Launch range and airspace scheduled by optimizer
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.description: Range (Eastern, Western, Starbase) and national-airspace scheduling for hundreds to thousands of launches and reentries a year is done by optimization tools that minimize hazard-area closures and conflicts, so range time stops being a cadence limit.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.status_oct2026: U.S. orbital launches: 198 in 2025 and 140 by Oct 7 2026 (Wikipedia). Musk projects Starship launching 'more than once per hour' within 3-4 years (Jan 2026). Range and FAA airspace integration are coordinated largely by human schedulers (general).
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.premise_tier: n/a; 124 is T1 per the KB catalog, conditional and not load-bearing (the repo's lean/docs/124.md lists a Lean main result with a Comparator challenge, 'Optimal three-machine unit-job scheduling', checked Oct 7 2026; T3 once the catalog is reconciled)
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.why: Launch windows, hazard areas and range assets form a precedence-constrained scheduling problem that mixed-integer programming and heuristics already solve at today's scale; the gap is expert time and integration with FAA air-traffic systems. At 1,000+ flights a year from one coast it becomes a real constraint. Family 124 (polynomial-time scheduling on three identical machines, T1 per KB catalog, conditional) is a theory result; its algorithm will not be what schedules ranges. The outcome is FAA and Space Force adoption inside airspace automation, on federal acquisition cycles, so the regulator-behavior cap used for physclock-regulator-ai-capacity applies.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.strongest_case_small: Range capacity is limited by physical assets, safety buffers and airline-disruption politics, not schedule optimization; at 2026-2028 cadence the range is not the binding gate.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.signpost: FAA or Space Force announcing automated hazard-area and airspace scheduling; FAA-reported airspace delay minutes per launch falling.

physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.title: A rulebook for trusting AI-made analysis
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.description: NASA-STD-7009, ECSS and Space Force test standards, or a faster NASA handbook, interim or engineering directive, or ECSS handbook, gain a defined way to count AI-generated analyses (with independently checked derivations, quantified model error and, where available, certified numerics) as verification evidence, graded by credibility level. How much test credit each level earns stays with programs and their Technical Authorities, as under NASA-STD-7009B.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.status_oct2026: NASA-STD-7009B (Mar 2024) sets model credibility and leaves acceptance criteria for results to programs (general). A NASA-sponsored aircraft certification-by-analysis guide (contractor report, May 2021) sets a vision for a notional 2040, and a NASA-led UQ position paper (Jan 2024) places widespread certification by analysis in 2040-2050 and calls tool credibility the open challenge; the NASA-FAA CM4QC strategy (Mar 2026) is aviation-focused, for additively manufactured metals. No space standard addresses AI-generated analysis (general). Outside aerospace, FDA issued final guidance on the credibility of computational modeling in medical-device submissions (Nov 2023, built on ASME V&V 40) and a draft risk-based, seven-step credibility framework for AI models used in drug and biologic regulatory decisions (Jan 2025).
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.why: Every test-substitution chain needs a rule saying what analysis evidence is worth. The named base standards revise every 8-10 years (NASA-STD-7009 2008, 2016 and 2024; GSFC-STD-7000 2013 and 2021; ECSS-E-ST-10-03 2012 and 2022, about 19 months from draft to publication), so the next base revision of 7009 falls around 2030-32. The faster route is a NASA handbook, interim or engineering directive, or an ECSS handbook. S2's independent checks (2026-27) and automated statement audits (capability-cheap-trust, 2028 after B-trunk) supply the evidence, so a first directive or handbook naming AI-generated analysis lands around 2029. Verified numerics (2028) strengthen the case but do not gate it: NASA-STD-7009B is already risk-based, and FDA wrote AI-credibility rules without machine-checked numerics. Capped at Medium because it is regulator acceptance. Test-reduction credit written into test standards is modeled in struct-35-test-standards-codify-ai-credit.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.strongest_case_small: NASA-sponsored aircraft studies put widespread certification by analysis at 2040-2050; base standards revise only every 8-10 years and follow experience and accidents, not capability; a single failure traced to AI analysis would freeze adoption.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.signpost: A NASA-STD-7009 revision, NASA engineering directive or ECSS handbook naming AI-generated analysis; a CM4QC pilot granting qualification credit.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] why: revision cycles corrected from '3-6 years (general)' to the named standards' 8-10 years (7009 2008/2016/2024; GSFC-STD-7000 2013/2021; ECSS-E-ST-10-03 2012/2022); the 2029 date now rests explicitly on the directive/handbook route. physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.title: Anomaly diagnosis 3-10x faster
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.description: AI agents do the cognitive part of anomaly investigations (telemetry forensics, fault-tree pruning, physics re-simulation of candidate causes, corrective-action analysis), so return to flight is set by hardware fixes and verification tests rather than diagnosis. Root-cause confirmation often still needs hardware reproduction tests.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.status_oct2026: The FAA authorized Falcon 9's return to flight 5 days after the Feb 1 2026 upper-stage deorbit-burn anomaly, with the FAA accepting SpaceX's findings (33FG). Starship loops in 2025 stretched to 82-91 days after the Flight 8 and 9 losses. New Glenn was grounded after an Apr 2026 upper-stage failure, and a May 28 2026 static-fire explosion destroyed a vehicle and damaged its pad (Wikipedia). The FAA accepts operator-led investigations (general).
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.why: Diagnosis is cognitive and sits on the critical path: when the cause is clear, return to flight takes days (Falcon 9, Feb 2026); when it is ambiguous, weeks to months. Searching the cause space 5-10x faster cuts the diagnosis share (illustratively 30-60% of a 60-90 day investigation, general) to days; redesign, requalification tests and FAA acceptance remain. No new regulator acceptance is needed: the FAA reviews findings, not the tools used to reach them. The physical-gate table gives diagnosis 3-10x faster but total return to flight only 0.5-0.8x, and only for non-hardware causes. One operator suffices: SpaceX, which owns a frontier lab and flies most often, generates the anomalies and data.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.strongest_case_small: The slow investigations are slow because hardware must be redesigned, rebuilt and retested or a pad rebuilt (New Glenn), none of which AI compresses; SpaceX already closes clear anomalies in under a week.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.signpost: An operator stating that AI tooling found a root cause; falling median time from mishap to FAA return-to-flight determination.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] Title 'Root cause in days, not months' -> 'Anomaly diagnosis 3-10x faster'; description notes hardware reproduction tests. [auditor] facts: FAA authorized return to flight 5 days after the anomaly; Starship 2025 gaps 82-91 days. S4 equals S3 (no S4 credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Low 2027, Medium 2028, High 2029: the speed-up shows only when an ambiguous anomaly occurs, so the odds build over one or two investigations. S1 Medium 2030, High 2034.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.note_2035: Routine by 2035 in every scenario. S4 equals S3: diagnosis is cognitive, and robots help only with the rebuild that follows.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.gate_note: Hardware reproduction tests bind; searching the cause space (cognitive) is the runner-up.

physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.title: License analyses drafted and checked by AI
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.description: AI agents produce and cross-check the Part 450 flight-safety analysis (debris, far-field overpressure, toxic release, expected casualty), the ground-safety analysis and the NEPA environmental documents that operators submit, turning months of specialist effort into days.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.status_oct2026: The FAA proposed (Oct 5 2026) consolidating flight-safety-analysis information requirements, dropping overpressure analysis for hypothetical public locations and simplifying containment; a revised draft AC 413.13-1A (Part 450 application guidance) was released for public comment on Jul 20 2026 (FR 2026-14576), alongside a draft AC 413.5-1 on pre-application consultation. Specialist consultancies and in-house teams prepare these analyses today (general).
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.why: These analyses use established methods (Monte Carlo debris dispersion, blast propagation, plume dispersion): expert-scarce, not research-hard. An AI running FAA-accepted methods needs no new acceptance; the FAA evaluates the outputs as it does today. Payoff: license modifications for new trajectories or cadence (for example New Glenn's 12-to-50-per-year review) are prepared in weeks. One operator or consultancy suffices for the signpost, and vertically integrated operators with in-house frontier models need not wait for industry-wide adoption.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.strongest_case_small: Preparation is rarely the long pole for an experienced operator; the long poles are environmental consultations, public comment and interagency review.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.signpost: An operator or consultancy publicly using AI-generated Part 450 analyses; shorter time from application to license modification.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.calibration_note: A3: Gate relabel, no band change: the why states the FAA evaluates outputs of already-accepted methods and no new acceptance is needed, so the binding gate is operator adoption, not regulation. With a regulatory gate the High band would breach the Medium cap.

physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.title: Analysis replaces some environmental qualification tests

physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.title: Nuclear launch safety cases in months
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.description: AI produces the reactor design analyses (neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, accident criticality) and the launch-accident nuclear safety analysis needed for NSPM-20 launch authorization of a space fission reactor, cutting a multi-year analysis cycle to months. LEU/HALEU fuel below 20% U-235 puts a launch in Tier II: the sponsoring agency head authorizes it after an Interagency Nuclear Safety Review Board (INSRB) review. Presidential authorization applies only to Tier III (non-LEU fuel).
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.status_oct2026: DRACO (nuclear thermal demo, Lockheed-BWXT contract Jul 2023 for a 2027 flight) was put on hold in Jan 2025 and cancelled in 2025, with DARPA citing falling launch costs. NASA unveiled Space Reactor-1 Freedom (over 20 kWe, nuclear-electric, two Mars flybys) in Mar 2026 for a Dec 2028 launch. Its estimate reached $2.1B by Sep 2026, while the House Appropriations Committee recommended $10M for it, within $50M for nuclear-electric propulsion, in May 2026 (Wikipedia). SR-1 uses HALEU uranium dioxide fuel, so its launch falls in NSPM-20 Tier II (NSPM-20, 2019).
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.why: Nuclear safety analysis is labor-dominated and export-controlled; on-demand applied math inside controlled networks compresses it from years to months. A fresh-fuel HALEU reactor has a low radiological inventory at launch, so its safety case centers on accidental criticality and the cycle is shorter than for Pu-238 RTG missions (general). The INSRB review, agency-head authorization and appropriations remain, so the node is capped at Medium. An AI-made safety case accelerates a reactor launch but is not a precondition for it (physclock-reactor-in-space).
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.strongest_case_small: Space reactor programs die of funding and politics (SP-100, Prometheus, DRACO), not analysis; HALEU fuel and fabrication bind.
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.signpost: NASA or DOE states that AI-generated neutronics and accident-criticality analyses were accepted in the SR-1 (Tier II) launch safety review, with review time under 6 months.

physclock-starship-full-reuse.title: Both Starship stages caught and reflown
physclock-starship-full-reuse.description: A Starship V3 booster and ship are each recovered and flown again, the threshold that turns a $200-250M expendable stack into an amortizable fleet.
physclock-starship-full-reuse.status_oct2026: Boosters were caught on Flights 5, 7 and 8 (Oct 2024-Mar 2025, pre-V3), and B14 and B15 reflew on Flights 9 and 11 (May and Oct 2025); B14's reflight followed inspection and replacement of 4 of its 33 engines. The open items are V3 landing-burn reliability, ship catch and ship reflight: the V3 boosters on Flights 12 and 13 failed in landing burns, and Flight 14 expended both stages by plan. Musk: Flight 15 attempts the first ship catch with odds of 'at least 50 or 60 percent', and ship and booster refly 'at the end of this year or more likely early next' (Mach33, Sep 2026).

physclock-starship-full-reuse.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor (flight tests of catch and reflight), so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Reuse is a flight-test result. Falcon 9 took 15 months from first landing (Dec 2015) to first reflight (Mar 2017). AI shortens failure analysis between attempts but does not change the number of attempts needed. Starship's booster went from catch to reflight in about 4.3 months (B14, Jan-May 2025), far faster than Falcon 9. For the ship, Falcon's 15-month landing-to-reflight lag applied to a first ship catch around late 2026 would give early 2028, so ship reflight in 2027 is roughly 50-60% (judgment); 2027 stays the earliest year. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). Consistent with Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 (wave 44 base, 23 Sep 2026): 3.3 flights per stack in 2027 and 4.8 in 2028.
physclock-starship-full-reuse.strongest_case_small: Ship catch and heat-shield refurbishment are unproven; repeated failures could push ship reflight into 2028 (Mach33 bear case).
physclock-starship-full-reuse.signpost: First ship-catch attempt (Flight 15, NET Oct 19 2026 per press, or a later flight); first reflight of a caught V3 booster and ship by mid-2027.

physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.title: Reflight cleared by data, not teardown
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.description: Reusable stages are cleared for reflight from flight sensor data and a probabilistic life model (a digital twin) instead of detailed inspection, enabling booster turnaround under a week and ship turnaround under two weeks.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 in 2025: 95% of launches on reused boosters, median booster on its 14th flight, 38-day median turnaround, 162 missions from 25 airframes; cohort lifetimes rose from 4.2 flights (2018 boosters) to 8.0 (2019) and 24 (2020) (Mach33). No V3 stage and no ship has reflown; two pre-V3 Super Heavy boosters were caught and reflown (B14: caught on Flight 7, Jan 16 2025, reflown on Flight 9, May 27 2025, after 4 of 33 engines were replaced; B15: caught on Flight 8, Mar 6 2025, reflown on Flight 11, Oct 13 2025).
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 372 is T1 (conditional) and not load-bearing
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.why: Mach33's base case has flights per stack at 3.3 (2027), 4.8 (2028), 8.9 (2029, about a 40-day average cycle) and 18 (2030, about 20 days), so record turnarounds under 7 days (booster) and 14 days (ship) fit 2030 in S2; Falcon 9 took 8 years from first reflight (Mar 2017) to a 9-day record (Mar 2025), and its 2025 median was still 38 days. Mach33's 2028 base-to-bull cost spread ($1.6B) covers every reuse driver; data-based clearance is one contributor and its share is not quantified, and because this node lands in 2029-30 it affects the 2029-31 manifests, not 2028. Chain (S2): first V3 reflights 2027 -> life twin 2028 -> rapidly reusable heat shield 2029 -> data-cleared turnaround on both stages 2030; S3 one year earlier (reuse learning 0.7-0.8x); S1: heat shield and life twin 2030 -> 2031, Low because both Medium prerequisites must land first. Life data still accrue one flight at a time. Family 372 (claims a proof that Lame moduli are uniquely determined from boundary data, smooth isotropic case; T1, so conditional) would support identifiability for inverse inspection in principle; damaged composites and welds lie outside its hypotheses. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.strongest_case_small: SpaceX scaled Falcon reuse through fleet-leader experience and inspection without formal twins; the limit is wear mechanisms (heat-shield tiles, engines) that only flights reveal.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.signpost: Starship booster turnaround under 7 days; SpaceX disclosing sensor-based reflight clearance.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.calibration_note: A3: Cross-domain consistency. Ship turnaround under two weeks requires a rapidly reusable heat shield, so this node cannot come earlier or be more likely than hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield (S2 2029, Medium in all scenarios). It also sat in the same year as its prerequisite prop-life-twin (S2 2028). Chain (S2): first Starship reflights 2027 -> life twin 2028 -> data-cleared turnaround on both stages 2029. physclock-reactor-in-space.title: A U.S. fission reactor launched
physclock-reactor-in-space.description: The first U.S. space fission reactor since SNAP-10A (1965) is launched: Space Reactor-1 Freedom (nuclear-electric, over 20 kWe) or a Fission Surface Power / Lunar Reactor-1 unit.
physclock-reactor-in-space.status_oct2026: SR-1 Freedom targets Dec 2028 at a $2.1B estimate (Sep 2026), with $10M recommended by the House Appropriations Committee (May 2026). NASA centralized space nuclear work under a Space Reactor Office (May 2026) and announced a streamlined management approach (Jun 2, 2026). SR-1 uses HALEU UO2 fuel and reuses the Gateway Power and Propulsion Element bus (three 12 kW AEPS and four 6 kW Hall thrusters); NASA paused Gateway in its current form on Mar 24, 2026. Fission Surface Power had three Phase 1 teams from 2022 (Lockheed Martin, Westinghouse, IX), a 2025 executive order prioritizing a lunar reactor, and a directive targeting launch readiness around 2030. NASA said in Mar 2026 that SR-1 data will inform Lunar Reactor-1 (Wikipedia).
physclock-reactor-in-space.why: HALEU fuel supply, reactor fabrication, zero-power criticality testing and integration take roughly 4-6 years from a funded start (general). The physclock lag ladder applies 0.9x in S2 and 0.8-0.9x in S3, while appropriations and politics compress 1.0x in every scenario. SR-1 flies past Mars twice and drops a helicopter capsule there (Wikipedia), so it launches only in a Mars window: Dec 2028, early 2031, about Apr 2033 or about mid 2035. It is underfunded for Dec 2028; the early-2031 window needs FY2027-28 appropriations of several hundred million dollars a year. The lunar unit is 2033 at the earliest after NASA reset the Lunar Reactor-1 procurement in Mar 2026 (struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe). A conventionally prepared Tier II safety analysis is sufficient, so the AI safety case (physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai) is an accelerator worth perhaps 6-12 months. It matters only if it moves a launch into an earlier window. Chain: funded start FY2027 -> fuel, fabrication, criticality tests, safety analysis and INSRB review -> ready about 2030 -> launch in the early-2031 Mars window, the earliest year in every scenario. Band Low in all scenarios because the binding gates do not depend on the scenario and every U.S. space-reactor program since SNAP-10A has been cancelled.
physclock-reactor-in-space.strongest_case_small: Every U.S. space reactor program since 1965 has been cancelled; cheap launch removed DRACO's rationale; the 2026 pause of Gateway in its current form and cancellation of Mars Sample Return show how fast NASA priorities shift.
physclock-reactor-in-space.signpost: FY2027 appropriation for SR-1; DOE fuel delivery; a reactor criticality test.
physclock-reactor-in-space.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder: a space reactor takes 4-6 years from a funded start (0.9x in S2, 0.8-0.9x in S3; appropriations 1.0x). SR-1 has $10M recommended by the House Appropriations Committee against a $2.1B estimate and Fission Surface Power had no confirmed Phase 2 award, so the earliest funded start is 2026-27. Chain (S2): funded start 2026-27 -> fuel, fabrication, criticality tests and AI-shortened safety case -> launch 2030 at the earliest. physclock-pad-propellant-infra.title: Pads and propellant plants for hundreds of heavy flights
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.description: At least four Starship-capable pads operate (Starbase pads 1 and 2, LC-39A, SLC-37 or equivalent) with on-site or pipeline propellant supply, removing pad count and cryogen trucking as cadence limits.
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.status_oct2026: Starbase has two pads; LC-39A's Starship debut is targeted around year-end at best (Mach33). A Starbase methane pipeline ('Starpipe') targets Jan 2027 service; SpaceX filed for a 32.4-mile Florida gas pipeline (Oct 2026); a $100B Louisiana campus (five complexes, two pads each) plans construction from 2027 and first launches as soon as 2029. Merchant supply needs about 389 tanker deliveries per flight (Mach33).
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor (pad construction, pipelines and propellant plants), so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Pad construction (2-4 years per heavy pad, general) and air-separation and liquefaction plants run on the physical clock. On-site propellant costs about $0.2M per flight against $1.7-2.7M merchant, and trucking becomes physically implausible above about 100 flights a year (106 deliveries a day) (Mach33). AI barely touches this; it bounds every high-cadence node. LC-39A has not launched Starship as of Oct 2026, against a late-2025 plan (Spectrum News 13, Mar 2025) and an H2-2026 target (Mach33, Apr 2026); SLC-37 was approved in Dec 2025 and is under construction; at 2-4 years per pad and 1-3 years for the Florida pipeline (filed Oct 2026), four pads with pipeline or on-site supply is a 2029 central year. The node is AI-independent, so all scenarios move together. Environmental caps also bind: Starbase 25 a year (FAA, May 2025), LC-39A 44 (Jan 2026) and SLC-37 76 (Dec 2025), so 100 flights needs both Florida sites running above half their caps. Chain (S2): first V3 reflights 2027 -> four pads with pipeline or on-site propellant 2029 -> 100+ flights 2030; S3 2029 only if the four-pad set is ready early that year; S1 about 2030 on SpaceX's own trajectory. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). physclock-licensing-in-weeks.title: Launch licensing in weeks
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.description: Routine license modifications (new trajectory, cadence or payload class) clear in under 30 days, new vehicle operator licenses in under 90 days from a complete application (against the 180-day statutory maximum), and FCC satellite approvals in months.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.status_oct2026: EO 14335 (Aug 2025) ordered Part 450 reform and NEPA streamlining; FAA proposed rules on Jul 30 2026 (waiving requirements under 13 laws) and Oct 5 2026 (cutting Part 450 analysis burdens); the FCC adopted a Part 100 'Licensing Assembly Line' (vote Jul 22 2026). The statutory review clock for a complete application is 180 days (general).
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.why: Chain (S2): FAA final rules on the Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026 proposals 2027-28 -> AI-assisted FAA review (physclock-regulator-ai-capacity) 2028, fed by AI-drafted Part 450 analyses (physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis) -> published median modification times under 30 days 2028-29. Reform alone gives about 1.2x (physical-gate table, S1); halving the statutory clock needs reviewer capacity, so regulator AI capacity stays a hard prerequisite, while operator-side drafting mostly shortens the time before the clock starts and is an accelerator. One route is a license that covers a whole analyzed flight envelope, so routine changes need no modification (Part 450 already lets one license cover multiple launches of a vehicle or family, 14 CFR 450.3, general). Capped at Medium because it is regulator behavior.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.strongest_case_small: Licensing was not the binding gate for SpaceX in 2025-26 (hardware was); NEPA litigation and environmental consultations remain; a public-safety incident would reverse reform.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.signpost: FAA final rules on the 2026 proposals; published license evaluation times; Starship license modifications approved without delaying flights.

[skeptic] physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis hard -> soft; skeptic's proposal to also soften physclock-regulator-ai-capacity rejected (the physical-gate table credits reform alone with only 1.2x). Chain (S2): data-cleared reflight 2030 -> acceptance on flight history plus AI evidence 2031; S3 one year earlier. physclock-cheap-mass-customer.title: Customers buy orbit under $1,000 per kg
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.description: Third-party customers can routinely buy dedicated heavy-lift launch below $1,000 per kilogram of customer payload delivered (not per kilogram of vehicle capacity), against a Falcon 9 dedicated median of about $5,300/kg and a rideshare floor of about $7,000/kg today.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.status_oct2026: Mach33 Launch Unlock model (Aug 2026): Starship third-party ticket enters at about $3,975/kg in 2027 and fades toward cost with a 2033 midpoint (2030-36 range) as competitors reach cadence; Voyager's $90M Starlab contract is about $900/kg of capacity on a 100 t vehicle for a launch NET 2028-29 (Mach33); on Starlab's delivered mass, which is not published, the price per kilogram is higher. physclock-cheap-mass-customer.why: Price follows competition and SpaceX's capacity-release decisions, not cost: Falcon 9 list prices were stable for a decade, and Mach33 finds a one-year delay in credible competitor cadence delays external crossover by about a year. AI math reaches this node only by speeding competitors' engineering. Mach33's 2035 simulations vary when SpaceX releases Starship's spare capacity to customers (2029-2033) as a main price driver, so competition accelerates this node rather than gating it, and SpaceX can price below $1,000/kg without a rival; internal orbital-compute demand can delay that release. Band S2 Low: Mach33's fade midpoint is 2033 (range 2030-36), so crossing by 2031 is roughly 20-30% (judgment), and AI moves it 0-1 year. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). Pinned to Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 customer side (wave 38b, 10 Sep 2026): the reference case opens Starship spare capacity to customers in 2031 (tested 2029 to 2033), with spot price $6,200/kg in 2029, $5,634 in 2030, $820 in 2031 and $562 in 2033, and a realized price (revenue per customer kilogram) median of $5,823/kg in 2030 and $945 in 2035. Opening in 2029 gives a 2030 spot of $921/kg. The node is the spot or dedicated price, so v1.3 crosses $1,000/kg in 2031; with the model's one-year lag the odds reach Medium in 2032 and High in 2034 in S2. It now needs customer access (physclock-customer-launch-access) as a hard prerequisite. Sensitivity: wave 45 (v1.4, ratified 21 Oct 2026) moves the hinge to 2030 (passed by 2030 in 53% of worlds); on that basis this node would move about a year earlier. The model stays pinned to v1.3.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.strongest_case_small: Anchor deals like Voyager's already price near $900/kg, so 'routine' is a soft threshold; the markets most sensitive to $/kg (Starlink, orbital compute) are SpaceX's own and see internal cost.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.signpost: Published Starship rideshare or dedicated pricing; a second Starship-class customer contract below $1,500/kg.

The incompressible core is thermal-vacuum time constants, real-time life and creep tests (a 10,000-hour creep test takes about 14 months), workmanship screening and statistical replicates. Commercial operators that skip tests on their own risk (physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual), accepted reliability priors (physclock-reliability-priors-credit), autonomous stands and printed-part certification accelerate it but are not preconditions. Capped at Medium; S2 Low because evidence on programs started 2028+ cannot report before about 2031.

physclock-dev-capital-cut.title: AI cuts new space hardware development cost by about 10-20%
physclock-dev-capital-cut.description: Non-recurring development cost for new spacecraft and launch vehicles falls about 10-20% under S2 as engineering labor for analysis, design, software and verification shrinks; hardware, test articles and facilities do not shrink.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.status_oct2026: Starship program spend exceeded $15B by 2026, against roughly $400M for Falcon 9 development, and SpaceX directed all $3B of its 2025 space-segment R&D to Starship (Reuters via 33FG). SpaceX held $100.8B in cash after an $85.7B IPO in June 2026.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.why: If engineering labor is 40-60% of development cost and analysis, design, software and verification are about half of it (general), S2's 5-10x cognitive speedup removes roughly 16-27% of total cost gross (merely halving that content removes 10-15%). physclock.json's capital row gives a 15-30% fall in development labor cost, which is about 6-18% of total cost, and an effective capital multiplier of 1.15-1.3x (13-23%). Scope growth takes some back, so the realized cut is about 10-20%. A second channel could add to it: standing-army costs scale with schedule, so shorter programs also trim time-proportional overhead. Chain (S2): engineering adoption 2028 -> programs started 2028 or later estimated with AI-reduced labor -> first program estimates showing 10-20% lower non-recurring cost 2029 -> completed-program evidence 2031 or later. S3: adoption 2028 with near-free cognition from 2029 -> 2029. S1: 2031. It matters most for capital-gated new entrants; for SpaceX capital is not binding through 2031. What binds is organizations changing practice, not capital.

physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.title: A new reusable launcher from start to orbit in three years
physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.description: A program in any country started in 2027 or later reaches orbit with a reusable medium or heavy launcher within three years of program start.
physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.status_oct2026: Historical: Falcon 9 about 5 years (2005-2010) and Electron about 5 years to orbit (2013-2018) (general); New Glenn announced 2016 for 2020 and flew Jan 2025; Neutron announced Mar 2021 and is NET Q4 2026; the BE-4 engine alone took from 2011 to first flight in Jan 2024 (Wikipedia).
physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.why: Even with cognitive work nearly free, engine development (hot-fire campaigns, turbopump failures), pad construction (2-4 years) and flight-test learning set a floor of about 4-5 years. AI's best case removes about a year, and only programs started after AI adoption (2027-28 in S2) benefit. The realistic path is a derivative built around an existing engine family: LandSpace's Zhuque-3 (TQ-12-family methalox engines from Zhuque-2) hopped in Jan 2024, reached orbit Dec 3 2025 and landed its first stage on its second flight, Aug 18 2026 (Wikipedia), on roughly a four-year derivative timeline without AI help (general). Clean-sheet multipliers of 0.8-0.9x (S2) and 0.7-0.8x (S3) on such a timeline give about 3.2-3.6 years in S2 and 2.8-3.2 years in S3 under 2031 conditions, so S2 is Speculative and S3 Low by 2031. To reach orbit by end-2035 a program must start by end-2032, so it runs under 2032-35 conditions: about 0.75-0.87x in S2 (3.0-3.5 years) and 0.66-0.76x in S3 (2.6-3.0 years) on the four-year base. About half of new launchers fail on their first flight, which adds 0.5-1 year. Applying the multipliers to a derivative base assumes the remaining work compresses like a clean-sheet program's; on the 5-13 year clean-sheet base no S3 program gets under 3 years, so the node rests on derivatives. FAA licensing reform and AI-run test stands help U.S. entrants but are not gates for every entrant.

physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.title: New satellite generations every year
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.description: Leading commercial constellation operators field a new satellite generation (new bus or payload, not only software) about every 12 months, against 18-36 months today.
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.status_oct2026: Starlink: v0.9 May 2019, v1.0 late 2019, v1.5 2021, v2 mini Feb 2023, v2 mini optimized (average satellite mass down from 623 kg to 575 kg, 96 Gbps), V3 (about 1 Tbps, about 2 t) first flown on Flight 13 (Jul 2026) and first orbited on Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026). V3's timing was gated by Starship, not the satellite. V2 mini production reached six a day by Mar 2023 (Wikipedia; Mach33). SpaceX's first compute satellite, Starmind AI1 (spec disclosed Jun 2026), uses modular, interchangeable chip inserts, and its power target rose from 150 kW (Jun) to about 250 kW (Oct 2026) (Mach33).
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.why: Chain (S2): engineering adoption 2028 -> first AI-era bus or payload designed, qualified and retooled in about 12-15 months -> fielded 2029 -> a second generation about 12 months later shows the cadence, 2030. S3: same adoption year, but commercial generations compress 0.5-0.7x (18-36 months becomes 9-25), so 2029 at the optimistic edge; an annual cadence sits at the favorable end even there, so Medium. Design, software and verification compress in S2; payload qualification, radiation testing, line retooling and the launcher bind (V3's timing was set by Starship). Upside not driven by AI math: orbital-compute satellites may track the accelerator makers' annual cadence (general) with modular chip inserts on a common bus, making a yearly payload generation a chip swap. Faster generations raise capacity per kilogram (V3 carries about three times V2 mini's capacity per kilogram, Mach33). Band: the P7 default (Speculative) is raised to Medium in S2 because the physical steps are commercial with no regulator, Starlink already fields generations every 18-36 months so only a 1.5-3x compression is needed, and the chain leaves a year of slack; not High because qualification, retooling and the launcher bind. S1 (F2 audit): adoption lands in 2029, so the first AI-era generation flies about 2030 and the second, which shows the cadence, about 2031; S1 moves 2030 -> 2031 and Medium -> Low, and the non-AI chip-swap path stays upside, not the base case. Bands are judgments.
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.strongest_case_small: Generation cadence is set by launcher steps and fleet economics (about five-year satellite life), not design speed; operators may prefer continuous incremental change.
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.signpost: A Starlink V3.x or V4 announcement within 18 months of V3; Amazon Leo's second-generation timeline.

plasma-vm-wellposed.title: Relativistic plasma equations proved well-behaved (checked)
plasma-vm-wellposed.description: The claimed proof that the 3D relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell system has global smooth solutions for smooth finite-energy data passes an outside Comparator run and a statement audit, moving from T3 to T4. The system is the kinetic equation for collisionless plasma coupled to Maxwell's equations; family 362 covers one species in 3D, per the release overview. This is the Glassey-Strauss global-regularity problem, open since the 1980s.
plasma-vm-wellposed.status_oct2026: Family 362 [L], T3: agent-written Lean main result in the repo, unchecked by outsiders as of 2026-10-07; no outside commentary on 362 found in search. Before the release, only continuation criteria (Glassey-Strauss 1986: smooth while momentum support stays bounded), small-data and symmetric results existed, e.g. vacuum stability for relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell-Boltzmann (Cao and Li, arXiv 2601.04018, Jan 2026).
plasma-vm-wellposed.why: The Lean proof exists, so a Comparator run is cheap; the slow part is the statement audit (does the Lean definition of the system, its function spaces and 'finite energy' match what physicists mean?). The March 2026 AI-assisted formalization of the Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equilibrium reported exactly these definition-alignment bugs and hypothesis creep, which is why the gate is formalization rather than cognition. Hexagon (launched Oct 6, 2026) exists to do this. Once T4, kinetic codes for the one-species relativistic system are known to approximate a solution that exists and stays smooth for all time: a confidence gain, per tl-position-2. Real plasmas have at least two species, so the multi-species case stays open.
plasma-vm-wellposed.strongest_case_small: Codes never waited for this; physicists assumed it. The theorem covers the whole-space relativistic system without walls, collisions or external circuits, while Hall-thruster, magnetic-nozzle and magnetosphere codes use electrostatic, non-relativistic, collisional or bounded-domain versions that are different equations. Nothing in a thruster, forecast or fusion device changes.
plasma-vm-wellposed.signpost: An outside Comparator report and statement audit for family 362 posted on Hexagon or by a kinetic-theory group within 12 months. The audit must state whether the Lean statement covers one species only and which data class it assumes (e.g. compact momentum support versus finite energy). A definition mismatch found in the audit would break this node.
plasma-vm-wellposed.revision_note: B-plasma-nuclear resolver (2026-10-07): Auditor (statement-gap rule, tr-position-2): title and description scoped to one species, 3D, per the release overview; signpost asks the audit to state species and data class. plasma-lean-kinetic-library.title: A formal library for plasma equations
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.description: Agreed, reusable Lean definitions of Vlasov-Poisson/Maxwell, Landau and Boltzmann collision operators, ideal and Hall MHD, and their standard solution concepts, so any claimed result about a plasma model can be audited against a fixed statement.
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.status_oct2026: Mathlib coverage of PDE is thin (3 of 16 PDE families in the release have Lean). Proof of concept: one mathematician supervising Gemini DeepThink, Claude Code and Aristotle formalized the Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equilibrium characterization in 10 days for about $200, writing no code (arXiv 2603.15929, Mar 2026).
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.why: A single statement audit can use bespoke definitions reviewed by experts, as in the 10-day, ~$200 VML case (arXiv 2603.15929). The shared library matters for reuse across 363, 364 and any future plasma theorem, and for machine-checked numerics (plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics). The limit is agreeing on definitions, not writing proofs. Under S2, Mathlib analysis/PDE coverage catches up 2027-29 and a plasma layer follows within a year; S3 follows S2 through 2027.
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.strongest_case_small: Engineering codes do not use Lean, and a definitions library mostly serves mathematicians. Matching a Lean object to the equation a physicist actually simulates still needs scarce human experts.
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.signpost: A Mathlib or Hexagon pull request adding standard definitions of the Vlasov-Maxwell system and its solution concepts, cited by a family-362 audit.

plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.title: Plasma simulations with certified error bars
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.description: Convergence proofs and computable error bounds for structure-preserving Vlasov-Maxwell, particle-in-cell (PIC) and MHD discretizations, increasingly machine-checked, so code verification can state 'discretization error below X' instead of relying on convergence studies.
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.status_oct2026: Structure-preserving (geometric) PIC and finite-element schemes exist with proved conservation properties (general). Convergence theorems assume a smooth solution on the time interval; local theory and continuation criteria already supply that on finite intervals, and family 362 [L, T3] would add global smoothness for one-species relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell. Engineering PIC (Hall thrusters, nozzles, magnetospheres) mostly solves electrostatic, non-relativistic Vlasov-Poisson, globally regular in 3D since 1991-92 (Pfaffelmoser; Lions-Perthame, general). PIC statistical noise and the electron-to-xenon mass ratio of about 1:239,000 (stiffness) lack rigorous error control (general).
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.why: Under S2, AI does numerics with certified error bounds by 2027-28 and the verified floating-point toolchain matures 2027-29, so the first certified kinetic-solver modules appear ~2029. Practical value: replacing grid- and particle-count convergence studies (often several times the cost of the production run, general) with proof-backed estimators, and giving ML surrogates a certified reference to be checked against. S3 High: formalization-gated work runs on the cognitive clock, which S3 compresses 20-50x from 2029; all S3 hard prerequisites are High by 2028; and the node needs only one code team to ship one machine-checked module (a Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau theorem took 10 days and ~$200 in Mar 2026, arXiv 2603.15929).
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.strongest_case_small: Turbulent plasma simulations are chaotic, so rigorous long-time error bounds grow with the Lyapunov time and can be valid but useless for the time-averaged transport engineers want. Model-form error (closures, wall physics) dwarfs discretization error in Hall-thruster and space-weather codes.
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.signpost: A plasma code team (e.g. WarpX, GEMPIC, GX) ships a module with a machine-checked convergence or conservation proof and uses it in a V&V report.

plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.title: Full-thruster kinetic simulation becomes affordable
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.description: AI-designed algorithms (implicit and asymptotic-preserving PIC, low-rank and sparse-grid Vlasov solvers, bounded learned subgrid models) make 3D whole-device kinetic simulation of a Hall thruster with real mass ratio, real geometry and wall physics a days-long rather than infeasible calculation.
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.status_oct2026: Facility-scale kinetic simulations of Hall thrusters do not yet exist at feasible cost (Whittaker, Marks, Gorodetsky, AIAA 2026). 3D PIC with wall charging, secondary emission and near-plume outflow (Liu, Zhao, Zhao, arXiv 2603.14849, Mar 2026) shows anomalous transport self-organizing into near-wall pathways, but at reduced scale. In fusion, GPU-native gyrokinetics (GX) already runs useful turbulence cases in minutes on one GPU.
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.why: Algorithm invention for multiscale kinetic problems is expert-scarce work that S2 makes on-demand by 2027-28 (P1), and its product is practical algorithms (P4). Order-of-magnitude cost today (general arithmetic, judgment): at real density, cells that resolve electron-cyclotron drift waves (~50-100 micrometres) give ~1e9-1e10 cells over a 5 kW thruster and its near plume. With ~100 particles per cell and ~1e7 cyclotron-resolving implicit steps for ~1 ms of simulated time, that is ~1e18-1e19 particle pushes, weeks to months on a full exascale machine. Implicit energy-conserving PIC already exists, so reaching 'days' needs another ~10-100x from algorithms (sparse-grid, low-rank, asymptotic-preserving, subcycling) plus 2028-31 hardware. That makes hero runs feasible, which is all this node claims. Design loops that need hundreds of evaluations stay out of reach, so design runs through the closure (plasma-hall-anomalous-closure). Band: S2 Medium, the P4 default, given the node's own strongest case (gains may stall near 10x); S3 High because recursive AI compounds algorithm gains after 2028.
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.strongest_case_small: The problem spans six-plus orders of magnitude in time scale; some cost may be irreducible and algorithm gains could stall near 10x. Even perfect kinetic simulations inherit uncertain wall, secondary-emission and facility-pressure physics, so cheaper runs do not automatically remove uncertainty.
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.signpost: A published full-device 3D PIC of a >=5 kW Hall thruster at real mass ratio and real geometry, with neutrals and wall emission, covering >=0.5 ms of simulated time and completed in under a week.

plasma-gk-surrogates.title: Millisecond fusion-turbulence models trusted in design
plasma-gk-surrogates.description: Neural and quasilinear surrogates of gyrokinetic turbulence that run in milliseconds, carry calibrated uncertainty, and are trusted inside reactor-design and scenario-planning loops in place of hours-to-weeks nonlinear simulations.
plasma-gk-surrogates.status_oct2026: Already arriving through ML, not frontier math: surrogates of the GX code trained on >200,000 nonlinear simulations over ~23,000 stellarator configurations run in ~ms and are used directly in equilibrium optimization (Churchill, Landreman et al., arXiv 2609.28730, Sep 23 2026); GyroSwin cuts fully resolved nonlinear gyrokinetics cost ~1,000x (arXiv 2510.07314); PQLS calibrates a quasilinear saturation rule by Bayesian inference, separating parameter and model-form uncertainty (arXiv 2609.29336, Sep 24 2026). Multiscale nonlinear runs can cost ~640,000 node-hours (general; reported for GKV on Fugaku, primary source not checked).
plasma-gk-surrogates.why: The training data and ML methods exist; DOE's Genesis Mission/STELLAR-AI (PPPL, Jan 2026) includes StellFoundry, an AI stellarator-design project. AI applied math adds out-of-distribution error bounds and principled UQ on top, raising trust from 'useful screening tool' to 'design-of-record input'.
plasma-gk-surrogates.strongest_case_small: This is ML engineering already underway, so the AI-math increment is small. Surrogates trained on adiabatic-electron simulations miss kinetic-electron and electromagnetic effects that matter at reactor-relevant pressure, so trust may stay limited to early design.
plasma-gk-surrogates.signpost: A fusion company publishes a design whose surrogate-predicted transport is later confirmed within its stated error bars by experiment (W7-X or a new device).

plasma-swx-data-assimilation.title: Sun-to-Earth ensemble forecasting with honest uncertainty
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.description: Coupled data assimilation from the Sun (SDO imagery and magnetograms, coronagraphs) through the solar wind (SOLAR-1 at L1) to the magnetosphere, ionosphere and thermosphere, producing ensemble forecasts with calibrated probabilities rather than single deterministic runs (demonstrated in a research or pre-operational testbed; operational transition is a later step).
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.status_oct2026: SOLAR-1 (ex-SWFO-L1) launched Sep 24, 2025 and reached L1 Jan 23, 2026. NOAA's WAM-IPE gives 2-day ionosphere-thermosphere forecasts (operational since July 2021, upgraded 2023). NASA/IBM's open Surya heliophysics foundation model (Aug 2025, 366M parameters, 9 years of SDO data) beats flare benchmarks by ~16% up to 2 h ahead. STEREO-A (70.6 degrees ahead of Earth, Oct 2026) and PUNCH (2025) add off-axis and 3D views. Density models rarely propagate uncertainty to orbit decisions (CPAESS 2026 workshop abstract).
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.why: Ensemble data assimilation for a nonlinear, sparsely observed coupled system (filter design, model-error estimation, localization, feature alignment of CME fronts) is bespoke, expert-scarce applied math; S2 makes it on-demand by 2027-28. Terrestrial weather shows what DA buys: roughly a day of useful lead time per decade (general).
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.strongest_case_small: Space weather is observation-starved: one L1 point, a few coronagraph viewpoints and no routine coronal magnetic-field measurement. Assimilation cannot create information that is not observed; Kay et al. (2024) attribute CME arrival-time errors mainly to input reconstruction and background solar wind.
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.signpost: A published assimilative ensemble Sun-to-Earth forecast system with reliability diagrams on CCMC benchmarks (research or pre-operational testbed) by 2028; SWPC or ESA operational transition by 2030.
