struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.title: Closing the mid-frequency vibration gap
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.description: Error-controlled prediction of launch vibroacoustic response in the mid-frequency band (roughly a few hundred Hz to ~1-2 kHz), where finite-element models are too costly and statistical energy analysis is invalid, via hybrid FE-SEA and reduced-order models with a posteriori error bounds.
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.status_oct2026: A long-standing open problem (general); practice envelopes predictions with margins and relies on acoustic and random-vibration tests. NASA NESC's Norton-Thevenin Receptance Coupling (2023-2024) cuts the cost of coupled loads analysis but does not address mid-frequency fidelity.
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.why: Mid-frequency is hard because modal and statistical descriptions both break down. AI can design and prove error estimators for hybrid methods quickly under S2, but validation needs reverberant-chamber and flight data with quantified uncertainty. If solved, component random-vibration levels could be set from prediction with smaller margins, feeding struct-launch-env-margins.
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.strongest_case_small: Qualification by test remains mandatory; uncertainty in the forcing (liftoff acoustics, transonic buffet) dominates structural model error, so even perfect structural models leave most of the margin in place.
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.signpost: A hybrid FE-SEA method with proven error bounds, validated against chamber data, ships in a commercial vibroacoustics code by 2029.

struct-shm-inverse-limits.title: Damage detection with proven detection limits
struct-shm-inverse-limits.description: Problem-specific stability estimates, optimal sensor placement and model-assisted probability of detection (MAPoD) for guided-wave, strain and electrical-resistance damage sensing, telling engineers what damage size a given sensor layout can and cannot see.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.status_oct2026: MAPoD for guided-wave SHM on composite cryogenic tanks for reusable launchers is active research (ONERA, Jul 2026); SHM is not yet qualified as an inspection replacement on launch vehicles (general). The release supplies a uniqueness claim (372, T1 per KB catalog, conditional) and a nonuniqueness result (365; only the 3D bounded-measurable scalar-conductivity part is formalized, T3), not stability constants.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 372 is T1 per KB catalog, conditional (repo lean/docs/372.md lists a Lean main result with a Comparator challenge, checked Oct 7 2026; T3 once the catalog is reconciled); 365 headline T1, formal scalar-conductivity part T3
struct-shm-inverse-limits.why: The question that earns inspection credit is not whether damage is identifiable in principle (372 claims yes, for smooth isotropic Lame moduli in 3D with full boundary data; conditional, and it does not cover anisotropic laminates or discontinuous damage) but how small a delamination N sensors detect at 90/95 confidence. That is quantitative stability plus statistics: solved in principle, expert-scarce, ideal for on-demand AI. 365's formal part (T3) shows nonuniqueness only for rough (bounded measurable) scalar conductivities in 3D; thin sensing skins are effectively 2D, where uniqueness for bounded conductivities is classical (Astala-Paivarinta 2006, general), and CFRP is anisotropic, so 365 sets no practical ceiling. The practical limit is the classical logarithmic stability of the Calderon problem (general). The node's main pathway is capability; the catalog adds only conditional confidence.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.strongest_case_small: Real SHM is limited by sensor aging, bonding and temperature/cryogenic compensation, not inverse-problem theory; regulators and operators accept POD from physical specimen tests, not proofs.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.signpost: Published MAPoD/POD curves for a guided-wave SHM layout on a cryogenic composite tank, validated against seeded-defect specimens, by 2029; SHM papers citing 365 or 372.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.calibration_note: A3: Premise label only: the why says the main pathway is capability and the catalog adds confidence. A4: Hard edge from struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations made soft. That node is T1-premised (Low/Medium/Medium), and this one is capability-driven (Medium/High/High), as its own why says (the catalog adds confidence). A hard edge would have rated the dependent likelier than its prerequisite. B-certification: 'one ceiling' dropped; 365 sets no practical ceiling for 2D or anisotropic sensing.

struct-verified-fe-solvers.title: Finite-element solvers with machine-checked error bounds
struct-verified-fe-solvers.description: Structural and thermal finite-element solvers (linear statics, modal, steady conduction-radiation) whose discretization and floating-point errors carry proved bounds (guaranteed a posteriori estimators plus verified arithmetic), so an analysis result ships with a certificate.
struct-verified-fe-solvers.status_oct2026: Guaranteed error estimators exist for model problems (general); verified floating-point toolchains are emerging at flight-software scale (verification domain); nothing at production FE scale; Mathlib coverage of PDE and numerics is thin.
struct-verified-fe-solvers.why: Certification by analysis rests today on solver verification by benchmark plus test correlation. Proof-carrying error bounds remove the code- and solution-verification layer of NASA-STD-7009-style credibility, freeing scarce reviewers for model-form questions. tl-position-6: formal verification is the bridge to safety-critical use, here applied to numerics rather than flight code.
struct-verified-fe-solvers.strongest_case_small: Discretization error is rarely the dominant uncertainty in structures (joints, boundary conditions, damping and loads are); a certificate on the wrong model is worthless (the specification problem).
struct-verified-fe-solvers.signpost: An open or commercial FE code ships certified error bounds for linear statics or modal analysis with a formal proof artifact by 2029.

struct-damage-tolerance-physics.description: Validated physics-based models of crack growth and composite damage progression under the low-cycle, high-amplitude, cryogenic and thermal-cycling spectra of reusable stages and tanks, replacing conservative empirical scatter factors and knockdowns.

struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.title: Predictive two-phase cooling physics in microgravity
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.description: Validated mechanistic models of flow boiling, condensation, critical heat flux and flow-regime transitions in microgravity pumped loops and heat pipes, at the heat fluxes 100-250 kW compute satellites need.
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.status_oct2026: Correlation-based. ISS flow boiling and condensation results published 2024-2025 (Int. J. Heat Mass Transfer); microgravity onset-of-boiling studies 2026. Two-phase pumped loops and oscillating heat pipes have flown, but not at AI1's heat flux, quantity or cost (33FG, Jun 2026).
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.why: Two-phase transport cuts heat-transport mass (33FG model: ~2.0 kg/kW for Starlink-like transport to ~0.8 kg/kW loop-based) and lets radiators run nearer chip temperature, which matters through T^4; below ~5 kg/m2, radiators rest on two-phase pumped loops or oscillating heat pipes not yet flown at this flux or quantity (33FG). Designers carry margins for microgravity uncertainty. Flight data bind: an ISS campaign yields hundreds of test points, while compute-satellite fleets will stream telemetry from ~2028-29, which S2 AI can turn into models; whoever owns the fleet owns the model. AI1's published radiator is a deployable liquid radiator, possibly single-phase, so its telemetry may not be two-phase data.
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.strongest_case_small: Engineers design around uncertainty with margin and favorable-orientation ground tests; the margin penalty may be only ~10-20% of heat-transport mass; SpaceX will iterate hardware faster than theory matures.
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.signpost: Operator telemetry from AI1 or Starcloud-class two-phase loops published or used in an open model; a microgravity critical-heat-flux model validated within about 15% by 2029.

struct-deployment-mechanics.title: Predictive simulation of large deployable structures
struct-deployment-mechanics.description: Validated models of deployment for 50 m to km structures: frictional contact and latching, stored-strain composite booms, tape-spring snap-through, membrane wrinkling and thermally induced vibration, where today's simulations lean on ground tests that gravity corrupts at scale.
struct-deployment-mechanics.status_oct2026: ACS3 (launched Apr 2024) deployed an ~80 m2 sail on 7 m composite booms; NASA says current booms support sails up to 500 m2 and follow-on booms up to 2,000 m2. Hinge misalignment in over-constrained deployable panels for space solar power is still being quantified (JSME, 2026). Rigid-body Coulomb friction has known existence and uniqueness pathologies (Painleve paradox, general).
struct-deployment-mechanics.why: At 100 m and beyond, gravity-offload rigs stop being representative, so qualification must be by analysis plus subscale and flight data, which requires models with understood error. AI supplies the math (nonsmooth dynamics, similitude scaling laws, tension-field wrinkling theory) quickly under S2, but validation needs flight deployments. Compute satellites will add many: each Starmind satellite deploys arrays on a ~75 m wingspan (up to 1,500 m2 of solar under the Sep 2026 filing), by the hundreds a year from ~2029, a far larger large-deployable dataset than today's few flights a year, though it covers the 50-100 m class rather than km scale and belongs to the operator.
struct-deployment-mechanics.strongest_case_small: Most deployment failures are workmanship and mechanism problems (snags, stiction, harness routing) that no model predicts; programs mitigate with simplicity and redundancy, not prediction.
struct-deployment-mechanics.signpost: A 500 m2-plus deployable flies with pre-flight predicted deployment shape and loads matched within stated bounds; NASA flies its follow-on boom technology.

struct-shell-knockdown-rules.title: Lighter buckling design rules for tanks and interstages
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.description: Probabilistic or mechanistic knockdown factors tied to measured imperfection statistics, beyond NASA SP-8007-2020's deterministic analysis-based approach, become routine agency and industry practice for cylinders and cones, including composite shells where a blanket 0.65 is still common.
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.status_oct2026: NASA SP-8007-2020/REV 2 (Dec 2020, NESC) already updates the 1965/1968 monograph with semi-empirical and analysis-based design approaches (Secs. 4.2-4.3) and records analysis-based design buckling loads for the Shuttle SRB cases and External Tank and the SLS core stage; it is a design guideline, not a requirement. NASA SBKF developed and test-validated analysis-based knockdown approaches on 8-ft metallic and composite cylinders (2010s-2022); a NASA review warns the universal 0.65 composite factor can be unconservative; Wagner et al. (2025) report weight savings above 14% and up to 31% in optimized configurations with a mechanistic design curve. Probabilistic knockdowns tied to measured imperfection statistics are not yet standard practice.
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.why: For unstiffened isotropic cylinders SP-8007 gives knockdowns of about 0.22-0.47 (R/t 1000-200), and buckling-critical wall thickness scales as KDF^-1/2, so raising a knockdown from 0.32 to 0.60 cuts that wall mass about 27%. 0.65 is SP-8007's recommended factor for moderately or heavily stiffened cylinders, whose load does not scale as t^2. Stiffened, sandwich and optimized shells see 14-31% with a mechanistic design curve (Wagner et al. 2025). Rules tied to measured imperfection statistics come from Monte Carlo on factory data plus certified margins; a worst-case imperfection theorem helps but is not required, since the analysis-based revision already happened without one. Standards and handbook revision (SP-8007, ECSS buckling handbook) and validation tests on representative shells bind, so the band is capped at Medium.
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.strongest_case_small: Buckling-critical structures (interstages, intertanks, unpressurized barrels, adapters) are a minority of dry mass; new-space firms test to failure and do not follow SP-8007 strictly; a kilogram saved on a booster buys only ~0.1-0.2 kg of payload (general).
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.signpost: A NASA SP-8007 or ECSS buckling-handbook revision adopting regime-aware or probabilistic knockdowns, or a launch-vehicle program citing them, by 2029.
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] Fact fix: SP-8007-2020/REV 2 already replaced the 1960s-only approach and analysis-based loads were used on SRB, ET and SLS core stage (text checked by resolver in the NTRS full text); description re-scoped to probabilistic knockdowns beyond it; scaling example corrected (0.65 is the stiffened-cylinder factor; unstiffened 0.22-0.47; 0.32 -> 0.60 cuts ~27%). struct-launch-env-margins.title: Tighter launch vibration and acoustic environments
struct-launch-env-margins.description: Component and spacecraft random-vibration, acoustic and shock test levels set with a reduced qualification margin over a model-predicted maximum predicted environment (MPE), from error-bounded predictions calibrated on early flight data, for new vehicles where flight data are sparse; published by a launch provider or disclosed by a vertically integrated provider-customer for its own payloads.
struct-launch-env-margins.status_oct2026: Maximum predicted environments are already statistical (P95/50 normal tolerance limits per NASA-HDBK-7005, general), and qualification adds about +3 dB (GEVS) to +6 dB (launch-vehicle units) over the acceptance or MPE level (general). Environments are enveloped flight data plus fixed qualification margins (for example qualification at acceptance +3 dB, general); NESC's NTRC methods cut coupled-loads cost (2023-2024); each coupled-loads cycle with a launch provider takes weeks (general).
struct-launch-env-margins.why: Random vibration sizes brackets, secondary structure and electronics boxes; a 3 dB margin doubles the test PSD (about 1.4x g-rms). Stating environments as exceedance probabilities is already practice, and for high-cadence vehicles empirical P95/50 envelopes from abundant flight data do the job without predictive models, so the AI-attributable gain is on new vehicles with sparse data, where calibrated predictions could justify a smaller margin. Forcing uncertainty dominates structural model error, so mid-frequency structural fidelity accelerates rather than gates. Launch-provider user guides and agency test standards gate adoption, so Medium is the cap; S2 Low because providers have little incentive to tighten published environments and a vertically integrated provider (SpaceX launches about three quarters of its own mass to orbit) rarely discloses its own.
struct-launch-env-margins.strongest_case_small: Launch providers have little incentive to tighten published environments; forcing uncertainty dominates; savings fall on small parts and test-failure rates rather than vehicle mass.
struct-launch-env-margins.signpost: A launch provider publishes environments derived from flight-calibrated predictive models with stated exceedance probability and a reduced qualification margin, or a vertically integrated provider discloses such environments for its own payloads.

struct-radiator-optimization.title: AI-optimized radiators and heat transport
struct-radiator-optimization.description: Coupled conduction-radiation-two-phase design optimization (panel topology, heat-pipe and loop layout, cold plates and heat spreading, view factors to Earth and arrays, micrometeoroid segmentation, deployment structure) that cuts thermal-subsystem mass and the chip-to-radiator temperature drop at fixed hardware technology.
struct-radiator-optimization.status_oct2026: 33FG model: Starlink V3-like thermal ~19.4 kg/kW at 310 K; StarThink V2 ~3.0-3.4 kg/kW at 370 K with 2.5 kg/m2 two-sided panels; proven radiators run 2.5-5 kg/m2, and values below ~5 rest on two-phase hardware not yet flown at this scale. AI1 June 2026 spec: 110 m2 deployable liquid radiator (~3.7 kg/m2 implied by 33FG's ~410 kg radiator allocation); ~1,400 W/m2 (two-sided, per m2 of planform) is Musk's stated figure, not the spec sheet. SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response caps the 250 kW-peak design below 200 m2 of radiator; 33FG's Oct 6 model needs ~134 C GPU logic and ~132 C HBM at 200 m2, or ~327 m2 to hold 105 / 95 C, unless heat spreading improves.
struct-radiator-optimization.why: The design space is large but well-posed (T^4 nonlinearity, view-factor coupling, MMOD puncture probability): expert-scarce, ideal for on-demand AI. At 765-1,400 W/m2 (from 33FG's Oct 2026 model holding HBM at 95 C up to Musk's June figure), a GW of waste heat needs ~0.7-1.3 km2 of panel, and each 1 kg/m2 of areal density is ~700-1,300 t per GW. If AI design cuts thermal mass 10-25% beyond SpaceX's own conventionally optimized second iteration (assumption; the AI-attributable increment may be nearer 5-15%), the saving is ~350-1,400 t per GW (~4-14 Starship flights at 100 t), ~2-9% of the ~16,000-18,000 t launched per GW. In cost terms, thermal is the largest single $/GW sensitivity in Mach33's orbital-data-center model (+/-30% thermal -> +/-8.9% $/GW), so a 10-25% cut is ~3-7% of $/GW, about 0.3-0.6 year on Mach33's base cost curve, which falls ~12% a year in 2028-31 (a single commercial forecaster's model). The biggest design lever is the chip-to-radiator temperature drop under the HBM limit: at the ~250 kW target, cold-plate and heat-spreading design set chip and HBM temperature and therefore chip life (33FG reference: 5.6 -> 3.4 years), so the gain shows up as service life and sustained draw as much as mass; how hot the chips may run is decided by qualification (struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification).
struct-radiator-optimization.strongest_case_small: Radiator physics is simple and SpaceX and Starcloud already optimize it with conventional tools; manufacturing cost per m2 at Starlink volume and chip-temperature limits matter more than design insight (33FG: thermal is not a physics blocker).
struct-radiator-optimization.signpost: A flown compute satellite discloses radiator areal density below 3 kg/m2; Starmind telemetry shows ~1,250-1,400 W/m2 sustained at stated chip and HBM temperatures.
struct-radiator-optimization.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: prerequisites cap-applied-math and cap-research-math-public replaced by cap-design-optimization (same years; this is a multiphysics design tool); gate fabrication -> adoption; the 2.5 kg/m2 target moved out of the description (it belongs to struct-radiator-lightweight-production). Skeptic: radiator flux 1,400 -> 765-1,400 W/m2 per the Oct 2026 33FG model and counterfactual set to SpaceX's own second iteration. Auditor: arithmetic fixed (2.5-6% was 2.5-9%; now ~2-9% on the revised mass per GW); 1,400 W/m2 attributed to Musk; chip-life channel added. Advocate: $/GW framing (Mach33 thermal sensitivity, verified) added; soft edges from struct-agentic-analysis-workflows, struct-two-phase-microgravity-models (all three lenses) and the new hot-chip node. Years and bands unchanged. | E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): 2035/S4 extension. band_2035: S1 Medium -> High. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Medium from 2028 (the design problem is well-posed and the tools exist); High once a second hardware iteration carries AI-optimized thermal design, 2030 in S2 and 2029 in S3/S4 (seed had 2028). S1 Medium 2031, High 2034 with its design-optimization prerequisite.

struct-cert-by-analysis.title: Qualification by analysis replaces some structural tests
struct-cert-by-analysis.description: Agencies (NASA, ESA, Space Force) accept AI-produced, uncertainty-quantified analysis in place of a strength qualification test beyond what NASA-STD-5001B already allows: for composite or bonded primary structure, or for metallic structure at tested-hardware factors of safety instead of the larger no-test factors. Derivative structure with correlated heritage test data comes first.
struct-cert-by-analysis.status_oct2026: NASA-STD-7009 provides a credibility framework. NASA-STD-5001B (Change 3, Oct 2022) already allows prototype or protoflight strength testing and, for metallic structures only, an analysis-alone (no-test) option with an engineering rationale and Technical Authority approval, generally at larger factors of safety; its example criteria include similarity to a test-verified predecessor with good test-analysis correlation (FSR 15-16, Sec. 4.1.2.3). It allows probabilistic criteria case by case (FSR 17). Composite, bonded and most new primary structure are still strength-tested (general).
struct-cert-by-analysis.why: A dedicated qualification article for launch-vehicle primary structure costs tens of millions of dollars and up to a year (general); a spacecraft unit's qualification model costs far less. The institutional route already exists for metals at a mass penalty, so what is new is credit at standard factors and for composites. It rests on certified UQ, AI-run test correlation and correlated heritage test data (5001B's no-test criteria lean on similarity and test-analysis correlation, hence the hard edge from struct-test-data-commons). Proof-carrying solver bounds help but do not gate, because discretization error is rarely the dominant uncertainty (struct-verified-fe-solvers). Chain (S2): credibility directive 2029 -> first use at a program's test-plan milestone 2030. Needs agency acceptance, so capped at Medium; S2 Low because the re-scoped step is harder than today's allowances and has one or two years of window after the rulebook (judgment, not a computed probability).
struct-cert-by-analysis.strongest_case_small: Test failures routinely expose what analysis missed (joints, workmanship); no agency will drop tests on first-of-kind primary structure; savings concentrate on derivatives.
struct-cert-by-analysis.signpost: A NASA, ESA or Space Force program grants model-based qualification credit, citing AI-produced analysis, in place of a planned strength test for composite or bonded primary structure, or for metallic structure at tested-hardware factors, by 2030-31.
struct-cert-by-analysis.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic+auditor] Fact fix: the status said tests are mandatory for primary-structure qualification; NASA-STD-5001B Change 3 Sec. 4.1.2.3 (FSR 15-16) already allows metallic no-test verification and FSR 17 allows probabilistic criteria (text checked by resolver). Description and signpost re-scoped to credit beyond those allowances (otherwise the node is met today with no AI attribution). [skeptic+advocate] struct-verified-fe-solvers hard -> soft. [skeptic] struct-test-data-commons added as hard prerequisite (5001B no-test criteria require similarity and correlation evidence). [skeptic] S2 band Medium -> Low because the re-scoped event is strictly harder; skeptic's year slip (S2 2031, S3 2030) not taken because the credibility standard stays at S2 2029; advocate's S2 2029/S3 2028 rejected (depended on a 2028 rulebook). | E-certification (2026-10-07): 2035 horizon and S4 review. Years: S1 >2031 -> 2033. band_2035 S1-S4 Low/Medium/Medium/Medium. S4 equals S3 (no S4 credit). | E-certification resolver (2026-10-07): S1 band_2031 Low -> Speculative (skeptic): the S1 year falls after 2031, and earliest year marks the first credible year. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S3 Medium 2030 (rulebook Medium 2029 plus a test-plan milestone); S2 Medium 2032: its rulebook reaches Medium in 2030 and the re-scoped step (credit at standard factors and for composites) is harder than today's allowances. Medium cap. Skeptic (2034: few test-plan milestones) vs advocate (2031: SDA buys): 2032.
struct-cert-by-analysis.note_2035: S1 lands about 2033, two years after its rulebook. S2 rises to Medium as more programs reach test-plan milestones; the regulatory cap holds. S4 equals S3 because the gate is agency acceptance.
struct-cert-by-analysis.gate_note: Agency acceptance binds; correlated heritage test data and certified UQ validation (data) are the runner-up.

struct-fsp-next-gen-design.title: Second-generation fission power designs
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.description: AI multiphysics optimization of reactor, shield, Brayton converter, radiator and lander integration for follow-on fission systems (lower kg/kWe at 100 kWe-plus, Mars or nuclear-electric variants) after the first unit's design is frozen.
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.status_oct2026: NASA directive (Jul 31 2025): at least 100 kWe, closed Brayton cycle, heavy lander with up to 15 t available, launch-ready by Q1 FY2030, awards to two providers within six months of the RFP; reactor under ~6 t (New Space Economy, Apr 2026). The final RFP was never issued: NASA made the draft Space Act Agreement path inactive on Mar 26 2026 and tied Lunar Reactor-1 to SR-1 experience. NASA spent over $200M since 2000 on 1-200 kWe concepts without flight readiness (directive).
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.why: A timing trap: first-of-a-kind systems freeze their designs (PDR not before ~2028, no provider yet) before AI multiphysics design capability matures (S2 ~2029), so AI-math gains land in second units, and a second-generation study presupposes a first unit under contract and frozen. Shield design rests on radiation transport, which the release does not touch; AI applied math helps there only under S2.
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.strongest_case_small: Space nuclear power is bounded by fuel supply, launch approval, nuclear ground testing and budgets, not design insight; a second-generation program may not be funded before the first unit operates.
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.signpost: NASA restarts the LR-1 procurement, awards providers and announces a follow-on (Mars-class or 200 kWe-plus) design study, ideally naming AI-assisted multidisciplinary optimization.
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Auditor: status corrected (final RFP never issued; Mar 26 2026 reset); PDR ~2027 -> not before ~2028; bands S1 Low -> Speculative, S2/S3 Medium -> Low. Years unchanged. | E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): 2035/S4 extension. earliest_year: S1 >2031 -> 2032; band_2035: S1 Speculative -> Low, S2 Low -> Medium, S3 Low -> Medium, S4 Low -> Medium. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): 30% needs a Lunar Reactor-1 award (procurement inactive since Mar 2026) plus a frozen first design before a follow-on study: S2 2034, S3/S4 2033 where design tools are ready a year sooner. Skeptic (no RFP, SR-1 unfunded) vs advocate (a second-generation study is cheap): Medium by 2035 kept, crossing late in the window.

struct-flown-lighter-structure.title: First flight structure sized with AI-certified margins
struct-flown-lighter-structure.description: A launch-vehicle barrel, interstage or large spacecraft primary structure flies after being sized with AI-derived knockdowns tied to measured imperfection statistics and certified uncertainty margins, beyond SP-8007-2020's analysis-based approach, at 10-30% lower mass for its buckling-critical parts. Commercial builders need no standards revision to do this.
struct-flown-lighter-structure.status_oct2026: No such flight attributed to AI-derived design rules. Human analysis-based design buckling loads were already used for the Shuttle SRB cases and External Tank and for the SLS core stage (first flown Nov 2022), per SP-8007-2020; new-space firms rely on test-to-failure (general).
struct-flown-lighter-structure.why: Chain (S2): worst-case imperfection theory and certified margins (2028) -> in-house design rule 2029 -> build and validation test of a primary-structure flight article (2-3 years for a new launch-vehicle subsystem, lag ladder) -> flight 2031. A standards revision (struct-shell-knockdown-rules) accelerates but does not gate, because commercial builders are not bound by SP-8007 or ECSS handbooks and the FAA does not certify structure. S3 gains little because the build-and-test cycle binds; its 1.3-1.5x physical speed keeps 2031 but raises the odds to Medium. Since human analysis-based knockdowns have already flown, the AI-attributable step is a further margin cut on a minority of dry mass. Vehicle-level payoff is modest: ~1-3% payload on an upper-stage-limited vehicle (analyst estimate).
struct-flown-lighter-structure.strongest_case_small: Attribution is nearly impossible because companies already push margins via test; vehicle-level mass savings of 1-3% are within normal design-iteration noise.
struct-flown-lighter-structure.signpost: A launch or spacecraft program publicly states that a flown structure was sized with AI-derived probabilistic or mechanistic knockdowns (by 2031).
struct-flown-lighter-structure.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder: primary structure. A launch-vehicle barrel, interstage or primary structure designed on 2028-29 AI capability flies 2031+ in S2 (new LV subsystem 2-3 years). Chain (S2): imperfection theory 2028 -> knockdown rules 2029 -> flight-article build and validation test 2-3 years -> flight 2031. S2 2030 -> 2031 (Medium -> Low); S3 2030 -> 2031 (1.3-1.5x physical speed still lands 2030-31; Medium kept); S1 unchanged. A4: Why text updated to match the A3 years and bands; it had still described the v0 values. A3's conditional sentence is kept.

struct-shm-inspection-credit.title: Sensor-based inspection credit for reusable stages
struct-shm-inspection-credit.description: Built-in structural health monitoring with quantified probability of detection replaces scheduled teardown or scanning inspection for defined zones of reusable stages or tanks between flights.
struct-shm-inspection-credit.status_oct2026: Demonstrated on specimens and subscale composite cryotanks (ONERA, 2026); an SHM payload for in-flight re-certification was prepared for ISS exposure (SPIE, Apr 2026); no launch vehicle uses SHM as formal inspection credit (general).
struct-shm-inspection-credit.why: Inspection is a large part of reuse cost: non-destructive testing of large structures is slow and access-limited (ONERA, 2026). Proven detection limits plus certified margins let operators set inspection intervals from data. Sensor qualification under thermal-cryogenic aging binds, which no amount of cognition compresses. Chain (S2): applied math public 2027 -> proven damage-detection limits and certified structural margins (2028) -> sensor systems qualified under thermal-cryogenic aging 2029 -> an operator sets inspection intervals from sensor data on a reusable stage 2030 (Medium; no regulator needed for an operator carrying its own risk).
struct-shm-inspection-credit.strongest_case_small: Commercial operators set their own regimes and may find visual and borescope inspection plus fleet leaders cheap enough; sensor reliability, not math, limits SHM.
struct-shm-inspection-credit.signpost: An operator or NASA program announces SHM-based inspection credit for a reusable stage or tank (POD curves accepted in place of a scheduled NDE inspection) by 2030.
struct-shm-inspection-credit.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder. Built-in SHM on a reusable stage is a new launch-vehicle subsystem (2-3 years from design-complete to flight, 1.5-2 years at S3 speed) and its own why says sensor qualification under thermal-cryogenic aging binds. Chain (S2): detection limits and certified margins 2028 -> sensor network design and qualification -> inspection credit on flying stages 2030. S1 2031 -> >2031, S2 2029 -> 2030, S3 2029 -> 2030; bands unchanged.

struct-highflux-radiator-flight.title: 100-kW-class deployable radiators fly on compute satellites
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.description: First flights of deployable liquid or two-phase radiators rejecting 100-250 kW per spacecraft (SpaceX Starmind: the June 2026 AI1 spec had 110 m2 at Musk's ~1,400 W/m2 for 150 kW; the Aug-Sep 2026 revision runs 175 kW average / 250 kW peak inside a filed radiator envelope under 200 m2, i.e. at least ~1,250 W/m2 at 250 kW unless the envelope grows; Starcloud-3, ~200 kW), on the physical clock and largely independent of AI mathematics.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.status_oct2026: June 2026 AI1 spec (150 kW peak, 120 kW average, 110 m2 radiator, 70 kW/t target, 70 m wingspan) superseded. SpaceX product page (Aug 2026): 175 kW average / 250 kW peak on a space-optimized Vera Rubin NVL72, 75 m wingspan. SpaceX FCC response (Sep 16 2026): under 4,000 kg, under 200 m2 radiator, under 1,500 m2 solar. Musk (Oct 1 2026): cautiously optimistic of ~250 kW average via Nvidia co-design. 33FG Oct 6 model: 250 kW in 200 m2 implies ~134 C logic / ~132 C HBM (with a higher-rated GPU package); holding 105 / 95 C needs ~327 m2. SpaceX targets first Starmind launches in Q4 2027 (Musk, Aug 25 2026); the design is not frozen. Starcloud-1 ran an H100 in orbit from Nov 2025; Starcloud-3 (~200 kW) is designed for Starship; Starship reached orbit Sep 28 2026 deploying 26 Starlink V3.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor on SpaceX's and Starcloud's hardware schedules, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Anchor node for the orbital-compute chain: the hardware arrives regardless, sized with conventional tools. 33FG's June reconstruction puts AI1's thermal system (June spec) at ~532 kg of 2.1 t (25%) and notes that below ~5 kg/m2 it relies on two-phase hardware SpaceX does not yet build in-house; the October reference satellite is ~4.0-4.5 t. Between June and October 2026 the power point moved twice and the radiator envelope grew from 110 to up to 200 m2, with thermal closure (HBM temperature) still open. With design-complete at best ~Q1 2027, a 12-18 month lag from design-complete to flight for a derivative payload (physclock lag ladder) and announced SpaceX schedules running 1.5-3x long, first flight lands in 2028 in every scenario. AI-math effects enter on the second iteration. High in every scenario (judgment): SpaceX targets Q4 2027 and Starcloud-3 is a second attempt, so a first flight by 2031 survives a slip of two to three years. Basis (R9): SpaceX's AI1 (the Starmind program's compute satellite) as Mach33 reconstructed it (17 Jun 2026): 150 kW peak and 120 kW average compute power, about 2.1 t (71 kW/t on peak), flying in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit (SSO). AI1's radiator is a 110 m2 deployable liquid loop at 1,400 W/m2 (two-sided) and its array 600 m2 at 250 W/m2; a later 250 kW generation would need the larger filed envelope.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.strongest_case_small: This node is the counterfactual baseline: everything here happens without any AI mathematics.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.signpost: First Starmind launch (Q4 2027 target) with published thermal telemetry: sustained ~1,250-1,400 W/m2 of planform, GPU and HBM temperatures.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Auditor + advocate + skeptic: status and description updated from the superseded June AI1 spec to the Aug 2026 product page, Sep 16 2026 FCC envelope and Oct 2026 statements; 'launch date not published' corrected (SpaceX targets Q4 2027). Skeptic: years 2027 -> 2028 in all scenarios (design not frozen, 12-18 month lag ladder, 1.5-3x slip calibration; same practice the trunk resolver applied to launch-clock nodes). Advocate's reliance on a Q4 2027 first flight rejected on that calibration. Bands High unchanged. No year or band change. | R9-orbital-compute (2026-10-27): AI1/SSO basis stated (review OC-1). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): SpaceX targets Q4 2027, so the odds pass 30% in 2028, but announced SpaceX schedules run 1.5-3x long: High (over 70%) from 2029, not 2028. struct-radiator-lightweight-production.title: Ultralight radiators in serial production
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.description: Two-phase or oscillating-heat-pipe deployable radiators at or below 2.5 kg/m2 planform, running at ~370 K chip temperature, built at Starlink-like volume (thousands of m2 per month).
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.status_oct2026: Lab and prototype panels reach ~1.9-3.9 kg/m2 (33FG survey of NASA and industry prototypes); commercial deployables ~3.5-4.9 kg/m2 (Redwire Q-Rad per 33FG); none in mass production at this areal density (general).
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.why: Not an AI-math implication: serial production of light radiators is a manufacturing and insourcing ramp on the physical clock, so this is an exogenous anchor and the P7 Speculative default does not apply; AI design and validated two-phase models are soft accelerators (P1). Going from ~3.7 kg/m2 (AI1 implied) to 2.5 kg/m2 saves ~850 t of radiator per GW at 1,400 W/m2 (~1,550 t at ~765 W/m2), ~9-16 Starship flights at 100 t. Prototypes already reach ~1.9-3.9 kg/m2 without AI design, so serial production is a manufacturing and insourcing problem; AI design (2028 in S2) and validated two-phase models shorten iteration but are not prerequisites. The manufacturing ramp and qualification bind, so S2 and S3 tie at 2030 (first flight of the new panel in 2029, then the production ramp). Economic pull is modest: 33FG finds the radiator is the subsystem with room to spare (each kg/m2 off the ~600 m2 solar array buys ~6x what the same cut buys on the radiator), and the October design is short of radiator area, not areal density. S3's AI-run factories speed a ramp but do not create demand for it. S1 is 2031 and Low because a capability plateau slows design iteration and weakens compute-satellite demand; S2 and S3 Medium (judgment) because prototypes already reach the target density but the economic pull is modest.
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.strongest_case_small: The gain rides on manufacturing learning curves and supplier insourcing, where AI mathematics plays a small role; 70 kW/t may already be economic without it.
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.signpost: SpaceX insources two-phase radiator production (33FG expects within a few years of first purchase) and discloses areal density for a Starmind version.
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder. Serial production at thousands of m2 per month comes after first flight of the new panel, which itself takes 12-18 months from the 2028 design (production ramp compresses only 0.9x in S2, 0.7-0.8x in S3). Chain (S2): AI-optimized radiator design 2028 -> first flight mid-2029 to 2030 -> serial production 2030. S1 2031 -> >2031 (Medium -> Low; S1 design lands 2030), S2 2029 -> 2030, S3 2029 -> 2030; S2/S3 bands unchanged. A4: Why text updated to match the A3 years and bands; it had still described the v0 values. A3's conditional sentence is kept.

struct-fsp-radiator-qual.title: Lightweight 600 K radiators qualified for fission power
struct-fsp-radiator-qual.description: Titanium-water or cesium-titanium heat-pipe radiator panels near 3 kg/m2 rejecting the ~230-300 kW of waste heat from a 100 kWe Brayton system, qualified for launch vibration, freeze-thaw and ~10 years of lunar micrometeoroid exposure.
struct-fsp-radiator-qual.status_oct2026: A Cs-Ti heat-pipe panel design reaches 2.98 kg/m2 and rejects >56 kWth at 600 K with launch stresses under 10% of yield (JBIS, Jul 2025; paywalled, unverified in review); ACT's SBIR Phase III work on Ti-H2O/graphite-fiber radiators added freeze-thaw tests and a 10-year lunar MMOD analysis (ICES, Jul 2026); titanium wick treatments studied (AIAA SciTech, Jan 2026). NASA reset the FSP procurement in Mar 2026; no provider is under contract.
struct-fsp-radiator-qual.why: At ~25-30% Brayton efficiency, 100 kWe means rejecting ~230-300 kWt; at an average radiating temperature near 450 K and ~3 kW/m2 net on the lunar surface (general), that is ~100 m2 and ~300 kg of panel at 3 kg/m2. The technology is on track without AI mathematics; qualification testing and program funding set the date.
struct-fsp-radiator-qual.strongest_case_small: The radiator is not the long pole of fission surface power; fuel, licensing and the lander are.

struct-reusable-life-management.title: Sensors and models track wear on reusable stages
struct-reusable-life-management.description: Fully reusable heavy launchers (Starship-class and peers) manage structural life with validated life models (data-driven or physics-based) and built-in sensors, sustaining fast turnaround without routine teardown inspection and with life limits set by analysis rather than fleet-leader experience alone.
struct-reusable-life-management.status_oct2026: Starship reached orbit on Sep 28 2026 with both stages expended at sea (33FG); booster and ship reuse at scale not yet operational; Falcon-class booster reuse relies on inspection and fleet-leader experience (general).
struct-reusable-life-management.why: Needs inspection credit (2030 in S2), data-cleared reflight from a probabilistic life twin (physclock-twin-reflight-clearance, S2 2030 after B-trunk), and flight cycles to build confidence (Mach33 base: 8.9 flights per stack in 2029, 18 in 2030). Physics-based damage closure (struct-damage-tolerance-physics) accelerates but does not gate: operators set life with data-driven models and fleet leaders first. Fleet experience accumulates only with flights, which no cognition compresses. S2 Low because it chains two Medium prerequisites and needs a public description of sensor-based inspection; S3 Medium.
struct-reusable-life-management.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may reach airline-like turnaround empirically, making the AI-math contribution unmeasurable; operators may never publish how they set life limits.
struct-reusable-life-management.signpost: A Starship booster or ship flies 10-plus times with publicly described sensor-based inspection between flights.

struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet.description: Compute satellites at ~100 kW/t (versus AI1's ~70 kW/t design point and a Starlink V3-like ~11 kW/t) built at hundreds to thousands per year.
struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet.status_oct2026: June AI1 spec target 70 kW/t (mass unpublished; ~2.1 t implied, ~71 kW/t on peak per 33FG). SpaceX's stated long-run goal is ~100 kW of compute per tonne (Feb 2026, press report). The Aug 2026 revision (250 kW peak / 175 kW average) and SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response (under 4,000 kg, under 200 m2 radiator, under 1,500 m2 solar) bound the next design at about 62 kW/t or more on peak; 33FG's Oct 6 reference case reaches ~4.5 t (~56 kW/t). kW/t fell as power rose. 33FG's StarThink V2 reference reaches ~100 kW/t with 2.5 kg/m2 radiators, improved solar and 370 K chips, and 33FG identifies solar areal density as the primary constraint.
struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet.pathway: P7 (AI math second-order via P1 thermal and structural design and P5 chip-life evidence)
struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet.why: Solar is ~56% of AI1's reconstructed mass, so 100 kW/t depends first on array specific power (struct-light-solar-array-production, then thinner or higher-efficiency cells), then on how hot chips and HBM may run (struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification), and only then on radiator areal density. From the ~55-62 kW/t of the Sep 2026 envelope, 100 kW/t in serial production by 2031 needs a ~60-80% gain within ~3 years of first flight, against a design trend that has run the other way; that is Low in S2. The AI-math contribution is design optimization of the thermal and structural share and faster accelerated-life evidence for hotter chips. In S3, yearly satellite generations and AI-run factories (1.2-1.3x) keep it Medium.
struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet.strongest_case_small: The October design moved away from 100 kW/t; with cheap launch SpaceX may prefer bigger satellites at ~55-65 kW/t, and solar areal density and chip power density move kW/t more than thermal design.
struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet.signpost: SpaceX discloses a Starmind version at or above 100 kW/t.
struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet.calibration_note: A3: Follows struct-radiator-lightweight-production (now 2030 in S2/S3); serial production of 100 kW/t satellites needs those radiators plus lighter arrays in a production line. struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe.status_oct2026: Directive (Jul 31 2025): at least 100 kWe, closed Brayton, heavy lander up to 15 t, launch-ready Q1 FY2030, two awards within six months of the RFP. On Mar 24 2026 NASA said Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be informed by Space Reactor-1 Freedom (Mars launch Dec 2028); on Mar 26 2026 it made the draft Funded Space Act Agreement posting inactive to reassess the development approach. No FSP/LR-1 provider award found as of Oct 2026. NASA-DOE MOU renewed (Jan 2026); a December 2025 executive order calls for a lunar surface reactor ready for launch by 2030.
struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe.why: Scenario-invariant on purpose: the binding gates are a heavy cargo lander able to land ~15 t (auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing, itself behind schedule), nuclear launch approval, HALEU fuel supply and nuclear ground testing. The Q1 FY2030 launch-ready target predates the Mar 2026 procurement reset; with no provider under contract and LR-1 now sequenced behind SR-1, a space reactor's 4-6 years from a funded start (physclock lag ladder) puts launch after 2031. AI mathematics does not move licensing, appropriations or lander schedules, and the first unit's design freezes before AI design tools mature.

struct-km-monolith.title: Kilometre-scale monolithic structure in orbit
struct-km-monolith.description: A single connected structure at least 1 km across (solar-radiator plane for GW compute, space solar power array or large antenna) deployed or assembled in orbit.
struct-km-monolith.status_oct2026: Starcloud's white paper (Sep 2024) sketches a 5 GW station with a ~4 km x 4 km array assembled modularly; Google Suncatcher (Nov 2025) instead flies 81 satellites within a 1 km radius at 100-200 m spacing; SpaceX said on Oct 6 2026 that Starmind needs ~10-satellite tight-formation clusters at ~10 Tbps; Chinese space-solar-power truss-assembly robotics is active (2026); Caltech's MAPLE beamed power in orbit (2023) with 50 m unit tiles planned.
struct-km-monolith.why: Formation flying is replacing structure: guidance, navigation and optical links give km-scale clusters without km-scale structures (Suncatcher places 81 satellites within 1 km; Starmind plans ten-satellite clusters), so the business case for a monolith weakens even as modeling improves. No km-scale program is funded. Robotic in-orbit assembly reaches the 100 m class by 2035 at best (robo-in-space-assembly, Low by 2035 in S3 and S4), and a 1 km structure has about 100 times that area. Deployment physics and certification by analysis (2029-30) are not the gate; capital and a buyer are. Every scenario is after 2035.
struct-km-monolith.strongest_case_small: Even with perfect models, nobody is paying for a monolith when formation flying works; the most likely km-scale builder (Chinese space solar power) runs on its own schedule.
struct-km-monolith.signpost: A funded km-scale assembly demonstration (for example a Chinese space-solar-power milestone), or an orbital-compute operator abandoning formation flying for a monolith.
struct-km-monolith.note_2035: Every scenario resolves to after 2035 and Speculative: no km-scale program is funded and formation flying meets the compute need. Robotic assembly reaches the 100 m class by 2035 at best and the gate is capital, so S4 gets no credit.

struct-design-cycle-compression.title: Structures and thermal analysis cycles 2-5x faster
struct-design-cycle-compression.description: Time from a requirement change to signed-off stress, loads and thermal analysis (not design-build-test) compresses 2-5x across the industry, cutting non-recurring engineering and allowing more design iterations per program.
struct-design-cycle-compression.status_oct2026: Agentic FEA is at research-prototype stage (2026); coupled-loads and thermal correlation cycles still take weeks (general).
struct-design-cycle-compression.why: Chain (S2): public applied math 2027 -> agentic FE workflows 2027 -> adoption at vertically integrated firms 2028, primes 6-12 months later -> industry-wide 2-5x 2029. The earliest and most certain effect in this domain. If structures and thermal analysis is ~10-20% of spacecraft non-recurring engineering (general) and agents cut its labor 50-80% (assumption), NRE falls ~5-15%; the larger benefit is more iterations per month, which compounds into lighter, better-margined designs. A 50-80% labor cut is a 2-5x speedup, and human sign-off time stays roughly constant, so turnaround compresses less than the 5-10x cognitive multiplier.
struct-design-cycle-compression.strongest_case_small: Program schedules are bound by hardware procurement and physical tests (thermal vacuum, vibration), not analysis; faster analysis can simply wait longer for the test chamber.
struct-design-cycle-compression.signpost: Primes or new-space firms report analysis cycle-time reductions, or stress-analyst hiring shifts toward review roles, by 2029.
struct-design-cycle-compression.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic+auditor] Title now says analysis turnaround, not design cycles; capability-engineering-adoption moved from accelerated_by to a hard prerequisite ('across the industry'); S2 2028 -> 2029 (primes follow 6-12 months after vertically integrated firms). struct-structural-mass-step.title: 5-15% lighter structures on new vehicles and spacecraft
struct-structural-mass-step.description: Vehicles and spacecraft designed from ~2028 show 5-15% lower structural mass for equivalent loads, spacecraft first and launch-vehicle primary structure later. The gains come from knockdowns (buckling-critical barrels), certified margins (strength-critical members), tighter launch environments (secondary structure and boxes) and design optimization; they apply to different parts of dry mass, so they do not simply add.
struct-structural-mass-step.status_oct2026: No measurable trend attributable to AI mathematics (general).
struct-structural-mass-step.why: Chain (S2): first flown AI-sized structure 2031 -> several new designs disclosing comparable dry-mass fractions after 2031; an industry-wide trend cannot show up in the year of the first flight. AI-native spacecraft and AI design optimization accelerate the spacecraft side.
struct-structural-mass-step.strongest_case_small: Launch economics are set by propulsion, reuse and cost, not structural mass (Starship deliberately uses heavier, cheaper stainless steel); measured mass fractions will not separate AI effects from normal improvement.
struct-structural-mass-step.signpost: New vehicle or spacecraft reveals citing AI-derived design rules with disclosed dry-mass fractions.

struct-gw-orbital-compute.title: 1 GW of compute operating in orbit
struct-gw-orbital-compute.description: Cumulative at least 1 GW of compute power in orbit, counted at peak rating, on AI1-class satellites in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit (SSO). At AI1's 150 kW peak that is about 6,700 satellites (about 8,300 at its 120 kW average); at about 2.1 t each (Mach33's reconstruction, 71 kW/t) about 14,000 t, or about 10,000 t at the 100 kW/t SpaceX's S-1 cites. A Starship carries about 60-90 t to SSO, so 1 GW is about 155-235 flights at AI1 density and 110-170 at S-1 density. The array is about 4 km2 at 250 W/m2, and the radiators about 0.7 km2 at 1,400 W/m2 two-sided. A 250 kW unit, if SpaceX flies one, is a later generation at S-1 density (about 2.5 t), not AI1.
struct-gw-orbital-compute.status_oct2026: SpaceX filed for up to 1 million orbital data-center satellites (Jan 2026). Musk (Aug 25 2026) targeted first AI satellites in Q4 2027, 'significant scale' in 2028 and 1 GW in orbit by end-2027, then ~10x a year, and cautioned listeners to treat the projections skeptically. SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response bounds each satellite under 4,000 kg. Mach33's AI1 reconstruction (Jun 2026): 150 kW peak, 120 kW average, about 2.1 t, dawn-dusk SSO; SpaceX's S-1 cites over 100 kW per tonne and deployment 'as early as 2028'. Starcloud raised $170M (Mar 2026); Google's first Suncatcher prototype launched Oct 1 2026; Starship reached orbit Sep 28 2026. Mach33 places scaled orbital-compute deployment in the early 2030s. Orbital compute in Oct 2026 is at kilowatt scale (general).
struct-gw-orbital-compute.pathway: P7 (not AI-math-driven; AI math second-order via P1 thermal and reliability design)
struct-gw-orbital-compute.why: Re-based on AI1 in dawn-dusk SSO (R9). 1 GW at AI1 density is about 6,700 satellites and 14,000 t, or 155-235 Starship flights at 60-90 t to SSO; the figure rests on the AI Compute Keystone's 1.5x SSO delivery placeholder (ODC_HEO_LEO_X) while the keystone's SSO re-base is open (wave 45 open item 5; TODO(source): the 16 Oct orbit ruling note). Fewer tonnes per GW than the earlier Starmind-class basis (16,000-18,000 t) but less payload per flight to SSO, so the flight count rises; the odds rise for a different reason. Mach33's own paths run well ahead of the tree: the AI Compute Keystone (v1.0, Aug 2026, model_series.csv) installs 1.5 GW in orbit in 2028 in its base and three other lenses and in 2029 in the cadence-bound lens, and reaches 437.9 GW by 2040; Launch Keystone v1.3's reference case books 38,600 t of SpaceX's own compute in 2030 and 71,500 t in 2031. Those are model paths, and this node is the odds that the milestone has happened. Chain (S2): AI1's first flight 2028 (struct-highflux-radiator-flight; SpaceX target Q4 2027, slipped per the tree's 1.5-3x calibration) -> paying operations 2029 (materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops) -> internal launch cost under ~$300/kg 2029 (physclock-cheap-mass-internal) and 100+ heavy flights a year 2030 (physclock-heavy-cadence-100) -> 155-235 SSO flights through 2030-31, about half of SpaceX's heavy flights, which matches the share v1.3 gives its own compute. Earliest 2031 in S2 (2030 in S3 and S4, where heavy cadence comes a year earlier). Odds (judgment): applying the tree's slip convention of one to two years to the keystone's cadence-bound 2029 crossing puts the 30% point in 2031, so S2 is Medium from 2031 (it was Low against the 16,000-18,000 t Starmind basis and without the keystone paths) and High from 2034 once SpaceX has had three years at 100+ heavy flights. S3 and S4 reach High in 2033 on a year's head start in cadence. S1 is Medium only in 2035 because a capability plateau weakens demand. Launch cadence sets the date; launch price does not move the cost crossover (in the AI Compute Keystone, x1.5 on launch price leaves the 2029 crossover in place, per the 26 Oct AI Compute review). AI math is second-order: AI radiator design saves ~350-1,400 t per GW at the old basis (~2-9% of launched mass), hotter qualified chips about as much again (struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification), and right-sized radiation mitigation ~5-20% compute per watt (assumption). Catalog family 107 (matrix multiplication exponent at most 9/4, Lean, T3) is a galactic algorithm and contributes nothing (P4 nil). Launch cadence, satellite and array fabrication, and chip supply bind.
struct-gw-orbital-compute.strongest_case_small: Thermal physics (T^4, junction-temperature limits) is unchanged, and the timing is set by Starship cadence and financing; AI mathematics could vanish from the chain without moving this node by more than months.
struct-gw-orbital-compute.signpost: AI1 production rate and dedicated SSO Starship flights per year; FCC authorization of a first AI1 tranche; SpaceX reporting deployed orbital compute in the hundreds of MW by 2030.
struct-gw-orbital-compute.calibration_note: A3: Follows struct-radiator-lightweight-production (now S3 2030). S3 2030 -> 2031; bands unchanged. (Note: 1 GW does not strictly need sub-2.5 kg/m2 radiators; the hard edge could be soft.) A4: Hard edge from struct-radiator-lightweight-production made soft. The why says sub-2.5 kg/m2 radiators save a few percent of launched mass (about 3-11 flights per GW), so 1 GW does not require them. Years stay >2031/2031/2031: launch cadence (100+ heavy flights a year, 2029 in S2), serial satellite production and capital bind, and S3's 1.3-1.5x physical multiplier does not fit 100-140 dedicated flights plus the satellite ramp into 2030. Bands Low/Medium/Medium kept.

verif-code-proof-agents.title: Agents that prove real flight code
verif-code-proof-agents.description: AI agents write contracts, loop invariants and proofs for production embedded code (C, Ada/SPARK, Rust) and discharge them in an existing checker (Frama-C, GNATprove, Verus, or Lean via extraction), at a marginal cost of compute hours instead of proof-engineer years.
verif-code-proof-agents.status_oct2026: Partly exists. Off-the-shelf LLMs produced verified code for 82% of Dafny, 44% of Verus and 27% of Lean specifications in the vericoding benchmark (Sep 2025). The best agent fully solved 27 of 43 repository-scale instances in Vero (Aug 2026), none of the hardest. AI coding agents wrote and verified a bare-metal Ada/SPARK security stack (classical and post-quantum crypto, TLS 1.3, IKEv2, X.509); GNATprove discharged 49,280 proof obligations at a claimed 20-40x lower supervision cost than hand verification, and the agents tried to bypass weak checks (Philipp, arXiv 2607.14340, Jul 2026 preprint). AdaCore released GNAT Foundry Intersection, an agent workflow gated by SPARK proof, requirements-based tests and MC/DC, described as a demonstration, not certification (Sep 14, 2026). OpenAI's pipeline formalized the main results of 162 papers in weeks (openai/math, Oct 6 2026; manuscripts dated Sep 10-Oct 6, formalization timing not separately reported; agent-written, review status unchecked, so T3 as evidence of the pipeline). No catalog family applies; the evidence is the pipeline itself.
verif-code-proof-agents.why: Formal methods in aerospace have been limited by proof labor, not tools: seL4 took about 25 person-years and roughly 27 lines of Isabelle per verified line of C. Proof writing is exactly what agents now do. The remaining gate is mature formal semantics for the target language: strong for SPARK and Frama-C C, weaker for C++ and for Rust in Lean. Under S2, with agent task horizons doubling every 6-9 months, repository-scale success moves from about 63% (Aug 2026) to routine during 2027. Under S1 public models get there by about 2028. 'Achieved' here means verifying a 10-50 KLOC real embedded codebase to functional-contract level with under 10% human proof effort.
verif-code-proof-agents.strongest_case_small: Benchmarks use clean specs and small repositories. Flight code is legacy C and C++ with hardware registers, interrupts, concurrency and undocumented assumptions, where proofs stall on modeling the environment rather than on proof search. A proof of an unreviewed spec adds little assurance.
verif-code-proof-agents.signpost: A tool vendor or agency (AdaCore, AbsInt, TrustInSoft, Galois, NASA, ESA) reports AI-generated SPARK or Frama-C proofs over more than 10 KLOC of real embedded code with human effort a small fraction of the seL4 ratio; Vero-class repository benchmarks pass 90%.

Auditor: 'in under four weeks' corrected (it describes manuscript dates). S1 a year behind each crossing (High 2030).

verif-code-proof-agents.gate_note: Formal semantics and proof labor bind; the agents' task horizon on repository-scale code (cognitive) is the runner-up.

verif-skolem-positivity.title: Skolem and Positivity problems for linear loops settled
verif-skolem-positivity.description: Decide whether a linear recurrence ever hits zero (Skolem) or always stays positive (Positivity), both open in general. They are the exact mathematical core of asking whether a discrete-time linear loop, such as a sampled control law or estimator update, ever crosses a threshold.
verif-skolem-positivity.status_oct2026: Open. Skolem is decidable only up to order 4, and Positivity up to order 5 (Ouaknine-Worrell 2014); extending Positivity to order 6 would require major breakthroughs in Diophantine approximation of transcendental numbers. Some results are conditional on number-theoretic conjectures (general). Not in the openai/math catalog.
verif-skolem-positivity.why: Either a decision procedure or an undecidability proof would fix the ceiling for exact, unbounded verification of linear loops with rational coefficients, and would feed invariant generators and termination provers. It sits at the intersection of logic and number theory, where the Sep-Oct 2026 releases show progress, but the order-6 barrier is a known one, unlike unforced Navier-Stokes, so the S2 band is one below that node (Low). Bands reflect the chance an AI system settles it by 2031, not that it changes flight practice.
verif-skolem-positivity.strongest_case_small: Flight verification never needs exact unbounded decidability. Engineers prove sufficient conditions (Lyapunov functions, linear matrix inequalities, bounded horizons, interval margins) that are already decidable or cheap, and flown code runs in floating point, not exact rationals. Expect a P3 ceiling result with near-nil effect on tools.
verif-skolem-positivity.signpost: A lab, Hexagon or arXiv claim with a Lean statement deciding Skolem at order 5 or above, or Positivity at order 6 or above; verification-tool papers citing it within a year.
verif-skolem-positivity.revision_note: B-math-frontier: [skeptic+auditor] Signpost fixed: Positivity is already decidable up to order 5 (Ouaknine-Worrell, SODA 2014), so it would have fired on a known result; order 6 needs breakthroughs in Diophantine approximation, a known barrier, so S2 band Medium -> Low (S3 stays Medium). Unsupported status sentence removed. [skeptic] pathway P3->P6 -> P3 (tool effect near nil). | E-math-frontier (2026-10-07): S1 >2031 -> 2033; band_2035 S2 Low -> Medium; S4 = S3. | R8 (2026-10-08): band set to Speculative where earliest year is after the checkpoint | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S3/S4 Medium moves 2028 -> 2030 (the order-6 barrier is known and may need Schanuel-type results); S2 Medium kept at 2033, when S2 cognition matches S3 in about 2030. Skeptic (transcendence barrier) vs advocate (logic and number theory show progress) resolved at those years; capped at Medium. Bands unchanged.

verif-game-solving-synthesis.title: Faster solvers for building correct-by-design controllers
verif-game-solving-synthesis.description: Family 104 claims quasipolynomial algorithms for mean-payoff, stochastic and parity games; its Lean part covers only a randomized algorithm for mean-payoff games. These games are the back end of reactive synthesis (building mode logic from temporal-logic specs) and of probabilistic model checking (fault management under random failures).
verif-game-solving-synthesis.status_oct2026: Family 104's Lean main result covers only a randomized quasipolynomial algorithm (success probability at least 7/8) for the zero-threshold winning set of finite mean-payoff games with signed binary weights, plus a counterexample to Truffet's elimination procedure (lean/docs/104.md); that part is T3, unchecked by outsiders. The stochastic-game and parity claims are manuscript-only (T1). Parity games have had quasipolynomial algorithms since 2017 (general). Practical solvers (strategy iteration, value iteration) already handle engineering-sized instances.
verif-game-solving-synthesis.premise_tier: T3 (randomized mean-payoff algorithm, Lean scope); T1 (stochastic games: conditional)
verif-game-solving-synthesis.why: Once independently checked (T4), the mean-payoff result resets the worst-case complexity map for quantitative synthesis; tool builders will cite it as a worst-case upper bound. The probabilistic model-checking implication rests on the stochastic-game part and is conditional (T1). Bands are one step below a checked result for that reason, in every scenario. The node is the result being established and known. Its effect on flight-verification practice is near nil: the 2017 quasipolynomial parity algorithms did not beat Zielonka-type solvers on benchmarks (van Dijk, TACAS 2018).
verif-game-solving-synthesis.strongest_case_small: Worst-case bounds do not govern practice. Real synthesis and model-checking problems are limited by state-space size and specification quality, and existing solvers rarely meet worst cases. No change to flight verification workflows is expected.
verif-game-solving-synthesis.signpost: An independent Comparator run on family 104 via Hexagon; any implementation that beats strategy iteration on standard probabilistic model-checking benchmarks.
verif-game-solving-synthesis.revision_note: B-math-frontier: [auditor] 104 statement gap (lean/docs/104.md, checked): Lean covers only a randomized quasipolynomial algorithm for mean-payoff games plus a Truffet counterexample; stochastic and parity claims are manuscript-only (T1). Bands High -> Medium in every scenario (the engineering link runs through stochastic games, conditional). [skeptic] pathway P3 -> P4 (an algorithm is an upper bound, not a ceiling); wording fixed. | E-math-frontier (2026-10-07): band_2035 = band_2031 (T1 rule); S4 = S3. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Checking family 104 takes about a year, so Medium 2028 in every scenario; T1 stochastic-game part keeps it below High. verif-spec-engineering.title: AI-drafted formal specifications
verif-spec-engineering.description: AI turns natural-language requirements, interface control documents and concepts of operations into formal, machine-checkable specifications (contracts, temporal logic, unit-typed interfaces). It checks them for consistency and realizability and flags hidden environmental assumptions for human sign-off.
verif-spec-engineering.status_oct2026: NASA's FRET turns structured English into temporal logic and, through Ogma and Copilot, into runtime monitors that flew in NASA's ICAROUS autonomy framework. Research pipelines (Forge, Jun 2026) close the loop from LLM-written code to Dafny, CSP and Isabelle checks. Spec writing remains scarce senior-engineer work, and no space program publicly uses AI-drafted formal specs for flight-critical functions.
verif-spec-engineering.why: Once proofs are cheap, specs become the bottleneck: a proof of the wrong property is worthless (tr-position-2). In all 9 software-related losses and near-losses in our failure table, the missing piece was an assumption, interface spec or process step, not proof capacity. AI cuts spec drafting and consistency checking several-fold (general). Each spec still needs a qualified engineer to accept that it says what the mission needs, so human review bandwidth binds. 'Achieved' means first use on a flight program for a safety-critical function; it does not imply the spec-review bandwidth that fleet-wide invariants (verif-constellation-verified-updates) or $5-20-per-line costs (verif-assurance-cost-collapse) assume, and those nodes carry that risk in their own bands.
verif-spec-engineering.strongest_case_small: AI drafts may encode the same wrong assumptions the team already holds and give them false authority by making them formal. For domain experts who are not fluent in temporal logic, reviewing a formal spec is not much faster than writing one.
verif-spec-engineering.signpost: NASA, ESA or a lander company publishes a case study of LLM-drafted FRET or contract specs accepted at a flight review; a certification-authority position paper on AI-authored low-level requirements.
verif-spec-engineering.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic: clarified that 'achieved' is first flight-program use, not review bandwidth at fleet scale. Auditor: 'losses' -> 'losses and near-losses'. Auditor's S1 High -> Medium rejected: the node is P1->P2 (P1 default High), and a single flight-program use by 2031 does not need certification or public models beyond the 2028 S1 release. Years and bands unchanged. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): lettered citation 'analyst position h' replaced with the KB position id tr-position-2. soft edge from frontier-applied-posing (B-math-frontier request 5). | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): no year or band change; note added. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Low 2027 (first use possible), Medium 2028, High 2029: first use on a flight program for a safety-critical function is an adoption step, not a capability step. S1 one year later (High 2030).

verif-spec-engineering.gate_note: Human spec review and program adoption bind; drafting specs that say what the mission needs (cognitive) is the runner-up.

verif-verified-gnc-numerics.title: Guidance code with proven floating-point math
verif-verified-gnc-numerics.description: Machine-checked bounds on round-off, overflow and conversion errors for guidance, navigation, control and estimation code, generated per module by agents. The tools are Astree, PRECiSA with Frama-C, or Lean FloatLib-class libraries. The result is that a proof about real-number math also holds for the code that flies.
verif-verified-gnc-numerics.status_oct2026: Solved in principle and expert-scarce. Astree proved absence of runtime errors in 132 KLOC of A340 primary flight-control code in 1 h 20 min (2003). NASA verified the floating-point C of the DAIDALUS detect-and-avoid well-clear module with PVS, PRECiSA and Frama-C, including round-off bounds and overflow freedom (2023). In Lean, FloatLib (Sep 2026) unifies IEEE binary and decimal formats, posits and P3109 with proofs; FloatSpec is a port of Flocq in progress.
verif-verified-gnc-numerics.why: Ariane 501 was lost to an unprotected 64-bit float to 16-bit integer conversion. Runtime-error analysis of that class is automatic today, and per-module round-off proofs in the DAIDALUS style become a compute job once agents write the annotations. The coverage gate is verified libraries for linear algebra, quaternion kinematics and filters with floating-point semantics.
verif-verified-gnc-numerics.strongest_case_small: Runtime-error freedom is already cheap with Astree-class tools, and numerical round-off rarely kills missions. The Ariane case needed the right input ranges, which is an assumption problem, not a proof problem.
verif-verified-gnc-numerics.signpost: A Lean or Coq library with a verified floating-point Kalman filter or quaternion propagator; NASA or ESA GNC teams publishing agent-generated round-off proofs on flight code.

verif-closed-loop-guarantees.title: Machine-checked stability for guidance and control
verif-closed-loop-guarantees.description: Proofs that a guidance, control and estimation loop stays inside a safe envelope, including actuator saturation, sampling, delay, sensor gating and mode switches. The proofs use barrier certificates, Lyapunov functions, reachability or differential dynamic logic, and are produced on request rather than by rare specialists.
verif-closed-loop-guarantees.status_oct2026: Tools exist: differential dynamic logic (KeYmaera X), sum-of-squares barrier certificates, reachability analyzers. They have been applied to aircraft collision avoidance (general). Building certificates for saturated, sampled, mode-switching loops is expert-scarce, and nonlinear hybrid verification at full-vehicle scale is partly open. Lean building blocks appeared in 2026: lyapunov-odes-lean (Zenodo, May 31 2026) and Doll and Shames' Lyapunov stability for hybrid systems plus the small-gain theorem in Lean (arXiv 2607.19727, Jul 2026). No catalog family applies (family 143, uniform limit-cycle bounds for Hilbert's sixteenth problem, Lean-formalized and unaudited, is theory-only context, not a premise).
verif-closed-loop-guarantees.why: This is the bespoke math, easier than the catalog's, that tl-position-4 says matters most: a stability or keep-out proof for one control law. Under S2, research-grade applied math is on tap from 2027, and existing provers (KeYmaera X differential dynamic logic, sum-of-squares barrier certificates) with agent-written proofs are a mature route that does not wait for Lean/Mathlib coverage of ODEs and hybrid systems. These certificates are over real numbers; the floating-point gap is closed separately by verif-verified-gnc-numerics or by runtime monitors, so neither the Lean library nor the floating-point node gates this one. 'Achieved' means a machine-checked stability or safety certificate for a flight-representative GNC loop (the flight control law with saturation, sampling delay and mode logic), published or delivered to a program; flight use is tracked in verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight and verif-rpo-assured-autonomy.
verif-closed-loop-guarantees.strongest_case_small: Most flown GNC is close to linear, with well-understood classical margins checked by Monte Carlo. Flight losses trace to sensor logic and assumptions more than to unstable control laws. Proofs over idealized dynamics may not survive unmodeled flexible modes, propellant slosh or plume effects.
verif-closed-loop-guarantees.signpost: An agent-produced, machine-checked barrier certificate for powered-descent or rendezvous guidance published with flight-like dynamics (saturation, delay, slosh).
verif-closed-loop-guarantees.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: All three lenses: family 143 removed from catalog_families (the node itself says it does not reach this workflow; it would draw a false 'family 143 unlocks GNC stability' edge); premise_tier -> n/a; 'achieved' no longer requires a flown loop (a tier-5 outcome). Skeptic + advocate: infra-mathlib-applied hard -> soft; advocate + auditor: verif-verified-gnc-numerics hard -> soft. Advocate: S2 2028 -> 2027 accepted, because the skeptic's reason to keep 2028 (the numerics edge) is gone and the KeYmaera X/SOS route is mature (mechanism in the verification domain's table; 2026 Lean Lyapunov work checked by the auditor). Downstream nodes do not move. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Low 2027, Medium 2028, High 2029: KeYmaera X and SOS routes are mature, but a certificate delivered for a flight-representative loop is likelier a year after the capability. S1 Medium 2031, High 2034.

verif-onboard-optimizer-certificates.title: Certified onboard trajectory optimizers
verif-onboard-optimizer-certificates.description: Embedded SOCP/QP solvers for powered-descent guidance, rendezvous MPC and collision avoidance with machine-checked proofs that, in the flight processor's floating-point arithmetic, they terminate within a fixed iteration budget and return an epsilon-feasible, epsilon-optimal solution or a certified infeasibility flag for every admissible state, paired with cheap runtime certificates (duality gaps) checked each control cycle. One reusable certified component for landers, docking systems and collision-avoidance planners.
verif-onboard-optimizer-certificates.status_oct2026: Onboard convex guidance (lossless convexification) has flight-test heritage on rocket test beds (general). Proofs that a specific solver implementation converges within a fixed iteration and timing budget are rare. Runtime duality-gap certificates are cheap but seldom used as safety evidence. Code-level formal verification of an interior-point algorithm for linear model predictive control has existed since 2018 (Davy, Feron, Garoche and Henrion, arXiv 1801.03833; Cohen's 2018 ENAC PhD continued the line) and was not adopted in flight, which suggests demand, not cognition, has bound.
verif-onboard-optimizer-certificates.why: Crewed landing and propellant transfer increasingly rely on onboard optimization. Certifying it needs both math (convergence and feasibility for every admissible state) and timing evidence on the flight processor. The math compresses under S2; timing characterization on radiation-tolerant processors and HIL qualification bind. Solver termination and epsilon-feasibility are properties of the convex program and the solver, not of closed-loop stability, and feasibility over the admissible set comes from astro-scp-guarantees; a generic SOCP or QP solver needs no astrodynamics library, so closed-loop guarantees and the formal astrodynamics library accelerate rather than gate this node.
verif-onboard-optimizer-certificates.strongest_case_small: Programs can avoid certifying the optimizer by wrapping it in runtime assurance with a simple backup guidance law, which is cheaper and already accepted practice.
verif-onboard-optimizer-certificates.signpost: A lander or HLS provider describing certified onboard optimization in an AIAA GNC paper or design review; verified convex-solver code with worst-case execution time bounds.
verif-onboard-optimizer-certificates.merge_note: A1: merged astro-verified-onboard-solver (same achievement: a proven onboard convex solver). verif had rated it 2031/2029/2028 Low/Medium/Medium with a qualification gate because it bundled timing evidence on radiation-tolerant processors and HIL; astro rated it 2030/2028/2027 Medium/High/High as a formalization milestone. Reconciled by scoping this node to the proofs plus runtime certificates (all hard prerequisites, including infra-verified-numerics and verif-verified-gnc-numerics, land by S2 2028), and leaving flight timing/HIL qualification to verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight and verif-hls-autonomy-certification. Astro's caution kept: a Jun 2026 audit found compilation-based metrics overstate numerical-analysis formalization quality (arXiv 2606.14000).
verif-onboard-optimizer-certificates.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic: verif-closed-loop-guarantees and astro-formal-astrodynamics-library moved from hard to soft (solver properties need neither); 2018 interior-point verification precedent added to status (checked: arXiv 1801.03833 is code-level IPM verification for linear MPC; the skeptic's 'SOCP with floating-point analysis' wording is not in the abstract, so it is not repeated). Years and bands unchanged (verified numerics still holds S2 2028). | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): band_2035 S1 Medium -> High. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Low 2028, Medium 2029, High 2030: the math is quick but certificates need timing evidence on the flight processor. S1 Medium 2031, High 2034 behind infra-verified-numerics. The why reads as if qualification binds; I kept formalization because the S2 year follows the verified-numerics chain.
