verif-nn-verification-scale.title: Verifying neural-network perception at flight scale
verif-nn-verification-scale.description: Proving robustness and correctness properties, over the operational domain, of neural networks used for terrain-relative navigation, hazard detection or pose estimation. This is genuinely open: exact verification is NP-hard, and 'correct perception' resists formal specification.
verif-nn-verification-scale.status_oct2026: VNN-COMP 2025 (8 teams, 16 regular and 9 extended benchmarks) shows steady progress on small and medium networks. Flight-scale vision networks and perception properties remain out of reach. SAE ARP6983 / EUROCAE ED-324 (joint G-34/WG-114; the first issue covers supervised offline machine learning; ED-324 publication scheduled Q4 2026; ARP6983's June 2026 target status unconfirmed as of Oct 2026) and EASA NPA 2025-07 base machine-learning assurance on data and process, not proof. No catalog family addresses it.
verif-nn-verification-scale.why: Exact verification of ReLU networks is NP-hard (general), and the property itself ('detects every hazardous crater') is defined by data, not by math. New relaxations and verification-friendly architectures from on-demand research math could move the frontier, but the gap in specification remains even in S3, which is why the band stays Low.
verif-nn-verification-scale.strongest_case_small: Space programs do not need to verify the network. They wrap it in runtime assurance or use it only for advisory functions, so this open problem may simply be routed around.
verif-nn-verification-scale.signpost: VNN-COMP results on networks at terrain-relative-navigation scale; ED-324/ARP6983 or EASA guidance granting credit for formal robustness proofs of neural networks.
verif-nn-verification-scale.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Auditor: ARP6983 June 2026 target marked unconfirmed (date has passed; only the ED-324 Q4 2026 schedule is confirmed). Years and bands unchanged. | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): S1 >2031 -> 2035 (S1 cognition reaches S2's 2030 level about 2035); band_2035 S1 Speculative -> Low, S2-S4 Low -> Medium. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Medium crossing S2 2034, S3-S4 2032: the cognitive gate is where S3's near-free research pays most, so S3 crosses two years ahead; S2 needs verification-friendly architectures and ED-324/ARP6983 domain specs to mature. Skeptic (NP-hardness and data-defined properties keep S2 Low to 2035) vs advocate (domain-limited specs make it tractable by 2032 in S2): S2 at 2034 keeps Medium by 2035 with little slack. S1 Low 2035, its earliest year.
verif-nn-verification-scale.note_2035: S1 gets the needed cognition only about 2035. By 2035 S2-S4 rise to Medium as verification-friendly networks and narrower operational-domain specs mature, while the spec gap keeps them below High; S4 equals S3 because robot fleets add demand for verified perception but no new cognition.
verif-nn-verification-scale.gate_note: Verification math for large networks (cognitive) binds; data-defined properties and operational-domain specs (data) are the runner-up.

verif-environment-assumption-models.title: Validated limits on sensor and terrain behavior
verif-environment-assumption-models.description: Formally stated, test-validated envelopes for what sensors and environments can do during critical phases: laser rangefinder and altimeter dropouts and reflectivity, IMU saturation durations, terrain discontinuities, lighting. Proofs can assume them and simulators can sample them.
verif-environment-assumption-models.status_oct2026: Ad hoc. Recent lunar losses trace to sensor and environment surprises: Hakuto-R M1's 3 km crater rim (2023), Resilience's late rangefinder readings (2025), Athena's altimeter interference, low-sun lighting and crater appearance mismatch (Mar 2025), and earlier Schiaparelli's 1 s IMU saturation (2016). LRO maps and flight telemetry exist but are not packaged as formal assumptions.
verif-environment-assumption-models.why: Proofs and tests are conditional on environment assumptions. AI can quickly fuse orbital maps, test data and telemetry into formal envelopes, but the envelopes are only as good as sensor characterization tests and the few landings that produce truth data. S3's autonomous labs speed sensor testing on the ground, not the supply of lunar truth data, which is why even S3 stays Medium. The achievement is packaging test and telemetry data into validated envelopes that change modeling practice (model confidence, P5), not new theory becoming tools, and Medium is the P5 default. It now gates verif-mission-loss-rate and accelerates assumption falsification and lander flight, so the interactive tree shows the assumption gate that the failure table says binds; AI-run test stands and autonomous labs accelerate the ground characterization.
verif-environment-assumption-models.strongest_case_small: Each new site, sensor and lighting condition differs, so envelopes generalize poorly and teams will still discover new failure physics in flight.
verif-environment-assumption-models.signpost: A shared, formally stated lunar-descent sensor and terrain envelope dataset (for example from NASA CLPS or ESA) adopted by two or more lander teams.
verif-environment-assumption-models.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Auditor: pathway P1->P6 -> P1->P5. Skeptic: orphan fixed (hard edge to verif-mission-loss-rate; soft edges to verif-assumption-falsification and verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight). Advocate: soft edges from physclock-ai-run-test-stands and cap-autonomous-labs accepted; advocate's S3 band Medium -> High rejected, because lunar truth data and shared adoption by two lander teams do not speed up with cognition (the node's own reasoning, unchanged by the advocate's evidence). verif-assumption-falsification.title: AI red-teaming of flight assumptions
verif-assumption-falsification.description: Agents search physics-based simulations and data for scenarios that break the assumptions under which flight software was proven or tested: terrain steps, saturation longer than designed, sensor delays, reboot timing, unit mismatches. Each finding becomes a test or a strengthened spec.
verif-assumption-falsification.status_oct2026: Monte Carlo dispersion campaigns and temporal-logic falsification tools exist (general). Hakuto-R M1's late landing-site change was not simulated against crater-rim terrain, and Schiaparelli's fault logic did not cover an IMU saturation lasting about 1 s.
verif-assumption-falsification.why: Counterexamples act fastest (fc-position-1): a found scenario changes the design within weeks. Agents can rerun targeted searches over terrain, sensor timing and fault combinations every time the design or landing site changes, which is exactly where Hakuto-R M1, Schiaparelli and Ariane 501 escaped. The gate is the fidelity of simulators and sensor models. Simulation-based falsification and Monte Carlo search run against existing requirements and need public research-grade models (P1), not AI-drafted specs adopted on a flight program, so spec engineering accelerates rather than gates it; validated environment envelopes widen what the simulator can represent.
verif-assumption-falsification.strongest_case_small: AI can only find failures the simulator can represent; Athena's and Resilience's sensor physics would not have appeared in typical simulations. Mature teams already run large dispersion campaigns.
verif-assumption-falsification.signpost: A lander team attributing a design change to AI-found falsifying scenarios; NASA CLPS asking for assumption-falsification reports at mission readiness reviews.
verif-assumption-falsification.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Auditor: hard edge from verif-spec-engineering made soft (falsification runs against existing requirements); hard edge from cap-research-math-public added so the P1 node keeps a capability gate (2028/2027/2027, equal to this node's years). Skeptic: soft edge from verif-environment-assumption-models. Years and bands unchanged. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): lettered citation 'analyst position c' replaced with the KB position id fc-position-1. | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): no year or band change; note added. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Medium 2027 (falsification runs on existing requirements with public models), High 2028. S1 a year later.
verif-assumption-falsification.note_2035: High everywhere before 2031, and simulator fidelity stays the limit through 2035. S4 equals S3 because the search is computational.
verif-assumption-falsification.gate_note: Simulator and sensor-model fidelity (data) binds; validation tests of those simulators (experiment) are the runner-up.

verif-fdir-model-checking.title: Exhaustive checks of fault logic and configuration
verif-fdir-model-checking.description: Agents build formal models of fault detection, isolation and recovery logic, mode machines, reboot and timing behavior, command sequences and parameter tables from code and interface documents. They then model-check them exhaustively, including emergency in-flight patches.
verif-fdir-model-checking.status_oct2026: Model checkers (SPIN, NuSMV, Kind 2) are mature; building faithful models is the cost. Failures and near-failures in this class: Starliner OFT (mission timer 11 h off, service-module valve-mapping error, 2019), Beresheet (a command to restart one IMU blocked the other IMU's data and set off a chain that shut down the main engine, 2019), Hitomi (wrongly updated thruster parameter, 2016), IM-1 (rangefinder safety switch left enabled; the in-flight patch missed a data-valid flag, per IM's CTO via SpacePolicyOnline, 2024).
verif-fdir-model-checking.why: Four of the nine software-related losses and near-losses in our failure table sit in this class. Agents can extract models from code and interface documents and check every fault combination and command sequence; this needs model extraction and model checking, not deductive code proofs, so verif-code-proof-agents accelerates rather than gates it. Agents can also check emergency patches within hours; IM-1's patch was written and uploaded mid-mission. The binding input is accurate hardware behavior (bus blocking, timer sources), which needs characterization data. Used as an engineering tool without certification credit, it travels P1 into P2, which is why S1 can be High.
verif-fdir-model-checking.strongest_case_small: Starliner's errors were also catchable by the end-to-end integrated test the program did not run (general). The root problem was process discipline, which cheap tools do not guarantee.
verif-fdir-model-checking.signpost: A CLPS or commercial-crew post-flight review crediting model checking with catching a fault-logic error before flight; NASA or ESA tools that automatically extract FDIR models from flight code.
verif-fdir-model-checking.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Auditor: 'losses' -> 'losses and near-losses'; pathway P2 -> P1->P2 (tool use without certification, which justifies S1 High); IM-1 data-valid flag re-cited to SpacePolicyOnline; Beresheet 'reboot loop' and Starliner 'skipped end-to-end test' were not in the cited articles, so the first is softened and the second marked general. Skeptic: verif-code-proof-agents moved from hard to soft (model extraction plus model checking needs no deductive code proofs). Years and bands unchanged. | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): no year or band change; note added. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Low 2027, Medium 2028, High 2029, following its hard prerequisite verif-spec-engineering. S1 one year later.
verif-fdir-model-checking.note_2035: High everywhere before 2031, and hardware characterization data stays the limit through 2035. S4 equals S3 because model checking is computational.
verif-fdir-model-checking.gate_note: Hardware-behavior characterization data binds; model extraction from code and interface documents (formalization) is the runner-up.

verif-runtime-assurance.title: Proven safety wrappers for unverifiable autonomy
verif-runtime-assurance.description: Instead of verifying a neural or learned controller, verify a small monitor, a recoverable-set (barrier) condition and a simple backup controller, and switch to the backup before safety is lost (the Simplex architecture). Agents make the proofs of the wrapper and the switching logic cheap.
verif-runtime-assurance.status_oct2026: ASTM F3269 and NASA guidance define runtime assurance. Monitors generated by FRET and Copilot flew in NASA's ICAROUS, and R2U2 targets rovers and small satellites. Spacecraft use is mostly research. The expensive parts are proving the recoverable set and the switching logic.
verif-runtime-assurance.why: Neural and learned components (hazard detection, terrain-relative navigation) cannot be verified directly (see verif-nn-verification-scale), so assurance moves to a small, provable monitor and a simple backup. Agents make the barrier-certificate and switching proofs cheap. The binding gate is showing, on hardware-in-the-loop rigs and in flight, that the backup really recovers. The band scores agent-proven Simplex wrappers in use on uncrewed programs, which need no certifier, so the regulator Medium cap does not apply; credit as a certification path (the signpost's second half) would be capped at Medium and is not required here.
verif-runtime-assurance.strongest_case_small: Conservative wrappers trigger too often and erode the performance that justified the learned component, and a proven wrapper built on a wrong recoverable-set model is still unsafe.
verif-runtime-assurance.signpost: A lunar lander or rendezvous mission flying a learned component inside a proven Simplex wrapper; runtime assurance referenced in ED-324/ARP6983 or NASA guidance as a certification path.
verif-runtime-assurance.revision_note: F2 audit (2026-10-07): regulator-cap check: binding gate 'qualification' with High bands; the why now says why the Medium cap does not apply. | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): band_2035 S1 Medium -> High. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | E-verified-autonomy resolver (2026-10-07): soft edge to robo-requal-standard added (advocate): a model update to a learned robot could otherwise count as a process change, and a proven guard on force, path and sequence limits is evidence that the process stays inside its qualified window. Years and bands unchanged. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Low 2028, Medium 2029, High 2030: proofs are cheap from 2027-28; the rig and flight evidence takes one to two years. No regulator cap applies (uncrewed use). S1 Medium 2031, High 2034.

verif-verified-onboard-stack.title: Formally verified onboard software stack
verif-verified-onboard-stack.description: Formally verified onboard software components fly on ordinary (non-research) missions: an seL4-class separation kernel or hypervisor, a telecommand parser, or software-update authentication; the first operational flight of any one of them counts. Spatial isolation is proven. Timing isolation on multicore processors is measured, not proven, so flight software and onboard AI payloads sharing one multicore processor also needs accepted interference evidence (AC 20-193-style analysis plus measurement).
verif-verified-onboard-stack.status_oct2026: seL4: 8,700 lines of C, 200,000 lines of Isabelle proof, about 25 person-years (estimated under 10 if redone), with 160 bugs found (144 during C verification). ECSS-E-ST-40C Rev.1 and ECSS-Q-ST-80C Rev.2 (Apr 2025) added explicit security requirements. Verified kernels remain niche in space. seL4 has been open source since 2014 and flew on the UNSW-EC0 CubeSat (QB50, 2017, general). MIT Lincoln Laboratory's port of NASA's core Flight System to seL4 took more than a year, mostly building OS services beyond the kernel rather than proofs (NDSS SpaceSec paper).
verif-verified-onboard-stack.why: Kernel proof cost is sunk: seL4 is open source and has flown. The binding costs are OS services, platform ports and drivers for radiation-tolerant processors, qualification, and multicore timing interference on HPSC-class processors, which is measured, not proven. Agent proofs mainly cut the cost of mission-specific telecommand parsers, update authentication and re-verification on new platforms: at seL4's ratio a verified 10 KLOC stack costs roughly $2-5M of proof labor (seL4: about 25 person-years including design and implementation, under 10 if redone), which becomes a compute bill plus spec review. Parsers and update authentication can be uploaded to buses already in orbit; separation kernels need a new bus. Chain (S2): proof agents 2027 -> verified parser and update-authentication stack 2028 -> integration or upload and qualification 12-18 months -> operational flight 2029 (A3 lag ladder). S3 equals S2 through 2028, so S3 is 2029. S2 is Medium, like every comparable tier-5 'flies' node, because adoption and qualification, not proof labor, have kept verified kernels niche.
verif-verified-onboard-stack.strongest_case_small: Isolation proofs assume correct hardware. Multicore timing interference, radiation upsets and processor errata are measured, not proven, and those qualification campaigns stay physical. seL4 is already the target of defense air programs (DARPA PROVERS/INSPECTA, Collins), yet it is niche in space: platform support on radiation-tolerant processors and qualification, not proof labor, bind.
verif-verified-onboard-stack.signpost: A constellation or lander operator announcing a verified kernel or hypervisor in flight; ESA or a defense constellation program requiring formally verified telecommand parsing.
verif-verified-onboard-stack.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder and cross-domain parity. Read as flown on ordinary missions (tier 5); its only prerequisite verif-code-proof-agents is 2027 in S2/S3, so a smallsat-class flight is 2028-29 at the earliest, and every comparable "proof-carrying flight software flies" node (verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight, astro-landing-guidance-proven-flight, comms-pq-ttc-flight-demo, auton-verified-autonomy-lunar-flight) is S2 2029. Chain (S2): proof agents 2027 -> verified kernel and command stack 2028 -> integration 12-18 months -> flight 2029. S1 2029 -> 2030, S2 2028 -> 2029, S3 2027 -> 2028.
verif-verified-onboard-stack.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic + auditor: S2 band High -> Medium and S3 2028 -> 2029 (kernel proofs are sunk and free; OS services, ports and qualification bind; S3 equals S2 until 2028); auditor: S1 Medium -> Low; skeptic: '$5M' -> '$2-5M'. Advocate's S2 2029 -> 2028 rejected (two lenses opposite; A3 lag ladder), but its scope point is adopted: the first operational flight of any one component counts, and parsers or update authentication can be uploaded to existing buses. Skeptic's proposed new node verif-multicore-timing-evidence not added: it is not necessary for this node as scoped, A1 already left timing and HIL evidence to the flight nodes, and its 2026 flight-qualification evidence could not be checked (source returned 403); the gate is stated in the description and why instead. | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): band_2035 S1 Low -> Medium, S2 Medium -> High. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Low 2029, Medium 2030, High 2032: a first operational parser or update-authentication upload is credible in 2029 but needs a year to be likelier than 30%; High once several missions use one. S3 High 2031 keeps its High-by-2031 band. S1 Medium 2033.

verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight.title: Lander flies proof-checked descent guidance and fault logic
verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight.description: A lunar lander flies terminal-descent GNC whose key properties are machine-checked, not only Monte Carlo-tested: altitude plausibility, measurement-rejection gates, engine-cutoff and reboot logic and the guidance law, plus, if the guidance uses an onboard optimizer, its convergence, feasibility and solver numerics. Its assumptions are red-teamed against terrain and sensor models.
verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight.status_oct2026: Commercial and agency landers 2016-2025: Schiaparelli (IMU-saturation logic), Beresheet (a command to restart one IMU set off a chain that shut down the main engine), Hakuto-R M1 (filter rejected valid altimetry after a crater rim), IM-1 (configuration and patch flag), Peregrine (helium valve), Resilience (rangefinder), Athena (altimeter, lighting, tipped over). No lander has publicly flown formally verified descent logic (general). Agency losses with logic or GNC causes also belong in this record: Chandrayaan-2's Vikram (2019, deviation during the braking phase) and Luna-25 (Aug 2023, engine failed to cut off on time after a control-unit fault) (general). Successes in the same period include Chandrayaan-3 (2023), SLIM (2024, landed on its nose) and Blue Ghost M1 (Mar 2025) (general).
verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight.why: New-entrant landers face no certifying regulator for mission software and have repeatedly lost missions to logic errors (Beresheet, Hakuto-R M1), so the incentive is strong. Chain (S2): research-grade applied math public 2027 -> verified numerics and fault-logic checks 2027-28 -> GNC toolchain adopted 2028 -> software freeze 12-18 months before flight -> first flight 2029-30 on a CLPS-class lander. Launch slots are not scarce (up to 30 CLPS landings planned from 2027); the development cycle, the freeze and one team's adoption decision bind, not cognition. S3 equals S2 through 2028, so a flown article cannot beat S2's 2029 in S3. Many CLPS-class landers fly closed-form or Apollo-derived guidance with no onboard solver, so optimizer certificates and SCP guarantees accelerate rather than gate this node. Bands: S2 Medium, because several landers fly each year from 2029 but a team must adopt and say so; S3 High, because cognitive work is near-free from 2029 and two flight years remain. No regulator is involved for commercial lunar landers, so there is no Medium cap. Both bands sit above the P7 default (Speculative) because the flown change is software on landers that fly anyway.
verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight.strongest_case_small: Half of recent lander losses were hardware or sensor physics (Peregrine's valve, Resilience's rangefinder, Athena's altimeter and lighting), which proofs do not touch. Teams may also adopt quietly and never disclose.
verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight.signpost: A CLPS or private lander team publicly stating formal verification of descent GNC and fault management in a readiness review or press kit. Precursor (does not count, since it has no launch gate): a terrestrial vertical-landing testbed flying the same proof-checked logic.

No regulator is involved for commercial lunar landers, so no Medium cap.

verif-rpo-assured-autonomy.title: Proof-checked autonomous docking, servicing and refueling
verif-rpo-assured-autonomy.description: Rendezvous, proximity operations, docking, servicing or debris capture, and ship-to-ship propellant transfer flown with machine-checked passive safety (collision-free under failures), keep-out zones, abort reachability and capture logic, plus runtime assurance on the guidance, used as primary safety evidence.
verif-rpo-assured-autonomy.status_oct2026: Starship reached orbit on Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026) and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Ship-to-ship propellant transfer has not yet been demonstrated: SpaceX's leaked Nov 2025 HLS schedule targeted June 2026, which slipped, and NASA Administrator Isaacman expected the demonstration in very early 2027, maybe at the end of 2026 (The Space Review, Sep 28 2026); a secondary listing giving Q4 2026 is unconfirmed. Artemis III was reprofiled to a crewed low-Earth-orbit rendezvous and docking test with HLS pathfinders from both SpaceX and Blue Origin (readiness no earlier than mid-2027). A landing needs about 15 tanker flights (Spaceflight Now, Jul 2026).
verif-rpo-assured-autonomy.why: Each lunar landing chains many autonomous rendezvous and transfers. Proven passive safety and abort logic lower the risk per operation and the test burden per software change. But confidence is gated by flight demonstrations, not by proof capacity, and launch cadence does not compress with cognition. Chain (S2): verif-closed-loop-guarantees 2027; astro-hybrid-rpo-verification, verif-runtime-assurance and astro-certified-gnc-toolchain 2028 -> proofs added as late verification evidence to an already-contracted servicing or inspection mission (contract to launch 2-4 years; software freeze 12-18 months) or to Starship transfer-flight software, which changes between flights -> first flight using them as primary safety evidence, accepted in an operator or NASA safety review, 2029-30. S3: identical through 2028 -> 2029. S1: prerequisites 2030 -> 2031 at the earliest. Starship transfer flights in 2027 fly baselines set before the toolchain exists. Band: S2 and S3 Medium, above the P7 default (Speculative), because the flown change is software and safety evidence on missions that fly anyway; Medium is also the cap when acceptance runs through a NASA safety review. S1 Low. Bands are judgments.
verif-rpo-assured-autonomy.strongest_case_small: SpaceX builds confidence through flight count; formal proofs may stay internal and invisible. Docking risk is dominated by hardware: mechanisms and cryogenic-transfer physics.
verif-rpo-assured-autonomy.signpost: Artemis III (late 2027) safety documentation citing formal verification of rendezvous abort logic; the first successful ship-to-ship propellant transfer.
verif-rpo-assured-autonomy.merge_note: A1: merged astro-verified-rpo-servicing (same achievement for a different customer: servicing/inspection/debris capture vs Starship/HLS transfer; astro >2031/2030/2029, verif 2031/2029/2029, both Low/Medium/Medium). Kept the verif id and its years for the first-of-kind flight of either type. Added astro's prerequisites (astro-hybrid-rpo-verification, astro-certified-gnc-toolchain) and sourcing: commercial servicing demos and ESA CREAM are under way, none uses formal proofs as primary safety evidence; missions take 2-4 years from contract to launch. Confidence is gated by flight demonstrations and launch cadence, not proof capacity.

verif-constellation-verified-updates.title: Proof-checked software updates across constellations
verif-constellation-verified-updates.description: Each over-the-air update to thousands of satellites is gated by automatic re-proof of key invariants: collision-avoidance decision logic, safe-mode entry, deorbit command and decision logic, command authentication. Proofs re-run in hours, enabling weekly verified releases. A proof covers the command and logic path, not physical deorbit capability such as propulsion health.
verif-constellation-verified-updates.status_oct2026: Starlink satellites made 207,152 avoidance maneuvers from Dec 2025 to May 2026 (more than 355,000 a year); they maneuver autonomously (general; the cited report gives counts, not where decisions are made). Update practices are proprietary, and the FCC requires maneuver reports, not software assurance.
verif-constellation-verified-updates.why: At this volume of onboard decisions, a logic regression in collision-avoidance or safe-mode code is a fleet-wide risk. Once the specs exist, re-proving a fixed set of invariants on every update is a compute job, with no regulator in the loop. The largest operator merged with a frontier AI lab (SpaceX acquired xAI, Feb 2026), so model access, ITAR handling and the update pipeline sit inside one firm, the vertical-integration path the capability domain names as the shortest from AI math to flown hardware. This node is a fleet-wide, strictly stronger instance of astro-proof-backed-flight-software-ops, so it is dated and banded no earlier or higher than that node. Chain (S2): proof agents, spec drafting and FDIR model checking 2027 -> operator writes reviewed invariant specs and proof-gated release pipeline 2028 -> first publicly disclosed fleet-wide proof-gated release 2029. Every invariant needs a reviewed spec, which is the bandwidth this branch says binds, and operators disclose little, so S2 is Medium. S3 equals S2 through 2028; it is High only because cognitive work is near-free from 2029.
verif-constellation-verified-updates.strongest_case_small: Operators already manage risk with staged rollouts, telemetry and fast rollback, which may be cheaper than proofs for non-catastrophic functions, and they disclose little.
verif-constellation-verified-updates.signpost: An operator (SpaceX, Amazon Kuiper, defense constellation contractors) or an FCC filing referring to formally verified collision-avoidance or deorbit logic.

verif-hls-autonomy-certification.title: Crewed lander autonomy certified with AI proofs
verif-hls-autonomy-certification.description: NASA human-rating (NPR 8705.2C with NPR 7150.2 Class A software), FAA commercial human-spaceflight rules or ECSS accept AI-produced machine-checked proofs as part of the certification evidence for crew-critical GNC autonomy (landing guidance, docking, abort and fault management). The likeliest first case is a block upgrade for a crewed lunar lander.
verif-hls-autonomy-certification.status_oct2026: The first crewed landing moved to Artemis IV in 2028 (a Nov 2025 leaked SpaceX HLS schedule reported by Politico Pro gave a crewed landing in Sep 2028, an uncrewed landing in Jun 2027 and a propellant-transfer demonstration in Jun 2026, which has since slipped; 33FG news). NPR 8705.2C requires single-failure tolerance to catastrophic events, crew override of automation, and autonomous capability for functions whose loss would be catastrophic. No human-rated system has used AI-written proofs as evidence.
verif-hls-autonomy-certification.why: The 2028 landing's software baseline will largely be set before public research-grade verification arrives, so AI proofs enter through block upgrades for 2029-31 landings. NASA's technical authority must accept the evidence, so the band is capped at Medium. Crewed acceptance needs the general regulator credit (infra-tool-qualification, Medium in S2 and S3) plus a human-rating step of its own, so it sits one band below that node: Low in S2 and S3.
verif-hls-autonomy-certification.strongest_case_small: Human rating relies on testing, redundancy and crew override, and proofs add to that evidence rather than replace it. After Starliner, NASA's risk posture favors more testing, not less.
verif-hls-autonomy-certification.signpost: NASA HLS or commercial-crew certification documents referencing formal proofs; NASA standards or software-engineering handbook guidance on AI-generated verification evidence.
verif-hls-autonomy-certification.calibration_note: A3: Cross-domain consistency: this is the HLS instance of astro-human-rated-proof-credit (AI proofs accepted for crewed GNC), so it cannot be earlier or likelier than that general node, and crewed acceptance should lag the first uncrewed certification credit (S2 2030, S3 2029). Chain (S2): checker-route credit 2030 -> NASA technical authority accepts proofs for an HLS block upgrade 2031 at the earliest. S2 2030 -> 2031, S3 2029 -> 2030; bands Low/Medium/Medium -> Speculative/Low/Low (regulatory, crewed). A4: Resolved the A1/A3 disagreement on S3 (A1 merge patch Medium; A3 Low). Set to Low. The node is conjunctive: infra-tool-qualification (S3 Medium) plus a crewed human-rating step, under a post-Starliner posture that favours more testing. A dependent of a Medium regulatory node with a further uncertain regulatory step belongs below Medium. This also matches the merged astro node's original Speculative/Low/Low. Final: >2031/2031/2030, Speculative/Low/Low.

verif-afss-part450.title: Proof-backed autonomous flight termination under FAA rules
verif-afss-part450.description: Autonomous flight safety system logic and other Part 450 computing-system safety items are licensed with formal proofs as an accepted means of compliance alongside RCC-319 testing.
verif-afss-part450.status_oct2026: Section 450.141 requires operators to identify computing-system safety items, set safety requirements by criticality and use a development process suited to that criticality. AC 450.141-1A, which includes an RCC-319 appendix on mission data loads, is an accepted means of compliance. There is no explicit credit for formal proofs, but the performance-based rule allows alternative means. Under 14 CFR 450.35(a), a means of compliance must be accepted before application acceptance for five items, including the highly reliable flight safety system (450.145(b)); computing-system safety items (450.141) are not among them. RCC 319 editions appeared in 2014, 2019 and 2025.
verif-afss-part450.why: Flight-termination logic is small, critical and well specified, which makes it the ideal first proof target in launch. Part 450 is performance-based and outside the DO-330 tool-qualification regime, so FAA AST acceptance is its own step rather than a consequence of DO-178C or NASA credit; infra-tool-qualification now accelerates rather than gates this node. For computing-system safety items an operator can include checker-verified proofs in its development process now; for the flight safety system itself the FAA must accept a proof-backed means of compliance under 450.35. Chain (S2): proof agents and FDIR model checking 2027 -> an operator includes proofs for computing-system safety items 2028-29 -> FAA accepts a proof-backed flight-safety-system means of compliance 2030. S2 is Low, not Medium: autonomous flight safety systems are already accepted through RCC-319 testing, applicants gain no license time from proofs (see strongest case), and FAA AST is a different office from the aircraft certification office that holds the DO-330 precedent. Regulator acceptance caps every scenario at Medium.
verif-afss-part450.strongest_case_small: License timelines are driven by environmental review, mishap investigations and public-safety analysis, not by software evidence (general). Flight-termination software is already heavily tested, so proofs will not speed licenses or raise launch cadence.
verif-afss-part450.signpost: A license record or FAA-accepted means of compliance citing formal verification of computing-system safety items or flight-safety-system logic. (An RCC-319 revision recognizing formal analysis is unlikely before 2031 on the 2014/2019/2025 cycle.)
verif-afss-part450.calibration_note: A1: its hard prerequisite verif-checker-not-generator was merged into infra-tool-qualification, which keeps the scenario premise for regulator credit for AI proofs (>2031/2030/2029); FAA Part 450 acceptance of proof-backed termination cannot precede that credit. Superseded by B-verified-autonomy: the hard edge from infra-tool-qualification is now soft (Part 450 sits outside DO-330), while years stay at >2031/2030/2029 on FAA AST's own acceptance chain.

verif-assurance-cost-collapse.title: Verified flight code 15-120x cheaper per line
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.description: The cost per functionally verified line (seL4-class full functional proof) falls from about $300-600 to roughly $5-20 under S2, a 15-120x fall (central about 35-40x), because spec review dominates what remains and compute costs cents per line. Turnaround to re-verify a small change drops from weeks to days. Program-level savings, which physical integration testing caps at about 2x, are tracked in astro-gnc-assurance-cost.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.status_oct2026: Baseline: DO-178 certification runs about $25-100 per line (Level A at the top of the range); verification can reach 80% of a DO-178B Level A project, and effective productivity is under 10 lines per person-day (Coverity/Black Duck whitepaper). seL4-class full functional proof costs roughly $300-600 per line (general, derived from about 25 person-years, including design and implementation, for 8.7 KLOC). Early evidence on unit cost: AI agents wrote an Ada/SPARK security stack whose 49,280 proof obligations GNATprove discharged at a claimed 20-40x lower supervision cost than hand verification (arXiv 2607.14340, Jul 2026 preprint; security software, not a flight program).
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.why: Per-line cost model (general, our assumptions; verification-domain cost table, values 'by 2029'): proof labor, the dominant cost of seL4-class verification, becomes agent compute, and the residual is human spec review and accountability. Under S1 the per-line cost falls to about $50-150 (2-12x); under S3 to about $1-5. Chain (S2): proof agents, spec drafting and FDIR model checking 2027 -> adoption on uncrewed programs that need no certification credit 2028 -> vendor or program case studies showing more than 50% fewer verification hours 2028-29. The per-line effect is measured on code, not on certified programs, so it needs no regulator; S2 returns to High now that the program-level claim, which waited on certification credit (A3), has moved to astro-gnc-assurance-cost. S3 equals S2 through 2028, so S3 is 2028, not 2027. The larger effect is assurance level per dollar and change turnaround.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.strongest_case_small: Software is a modest share of mission cost and schedule. HIL rigs, environmental testing and integration remain physical and set program pace.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.signpost: Program cost reports or vendor case studies showing more than 50% reduction in verification hours on a safety-critical flight program.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.calibration_note: A3: Tier-7 rule: the 30-100x cost of a verified line follows directly from S2, but the programme-level "about 2.4x cheaper" claim needs programmes to adopt and finish, and any certified programme waits for first certification credit (S2 2030). S2 High -> Medium; S3 High kept.

verif-assurance-cost-collapse.note_2035: By 2035 S1's per-line cost also falls 15x or more, so S1 reaches High. S4 equals S3 because the remaining cost is proof compute plus human spec review.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.gate_note: Adoption on uncrewed programs binds; the residual human spec review (cognitive) is the runner-up.

verif-new-entrant-advantage.title: Assurance stops being a moat for primes
verif-new-entrant-advantage.description: Small teams (lander and constellation startups) reach assurance levels that once required large verification departments, on uncrewed commercial and government work that needs no certification credit. Primes' advantage shifts from process capacity to certification relationships, which still matter for crewed and certified work, while qualified-checker vendors and AI-model providers capture new value.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.status_oct2026: Primes hold certification know-how and large V&V departments. New entrants run small teams and account for most recent software-caused lander losses and near-losses (Beresheet and Hakuto-R M1 lost; IM-1 landed but tipped over after a configuration and patch error).
verif-new-entrant-advantage.why: Uncrewed commercial missions have no certifying regulator for mission software, so new entrants can adopt as soon as the tools work, while primes on cost-plus contracts have weaker incentives to cut verification hours. Value concentrates where trust is scarce: in the small set of qualified checkers (AdaCore, AbsInt, TrustInSoft and similar) and in access to frontier models. Chain (S2): per-line cost collapse 2028 -> new entrants bid formal assurance as a discriminator 2028-29 -> a NASA, ESA or defense award citing it 2030; procurement runs 1-2 years from RFP to award, and politics and appropriations do not compress. Certification credit accelerates the effect on certified work but does not gate it.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.strongest_case_small: Primes adopt the same tools quickly (Airbus led formal methods in avionics) and keep the regulator relationships. Value may accrue to AI labs and checker vendors rather than to either group of space companies.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.signpost: A new entrant winning a NASA, ESA or defense contract with formal assurance as a cited discriminator; a prime reorganizing its V&V department around spec engineering.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.calibration_note: A1: its hard prerequisite verif-checker-not-generator was merged into infra-tool-qualification (>2031/2030/2029, the scenario premise for regulator credit), so the moat cannot fall before certification credit for AI proofs exists. Superseded by B-verified-autonomy: the hard edge from infra-tool-qualification is now soft, because the node is rescoped to work that needs no certification credit; years kept on a procurement-lag chain.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic (alternative) + advocate: hard edge from infra-tool-qualification made soft and scope limited to work that needs no certification credit, since the node's own why says uncrewed work has no certifying regulator. Years and bands kept: skeptic's S2 2031/S3 2030/S2 Low depended on the zero lag after credit, which no longer applies, and advocate's S2 2029/S3 2028 ignores the 1-2-year procurement lag (politics 1.0x). Auditor: IM-1 is a near-loss, not a loss. | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): S1 >2031 -> 2032 (cost collapse S1 2030 plus 1-2 years from RFP to award); band_2035 S1 Low -> Medium, S2-S4 Medium -> High. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | R8 (2026-10-08): band set to Speculative where earliest year is after the checkpoint | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Medium 2031, a year after the first credible award; High 2034 after several procurement cycles; S3 a year earlier. S1 Medium 2034.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.note_2035: S1 follows its 2030 cost collapse by two procurement years, so 2032. By 2035 S2-S4 are High, and S4 equals S3 because procurement cycles are institutional.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.gate_note: Procurement adoption binds; RFP-to-award cycles and appropriations (capital) are the runner-up.

verif-mission-loss-rate.title: Fewer missions lost to software logic (hard to see by 2031)
verif-mission-loss-rate.description: The share of mission losses caused by software logic, configuration and fault-management errors falls measurably.
verif-mission-loss-rate.status_oct2026: Of the 12 notable losses and near-losses in our failure table (1996-2025), 9 were primarily or partly software, logic or configuration errors. Of the six commercial lunar missions in the table since 2019, three losses (Peregrine, Resilience, Athena) were primarily hardware or sensor physics. The table lists failures only. Successes in the same period include Chandrayaan-3 (2023), SLIM (2024, landed on its nose) and Blue Ghost M1 (Mar 2025), and agency losses with logic or GNC causes include Chandrayaan-2's Vikram (2019) and Luna-25 (2023) (general).
verif-mission-loss-rate.why: Even if verified software works as intended, only a few dozen lander and RPO flights will occur by 2031, too few to separate a lower software-caused loss rate from noise. Three of the six commercial lunar missions in the failure table (2019-25) had software- or logic-related causes (with Blue Ghost M1 added, p0 is about 0.4-0.5). With zero software failures in n verified landings the one-sided p is about 0.6^n, so at least 6 verified landings are needed for p < 0.05. S2 gives a first verified lander in 2029 and perhaps 2-5 by 2031, confounded by non-AI learning (Blue Ghost M1 succeeded without proofs), so S2 is Speculative, the P7 default; S3 stays Low. All 9 software-related cases in the table were assumption, spec or process misses, so the outcome also hinges on validated environment assumptions (verif-environment-assumption-models, now a hard prerequisite), not only on proof flights. Hardware and sensor failures keep the total loss rate high.
verif-mission-loss-rate.strongest_case_small: With cheap proofs, teams may ship more ambitious autonomy faster, keeping the loss rate flat while capability rises (risk homeostasis, general).
verif-mission-loss-rate.signpost: Root-cause reports of 2027-2030 lander or RPO failures: a shift from logic and configuration causes toward hardware and sensor causes would support the chain.
verif-mission-loss-rate.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic + auditor: S2 band Low -> Speculative (P7 default; at least 6 verified landings needed to see the effect). Auditor's S3 Low -> Speculative and S3 2031 -> >2031 rejected to keep a scenario spread: S3 adds lander flights and near-free cognition from 2029, which makes Low (10-30%) defensible. Skeptic: hard edge from verif-environment-assumption-models added (the direct edge from verif-assumption-falsification is omitted because it already sits upstream through the lander node). Auditor: success denominator added. | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): S1 >2031 -> >2035, S2 >2031 -> 2033 (2-5 verified landings by 2031 plus several a year after); band_2035 S1 Speculative -> Low, S2 Speculative -> Medium, S3-S4 Low -> Medium. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | E-verified-autonomy resolver (2026-10-07): advocate's S2 2033 -> 2032 accepted (4-9 verified landings by end-2032 make six reachable at the upper case, one year after S3). Skeptic's S2 2034 and band_2035 Low rejected: the power argument belongs in the band, and with a residual rate near 0.1 S2's 10-12 landings give 74% power or more (near 0.2, 38-41%), which averages to about even odds. Advocate's S3-S4 High rejected: effect size and risk homeostasis bind, not landing count. Soft edge from verif-35-mars-verified-landing added (Mars losses count in the share). | R8 (2026-10-08): band set to Speculative where earliest year is after the checkpoint | R9-launch (2026-10-27): gate launch -> launch-external (an outside customer buys the flight). Hard prerequisite physclock-customer-launch-access added: customers wait for capacity to reopen (v1.3 reference 2031, tested 2029 to 2033). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Medium S2 2034, S3-S4 2033: six clean verified landings are possible in 2032 (S2) but a 30% chance of a visible rate change needs 10+ landings; S3 has more flights. Skeptic (low test power and risk homeostasis keep it Low) vs advocate (dozens of landings by 2033 in S3): settled one year apart, both Medium by 2035.
verif-mission-loss-rate.note_2035: S2 can reach six verified landings with no software loss (p about 0.05 against a 0.4 baseline) in 2032 at the earliest. By 2035 S2 has 10-12 verified landings and S3-S4 dozens, but with a residual rate near 0.2 the test has only about 40% power at 10-20 landings, and risk homeostasis can hold the rate flat, so S2-S4 stay Medium; S4 equals S3 because the landing count sets the pace.
verif-mission-loss-rate.gate_note: Flight count binds; statistical power and validated environment assumptions (data) are the runner-up.

capability-random-sample-audit.title: Published error rate for openai/math results
capability-random-sample-audit.description: An independent expert team audits a random sample of 30 or more openai/math families (formalized and unformalized), checking statements against manuscripts and proofs or Comparator runs, and publishes an error and scope-gap rate. This turns the catalog-wide trust level from an assumption into a measured number.
capability-random-sample-audit.status_oct2026: Not yet. The only audit of an earlier OpenAI release covered ten results (arXiv 2608.14673); the first outside Comparator run (Kingy AI, Oct 6, 2026) covered three targets with no statement audit and found the Pi Exponent formal statement omits a manuscript consequence. Hexagon (beta, launched Oct 6, 2026; Buzzard on its advisory board) and AGMAI (guidelines Sep 29, 2026) supply venues and norms but hold no OpenAI deposits.
capability-random-sample-audit.pathway: P2/P3 (verification of the premise base, not certified use)
capability-random-sample-audit.premise_tier: n/a (measures the trust tier of the T1 and T3 catalog families)
capability-random-sample-audit.why: A measured error and scope-gap rate decides whether the 245 unformalized families (T1) stay 'conditional' in every downstream node and calibrates capability-cheap-trust; statement gaps are already visible in the first outside run. It is a human-bandwidth task (a few expert-days per family, general), so its year does not depend on the scenario; AI-assisted checking in S2 and S3 makes it cheaper, not earlier. Band above the P2 default because this is a research audit, not certified use.
capability-random-sample-audit.strongest_case_small: Experts may prefer headline families or their own research; a sample of 30 across many fields needs dozens of specialists; a low error rate on lab-chosen, mostly discrete problems says little about engineering statements.
capability-random-sample-audit.signpost: A published random-sample audit of 30 or more openai/math families (Hexagon, AGMAI, Epoch or an academic group) reporting proof-error and statement-gap rates.
capability-random-sample-audit.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the auditor (proposed as verif-random-sample-audit; renamed to the trunk's domain prefix). Bands unchanged.
capability-random-sample-audit.note_2035: Expected in 2027, so nothing changes in 2032-35. S4 equals S3 because the node is a disclosure.

capability-compute-launch-demand.title: AI compute becomes Starship's second anchor customer
capability-compute-launch-demand.description: Orbital-compute satellites (SpaceX Starmind AI1 and peers) fill at least 10 Starship flights in one calendar year, so Starship cadence and production learning depend on AI compute demand as well as Starlink. This couples the launch clock to the AI capability curve through demand, not through mathematics.
capability-compute-launch-demand.status_oct2026: Not yet. SpaceX disclosed AI1's first specification in Jun 2026 (150 kW peak; about 2.1 t per Mach33's reconstruction; modular, interchangeable chip inserts), then raised it on its Aug 2026 product page to 175 kW average / 250 kW peak; its Sep 16 2026 FCC response bounds each satellite under 4,000 kg, and 33FG's Oct 2026 reference satellite is about 4.0-4.5 t and partnered with Nvidia on its compute payload (Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs; SpaceX, Aug 4 2026, via 33FG). Mach33 reports the power target rising to about 250 kW by Oct 2026 and calls space datacenters the largest uncertainty in its Starship launch-revenue model (Sep 2026). 100-kW-class radiators first fly in 2028 in every scenario (struct-highflux-radiator-flight; SpaceX targets Q4 2027).
capability-compute-launch-demand.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous demand: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
capability-compute-launch-demand.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous demand anchor that couples the launch clock to the AI capability curve, not to AI mathematics, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Full chain (S2): both Starship stages reflown 2027 -> first 100-kW-class compute satellites flown 2028 (struct-highflux-radiator-flight) -> paying 100-kW-class operations in orbit 2029 (materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops) -> internal launch cost under ~$300/kg, Mach33's orbital-compute base-case input, 2029 -> 10 or more compute flights in one year, 2030, with little slack. At AI1's 2.1 t (Mach33's reconstruction: 150 kW peak, 120 kW average, dawn-dusk SSO), 10 flights at 60-90 t to SSO carry roughly 290-430 satellites, about 40-60 MW at peak. This is where the AI curve meets the launch clock: frontier training compute grows ~5x a year and a GW-scale ground site takes ~2.1 years (Epoch), so S2 and S3 raise demand for compute that needs no grid interconnection. S3 is a year earlier because demand and the physical multiplier both rise from 2028; S1 is later because a capability plateau slows the build-out. More flights also speed Starship production learning. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). Medium in S2 and S3 (judgment): the chain has little slack and the economics are unproven (strongest case).
capability-compute-launch-demand.strongest_case_small: The economics are unproven and Mach33 itself treats space datacenters as the largest uncertainty in launch revenue; running chips hot shortens their life (33FG's Oct 2026 model puts logic near 134 C at 250 kW in a 200 m2 radiator; struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification); Starlink V3 competes for the same flights through 2028; and ten compute flights in a year is a SpaceX demand decision it can defer.
capability-compute-launch-demand.signpost: First AI1 launch and on-orbit operation; SpaceX disclosure of a compute-satellite production rate; Starship flights carrying compute satellites in 2029 (5 or more keeps S2 on track).
capability-compute-launch-demand.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the advocate (proposed as physclock-compute-manifest-anchor; renamed to the trunk's domain prefix). Years moved one year later than proposed (S1 2031 / S2 2030 / S3 2029) to follow physclock-cheap-mass-internal (now 2029) and the launch-slip calibration; S3 High -> Medium (economics unproven). Labelled as an AI-capability demand effect, not AI math. Not a duplicate: struct-gw-orbital-compute is the 1 GW cumulative outcome downstream. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): status, chain and strongest case re-based on the orbital-compute branch: radiator first flight 2028 and paying ops 2029 (was 2027/2028), AI1 ~4.0-4.5 t (was 2.1 t), 10 flights ~220-250 satellites / ~40-60 MW (was ~450 / 70-110 MW); soft edge to struct-gw-orbital-compute added. Years and bands unchanged (S2 2030 Medium matches the GW node chain). | F2 audit (2026-10-07): classified as an exogenous physical anchor: pathway set to 'P7 (exogenous)', standard premise label, and the why now says plainly that it is not an AI-math implication (previous pathway: 'P7 (demand coupling from AI capability, not an AI-math effect)'). | E-trunk (2026-10-07): 2035/S4 extension. band_2035: S1 Low -> Medium, S2/S3/S4 Medium -> High (10 flights is about 40-60 MW a year). Years unchanged. | R9-orbital-compute (2026-10-27): flight arithmetic re-based on AI1 in SSO (review OC-2). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): The S2 chain has little slack (AI1 flights 2028, paying operations 2029), so Medium 2031 and High 2033; S3/S4 Medium 2030, High 2032. Skeptic (unproven economics) vs advocate (Launch Keystone v1.3 books 38,600 t of own compute in 2030) resolved one year after the earliest year. Bands unchanged.

frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.title: Clay rules on the forced Navier–Stokes breakdown claim
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.description: The Clay Mathematics Institute states whether OpenAI's Sep 8, 2026 forced blowup result satisfies its official breakdown statements (C)/(D), which permit a smooth, decaying force. Clay rules need publication in a qualifying outlet, two years, and general acceptance. OpenAI says it will not claim the prize, so the ruling may come only as a change to Clay's 'unsolved' listing. This is the event readers will hear as 'AI solved Navier-Stokes'. Its engineering effect is nil.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.status_oct2026: Clay still lists Navier-Stokes as unsolved; its president Martin Bridson called the evaluation 'deliberately unhurried' and 'absolutely rigorous'. OpenAI says the result establishes statement (C), and also (D), and will not pursue the prize. The underlying Lean claim is T3 with no independent Comparator run or statement audit; the manuscript is not yet published in a refereed outlet.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.premise_tier: T3 (forced NS Lean claim, pending independent check)
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.why: Chain: a Comparator run and statement audit (prop-ns-forced-verified, T4), then refereed publication (earliest 2027), then the two-year rule and general acceptance, then a Clay statement. The institutional clock runs at 1.0x in every scenario, so the earliest year is 2029 in all three. Band Low (judgment, not a computed probability): the check is likely, but publication of a 166-page manuscript, Clay's unhurried review, open questions about whether the force meets (C)'s decay conditions on [0, infinity), and the lack of a claimant make a Clay statement by 2031 less likely than not. Separates the reader-facing 'Millennium problem' headline from frontier-ns-unforced, the force-free question most analysts mean. Engineering effect nil (tl-position-2).
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.strongest_case_small: Clay may never rule if nobody claims the prize, and most mathematicians already treat the unforced question as the real problem, so the ruling changes nothing for mathematics or engineering beyond headlines.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.signpost: A Clay Institute statement, or a change to its Millennium Problems listing, on whether the forced result satisfies (C)/(D); a refereed publication of the OpenAI manuscript starts the two-year clock.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.revision_note: B-math-frontier: [auditor] New node: separates the Clay (C)/(D) ruling on the forced claim from the unforced question. Band lowered from the auditor's Medium to Low (publication plus two-year rule plus unhurried review plus no claimant; 1.0x institutional clock). Clay facts checked (implicator.ai). | R review (2026-10-07): dash normalization | E-math-frontier (2026-10-07): band_2035 Low -> Medium in all scenarios; S4 = S3. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Kept Medium 2033 in every scenario: publication about 2027-28, two-year rule, then a board and committee; the only precedent took about seven years. Skeptic (Clay may never rule on a forced claim) vs advocate (dispute forces a statement) resolved as about even by 2035. Bands unchanged.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.note_2035: By 2035 the publication and two-year rules have run for years, so a Clay statement is about as likely as not in every scenario. The clock is institutional, so S4 equals S3.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.gate_note: Clay's unhurried process binds; whether the forced result meets statements (C)/(D) (cognitive) is the runner-up.

verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.title: Reusable launchers re-prove flight software every flight
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.description: A reusable launch operator flies engine-control, redline, abort, fault-management and termination-interface logic whose key invariants are machine-checked, and re-proves them automatically on every software change between flights, and says so publicly. No certification is required: Part 450 reaches only public-safety computing items. This is the uncertified, flown counterpart of prop-verified-engine-software.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.status_oct2026: None known publicly. Falcon 9 flew 165 times in 2025 with no failures, and Starship flew at 48-91-day intervals in 2025 and 63-66 days in 2026 with software changes between flights (physical-clock domain). Under 14 CFR 450.35(a) the FAA requires an accepted means of compliance for the flight safety system (450.145(b)) but not for computing-system safety items (450.141). Newsletter commentary named a sensor trip as one hypothesis for the 2026 Raptor 3 boostback shutdowns (unverified). The largest launch operator owns a frontier AI lab (SpaceX acquired xAI, Feb 2026).
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.why: Two curves combine. The launch exponential means reusable vehicles fly often and change software between flights, so a regression in redline or abort logic is a recurring risk and re-verification sits on the turnaround path. The cognitive exponential cuts re-verification of a change from 2-6 weeks to 1-3 days, with proof repair in hours (verification-domain cost table), and software-only changes avoid the hardware lag ladder. Launch mission software has no certifying regulator beyond 450.141, and the leading operator owns a frontier lab. Chain (S2): proof agents, spec drafting and FDIR model checking 2027 -> integration into a vehicle software pipeline with reviewed invariant specs 2028 -> first publicly stated flight with re-proved engine and abort logic 2029. S3 equals S2 through 2028, and the binding gates (adoption and disclosure) do not move with cognition, so S3 is also 2029 and Medium. Most launch failures are hardware, so this changes software risk per flight, not cadence.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.strongest_case_small: Most launch failures are hardware; simulation plus HIL regression is already fast at leading operators; and adoption may never be disclosed, which is why S2 is Medium, not High.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.signpost: A launch operator stating, in a mishap report, conference paper or hiring material, that engine-control or abort logic is machine-checked on every release; an FAA license modification citing formal verification of computing-system safety items.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: New node from the advocate (the uncertified counterpart of prop-verified-engine-software, joining the launch-cadence and cognitive curves). Advocate's 2030/2028/2028 Low/Medium/High tempered to 2031/2029/2029 Low/Medium/Medium: the A3 lag ladder puts proof-carrying flight software in flight at S2 2029, S3 equals S2 through 2028, and disclosure, not cognition, binds the public signpost. physclock-flight-test-cadence made soft, because Falcon 9 already gives a reusable vehicle with frequent software changes. Not a duplicate: prop-verified-engine-software is the certified crewed-program version and astro-proof-backed-flight-software-ops covers spacecraft, not launch vehicles. Soft unlocks are limited to this branch's nodes; edges into external nodes (physclock-test-loop-monthly) are left to that branch. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): Starship interval aligned with physclock-flight-test-cadence (48-91 days in 2025; 63-66 in 2026). | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): band_2035 S1 Low -> Medium, S2-S4 Medium -> High. S4 = S3 (no four-condition credit). | E-verified-autonomy resolver (2026-10-07): skeptic's band_2035 S2-S4 High -> Medium accepted: the node's achievement requires the operator to say so publicly, and its own strongest case puts disclosure as the reason S2 is Medium; more operators by 2035 raise the odds only to about 0.6. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2-S4 Medium 2030, a year after the first credible stated flight; disclosure keeps High out of reach by 2035. S1 Medium 2033.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.note_2035: Adoption is likely by 2035, but a public statement is not, so S1-S4 stay Medium. S4 equals S3 because adoption and disclosure bind.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.gate_note: Adoption and public disclosure bind; proof-repair turnaround inside the vehicle pipeline (formalization) is the runner-up.

verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.title: Onboard AI agents fly under proof-checked command guards
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.description: An operational spacecraft (not a shadow-mode experiment) lets an unverified learned or language-model agent issue commands directly (tasking, health management, pointing, conjunction response, surface operations), with every command passing through a small guard whose invariants are machine-checked: a recoverable-set or barrier check, resource and keep-out invariants, and command authentication. The agent is never verified; the guard and its isolation are. This applies Simplex runtime assurance to generalist agents.
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.status_oct2026: Unverified guards already fly. Shield AI's Hivemind managed imaging tasking, health diagnostics, battery state of charge and pointing onboard a NOVI Space satellite, with 189 autonomous commands validated by Sedaro's SAFE edge framework, which is simulation-based rather than formal (Satnews, Aug 24 2026). An LLM agent supervised a reinforcement-learning thermal controller on flight-heritage hardware aboard the ISS (ASTREA, arXiv 2509.13380). AFRL flew neural-network attitude control with watchdog and guardrail runtime assurance in shadow mode (Jul 28, 2026). NASA's core Flight System has been ported to seL4, an isolation base.
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.why: Three curves meet. Cheap proofs make a small guard verifiable at compute cost; onboard compute and cheap launch put capable models in orbit; and fleet scale (more than 355,000 avoidance maneuvers a year at Starlink) and cislunar latency create demand for autonomy. Chain (S2): runtime-assurance proofs 2028 -> guard with machine-checked invariants uploaded to an existing smallsat bus (or flown on a new one, with a verified separation kernel if agent and guard share a processor) -> first operational mission with an agent commanding through the guard 2029. No certifying regulator is involved for uncrewed missions. S3 equals S2 through 2028, so S3 is 2029, but near-free cognition from 2029 and fast-moving defense and commercial demand make it High.
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.strongest_case_small: Conservative guards veto most useful agent actions, and a guard over a wrong recoverable-set model is still unsafe; if agent and guard share a multicore processor, timing isolation is measured, not proven; verification of neural perception stays open (verif-nn-verification-scale).
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.signpost: A satellite operator or defense program stating that an onboard AI agent commands the spacecraft in operations through a formally verified guard (machine-checked invariants), rather than in shadow mode or behind a simulation-only check.
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: New node from the advocate (onboard AI agents under proof-checked guards; the operational instance of verif-runtime-assurance for generalist agents). Kept the advocate's bands Low/Medium/High; S3 2028 -> 2029 because S3 equals S2 through 2028 and its prerequisite runtime assurance is 2028 in both. verif-verified-onboard-stack made soft rather than hard, because the guard can run on the existing flight computer while the agent runs on a payload computer, as current demonstrations do. Evidence checked: Satnews Aug 24 2026 (SAFE is simulation-based, not formal), ASTREA arXiv 2509.13380. Not a duplicate: verif-runtime-assurance is the tier-4 tool, and the auton nodes cover surface robots. Soft unlocks into external nodes (astro-autonomous-ca-at-scale, auton-*) are left to those branches. | E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): band_2035 S1 Low -> Medium, S2 Medium -> High. comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.title: AI lowers the quantum cost of breaking today's encryption
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.description: AI-designed quantum error-correcting codes (qLDPC and bivariate-bicycle families), logical instruction sets and arithmetic circuits lower the published spacetime cost (physical qubits x runtime) of Shor's algorithm for RSA-2048 or P-256 by at least 2x below the Oct-2026 best estimates for the same hardware assumptions: under 100,000 superconducting qubits (Pinnacle) or 10,000-26,000 neutral atoms (Cain et al.). Achieved means a published resource estimate that credits an AI-found code or circuit. This lowers the bar hardware must clear; it does not build the hardware.
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.status_oct2026: Human work cut RSA-2048 estimates from about 20 million noisy qubits (2019) to under one million (Gidney, arXiv 2505.15917, May 2025), to under 100,000 physical qubits with qLDPC codes at 1e-3 error and 1 us cycles (Pinnacle, arXiv 2602.11457, Feb 2026), and to as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atoms (Cain et al., arXiv 2603.28627, Mar 2026). LLM-guided search found new bivariate-bicycle qLDPC codes for about $400 of inference (arXiv 2606.02418). We know of no published Shor estimate that credits an AI-found code or circuit (not searched exhaustively).
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.premise_tier: n/a (capability; no catalog family is load-bearing)
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.why: The 2019-2026 gains came from code choice, arithmetic tricks, magic-state factories and layout: expert-scarce search of exactly the kind AI already does (the $400 qLDPC search). This is the main route by which AI mathematics moves the code-breaking threat to satellite links, and it runs against defenders: it raises the urgency of crypto-agility without changing the fabrication gate on comms-crqc-before-2031. In S2, research-grade applied math is public in 2027 and a resource-estimate paper takes about a research cycle, so 2028; S3 follows S2 through 2027. Bands are judgments on the P1->P4 convention for a negative (for defenders) result.
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.strongest_case_small: Estimates were already falling fast through human work, so AI credit may be marginal. The dominant costs (physical error rates, cycle times, connectivity, decoding latency) are hardware, a lower estimate does not change when a machine exists, and the 2026 estimates already assume hardware no one has at scale.
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.signpost: A resource-estimate paper for RSA-2048 or P-256 crediting an AI-found code, magic-state factory or arithmetic circuit; a quantum-hardware vendor roadmap citing AI-designed codes.
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. Years kept. band_2035 S1 Medium -> High. S4 = S3. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2-S4 Low and Medium 2028, High 2029: a resource-estimate paper takes about a research cycle after public applied math, and no published Shor estimate yet credits an AI-found code. S1 Medium 2030, High 2034 (applied math S1 High 2034). Bands unchanged.
