comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.title: Real-time spectrum sharing among rival constellations
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.description: Three or more NGSO operators in a shared band exchange ephemerides and beam plans and coordinate beams and power dynamically, under a protocol that carries machine-checked bounds on each party's throughput degradation (the FCC's 3% / 0.4% criteria) and proven convergence and fairness, replacing static band-splitting and exclusion angles. Achieved means such an arrangement operates in at least one band in at least one jurisdiction.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.status_oct2026: NGSO-NGSO sharing under FCC 24-117 uses 3% time-weighted throughput degradation and 0.4% added unavailability judged by orbital simulation (Roberts, arXiv 2609.36122); FCC 26-26 (Apr 2026) extended performance-based criteria to NGSO-GSO sharing. Game-theoretic power control for equal-priority NGSO coexistence has convergence and Nash-uniqueness conditions (arXiv 2609.38935); tight guarantees for three or more equal-priority operators remain open (comms research). Amazon filed for a 5,105-satellite direct-to-cell constellation in Jul 2026 (Roberts). No dynamic multi-operator arrangement is known.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.why: Multi-operator coexistence guarantees are genuinely open math, a cognitive bottleneck that S2 attacks (P1), and certified bounds that every party can re-check remove the trust barrier to sharing proprietary beam plans (P2). As filings multiply (Starlink, Amazon Leo, AST, Chinese filings), pairwise static coordination wastes spectrum. But the arrangement needs rival operators and a regulator to accept it, which caps the band at Medium, and commercial and political acceptance runs at 1.0x in every scenario: math solved around 2028 (S2), protocols and trials 2029-30, operation 2031 at the earliest. Low in S2 and S3.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.strongest_case_small: Operators prefer bilateral agreements and band segmentation that protect proprietary beam plans; the largest incumbent gains little from sharing; real-time exchange raises antitrust and security concerns; and static rules may be good enough at 2031 densities.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.signpost: Three or more NGSO operators announcing a dynamic coordination or data-exchange protocol; an FCC or ITU-R WP4A contribution proposing dynamic multi-operator sharing with verifiable bounds.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. S1 >2031 -> 2034 (S1 math about 2031, then protocols and trials at 1.0x). band_2035: S1 Speculative -> Low, S2-S4 Low -> Medium (regulator cap). S4 = S3. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Medium 2034, S3/S4 2033 (seed 2033 for both): acceptance runs at 1.0x, and from a 2031 (S2) or 2030 (S3) first operation it takes about three years before a multi-operator arrangement is more likely than not to be under way at 30%. Skeptic (rivals do not share beam plans) against advocate (FCC 24-117 fallback criteria push sharing): 2034 in S2. Bands unchanged.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.note_2035: S1 reaches it around 2034. Rival operators and a regulator must accept it, so S2-S4 stay capped at Medium by 2035; S4 adds nothing to a commercial and regulatory gate.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.gate_note: Rival operators and a regulator accepting the arrangement (adoption) bind; tight guarantees for three or more equal-priority operators, still open math (cognitive), are the runner-up.

physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.title: Operators fly new hardware qualified mainly by AI analysis
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.description: A commercial operator or bus vendor that carries its own risk (no regulator, insurer or government customer accepts the evidence) flies a new-design, not heritage-derived, spacecraft subsystem or structure whose qualification rests mainly on AI-produced analysis with stated uncertainty plus development tests and acceptance-level workmanship screening, skipping protoflight- or qualification-level environmental tests that its own practice would otherwise run. Today's common practice of protoflight testing instead of a dedicated qualification unit does not count.
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.status_oct2026: Not yet attributed to AI. Commercial operators already set their own test programs: FAA Part 450 licenses public safety, not vehicle or payload qualification (CRS R48582), and FCC licensing does not review structural qualification (general). Protoflight testing of new designs is common commercial practice, and some risk-tolerant smallsats skip thermal-vacuum testing (general). Most mass to orbit belongs to an operator that answers to no qualification authority: Starlink carried 1,975 t in 2025 against a contested external market of 347 t, about 5.7:1 (research/physclock.json, Mach33).
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.pathway: P1 (process outcome; flight step written out as a chain)
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.why: Chain (S2): AI agents run and check structural and thermal analysis (2027) -> information-optimal development tests (2028) -> a new subsystem designed and qualified mainly on that evidence in 2028 -> 12-18 month smallsat or derivative build (lag ladder) -> flies 2029-30. No Medium cap applies because the operator, not a regulator or customer, accepts the evidence. The AI-attributable step is extending test skipping from heritage derivatives to new designs on the strength of checked analysis. For constellation operators the fleet itself can serve as the test stand (in-orbit statistics from hundreds of units), which counts here when it replaces ground tests on a new design. S2 Medium, not High (judgment, not a computed probability): tests catch workmanship and unmodeled behavior that analysis cannot, a fleet-wide defect costs far more than a protoflight campaign, and the step must be stated publicly to count. S3 High: near-free cognition from 2029 makes analysis-led qualification the default for AI-native builders. Workmanship screening and thermal-vacuum time constants remain.
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.strongest_case_small: Risk-owning operators already skip tests they judge not worth it (protoflight, minimal smallsat testing) without AI, so attribution will be murky; an operator that loses hardware to an analysis miss will revert; insurers of commercial GEO satellites require qualification evidence (general).
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.signpost: An operator or bus vendor states that a new-design subsystem flew without protoflight- or qualification-level environmental testing on the strength of AI-produced analysis, by 2030.
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.revision_note: B-certification: New node from the advocate (commercial self-risk track). Resolver re-scoped it beyond today's protoflight practice (otherwise met today), set S2 High -> Medium, and S3 2028 -> 2029 (S3 equals S2 through 2028; a 2028 flight needs 2027 design). Soft edges into external nodes (capability-program-cycle-compression, physclock-satellite-gen-cadence, physclock-dev-capital-cut) left as cross-branch requests. | E-certification (2026-10-07): 2035 horizon and S4 review. Years kept. band_2035 S1-S4 Medium/High/High/High. S4 equals S3 (no S4 credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Medium 2030, High 2033 as analysis-led qualification becomes common at AI-native builders; S3 High 2031. No cap (operator accepts its own risk). S1 Medium 2033.
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.note_2035: By 2035 analysis-led qualification is common practice at AI-native builders in S2-S4 and plausible in S1. S4 equals S3: robots speed integration and test, and the step here is the decision to skip tests.
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.gate_note: An operator's decision to skip tests binds; the 12-18 month build of the new subsystem (fabrication) is the runner-up.

physclock-reliability-priors-credit.title: Models cut the test flights needed to prove reliability
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.description: Launch and spacecraft certifiers (Space Force NSSL new-entrant certification, NASA Launch Services Program risk categories, human-rating boards, or component reliability demonstrations) accept AI-produced, credibility-graded physics and flight-data models as Bayesian priors in reliability demonstration, cutting the certification flights or zero-failure trials needed for a stated reliability and confidence.
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.status_oct2026: Reliability demonstration by test needs about 230 zero-failure trials for 0.99 reliability at 90% confidence (n = ln(1-C)/ln R); the physical-gate table marks this unchanged unless model-based priors are accepted (then 0.3-0.6x), and no node used that row. Certifiers already trade flights for insight: Space Force certified Vulcan for NSSL in Mar 2025 after two certification flights, and the New Entrant Certification Guide pairs flight-count options with design review (general). NASA-STD-5001B FSR 17 allows probabilistic structural criteria case by case. EO 14335 (Aug 2025) Sec. 3(b)(iii) directs the FAA to review whether to expand the conditions that demonstrate reliability for a reentry vehicle under Part 450 (whitehouse.gov). It concerns public safety on reentry, and mission-assurance certifiers fall outside it.
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.why: Chain (S2): certified rare-event methods 2027-28 -> credibility directive 2029 -> a certifier accepts model priors in a reliability case at its next review cycle 2030. Statistics, not physics, bind: with accepted priors the zero-failure trials needed fall 0.3-0.6x (physical-gate table). Capped at Medium because it is certifier acceptance; S2 Low because it chains on a Medium rulebook with one or two years left, and certifiers already accept two-flight certification with heavy insight, so the next step is small and slow (judgment, not a computed probability).
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.strongest_case_small: Certifiers count flights because priors can be tuned to any answer, and rare-event model-form error is what NASA's 2024 UQ position paper calls unsolved (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20230016541).
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.signpost: A Space Force, NASA LSP or human-rating certification plan, or a component reliability demonstration, that cites model-based priors from AI-produced analysis to reduce required flights or trials, by 2030.
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.revision_note: B-certification: New node from the auditor (uses the physical-gate table's reliability-demonstration row). Resolver set S2 Medium -> Low (chains on a Medium rulebook with little window). Soft edge into external physclock-critical-payload-reuse-acceptance left as a cross-branch request. | E-certification (2026-10-07): 2035 horizon and S4 review. Years: S1 >2031 -> 2033. band_2035 S1-S4 Low/Medium/Medium/Medium. S4 equals S3 (no S4 credit). | E-certification resolver (2026-10-07): S1 band_2031 Low -> Speculative (skeptic; S1 year 2033). Advocate's S3/S4 High rejected: EO 14335 Sec. 3(b)(iii) (text checked) asks whether to expand reentry reliability conditions for public safety, commits no certifier to model priors, and the hard prerequisite physclock-credibility-evidence-standard is Medium. EO added to status; soft edge from physclock-heavy-cadence-100 added; carrying a flight record across vehicle versions is read as a use of model priors here. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S3 Medium 2030; S2 Medium 2033, three years after its rulebook, because certifiers already accept two-flight certification with insight and the next step is small and slow. Medium cap.

prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.title: Public flight data on storing cryogenic propellant in orbit
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.description: NASA and Eta Space's LOXSAT (Electron launch, nine months in LEO) completes its liquid-oxygen demonstration of zero-loss storage, high-accuracy gauging, automated pressure control and transfer, and NASA publishes comparisons of its predictive models against the flight data.
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.status_oct2026: Integration was finalized in May 2026 for a launch no earlier than Jul 17, 2026 on Electron; the mission is to validate 11 cryogenic fluid management technologies over nine months and inform Eta Space's Cryo-Dock depot (target 2030) (satnews, May 17, 2026). Whether it has launched could not be confirmed (unverified). NASA's CFM portfolio lists maturing predictive models through flight comparisons as an objective.
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.why: Not an AI-math implication: a physical-clock anchor with nil AI-math effect on its date, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. It supplies public microgravity validation data that does not depend on SpaceX releasing its Starship transfer data, which prop-cfm-models' strongest case says SpaceX will keep. Chain: Electron launch (NET Jul 2026, unverified) -> nine months of LOX storage, gauging and transfer tests (to about mid-2027) -> NASA model-versus-flight comparisons published (2028 at the earliest). The data are small-tank and LOX-only, so they calibrate models (soft links to prop-cfm-models and prop-mass-gauging) rather than validate Starship-scale methane behaviour. Medium, not High, in every scenario: launch, spacecraft performance over nine months and publication must all go right (the 2019 Robotic Refueling Mission 3 lost its methane early when its cryocooler failed, general).
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.strongest_case_small: Small tanks and LOX only: scale-up to depot-class tanks and methane still needs Starship data, so the public dataset may not move operational margins.
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.signpost: Confirmed LOXSAT launch and nine-month operations, then NASA or Eta Space papers comparing model predictions with flight pressure, boil-off and gauging data.

hyper-model-form-error-bounds.title: Error bounds for carrying ground-test heating data to flight
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.description: Rigorous or coverage-calibrated bounds on the error of aerothermal and material-response models when extrapolated from arc-jet and shock-tube conditions to flight, so that a probabilistic TPS margin can carry model-form error with stated coverage instead of a judgment factor. Achieved when a published TPS sizing carries a ground-to-flight model-form term calibrated against instrumented flight bondline or heating data.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.status_oct2026: Open. The SRL alternative-margining Monte Carlo sampled aerothermal error only between 1 and the existing factors (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20260005218/downloads/SRL_TPS_IPPW.pdf, slide 13), while at the same 8 km/s entry baseline simulations under-predicted VUV by up to 2x against EAST and three UQ methods disagreed between 30% and 100% (Hansson, ESA, 24 Sep 2026). BOLT-1B showed flight transition differs from tunnel transition (Jan 2026). Paired ground-flight datasets are starting to exist: W-6 (May 2026) flew two NASA Ames instrumented eChar tiles.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.why: AI doing research-grade applied math can derive model-discrepancy frameworks with coverage guarantees cheaply (P1), but demonstrating coverage needs paired ground and flight datasets (Varda/Ames instrumented tiles, BOLT-class flights, Orion), which accrue at flight cadence. This is what decides whether the ~25% SRL-style thinning survives once aerothermal error is not assumed to sit inside the existing factors. It matters most where radiation is significant (Mars, Venus, 12+ km/s return) and least for convectively dominated LEO capsules. S2 lands the method by ~2029 and the first flight-calibrated application by ~2030; S1 lacks both the capability and the data in time.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.strongest_case_small: Model-form error under extrapolation may be irreducible without flight data at the exact condition; a few paired datasets a year may not support stated coverage, and engineers may keep judgment factors regardless.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.signpost: A published TPS sizing whose ground-to-flight model-form error term is calibrated against instrumented flight bondline data (e.g. Varda W-6 Ames tiles, Orion) and carried through to a reliability statement.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.revision_note: B-entry: New node. [auditor] Split from hyper-certified-margin-uq, whose own why called model-form error 'genuinely open'. [skeptic] Signpost and data gate taken from the skeptic's certified-margin finding. Links to hyper-probabilistic-tps-sizing and hyper-12kms-entry-design-basis are soft, as the auditor proposed: LEO capsules can size probabilistically without it. | E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. S1 >2031 -> 2033 (S1 applied math 2029 plus paired datasets). band_2035 S1 Low -> Medium, S2-S4 Medium -> High. S4 = S3 in year and both bands. | R8 (2026-10-08): band set to Speculative where earliest year is after the checkpoint | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Medium a year after the earliest year (the first flight-calibrated application needs a capsule campaign). High 2034 in S2 and 2033 in S3 as instrumented-tile data accumulate. Bands unchanged.

hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.title: Fleet-trained reentry heating model for one reusable vehicle
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.description: A physics-constrained model of reentry heating and TPS thermal response specific to one reusable vehicle family (Starship first), assimilated from 50 or more instrumented orbital reentries of that family (thermocouple and load-sensing tiles, imagery, trajectory reconstruction). It predicts per-zone heating for the next flight within ~+/-15-20% and is used to shape entry trajectories and plan tile work. For the owner it turns the open transition and SBLI problems into a fitting problem inside the flown envelope; it does not transfer to other vehicles or to CO2 (Mars) entry. Achieved when the operator states that entries are shaped or tile work is planned from such a model.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.status_oct2026: Starship ships have re-entered on most integrated flights since 2024; Flight 10 (Aug 2025) deliberately removed tiles and flew metallic and actively cooled tiles, and Flight 13 (Jul 2026) flew load-sensing and reflown tiles in a heat-shield stress test. Starship flew 3 times in 2026 to Oct 7; physclock-flight-test-cadence expects 12+ a year from 2028 (2027 about a coin flip), and Mach33's reference case has ~90 flights in 2028. SpaceX does not publish its heating models; no ship has been caught.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.why: Two curves combine. Launch cadence supplies the owner with the flight data that the general tier-3 closure nodes lack: roughly 8-10 ship reentries with data through Oct 2026 (general count), about a dozen flights a year from 2028 (physclock-flight-test-cadence; 2027 is about a coin flip) and more once physclock-heavy-cadence-100 is reached (S2 2030, S3 2029), so ~50 instrumented reentries of one family accumulate around 2029. On-demand applied math (S2 2027) makes data assimilation, inverse heat conduction and Bayesian updating cheap to build and maintain. The general transition and SBLI nodes exclude per-vehicle tuning by definition, yet per-vehicle tuning is what an operator needs, so for the owner the open physics leaves the critical path while it stays open for everyone else. The data clock is the launch curve, which is largely independent of AI (S3 runs 0.5-1 year ahead), so S1 and S2 share a year. P6 defaults to Low; Medium because the owner needs no outside acceptance, held below High because the operator may never say it uses such a model.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.strongest_case_small: SpaceX builds this with or without frontier AI mathematics, so AI pulls it forward by months, not years. A per-vehicle fit can fail outside the flown envelope (new trajectories, Mars entry), and the operator may never disclose it.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.signpost: SpaceX or another reusable-vehicle operator states that entry trajectories or tile replacement are set from a model trained on its own fleet's reentry data, or publishes per-zone predicted-versus-measured heating.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.revision_note: B-entry: New node from the advocate, narrowed. Carries the owner-data curve that the skeptic and auditor removed from hyper-flight-data-pipeline. Scoped to heating so it does not duplicate hyper-tile-damage-accumulation (tile fatigue) or physclock-twin-reflight-clearance (reflight clearance); hard prerequisite is the flight-cadence node rather than ship reuse because reentries accrue on expended ships too. Advocate's bands Medium/High/High and years 2029/2028/2028 lowered to Medium x3 and 2029/2029/2028: disclosure risk does not vary by scenario, and the launch curve moves S2 by at most 0-0.5 year. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): S3 2028 -> 2029 and why/status re-based on B-trunk's launch clock (12+ flights a year from 2028, not 2027; heavy cadence S3 2029): ~50 instrumented reentries accrue around 2029 at the earliest in every scenario. Soft edge from physclock-heavy-cadence-100 removed: it lands after this node in every scenario and closed the only soft loop in the graph (heatshield -> heavy cadence -> this node -> heatshield); the later data growth stays in the why. | E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. Years kept. band_2035 Medium -> High in all scenarios (disclosure risk shrinks with hundreds of flights). S4 = S3 in year and both bands. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Medium 2030, a year after ~50 reentries accumulate. High 2033 in S2, 2032 in S3 (cadence a year ahead), 2034 in S1. Bands unchanged.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.note_2035: Hundreds of instrumented reentries of one ship family accumulate by the early 2030s in every scenario, so an operator statement that entries or tile work are set from a fleet model is likely by 2035. Launch cadence sets the data clock, so S4 equals S3.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.gate_note: Instrumented reentries bind; the operator's statement that entries are set from a fleet model (adoption) is the runner-up.

struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.title: AI chips and memory qualified to run hot in orbit
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.description: Accelerator logic and HBM stacks are shown, by accelerated life tests, physics-of-failure models (electromigration, gate-oxide breakdown, bias-temperature instability, HBM retention and refresh, solder and through-silicon-via fatigue, combined with dose) and on-orbit telemetry, to survive a 3-5 year orbital mission at elevated temperature (roughly 110-135 C logic and 110-130 C HBM, against the ~105 C / 95 C comparison limits in 33FG's model), so compute-satellite radiators can run hotter and smaller.
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.status_oct2026: 33FG's Oct 6 2026 StarMind model fits 250 kW in the filed radiator envelope under 200 m2 only at ~134 C logic / ~132 C HBM (with a higher-rated GPU package); holding 105 / 95 C needs ~327 m2. 33FG found no publicly disclosed flight-qualified part with the required characteristics and estimates chip wear-out life falls from 5.6 to 3.4 years when the stock chip is pushed harder. Musk (Oct 1 2026): the SpaceX version of the VR72 is co-designed with Nvidia for ~250 kW average. Commercial HBM is specified for operation near 85-105 C (general).
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.why: Not an AI-math implication: qualification here is a vendor and operator program (life tests, flight telemetry, re-specification), so this is an exogenous anchor and the P7 Speculative default does not apply; AI applied math (P1/P5 accelerated-life models) is a soft accelerator. Radiator area scales as 1/T^4 of the radiating temperature, so allowable chip and HBM temperature is the largest thermal lever. Raising the radiating temperature from ~368 K (95 C) to ~407 K (134 C) cuts panel area ~33% at fixed heat (calculation); 33FG's model puts the gap at ~200 versus ~327 m2 for a 250 kW satellite. At ~3.7 kg/m2 that is ~470 kg per satellite (~10% of a ~4.5 t satellite), or ~1,900 t (~19 Starship flights at 100 t) per GW of 4,000 satellites, more than the whole AI radiator-design lever (~350-1,400 t per GW). Physics stays fixed: DRAM retention roughly halves per ~10 C, so hotter HBM needs faster refresh at a bandwidth cost, and Arrhenius wear-out shortens life (general), so the trade is service life (3-5 years, matching chip obsolescence) against radiator mass. The AI-math role is P1/P5: hierarchical Bayesian accelerated-life models, competing-risk wear-out and optimal accelerated-test design let qualification rest on weeks of high-temperature operating life tests (~1,000 h, general) plus first-flight telemetry rather than years of exposure. Chain (S2): first 100-kW-class flights 2028 -> life tests and telemetry 2028-29 -> vendor re-specification of HBM and a published orbital operating envelope 2029. The gate is qualification by the operator and chip vendors, with no regulator, so S2 and S3 tie. Medium in every scenario (judgment): first flights in 2028 leave two to three years for life data and a published envelope, but SpaceX may instead accept a shorter chip life, a larger radiator or a cooler package (strongest case).
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may simply accept a shorter first-generation chip life (33FG notes a first generation could trade life for earlier deployment and data), enlarge the radiator or its filing envelope, or use a cooler-running package; vendors, not AI mathematicians, own HBM reliability data, and the qualifying evidence is life tests and telemetry, not proofs.
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.signpost: A published orbital operating envelope above standard junction limits (HBM at 110 C or more) backed by accelerated-life data, or Starmind telemetry showing sustained chip or HBM temperatures of 110 C or more, by 2029-30.

struct-light-solar-array-production.title: Lightweight solar arrays at compute-constellation volume
struct-light-solar-array-production.description: Flexible or roll-out arrays at array-level specific power of roughly 125-140 W/kg or better (for example silicon at ~250 W/m2 on ~1.8-2 kg/m2 blankets) built at compute-constellation volume, hundreds of thousands of m2 a year. This is the mass lever 33FG identifies as the primary constraint on compute satellites, and the non-AI baseline against which the perovskite and specific-power chain is measured.
struct-light-solar-array-production.status_oct2026: 33FG's June 2026 AI1 reconstruction: array ~1,178 kg, 56% of the implied 2.1 t, ~127 W/kg over ~600 m2; the 2.1 t budget closes only if the array reaches ROSA-class ~1.8-2 kg/m2. SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response allows up to 1,500 m2 of solar under 4,000 kg per satellite. Roll-out arrays fly today at kilowatt to tens-of-kilowatt scale per wing (general); none is produced at hundreds of thousands of m2 a year.
struct-light-solar-array-production.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
struct-light-solar-array-production.why: Not an AI-math implication: array production at constellation volume is a manufacturing ramp that happens without AI mathematics, so this is an exogenous anchor and the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Solar is the largest mass block on a compute satellite; every kg/m2 off a ~600 m2 array buys ~6x what the same cut buys on a ~110 m2 radiator (33FG). At ~1,000-1,500 m2 per 250 kW satellite, 1 GW needs ~4-6 km2 of array, many times Starlink's yearly array output (assumption), so array production rather than radiator design is the fabrication gate at GW scale. Reaching 100 kW/t needs this and more: the June AI1 design already assumed ROSA-class arrays to reach ~70 kW/t, so 100 kW/t also needs thinner or higher-efficiency cells (materials-perovskite-primary-power) and hotter chips. Chain (all scenarios): first Starmind flights 2028 -> serial satellite production with arrays at constellation volume 2029. Medium rather than High because the filing allows a heavier 1,500 m2 array within 4,000 kg, so SpaceX may not need the light blanket at volume.
struct-light-solar-array-production.strongest_case_small: SpaceX already builds Starlink arrays in-house at scale and the filing allows a heavier array within the mass envelope, so volume may come with modest areal density; this node is the counterfactual baseline that happens without AI mathematics.
struct-light-solar-array-production.signpost: SpaceX discloses array areal density or W/kg for a Starmind version, or a Starmind production rate implying hundreds of thousands of m2 of array a year.

struct-formation-compute-clusters.title: Tight-formation compute clusters operate in orbit
struct-formation-compute-clusters.description: Operational clusters of about 10 or more compute satellites holding station within a few hundred metres (inside ~750 m), linked by terabit-class optical crosslinks (~10 Tbps per cluster per SpaceX), running models too large for one satellite. Formation flying is the route to large coherent compute in place of km-scale monolithic structures.
struct-formation-compute-clusters.status_oct2026: SpaceX VP Michael Nicolls (Oct 6 2026): Starmind needs clusters of ~10 satellites in tight formation with ~10 Tbps between them (via 33FG). Google Suncatcher's design places 81 satellites within a 1 km radius at ~100-200 m spacing; its first prototype launched on Transporter-18 on Oct 1 2026 and a two-satellite laser-link test is planned for 2027. Close formation at hundreds of metres has flown since TanDEM-X (2010, general).
struct-formation-compute-clusters.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
struct-formation-compute-clusters.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor (optical terminals, station-keeping propellant and the compute fleet), so the P7 Speculative default does not apply; AI math enters only through soft inputs (P2 collision-safety proofs, certified link scheduling). Forcing a frontier model into one satellite forgoes up to 44% of achievable serving output (33FG, Jul 2026); tight clusters recover much of it, and microsecond-scale synchronization bounds a coherent domain to under ~750 m (Mach33). Chain (S2): first 100-kW-class Starmind flights 2028 -> a batch of ten or more satellites launched and phased into formation, with Google's two-satellite link test (2027) as a precursor -> operational cluster 2029-30. AI math lowers risk and operations cost (machine-checked collision safety for dense multi-year formations under thruster faults and communication loss; certified gaps for link scheduling) but does not set the date. Physical gates do not move: optical-terminal throughput, differential-drag and J2 station-keeping propellant, and the debris consequence of a dense cluster. S3 equals S2 in band because the gates are physical and no cluster has flown. S1 is Low because a capability plateau weakens demand for models too large for one satellite and delays the compute fleet (as in capability-compute-launch-demand); S2 and S3 are Medium (judgment) because SpaceX has stated the requirement and Google has a precursor test, but no cluster has flown. Basis (R9): SpaceX's AI1 (the Starmind program's compute satellite) as Mach33 reconstructed it (17 Jun 2026): 150 kW peak and 120 kW average compute power, about 2.1 t (71 kW/t on peak), flying in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit (SSO). A ten-satellite AI1 cluster is about 1.5 MW peak; clusters stay in the dawn-dusk band where the fleet flies.
struct-formation-compute-clusters.strongest_case_small: Software (smaller or satellite-sized models, better parallelism) may shrink the single-satellite penalty toward parity (33FG), removing the need for tight formations; dense clusters raise collision and debris risk that licensing may restrict.
struct-formation-compute-clusters.signpost: Ten or more compute satellites holding sub-km formation with terabit-class crosslinks in operation; Google's 2027 two-satellite link test meeting its bandwidth target.

auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.title: Heavy cargo landed on the Moon
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.description: A refueled Starship or Blue Moon Mk2 cargo lander delivers at least 15 t of useful payload to the lunar south-pole region in one landing. This is where the launch-cost exponential enters the lunar chain: reactors, LTVs, ISRU pilot units, habitats and spares. Smaller Mk1-class deliveries (about 3 t; VIPER, LTVs) are covered in the ground-truth and base chains.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.status_oct2026: No heavy lunar cargo landing yet. Starship reached orbit on Flight 14 (Sep 28, 2026), and ship-to-ship propellant transfer is expected in early 2027. In Feb 2026 SpaceX made a lunar 'self-growing city' its priority and told investors it targets an uncrewed lunar landing in Mar 2027 (WSJ via NBC News). NASA's Moon Base plan says heavier infrastructure arrives as cargo-capable HLS come online, and bulk launch buys pairing 4-5 rockets with commercial landers were reported near (Bloomberg via 33FG, Oct 6, 2026). Blue Origin's lunar schedule is exposed to the May 28, 2026 LC-36 loss. struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe names a ~15 t lander as its binding gate.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor on SpaceX's and Blue Origin's launch and refuelling programs, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Launch cadence and refueling, not cognition, set this date. AI contributes at the margin through boil-off and transfer models (prop-cfm-models), faster anomaly closure and PSI-informed site selection: 0-0.5 year in S2 and 0.5-1 year in S3 (physclock launch row). Chain (S2): ship-to-ship transfer 2027 -> full refuel campaign 2029 -> uncrewed or cargo-configured landing carrying 15 t or more 2029, under the Moon Base bulk-buy model. Chain (S1): the same curve without AI-assisted anomaly closure -> 2030. Chain (S3): refuel 2028 -> cargo landing 2028. The band is Medium in every scenario: it cannot exceed the refuel campaign's Medium in S1 and S2, announced schedules slip 1.5-3x, and a first landing of a new vehicle class on south-polar terrain carries real tip-over risk even in S3. Second-order unlock where the two curves combine: once landed mass is cheap and design iterations cost almost nothing, lunar hardware can be built mass-tolerant and rich in spares. That shifts reliability gates (ECLSS MTBF, MRE anode life) from 'demonstrate MTBF' toward 'carry spares and let robots swap them'.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.strongest_case_small: This node is almost entirely SpaceX's and Blue Origin's physical program; AI math moves it by months at most, and a single landing failure or refuel-campaign slip costs a year regardless of analysis speed.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.signpost: A Starship or Blue Moon Mk2 landing on the Moon with a declared payload of 15 t or more; NASA bulk lunar-delivery contracts naming heavy cargo flights.

auton-moon-base-infrastructure.title: Moon Base Phase 2 infrastructure on the surface
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.description: At one south-polar site, the following are landed and operating: night-surviving surface power of tens of kW (ridge-site solar with storage, or fission), surface communications, LTVs and a logistics cache, plus at least one semi-habitable element. This is the physical base that 'runs itself between crew visits' would maintain. It has no AI-math pathway and exists to show the gate.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.status_oct2026: NASA's Moon Base plan (Mar 24, 2026) has three phases: Build, Test, Learn (CLPS and LTVs, up to 30 robotic landings from 2027); Establish Early Infrastructure (semi-habitable infrastructure and regular logistics); and long-duration presence once cargo-capable HLS come online. Reporting dates Phase 2 to 2029-2032 and Phase 3 to 2032 onward (NBC; NASA's release gives no years). Budget reported at ~$30B (Bloomberg via 33FG). LTV awards in May 2026 (Astrolab $219M, Lunar Outpost $220M). Lunar Reactor-1 is to land in 2030. Astrobotic's LunaGrid-Lite (1 kW over 1 km of cable) is a power-distribution precursor.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.why: This is the gate auton-crew-optional-lunar-ops names for itself: there must be enough base to operate. Phase 2 runs 2029-2032. Politics and appropriations compress 1.0x, government flagships slip 2-7 years (physclock), and the first crewed landing has already slipped about four years. Chain (S2): refuel campaign and first heavy cargo landing 2029 -> Phase 2 power, LTVs, logistics cache and a semi-habitable element delivered over several heavy and CLPS landings 2030-31 -> all operating at one site by late 2031 (Low). Chain (S3): heavy cargo 2028 -> launch cadence 0.5-1 year earlier plus near-free design -> operating 2030 (Medium). Chain (S1): the same as S2, with the 2030 heavy-cargo date making 2031 the edge of the horizon (Low). SpaceX's Moon-first priority is an upside a NASA-only schedule would not show.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.strongest_case_small: Nothing here depends on AI mathematics; the base is built when appropriations, landers and landing success allow, and AI only trims engineering labor.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.signpost: NASA Moon Base Phase 2 contracts for a semi-habitable element and surface power with named delivery dates; a surface power system of 10 kW or more operating through more than one lunar day at the south pole.

auton-robotic-landing-pad.title: First robot-built landing pad or blast berm on the Moon
auton-robotic-landing-pad.description: Autonomous machines build a landing pad or blast berm of tens of square meters or more from local regolith on the Moon (sintered, melted or 3D-printed), using process windows from auton-sinter-process-control. The structure then survives the plume of a lander or a dedicated plume-test thruster.
auton-robotic-landing-pad.status_oct2026: NASA's MMPACT work with ICON (Project Olympus, $57.2M) aimed at a south-pole pad and blast-shield demonstration, originally targeted for about 2026, and no flight is manifested as of Oct 2026 (general). Lunar construction startups: Lunar Forge (Jul 2026); Astroport with Vermeer on autonomous construction machinery (Apr 2026). Microwave-sintered regolith cracks when cooled faster than ~16 C/min (Coatings, Feb 2026). SCALPSS imaged plume erosion on Blue Ghost Mission 1 (2025).
auton-robotic-landing-pad.why: Pads and berms matter because landing plumes eject regolith at high speed, and the hazard grows with Starship-class landers and repeated landings at one base site. Chain (S2): AI-mapped process windows and cooling-rate control 2029 -> flight unit after a 12-18 month smallsat-class lag -> landing 2031 -> pad-scale area sintered within one lunar day and plume-tested (Low). Chain (S3): process control 2028 -> landing 2030 (Low). The physics that does not compress, sintering power of kW to hundreds of kW and thermal-cycling cracking, keeps even S3 at Low, along with landing odds and the lack of a manifested flight.
auton-robotic-landing-pad.strongest_case_small: Operators can engineer around plumes with mid-body landing thrusters, throttling and standoff distance, so a pad may not be needed before the base has many landings, and the binding constraint is power, not recipes.
auton-robotic-landing-pad.signpost: A CLPS or Moon Base Phase 1 manifest that includes a construction or pad-sintering payload; a relevant-environment test in which a sintered pad survives a rocket plume.

science-private-observatories.title: A privately funded space telescope returns data
science-private-observatories.description: A philanthropically or commercially funded space telescope of 1 m aperture class or larger, built outside agency selection and appropriations, returns science data. The only current instance is Schmidt Sciences' 3 m Lazuli (announced Jan 2026, launch target July 2028). Smaller subscription missions (Blue Skies Space's 13 cm Mauve, 45 cm Twinkle planned) show the business model but are below the threshold. AI-run analysis, test-anomaly diagnosis and operations can trim its slips; they did not create it.
science-private-observatories.status_oct2026: Schmidt Sciences announced the 3 m Lazuli space telescope in Jan 2026 with a July 2028 launch target; its team calls two years to launch 'admittedly aggressive' and targets about four hours, or as little as 90 minutes, from command to photons (Sky & Telescope, Jan 14 2026). Blue Skies Space delivered first data to its Mauve science programme on Jul 6 2026 from a 13 cm telescope; Twinkle (45 cm) is planned (bssl.space).
science-private-observatories.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
science-private-observatories.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor (foundation capital, mirror and detector fabrication, test and launch), so the P7 Speculative default does not apply; AI assists only in integration, test and operations (soft). Full P7 chain: (1) capital was committed by a foundation in Jan 2026, not by appropriations; (2) design and build run 2026-28, mostly before public research-grade applied math (S2 2027), so AI's share is integration analysis, test-anomaly diagnosis (physclock-ai-mishap-analysis, S2 2027) and operations; (3) mirror and detector fabrication, thermal-vacuum testing and integration stay physical (1.05-1.3x); (4) launch is not scarce; (5) commissioning, then data. Announced schedules run 1.5-3x long (physclock slip table), so a 2.5-year plan from Jan 2026 implies launch from late 2029 to 2033 and data by 2031 at roughly even odds: Medium in every scenario (judgment). AI trims slips at the margin but does not change the earliest year, so the node is identical across scenarios. It qualifies 'no observatory flies sooner': outside agency selection and appropriations, the physical clock is the only clock. A second, AI-native private observatory started in 2028 and flying by 2031 would need an unannounced funder and is not counted.
science-private-observatories.strongest_case_small: One program carries the node; private projects slip too (Twinkle has been planned for years, general), and a 3 m space telescope built in 2.5 years has no precedent.

science-onboard-science-inference.title: Spacecraft send answers, not raw data, with error bounds
science-onboard-science-inference.description: A science mission (smallsat, hosted payload or Explorer-class; new, or by software upload to an operating spacecraft) runs onboard inference that turns raw instrument data into science products (event detections, classifications, spectral fits, compressed fields) with certified error bounds (stated false-negative and distortion rates) that its science team accepts in place of raw data for a stated share of its downlink, and retargets observations on those products. It cannot recover information the photons never carried; the gain is selection and compression of what is recorded.
science-onboard-science-inference.status_oct2026: Onboard autonomy for science is not new: EO-1's Autonomous Sciencecraft Experiment detected events and retargeted from 2004 (general); AEGIS selects rover targets onboard Curiosity and Perseverance (general); ESA's Phi-sat-2 (launched Aug 2024) runs onboard AI applications including image compression and cloud detection (ESA). Missing are certified error bounds that let a science team discard raw data; most science instruments still downlink raw or losslessly compressed data (general).
science-onboard-science-inference.why: Two curves combine: onboard compute is becoming routine (COTS AI chips in orbit, materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops, S2 2029) and AI applied math makes instrument-specific error analysis cheap. Chain (S2): cap-applied-math 2027 -> error-bounded detection and compression for a specific instrument 2028 -> software upload to an operating mission or a rideshare smallsat (12-18 month lag ladder for derivative payloads) -> operating with a stated downlink saving in 2029. It attacks downlink, part of the domain's dominant data-supply bottleneck (research/science.json). S2 Medium because science teams are conservative about discarding raw data and certification is the novelty, not the inference; S3 High because cognition is near-free from 2029 and one mission (a university smallsat is enough) clears the bar with two years of slack; S1 Low because applied math reaches outside teams only in 2029. S3 equals S2 through 2028. Bands are judgments.
science-onboard-science-inference.strongest_case_small: Distribution-free error bounds (conformal prediction, lossy-compression bounds) already exist, so the mathematics is not the barrier; and optical downlinks may relieve the bottleneck faster than onboard inference.
science-onboard-science-inference.signpost: A science mission team publishes onboard-derived products with certified error bounds and reports the share of downlink saved.

astro-small-debris-catalog.title: Screening-grade catalog of small debris
astro-small-debris-catalog.description: Tracking data shared with operators that keeps custody of at least 100,000 LEO objects, reaching about 5 cm in the main constellation shells (450-600 km), with covariances good enough for conjunction screening. Most of the ~1.2 million 1-10 cm fragments would still be untracked; full 1-10 cm custody (of order a million objects) is beyond 2031 in every scenario.
astro-small-debris-catalog.status_oct2026: ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report counts more than 40,000 catalogued objects against about 54,000 larger than 10 cm and about 1.2 million of 1-10 cm. Space Fence (operational 2020, general) has not visibly grown the public catalog several-fold. LeoLabs' sub-10 cm RANGER radar is still in development (LeoLabs). SpaceX Stargaze (Jan 30, 2026) adds minutes-latency tracking from about 30,000 star trackers, but star-tracker sensitivity limits it to roughly 10 cm and larger at useful ranges (general estimate), so it does not close the small-debris gap. The FY2027 request cuts the Office of Space Commerce (TraCSS) from $52.5M to $11M.
astro-small-debris-catalog.pathway: P1 (track association and orbit determination); sensor build-out and data sharing are not AI-math-driven
astro-small-debris-catalog.why: This is the sensor gate that astro-leo-safety-at-scale names as binding. Physical sensors (radar power-aperture, optical revisit) and data-sharing policy bind; AI applied math helps only with the cognitive share: associating uncorrelated tracks and determining initial orbits from sparse detections at 10^5-10^6 scale. Chain (S2): existing radars (Space Fence, commercial S-band) plus at least one new sub-10 cm sensor 2028-30 -> AI-built association and orbit determination for uncorrelated tracks from 2028 -> a shared screening-grade catalog above 100,000 objects in 2031. S3 is a year earlier only because association and orbit determination become nearly free from 2029 and existing sensors may already detect more than is catalogued; sensor deployment compresses only about 1.0-1.3x (physclock fabrication row) and data-sharing politics 1.0x.
astro-small-debris-catalog.strongest_case_small: The binding constraints are radar power-aperture, funding and willingness to share: US civil SSA funding is being cut and the Space Force may track more than it releases. Lower operating altitudes (Starlink 480 km) reduce exposure to long-lived small debris without any tracking.
astro-small-debris-catalog.signpost: A public or commercial catalog above 100,000 LEO objects with screening-grade covariances; operational acceptance of LeoLabs RANGER or a comparable sub-10 cm radar; TraCSS or Space-Track publishing small-object conjunction data.
astro-small-debris-catalog.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. S1 '>2031' -> 2032 (sensors are exogenous; S1 lags only on association, 2030). band_2035 S1 Speculative -> Low, S2 Low -> Medium. S4 = S3. | E-safe-orbits resolver (2026-10-07): Advocate's S3/S4 High by 2035 rejected: single-site 2 cm detection has existed since 2019 without producing the catalog. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Medium 2032 (seed 2033): sensors are the same in S2 and S3 and S3 is a year earlier only on association, so S2 trails S3 (Medium 2031, was 2030) by one year. Skeptic (no 100,000-object catalog seven years after Kiwi, TraCSS cut, 2034) against advocate (existing radars detect more than is catalogued, 2031): 2032. Bands unchanged.
astro-small-debris-catalog.note_2035: S1 follows in 2032, once AI association is cheap there. LeoLabs' Kiwi radar was designed in 2019 to track objects down to 2 cm, yet seven years on no catalog of 100,000 objects exists, so revisit, sensitivity at range, funding and data sharing bind through 2035. S3 stays Medium. S4 adds nothing because capital and data sharing bind the sensor build-out.
astro-small-debris-catalog.gate_note: Sensors and data sharing (data) bind; associating uncorrelated tracks and orbit determination at 10^5-10^6 scale (cognitive) are the runner-up.

astro-constellation-hosted-ssa.title: Constellations track debris with honest error bars
astro-constellation-hosted-ssa.description: Star trackers and hosted cameras on at least one megaconstellation (SpaceX Stargaze today) feed conjunction screening used beyond the owner's fleet, by other operators and a government or commercial catalog, with minutes latency and published, validated covariance realism for the trackable population (roughly 10 cm and larger). AI-built association, too-short-arc initial orbit determination and covariance-realism pipelines handle tens of millions of detections a day. This improves the input that dominates Pc error and storm-time custody; it does not see the 1-10 cm population.
astro-constellation-hosted-ssa.status_oct2026: SpaceX Stargaze (Jan 30, 2026): about 30,000 star trackers and about 30 million transits a day, orbit estimates and collision predictions within minutes versus hours industry-standard, screening offered free to other operators (Starlink via 33FG). SpaceX built it before the openai/math release. No published covariance-realism statistics or government catalog ingest of Stargaze data were found in the sources reviewed. An analytical framework for proliferated-LEO optical SSA gives 0.4-5.7 day revisit at 552-650 km (arXiv 2605.01241).
astro-constellation-hosted-ssa.pathway: P1 (association, orbit determination and covariance realism); the sensor network itself is not AI-math-driven
astro-constellation-hosted-ssa.why: Two curves combine. The constellation and launch exponential puts the sensors up at no marginal cost, and the cognitive exponential turns tens of millions of short streaks a day into catalog-grade orbits with honest uncertainty: multi-target association, too-short-arc orbit determination and covariance-realism validation are expert-scarce estimation work, on demand from 2027 in S2 (P1). Chain (S2): Stargaze operational 2026 -> covariance-realism validation and third-party ingest built with on-demand applied math 2027-28 -> published realism statistics and use by a government or commercial catalog 2028. The sensing and the free screening offer exist without AI math, so the AI-math share is the realism and validation increment, and whether it is published or shared is SpaceX's choice, which is why S2 is Medium. Physics floor (general estimate): a 10 cm object at 100 km is about magnitude 7-8 at good phase before trailing losses, against a star-tracker limit near 6-7, so cm-class fragments stay invisible.
astro-constellation-hosted-ssa.strongest_case_small: SpaceX built Stargaze before the release and may keep its covariance statistics proprietary; the government catalog faces an ~80% Office of Space Commerce cut, so third-party ingest may not happen; better tracking of 10 cm-plus objects leaves the dominant small-debris risk untouched.
astro-constellation-hosted-ssa.signpost: Starlink's Jun-Nov 2026 semiannual FCC report (the first full Stargaze period); TraCSS, Space Force or a commercial SSA firm ingesting Stargaze data; published covariance-realism statistics for constellation-hosted tracking.
astro-constellation-hosted-ssa.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. Years kept. band_2035 S1 Low -> Medium, S2 Medium -> High. S4 = S3. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Medium 2029 (was 2028, the earliest year), High 2033; S3 Medium 2029, High 2031 (was 2028). S1 unchanged. Bands unchanged.

plasma-side-view-monitors.title: Side-view and upstream solar-wind monitoring
plasma-side-view-monitors.description: Operational, guaranteed real-time off-Sun-Earth-line coronagraph and heliospheric imaging (ESA Vigil at L5 with NOAA's CCOR coronagraph) and/or an in-situ monitor well upstream of L1 (sub-L1), giving CME speed, direction and early magnetic-structure data well before arrival, rather than opportunistic views from aging research spacecraft. Vigil's quasi-nominal real-time service from the 30-degree mid-course point counts.
plasma-side-view-monitors.status_oct2026: Vigil is planned to launch in 2031 (ESA), so routine L5 data cannot arrive by end-2031. STEREO-A, a 2006 research spacecraft, is 70.6 degrees ahead of Earth (Oct 7, 2026, STEREO Science Center) and gives an opportunistic side view now. PUNCH (2025) adds polarimetric 3D imaging; CCOR coronagraphs fly on GOES-19 and SOLAR-1, both on the Sun-Earth line. No operational sub-L1 monitor is scheduled to fly before 2031 (general).
plasma-side-view-monitors.why: A physical anchor with no AI-math prerequisite, like the physclock nodes. Kay et al. (2024) attribute arrival-time error mainly to CME reconstruction and background solar wind, which side views constrain; Bz a day ahead needs routine coronal magnetic-field measurement or in-situ sampling well upstream of L1. Launch dates do not move with the cognitive clock, so the node sits beyond 2031 in all scenarios and shows the gate AI math cannot move for plasma-cme-arrival-skill (full gain) and plasma-bz-forecast.
plasma-side-view-monitors.strongest_case_small: STEREO-A already provides a side view, and earlier side-view periods did not cut arrival-time error much; the main gain may come from better background solar-wind modeling, which is mathematics, not a new spacecraft.
plasma-side-view-monitors.signpost: Vigil launch and commissioning (planned 2031); funding of a sub-L1 in-situ space-weather monitor.

ESA plans Vigil on Ariane 6, so customer access to SpaceX capacity does not bind it. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Seed kept: Low 2033 (quasi-nominal operations on plan), Medium 2034, never High. Skeptic (ESA missions slip a year or two at this stage) against advocate (an operational Space Safety mission with NOAA partnership): Medium 2034.

plasma-aeps-life-qual.title: 12 kW Gateway thruster passes a three-year wear test
plasma-aeps-life-qual.description: The AEPS QM-2 thruster completes its long-duration wear test to at least 100% of the PPE mission-based per-thruster xenon throughput requirement (1,770 kg, with the 50% margin shown by analysis under NASA's existing practice). That qualifies the first U.S. 12 kW-class Hall thruster. The node is the physical-clock anchor for EP life qualification and the dataset that model-based life credit will be judged against.
plasma-aeps-life-qual.status_oct2026: Three flight thrusters were delivered (2025) for the PPE bus, now repurposed for SR-1 Freedom; QM-1 completed environmental qualification (TVAC early 2026). QM-2 enters wear testing in GRC's VF-5 in fall 2026 after a xenon feed-system upgrade. Testing is planned through Sep 2029, and the SEP project closes out in 2029. NASA expects QM-2 to meet the throughput requirement given very limited erosion over thousands of hours of development testing (Williams et al., Space Propulsion 2026).

plasma-ai-fusion-operations.title: AI runs fusion-device experiment campaigns and control
plasma-ai-fusion-operations.description: At least one major fusion device (SPARC, Helion Polaris or Orion, W7-X, JT-60SA, DIII-D or KSTAR) runs its main experimental campaign with shots designed in differentiable integrated-modeling codes (e.g. TORAX) and executed under learned controllers (shape, density, heating, disruption avoidance). The team reports a shorter time from first plasma, or from campaign start, to target performance.
plasma-ai-fusion-operations.status_oct2026: Deep reinforcement-learning magnetic control was demonstrated on TCV (Degrave et al., Nature 602:414, 2022). Google DeepMind and Commonwealth Fusion Systems announced a research partnership on Oct 16, 2025 with three parts: the open-source, differentiable (JAX) simulator TORAX for virtual experiments before SPARC operates; reinforcement learning and evolutionary search for operating configurations that maximize fusion output within safety margins; and RL agents for real-time control. No deployment dates were given. SPARC first plasma is targeted for 2027.
plasma-ai-fusion-operations.why: Capability transfer (P1), like plasma-gk-surrogates, not new mathematics. Scenario development from first plasma to target performance is a shot-by-shot optimization loop. Differentiable modeling plus learned controllers cut the shots wasted on disruptions and mis-set scenarios. This is the concrete mechanism behind the 1.3-1.5x experiment multiplier S3 applies to fusion campaigns after 2028. Device availability binds: the year follows SPARC's 2027 first-plasma target and its history of slips (2025 -> 2026 -> 2027). The tooling already exists in every scenario, so years and bands do not differ by scenario. It speeds net gain (plasma-fusion-net-gain) and D-He3 campaigns (plasma-dhe3-burn-physics) only as soft edges: magnets, vessels, heating power and tritium handling still set those dates.
plasma-ai-fusion-operations.strongest_case_small: Fusion programs fail on hardware (magnet quenches, vessel and tritium-system problems) more than on scenario design. RL control has been shown on existing devices but not yet as the backbone of a first campaign, and operators may keep it advisory.
plasma-ai-fusion-operations.signpost: CFS (or another device team) reports that its first-campaign shots were designed with TORAX or a similar differentiable code and run under learned controllers, with a stated reduction in shots or time to target performance.
plasma-ai-fusion-operations.revision_note: B-plasma-nuclear resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the advocate (partnership facts verified on the DeepMind blog, Oct 16 2025). science-eo-retrieval-uq.title: Earth-observation retrievals with honest error bars
science-eo-retrieval-uq.description: Identifiability limits and analysis-backed, validated uncertainty for the inverse problems that turn Earth-observation measurements into numbers people act on: methane and CO2 point-source emission rates from shortwave-infrared and hyperspectral imagers; ground deformation from radar interferometry (InSAR phase unwrapping and atmospheric correction) and SAR image formation; and soil-moisture, biomass and hyperspectral-unmixing retrievals. Achieved means at least one operational data provider or agency science team ships per-source or per-pixel uncertainty that comes from an identifiability or error analysis, not only empirical scatter, whose stated coverage holds in blind validation (controlled methane releases, GNSS stations for InSAR), with scenes flagged where the quantity is not identifiable.
science-eo-retrieval-uq.status_oct2026: Facility-scale methane quantification is operational, but its error is dominated by wind and surface assumptions rather than by the spectra (general). MethaneSAT, launched Mar 4 2024, lost contact on Jun 20 2025 and was declared unrecoverable in Jul 2025 (Wikipedia); Carbon Mapper's Tanager-1 hyperspectral satellite launched in 2024 (Wikipedia). UNEP's International Methane Emissions Observatory publishes satellite detections through its Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) (European Commission). Blind controlled-release tests of satellite methane quantification have been run (general), but providers do not publish coverage statistics for their stated uncertainties (general). The same optimal-estimation machinery underlies exoplanet retrievals (science-retrieval-identifiability). No catalog family is load-bearing: the release's inverse-problem families (365, 372) concern recovering elastic or metric coefficients from boundary data, not atmospheric retrieval (nil). Minimum-discontinuity (L0) InSAR phase unwrapping is NP-hard and is solved heuristically (Chen and Zebker 2000, general). Earth observation had no node in graph-v2.
science-eo-retrieval-uq.why: Retrieval error budgets are bespoke, expert-scarce statistics: whether a plume's emission rate is identifiable given wind uncertainty, model-form error in fast radiative-transfer emulators, phase-unwrapping ambiguity in InSAR. On-demand applied math (S2 2027) turns each into a posed problem with a stated answer (P1), and calibration against controlled releases makes the coverage claim checkable, which changes how far users trust the product (P5). The data gate is validation (controlled releases, wind truth, GNSS stations): cheap and repeatable next to space hardware, but paced by field campaigns. S2 is Medium rather than the P1 default because the achievement is adoption by an operational provider, the AI-math increment over existing validation practice may be small, and buyers may not pay for it; S3 is High once cognitive work is near-free from 2029; S1 is Low because public applied math arrives about 2029, leaving one adoption year. The same optimal-estimation machinery underlies exoplanet retrievals (science-retrieval-identifiability), linked softly. Users of radar flood and crop indices in parametric insurance gain the same honest uncertainty (general).
science-eo-retrieval-uq.strongest_case_small: Honest error bars are mostly wider error bars: wind, surface reflectance, atmospheric transport, calibration and cloud dominate, and no theorem adds photons. Providers already publish validation-based uncertainties and can calibrate them against controlled releases with standard statistics, so the AI-math increment may be small and buyers may not pay for it.
science-eo-retrieval-uq.signpost: A methane or InSAR data provider (commercial or agency) publishing coverage statistics for its stated uncertainties from blind controlled-release or GNSS validation, with the uncertainty derived from an identifiability or error analysis, by 2029.
science-eo-retrieval-uq.revision_note: C-final integrator (2026-10-07): new node; merged C-sectors science-eo-retrieval-uq with its duplicate C-disciplines science-eo-retrieval-certified. Bands set Low/Medium/High (sectors proposed Medium/High/High, disciplines Medium/Medium/High): adoption by an operational provider under a data gate is Medium in S2, and S1 has one adoption year. | E-science (2026-10-07): 2035/S4 extension: band_2035 S1 Low->Medium, S2 Medium->High. S4 equals S3 (no S4 credit). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Medium a year after the earliest year (S2-S4 2029); High S2 2033 once CO2M and repeated controlled releases make coverage routine, S3 2030; S1 Medium 2032. Bands unchanged.

science-eo-ghg-enforcement-grade.title: Satellite methane data used as compliance evidence
science-eo-ghg-enforcement-grade.description: A regulator, accredited verifier or treaty body uses satellite emission-rate quantification (methane super-emitters, CO2 point sources), with its stated uncertainty, as evidence in a compliance determination, a penalty, a verified correction to reported company or national emissions, or an importer equivalence assessment, rather than only as a tip-off for follow-up inspection.
science-eo-ghg-enforcement-grade.status_oct2026: Satellites already trigger notifications: UNEP IMEO's MARS sends satellite-detected plumes to governments and operators (European Commission). The EU Methane Regulation (EU 2024/1787) entered into force on Aug 4 2024 and phases in requirements for importers (European Commission), with MRV equivalence for new import contracts from 2027 and methane-intensity limits from 2030 (dates general); the Commission issued recommendations on model contract clauses and penalties in Jul 2026 (European Commission). U.S. federal methane rules went under reconsideration in 2025 (general). Measurement capacity is uneven: MethaneSAT was lost in Jun 2025, while Tanager-1 (2024) and GHGSat's satellites operate (Wikipedia; general).
science-eo-ghg-enforcement-grade.pathway: P1->P5 (adoption into regulation; no hardware change)
science-eo-ghg-enforcement-grade.why: Detection is already accepted; the legal barrier to using a satellite number as evidence is a defensible uncertainty, which is the AI-math increment. Chain (S2): applied math public 2027 -> retrieval uncertainty validated in blind releases 2028 (science-eo-retrieval-uq, Medium) -> a verifier or regulator methodology that references satellite quantification 2029 -> first compliance or verified-inventory use 2030, as EU importer and methane-intensity rules take hold. No hardware step: existing constellations suffice. It needs regulator acceptance, so it is capped at Medium; with a Medium prerequisite and a regulatory step chained, S2 is Low, in line with the tree's other regulator-gated outcomes. S3 reaches the cap (Medium) but gains a year only on the methodology step, because regulatory clocks compress little and politics not at all. S1 waits for applied math (2029) and is Speculative.
science-eo-ghg-enforcement-grade.strongest_case_small: Regulators may keep satellites as tip-offs and base penalties on ground or aerial measurement, which is easier to defend; U.S. federal methane enforcement is receding; and the EU importer regime rests on exporters' own reporting, so a satellite number may never be decisive. Detection thresholds and revisit rates, set by hardware and orbits, limit what satellites can show in the first place.
science-eo-ghg-enforcement-grade.signpost: An EU verifier, member-state authority or national regulator citing satellite quantification with uncertainty in a compliance finding; the EU methane-intensity methodology naming satellite or other top-down measurement; MARS reporting a rising share of notifications that led to verified corrections.

astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.title: Proven error and spoofing bounds for satellite navigation
astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.description: Provable integrity for Earth users who combine GNSS with low-orbit navigation signals, inertial sensors and signals of opportunity: error overbounds that hold for heavy-tailed, non-Gaussian and correlated errors, protection levels with stated missed-detection probabilities (aviation targets are of order 1e-7 per approach, general), and jamming and spoofing detectors with stated false-alarm and missed-detection rates under an explicit threat model. Distinct from astro-nav-filter-guarantees, which covers onboard spacecraft navigation in cislunar and deep space. Achieved means a LEO-PNT or GNSS-augmentation provider, or an RTCA or EUROCAE working group, uses such overbounds or detector guarantees in a published integrity analysis.
astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.status_oct2026: Civil GNSS interference is now routine: OPSGROUP counted about 1,500 spoofed flights a day in Jul-Aug 2024, up from about 300 in the first half of 2024, across the Mediterranean, Black Sea, Russia and the Baltic, and the India-Pakistan border (OPSGROUP, Sep 6 2024). Iridium launched a PNT ASIC for jam- and spoof-resistant devices (Oct 27 2025; Iridium via 33FG). ESA's Celeste LEO-PNT demonstrator (11 satellites planned) launched its first satellites on Mar 28 2026, broadcast its first navigation signal from LEO on Apr 10 2026 and demonstrated 5G positioning signals on Sep 15 2026 (ESA). Gaussian overbounding of heavy-tailed GNSS errors is an established but expert-scarce craft (ARAIM, general), and new LEO constellations have no fault-rate history to bound. Catalog: nothing direct.
astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.why: Integrity is tail-probability mathematics: proving that a protection level is exceeded less often than about 1e-7 when errors are non-Gaussian and faults are correlated, and that a spoofing detector misses less often than a stated rate against a defined adversary. Both are bespoke, expert-scarce applied math that certified rare-event methods (frontier-rare-event-certified, S2 2028) and on-demand capability make routine, so the P1 default (High) holds in S2. The data gate is fault history: overbounds for a new LEO constellation need its own signal-in-space fault statistics, which accumulate only with operating years; proofs can say how much data is enough, not supply it. S1 follows the later rare-event methods (2030).
astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.strongest_case_small: Accuracy and jam resistance come from signal power, bandwidth, antennas and clocks, not proofs; a spoofing guarantee holds only inside its threat model, and adversaries adapt; aviation integrity standards change over a decade, not two years.
astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.signpost: A LEO-PNT provider (Xona, Iridium, ESA's Celeste follow-on) publishing an integrity support message or fault-rate overbound; RTCA or EUROCAE working papers using formally derived overbounds; a spoofing-detection standard with stated missed-detection rates.
astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. Years kept. band_2035 S1 Medium -> High. S4 = S3. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2-S4 Low 2028, Medium 2029, High 2030: certified rare-event methods arrive 2028, but overbounds for a LEO constellation need its own fault statistics, so High waits two years; data-bound, so S3 equals S2. S1 Medium 2031, High 2034. Bands unchanged.
astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.note_2035: LEO navigation fleets accumulate several years of fault history by 2035, so S1 reaches High. S4 adds nothing because the data gate runs in real time.
astro-pnt-integrity-overbounding.gate_note: Fault history that accumulates with operating years (data) binds; tail-probability overbounding math (cognitive) is the runner-up.

astro-leo-pnt-assured-service.title: Low-orbit navigation service with published error bounds
astro-leo-pnt-assured-service.description: A low-Earth-orbit PNT service (Xona Pulsar, Iridium PNT, a European LEO-PNT follow-on, or a megaconstellation's navigation signal) publishes an integrity specification (alert limit, protection level, time to alert, fault rates) backed by derived overbounds, and paying critical users (telecom and power-grid timing, maritime, automated vehicles, or aviation trials) rely on it as a GNSS backup or complement. Aviation certification is not required and is not expected by 2031.
astro-leo-pnt-assured-service.status_oct2026: Xona plans 258 small satellites at 1,080 km, broadcast its first commercial navigation signal in 2025 and announced on Oct 7 2026 that Pulsar is entering scaled production (Xona). Iridium sells timing and location services and launched a jam- and spoof-resistant PNT ASIC in Oct 2025 (Iridium via 33FG). ESA's Celeste demonstrator broadcast its first LEO navigation signal on Apr 10 2026 (ESA). None publishes an integrity specification comparable to aviation GNSS augmentation (general).
astro-leo-pnt-assured-service.pathway: P1->P7 (service deployment; the integrity layer is the AI-math share)
astro-leo-pnt-assured-service.why: Chain (S2): integrity overbounds 2028 -> provider fault-rate monitoring over one to two years of signal history -> a published integrity specification and paying critical-infrastructure users 2029-30. The service itself runs on the launch and capital clock: hundreds of satellites for continuous global coverage, mostly rideshare-launched, with Xona only now in scaled production, so S3 gains nothing over S2 (launch cadence follows its own curve). Demand is real (about 1,500 spoofed flights a day in 2024), but buyers may take an unbounded backup before an integrity-bounded one, which is why S2 is Medium, not High. S1 follows the later overbounds (2030) plus a year. Against the P7 default (Speculative): the physical part is an exogenous service deployment (Xona, Iridium, Celeste) and the AI-math share is the integrity layer, so the band is set by provider adoption and buyer demand: Medium in S2 and S3, Low in S1.
astro-leo-pnt-assured-service.strongest_case_small: Timing and positioning customers buy availability and jam resistance, which come from signal power and constellation size; integrity specifications matter mainly to aviation, which will not certify a LEO service by 2031; and the largest LEO operator may offer navigation without publishing anything.
astro-leo-pnt-assured-service.signpost: Xona or Iridium publishing alert limits and time to alert; a telecom, grid or maritime authority approving LEO PNT as a GNSS backup; EU or ESA decisions on a Celeste follow-on constellation.

astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.title: Certified merging of tracks from many sensors
astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.description: Methods that fuse detections from hundreds to thousands of space-based sensors into tracks of many objects at once, with certified optimality gaps on the data-association step (which detection belongs to which object), consistent covariances under sensor bias and dropouts, and stated rates of mis-association and lost custody. Serves space situational awareness (constellation-hosted star-tracker networks) and, at a high level, missile warning and tracking layers, where the same estimation problem appears with faster, maneuvering targets.
astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.status_oct2026: Multi-frame data association is NP-hard for three or more scans (classical, general), so operational fusion uses multiple-hypothesis, random-finite-set or Lagrangian-relaxation methods without certified gaps at proliferated scale (general). SpaceX Stargaze turns about 30,000 star trackers into about 30 million transits a day (Jan 2026; see astro-constellation-hosted-ssa). The Space Development Agency adds infrared tracking satellites in tranches: 28 in Tranche 1 from two vendors and 54 in Tranche 2 from three vendors ($2.5B awarded Jan 2024, first launches targeted from Aug 2026), with MDA's HBTSS medium-field sensors cued by SDA's wide-field sensors (Wikipedia; launch status not independently checked). Catalog: nothing direct; the 102 ceilings (T3) concern Max-Cut and vertex cover, not assignment.
astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.why: Association and covariance realism are the inputs that dominate tracking error, and both are estimation problems solved in principle but scarce in expert time, which is what on-demand applied math (S2 2027) makes cheap. Lagrangian duality already yields certificates of the optimality gap for assignment (general), so the work is scaling and checking them on proliferated scenes, not new theory; constants are practical, so the P4 step does not cut the band. One year of adoption after 2027 gives S2 2028 (High); S1 follows applied math (2029) plus a year.
astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.strongest_case_small: Sensor geometry, revisit and noise set tracking quality; heuristics already work on structured scenes; and in the defense case the binding gates are classified data access and acquisition, not math.
astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.signpost: Published certified-gap association results on proliferated-LEO benchmarks; Stargaze or a commercial SSA network publishing mis-association statistics; Space Force or SDA ground-segment awards naming certified fusion.
astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. Years kept. band_2035 S1 Medium -> High. S4 = S3. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Low 2028, Medium 2029, High 2030; S3 High 2029. One year of adoption after public applied math gives the earliest year, and routine use at proliferated scale takes one more. S1 Medium 2031, High 2034 (applied math S1 High 2034). Bands unchanged.
astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.note_2035: Certified association at proliferated scale is routine by 2035 in every scenario. S4 adds nothing because the work is cognitive.
astro-multitarget-track-fusion-certified.gate_note: Scaling and checking Lagrangian gap certificates (cognitive) binds; real proliferated-scene sensor data (SDA tranches, Stargaze) is the runner-up.

astro-proliferated-tracking-custody.title: Missile-tracking satellites cite certified track merging
astro-proliferated-tracking-custody.description: At a high level: a government proliferated-LEO missile-warning and tracking architecture delivers continuous custody of maneuvering targets by fusing detections across many satellites, and its operators publicly attribute part of the result to fusion and covariance methods of the certified kind (bounded mis-association, validated covariance), in a publicly reported test.
astro-proliferated-tracking-custody.status_oct2026: SDA's Tranche 1 and Tranche 2 tracking satellites are being built and launched on the agency's roughly two-year tranche cadence (Wikipedia; general; launch status not independently checked). Ground fusion software is classified and its methods unpublished (general). OpenAI, Google, xAI and others were cleared for classified networks in May 2026 (see capability-controlled-data-access).
astro-proliferated-tracking-custody.pathway: P1->P4 (ground software; sensors and launch are not AI-math-driven)
astro-proliferated-tracking-custody.why: Chain (S2): certified fusion methods 2028 -> usable on classified networks 2028 -> integrated into a tracking ground segment through a defense acquisition cycle 2029-30 -> a publicly reported custody test that credits the method 2030. Sensors, launch and appropriations decide whether custody happens at all (politics 1.0x), and classification limits what anyone outside can observe, so even if the math lands, attribution by 2031 is unlikely: Low in S2 and S3. The resilience question (does coverage survive the loss of satellites) is constellation-design math, linked softly from comms-constellation-design-optimizer.
astro-proliferated-tracking-custody.strongest_case_small: Tracking quality is set by infrared sensitivity, revisit and transport-layer latency; programs will use whatever fusion works without publishing it; and access to frontier models on classified networks depends on policy decisions that can change.
astro-proliferated-tracking-custody.signpost: SDA or MDA test reports of fire-control-quality tracks from fused space sensors; ground-segment contract language on certified association or covariance realism; unclassified government-lab papers on certified fusion at proliferated scale.
