robo-lab-bench-useful.title: Robots do general lab bench work at scale
robo-lab-bench-useful.description: At least 50,000 general-purpose robots do the bench work people still do in automated labs (reagent prep, plate loading, instrument tending, moving samples between workcells), so leading autonomous labs run without human hands in the loop.
robo-lab-bench-useful.status_oct2026: Specialized workcells already scale: A-Lab ran 100-200 samples a day, 50-100x a person (LBNL); Ginkgo runs over 50 automated carts and plans 50 more by end-2026; PNNL is buying 97 robots and over 100 instruments for $47M by 2030. People still do reagent prep and plate loading: in OpenAI's GPT-5 run on Ginkgo's cloud lab (36,000 compositions over about 6 months), humans prepared reagents and loaded plates (Feb 2026). Medra leased 38,000 sq ft for hundreds of arm-based robots (Feb 2026).
robo-lab-bench-useful.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
robo-lab-bench-useful.why: Workcells are S2/S3 baseline. General robots add the long tail of non-standard steps that keeps people in the loop. Chain (S4): robots useful in multi-task factory work 2029 -> lab variants with finer manipulation 2030; the base fleet in labs is about 58,000 in 2030 and 0.12M in 2031 (Medium by 2031, since bench dexterity is harder than factory handling). S2 and S3 (slow path): 1% of a 4.65M fleet is about 46,000 lab robots in 2035, just short of the line, so after 2035 (Low by 2035). S1: after 2035 (Speculative). Characterization and interpretation then bind: A-Lab's corrected paper confirmed 36 of 40 reported syntheses.
robo-lab-bench-useful.strongest_case_small: Lab capacity already grows 16-100x by 2031 through capex and specialized automation. General robots add breadth and better odds, and a drug program gains only about 0.9 year over S3.
robo-lab-bench-useful.signpost: An autonomous lab reports no human reagent prep or plate loading over a multi-month campaign; Medra or Lila report hundreds of robots in service.
robo-lab-bench-useful.note_2035: S4's base path has about 0.6M lab robots and 20% of lab technician labor by 2035; S1-S3 stay under 1% and just short of 50,000 robots. Materials and biology nodes gain throughput and replicate counts in S4, while characterization, creep hours and trial clocks still set their dates.
robo-lab-bench-useful.revision_note: E-robots (2026-10-07): new node in the robots branch (S4 Embodied, horizon 2035). S1-S3 follow the slow robot path, S4 the base path; the fast path is S4 upside. robo-launch-refurb.title: Robots inspect and refurbish rockets between flights
robo-launch-refurb.description: General-purpose robots do routine post-flight inspection, heat-shield tile handling and replacement, and refurbishment tasks on a reusable heavy launcher at a leading firm, beyond the single-purpose tile and pin machines already in use.
robo-launch-refurb.status_oct2026: SpaceX's Starfactory uses robotic cutters, welders and tile installers, and robotic heat-shield pin installation began in early 2026 (NASASpaceflight). These specialized machines are S2/S3 baseline. No Starship ship had been caught or reflown as of Oct 2026; Starship flew 5 times in 2025 and 3 times in 2026 to Oct 7. Musk said in Jan 2026 that no Optimus did useful work at Tesla.
robo-launch-refurb.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
robo-launch-refurb.why: Handling, inspection and refurbishment are the first aerospace tasks general robots can take: they need looser tolerances than assembly and little requalification on a firm's own vehicle. Chain (S4): multi-task factory robots 2029 -> deployed on ship and booster turnaround at a leading firm 2029 (Medium by 2031). S2 and S3 (slow path): 2031 (Low). S1: 2033. Cadence credit is conditional: refurbishment robots matter for dates only once ship turnaround falls under about a week, when labor and shifts become the binding step. Pads turn around between launches too. Flame deflector, deluge and quick-disconnect repair are shift labor of the same kind, and robots that work outdoors on pads arrive with construction-trade robots after 2031. At about one heavy flight a day, this is the main S4 lever within the brief's limit of about 1.4x on launch campaigns by 2035.
robo-launch-refurb.strongest_case_small: Vehicles are already ahead of flights. Starship hulls were built through at least Ship 48 by Apr 2026, so faster refurbishment may not raise cadence while failures, pads and propellant bind.
robo-launch-refurb.signpost: SpaceX discloses robot counts at Starbase, or a ship turnaround under 1 week; humanoids doing tile inspection or replacement.
robo-launch-refurb.note_2035: With hundreds of heavy flights a year by the mid-2030s, vehicle and pad turnaround labor scales with flights, and S4 robots carry that load at leading firms. S1-S3 keep using specialized machines and people. Pads, propellant and airspace still cap cadence.
robo-launch-refurb.revision_note: E-robots (2026-10-07): new node in the robots branch (S4 Embodied, horizon 2035). S1-S3 follow the slow robot path, S4 the base path; the fast path is S4 upside. R-robots (2026-10-07): Pad turnaround added to why and note_2035 as the mechanism at about one flight a day (advocate accepted in part). The threshold stays on vehicles, since outdoor pad work arrives with construction-trade robots after 2031. Years and bands kept. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S4 Medium 2031, after multi-task factory robots reach Medium (2030), and High 2033. S2-S3 Medium 2033. Skeptic: specialized machines already do it, so 2035. Advocate: Optimus at SpaceX, so 2032. Resolved 2033, when structured factory work is High on the slow path. Bands at 2031 and 2035 unchanged.

robo-aerospace-tolerance-work.title: Robots assemble flight hardware at leading space firms
robo-aerospace-tolerance-work.description: General-purpose robots do paid assembly, integration or test work on flight hardware at aerospace tolerances (torque records, traceability, sub-millimeter fits) at one or more leading space firms, under a requalified process.
robo-aerospace-tolerance-work.status_oct2026: Figure 02 at BMW loaded parts at a 5 mm tolerance for 11 months (Figure, Nov 2025); aerospace assembly needs tighter fits, torque and traceability records and per-process qualification. UBTech robots are in concept testing at Airbus. SpaceX builds about 70 Starlink satellites and about 200,000 terminals a week (S-1/A) with specialized automation. The S4 analysis puts about 1% of the base fleet in aerospace in 2031, about 0.06M robots, against a need of 0.05-0.17M for space.
robo-aerospace-tolerance-work.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
robo-aerospace-tolerance-work.why: Chain (S4): first process requalified on a single-task deployment 2029 (robo-requal-standard) and multi-task factory robots 2029 -> assembly processes requalified and paid tolerance work at a robot-first firm 2030 (Medium by 2031, after 3-12 months of requalification drag per process at leading firms (an estimated 6-24 months per process per supplier in general)). This is the early end of the S4 analysis's 2030-31 for leading firms. Suppliers follow after 2031 (robo-aerospace-supplier-tier). S2 and S3 (slow path): 2032 (Low by 2031). S1: 2034. The labor gain over S3 at robot-first firms is about 1.4x in 2031 (0.9-2.0x) and 2.3x in 2035 (1.6-3.1x), from 24/7 hours, productivity and parallel crews.
robo-aerospace-tolerance-work.strongest_case_small: Where automation already works, launch binds. Rocket Lab's Rosie cut composite work 33x, yet Electron's cadence rose 3.5x in six years; robots may raise output without moving any date in the tree.
robo-aerospace-tolerance-work.signpost: Humanoids in paid aerospace assembly or test work (Airbus, SpaceX, Tesla-adjacent firms); a prime's supplier bulletin that allows robot workmanship.
robo-aerospace-tolerance-work.note_2035: By 2035 robots supply just under a quarter of aerospace production labor on supply alone in the base path, and less after requalification. Robot-first firms then run fabrication about 1.9x and integration and test about 2.2x faster than in 2026; typical programs gain less.

robo-24x7-integration-test.title: Robots run integration and test around the clock
robo-24x7-integration-test.description: At a leading space firm, robots run a spacecraft or stage integration-and-test line 24/7 (handling, harnessing, mating, test setup and environmental-test loading) with people supervising. Integration and test calendar time falls at least 1.15x against the same firm's crewed line (about 1.75x against 2026 practice, of which about 1.5x is S3's gain).
robo-24x7-integration-test.status_oct2026: Integration and test is about a quarter of a new space program's critical path in the model. SpaceX runs 15 specialized engine test stands at McGregor (S-1/A), and the model's S3 already includes AI-run test stands (2028). Firefly traced a 2025 ground-test explosion to a contamination process error during stage integration, a reminder that workmanship risk sits in this step. GEVS thermal-vacuum minimums (4 cycles, 12 h plateaus) do not compress.
robo-24x7-integration-test.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
robo-24x7-integration-test.why: Robots compress the labor and shift share of integration and test: about 45% of an environmental qualification campaign and 35% of a satellite generation. Their own gain over S3 is modest: about 1.75/1.5, or 1.17x, at robot-first firms in 2031, and about 2.2/1.67, or 1.3x, in 2035. Chain (S4): tolerance work 2030 -> the line's other processes (harnessing, mating, test setup, chamber loading) requalified in parallel at 6-24 months each, plus fleets at 1,000 h between interventions 2030 -> a robot-first firm runs integration and test around the clock in 2031 (Low by 2031; the S4 Amdahl table counts it only for robot-first firms). S2 and S3 (slow path): 2033. S1: 2035. Thermal-vacuum dwells, hot-fire findings and reliability statistics stay fixed, so a program's compression ceiling rises from 51% (S3) to 56-60% at a robot-first firm in 2031.
robo-24x7-integration-test.strongest_case_small: Test-facility queues and dwell times may dominate. If chambers and stands are the bottleneck, extra shifts of handling add little, and S4 output raises demand for test slots too.
robo-24x7-integration-test.signpost: A satellite or stage maker reports robot-run 24/7 integration; integration and test durations below 0.57x of 2026 values (1.75x) at a robot-first firm.
robo-24x7-integration-test.note_2035: By 2035 robot-first firms run integration and test about 2.2x faster than in 2026, about 1.3x beyond S3, and typical programs gain less; the S4 ceiling reaches 66-67% at robot-first firms. S1-S3 keep human crews with specialized automation.

robo-supply-chain-loop.title: Robots work in the plants that make robot parts
robo-supply-chain-loop.description: General-purpose robots do at least 10% of labor hours in reducer, roller-screw, motor or magnet plants of a leading robot supply chain. With robots making robot parts, the robots-build-robots loop extends past final assembly.
robo-supply-chain-loop.status_oct2026: The loop is open. Humanoid factories are built and staffed by people and conventional automation; Figure ramped BotQ 24x in under 120 days with human labor (Apr 2026). FANUC has built robots with robots since 2001, yet its output doubled only about every 7 years because demand set the rate. Forethought estimates about a 1-year doubling for self-replicating robots with abundant AI and a few years with real frictions (May 2025).
robo-supply-chain-loop.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
robo-supply-chain-loop.why: Robot-production labor is small: 3.4M robots a year at 100-300 labor hours each is 0.2-0.5M worker-equivalents, 3-8% of the 2031 fleet's labor. So the loop adds little by 2031, about 1.0-1.2x on the fleet. Chain (S4): robot makers' own lines 2029-30 -> robots enter reducer, screw and motor plants about 2032 (High by 2035), so base growth eases only to 1.8x and then 1.6x a year. S2 and S3 (slow path): 2035 (Low). S1: after 2035. Holding a 12-month doubling to 2035 would give about 104M robots against the base 62M.
robo-supply-chain-loop.strongest_case_small: Robot output is bound by grinding machines, magnets, chips, capital and certification. Robots in parts plants leave machine-tool lead times of 6-14 months unchanged.
robo-supply-chain-loop.signpost: Humanoids doing final assembly of humanoids (Figure BotQ, Tesla, UBTech), then working in reducer, screw or magnet plants.
robo-supply-chain-loop.note_2035: The loop is why S4's base path keeps growing 1.6-1.8x a year after 2031, against the 1.2-1.3x of past ramps. It does not make growth super-exponential before 2035.

robo-construction-trades.status_oct2026: Construction robots are single-task. robo-earth-pads-plants.title: Robot crews build a launch pad or propellant plant
robo-earth-pads-plants.description: A heavy-launch pad or on-site propellant plant (air separation, methane liquefaction, storage) is built with general-purpose robots doing most field trade labor around the clock, in about half the 2026 calendar time. Calendar time runs from groundbreaking to first use; long-lead equipment and permits run before it.
robo-earth-pads-plants.status_oct2026: Starbase Pad 2 took about 16 months from flame-trench start to first launch on May 22 2026. SpaceX plans four operational Starship pads by end-2027 (S-1/A). On-site propellant production cuts variable propellant cost per flight about 90% and replaces roughly 389 tanker deliveries per flight (33FG estimate, Aug 2026). Large transformers take 128-144 weeks, and generator step-up units over 160 weeks.
robo-earth-pads-plants.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
robo-earth-pads-plants.why: Pads and propellant plants split about 35% labor, 15% physics, 35% materials and capital and 15% institutions (S4 analysis). Robots compress the labor share and allow 24/7 work; equipment lead times and permits stay. A leading firm reaches 0.75-0.85x of the 2026 calendar in 2031 with specialized machines, about 0.63-0.71x in 2033 and 0.50-0.57x in 2035 (linear between the S4 analysis's values). Chain (S4): construction trade robots 2032 -> a robot-built pad started 2033-34 -> done 2035 at about half the calendar (Low by 2035). S1-S3: after 2035 (Speculative). The pads for 100+ flights a year come first, built by people and specialized machines by 2029.
robo-earth-pads-plants.strongest_case_small: Transformers, compressors, cryogenic plant, concrete cure and NEPA review set most of a pad's calendar. A robot crew may shave only months off a 2-4 year build.
robo-earth-pads-plants.signpost: A launch provider reports a pad or propellant plant built mostly by robots; transformer lead times under 100 weeks while demand still rises.
robo-earth-pads-plants.note_2035: This is S4's lever on the mid-2030s launch clock, when hundreds of heavy flights a year are bounded by pads, propellant and airspace. A leading firm reaches about half the 2026 calendar only around 2035, too late to move launch nodes in the tree.

robo-lunar-construction.title: Robots build lunar pads, berms and roads at outpost scale
robo-lunar-construction.description: Multi-task robots build and maintain lunar surface infrastructure at outpost scale: at least two landing pads sized for heavy landers, plus blast berms and roads, about 10,000 m2 of prepared surface in all, kept in use over six or more lunar days.
robo-lunar-construction.status_oct2026: No construction payload is manifested. NASA's Project Olympus with ICON ($57.2M, through 2028) develops lunar construction methods. Northrop Grumman's robotic servicing vehicle launched Jul 21 2026. SpaceX paused Mars plans to prioritize the Moon, with an uncrewed lunar landing target of Mar 2027 (AIAA, Feb 2026). The lunar fission reactor target is 100 kWe, launch-ready in late 2029. Microwave-sintered regolith cracks when cooled faster than about 16 C/min (Coatings, Feb 2026).
robo-lunar-construction.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
robo-lunar-construction.why: Off Earth, robots are the product, so S4 changes capability most here; landed mass, power, lunar-night survival and flight demos still set dates. A 50 m pad covers about 2,000 m2, so the threshold lies well beyond the first robot-built pad (auton-robotic-landing-pad, a hard prerequisite). Work content is small and power sets the pace. Grading 10,000 m2 to 0.3 m moves 3,000 m3, about 150 days for 20 robots at 1 m3 a day each. Sintering two 50 m pads 5 cm deep heats about 350 t of regolith with about 280 MWh: about 4 months at 100 kW, or 1.5-2 years on 40 kW of daytime solar (estimates). Chain (S4): heavy cargo 2028 -> first robot-built pad 2030 -> landers carry robot variants of Earth designs from 2032 -> outpost-scale surface 2033 (Medium by 2035, if cargo landings reach 10 or more a year). The S4 analysis puts lunar construction at 0.4-0.6x of S3's calendar by 2035 on that condition. S3: dedicated machines and the slow robot path, 2035 (Low). S1 and S2: after 2035.
robo-lunar-construction.strongest_case_small: Landers can avoid pads with standoff distance and mid-body thrusters, and power limits sintering at kW to hundreds of kW. Robot count may not be the binding variable.
robo-lunar-construction.signpost: A CLPS or Moon Base manifest with a construction payload; a sintered pad that survives a plume test; 10+ cargo landings a year planned.
robo-lunar-construction.note_2035: S4 credit appears only after 2031, when robot variants of Earth designs reach lunar hardware. By 2035 the S3-S4 gap is about two years, bounded by cargo landings and power.

robo-in-space-assembly.title: Robots assemble large structures in orbit at scale
robo-in-space-assembly.description: Robots assemble structures larger than any fairing in orbit (100 m class, or radiators and arrays for 100 kW-class and larger platforms) as a repeated commercial operation, beyond one-off demonstrations.
robo-in-space-assembly.status_oct2026: NASA's OSAM-1 grew from $626-753M to over $2B and was cancelled in Mar 2024. Northrop Grumman's MRV launched Jul 21 2026 with two robotic arms and three Mission Extension Pods. Orbital compute needs large radiators: 100-kW-class deployable radiators fly about 2028 in the model.
robo-in-space-assembly.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)

One assembler doing several jobs under contract counts as repeated. Chain (S4): flight demo of certified assembly skills 2030 -> a commercial assembler designed alongside the demo on terrestrial actuators, models and contact simulation -> space qualification of mechanisms, 6-18 months (vacuum lubrication, thermal cycling, radiation-tolerant compute) -> launch 2032 -> repeated assembly 2033 (Low by 2035, since demand and space qualification bind). robo-in-space-assembly.strongest_case_small: Deployables and Starship's 9 m fairing may cover most needs through 2035, and OSAM-1 shows the cost risk of in-space assembly.
robo-in-space-assembly.signpost: A commercial assembly mission contracted after a successful demo; an orbital-compute operator specifying assembled radiators.
robo-in-space-assembly.note_2035: S4 brings the first repeated assembly about two years ahead of S3, through cheaper actuators and manipulation software. Space qualification and flight demos set the date, and deployables cover most needs, so both stay Low by 2035.

robo-aerospace-labor-quarter.status_oct2026: Near zero for general-purpose robots. Space production relies on people plus specialized automation: SpaceX had over 22,000 employees on Mar 31 2026 (S-1/A).
robo-aerospace-labor-quarter.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous robotics premise: the robot path defines S4; not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)

robo-aerospace-labor-quarter.strongest_case_small: Aerospace is low-volume and tightly regulated. Firms may automate a few high-rate lines (satellites, terminals) and leave most of the workforce untouched.
robo-aerospace-labor-quarter.signpost: Aerospace firms reporting robot-hours in production; supplier requalifications passing 100 processes.
robo-aerospace-labor-quarter.note_2035: This is where S4 departs most from S3 in aerospace production: just under a quarter of the labor on supply alone in 2035, against under 1%. Requalification at suppliers keeps the 25% line beyond 2035 on the base path.

capability-35-heavy-cadence-300.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor. 300 flights a year is about one a day. Approved Starship caps total about 145 a year (Starbase 25, LC-39A 44, SLC-37 76), and they come from completed reviews. Caps for 300+ need new site environmental assessments or impact statements (EIS median about 2.2 years, plus litigation risk) that are not yet filed. EO 14335 speeds reviews. It sets no caps. New pads take 2-4 years each, and large transformers take 128-160 weeks. Demand comes from Starlink V3 and later, orbital compute (capability-compute-launch-demand) and lunar tanker campaigns. Chain (S2): 100+ flights 2030 -> new site reviews filed 2027-28 and decided 2029-30 -> new pads and raised caps 2031-32 -> 300+ flights 2033. S3 2032: cadence runs a year ahead and compute demand is stronger. S1 2034: the plateau weakens compute demand, and Starlink alone needs far fewer flights. AI moves cadence by months through anomaly closure and range scheduling. Mach33's reference tonnage (about 35,400 t in 2029, or 240-320 flights at 112-150 t each) runs well above approved caps, so it cannot date this node. S4 gets no year or band: approvals, airspace and environmental caps bind, and robots do not touch them. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). Bands (judgment): Medium by 2035 in S2-S4 under the regulatory cap, because no review covering 300+ launches a year is filed; raise S2-S4 to High once one is. S1 Low. Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3's reference tonnage (10 Sep 2026: 71,500 t of own compute alone in 2031) implies far more than 300 flights a year; approved site caps, not demand, date this node.
capability-35-heavy-cadence-300.strongest_case_small: Starship has never met a yearly flight plan, and each failure grounds the fleet for weeks to months. Airspace closures, local opposition and litigation can cap cadence below what vehicles and pads allow.
capability-35-heavy-cadence-300.signpost: A filed environmental review covering 300 or more Starship launches a year across sites (raises S2-S4 to High); 150 or more Starship flights in 2031; a fourth Starship launch site approved; per-site caps raised above 100 a year.
capability-35-heavy-cadence-300.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. Approvals bind: caps for 300+ a year need new site reviews that are not yet filed, so S2-S4 are Medium by 2035. S4 adds nothing because approvals, airspace and environmental caps do not compress.

capability-35-internal-cost-100.title: Starship internal cost under $100 per kg
capability-35-internal-cost-100.description: SpaceX's internal cost to put a kilogram in low orbit on Starship falls below $100/kg, a third of the $300/kg milestone. Development, pads and factories are excluded.
capability-35-internal-cost-100.status_oct2026: Not yet. Flight 14 (Sep 28, 2026) cost about $4,915/kg with both stages expended (Mach33). Mach33's base case: $656/kg in 2027, about $300/kg in 2028, 8.9 flights per stack in 2029 and 18 in 2030, $13/kg in 2035 and $10/kg in 2040 (Launch Keystone v1.3, Sep 23, 2026).
capability-35-internal-cost-100.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
capability-35-internal-cost-100.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor set by flights per stack, payload per flight and production learning (Mach33 splits the early decline 56% reuse, 32% payload, 12% learning). A $85-100M stack flying 18 times with $4M of operations and 112 t of payload costs about $80-85/kg (estimate), so the threshold needs ships flying about 10 times or more as well as boosters flying 20-30 times. Mach33's base reaches 18 flights per stack in 2030, and its 0.85 learning rate per doubling of delivered mass takes the $143M stack of 2028 to about $85-100M by 2030 (estimate), so Mach33 crosses $100/kg in 2030. The model dates $300/kg a year after Mach33 (2029 against 2028); the same lag puts $100/kg at 2031. Ship reuse at that count needs the rapidly reusable heat shield, a hard prerequisite (hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield: S1 2031, S2 2030, S3 2029), so S1 follows in 2032. Band by 2031: S2 Low because the heat shield is only Medium by 2031 and the chain has no slack; S3 and S4 Medium with two years of heat-shield slack; S1 Low. S4 gets no credit: reuse and payload set cost, and refurbishment robots trim an operating cost that is already a small share. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). High by 2035 in every scenario (judgment): Mach33's 2035 base sits about 8x below the threshold, so only a failure of ship reuse keeps cost above it. That High holds only while the heat shield is High by 2035. Against Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 (wave 44 base, 23 Sep 2026): 8.9 flights per stack in 2029 and 18 in 2030 take internal cost through $100/kg in 2030; the model's one-year lag puts the node at 2031.
capability-35-internal-cost-100.strongest_case_small: If tiles are a dead end for ship reuse, ships stay near single use and cost stays near $300/kg (a $40M ship over 150 t, plus booster and operations; estimate). Internal cost also does not reach customers: Mach33's median 2035 customer revenue is about $945/kg.
capability-35-internal-cost-100.signpost: Disclosed ship flights per stack above 10; payload per flight near 150 t; cost estimates below $150/kg. SpaceX does not report cost per kg, so the signpost rests on estimates; Mach33's $13/kg for 2035 is one commercial model.
capability-35-internal-cost-100.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. The launch clock runs without AI math, so S2-S4 share the year and S1 follows its later heat shield. High by 2035 holds only while hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield is High by 2035; if the entry branch keeps it Medium, this node drops to Medium in all four scenarios. S4 gets no credit.

capability-35-cycle-halved.title: Leading firms halve development cycles
capability-35-cycle-halved.description: A leading firm completes a launch vehicle, crew or cargo vehicle, or new large spacecraft program, whose own pre-2027 comparable took 3 years or more, in at most half that time, with a published schedule analysis. Repeat constellation generations do not count (see physclock-satellite-gen-cadence); typical programs are covered by capability-program-cycle-compression.
capability-35-cycle-halved.status_oct2026: Not yet. Comparable programs today: clean-sheet launchers take 5-13 years, new engines 6-13 years and human rating about 6 years (model gate table); Starship SN8-SN15 flew in 147 days with human crews. Only a few thousand humanoids do paid work, most need teleoperation (IFR, Sep 30, 2026), and none do flight-hardware assembly.
capability-35-cycle-halved.why: Amdahl with physics held fixed (s4-embodied): 2035 ceilings are about 42-52% in S2 (judgment from the model's program shares), 56% in S3, 58-62% in S4 for typical and leading programs, and 66-67% at robot-first firms. Realized gains run below ceilings: 40-48% in S3, 42-54% in S4 typical and leading, 50-58% at robot-first firms. These ranges apply to programs run under that year's conditions, so a program finished in 2034 ran under 2032-34 conditions. Chain (S4): robots in paid flight-hardware work at leading firms 2030-31 (robo-aerospace-tolerance-work) -> processes requalified by 2032 (6-24 months each; early adopters dip first) -> program started 2032 -> completed 2034 under 2032-34 conditions, with a robot-first realized gain of about 45-54% -> published analysis 2034. S3: programs run under 2033-35 conditions realize 40-48%, so halving sits above the range and first becomes credible in 2035. S1 and S2 stay after 2035 because their ceilings sit near or below 50%. S4 credit passes all four tests: integration, test and fabrication labor bind at the firm; robots are useful there from 2030-31; no hard prerequisite lands later; and general-purpose robots go beyond the specialized test stands already in S3. Band: the P7 default (Speculative) holds for S1 and S2. S3 is Low and S4 Medium (judgment), because 50% sits inside the S4 robot-first range and above S3's. S4 Medium is a ceiling: it falls to Low if robo-24x7-integration-test is below High in S4 by 2035. Bands are judgments.
capability-35-cycle-halved.strongest_case_small: At a robot-first firm in 2035, physics time constants, reliability statistics and institutions still make up about 44% of the remaining critical path, so one anomaly or a requalification dip erases the margin. Firms may spend the gain on scope, and attribution to AI and robots will be disputed.
capability-35-cycle-halved.signpost: A firm reports a new vehicle or large spacecraft program at half the duration of its own predecessor; humanoids in paid aerospace integration and test; the first robotic-process requalification for flight hardware.
capability-35-cycle-halved.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S4 reaches it about a year before S3 (2034 against 2035) and is Medium against Low, carried by robot-first integration and test on requalified processes.
capability-35-cycle-halved.revision_note: E-trunk (2026-10-07): new node extending the spine past capability-program-cycle-compression; the main S4 outcome in the trunk. | E-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic accepted: scope narrowed to vehicles and large spacecraft whose pre-2027 comparable took 3 years or more, excluding constellation generations (as written, a 24-to-12-month satellite generation satisfied it and duplicated physclock-satellite-gen-cadence). Years S3 2034 -> 2035, S4 2033 -> 2034 (realized ranges apply to programs run under that year's conditions; a 2033 completion ran on 2031-32 robots at 40-50%). Bands kept (S3 Low, S4 Medium as a ceiling). Advocate's S2 2035/Low, S3 2033/Medium, S4 2032/High and the soft edge from physclock-satellite-gen-cadence rejected: they rested on satellite generations, which the narrowed scope excludes. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Kept: realized cuts reach 50% only at robot-first firms under 2033-35 conditions, so S4 Low 2034 and Medium 2035, S3 Low 2035. Bands unchanged.

capability-35-ai-native-large-system.title: A launcher or large spacecraft engineered mostly by AI flies
capability-35-ai-native-large-system.description: A launch-vehicle stage, a crew or cargo vehicle, or a non-constellation spacecraft over 5 t dry mass, whose design analyses, trades and verification artifacts were mostly AI-generated (with human review), flies and operates. Constellation satellites are covered by capability-ai-native-spacecraft.
capability-35-ai-native-large-system.status_oct2026: Not yet. AI-generated engine and structural geometry and agentic chip design exist piecemeal. SpaceX owns a frontier lab (SpaceXAI) and flies Starlink V3 at about 2 t. Constellation satellites do not count here.
capability-35-ai-native-large-system.why: Second-generation step: the AI-native process (capability-ai-native-spacecraft) applied to a stage, a crew or cargo vehicle, or a large non-constellation spacecraft, where hot fire, integration and qualification bind whoever does the design. Constellation satellites are excluded so that one AI-designed Starlink generation cannot satisfy both nodes. Chain (S3): AI-native smallsat flies 2029 -> stage or vehicle design starts 2029 -> a four-year derivative program at 0.7-0.75x flies 2032. S2: 0.8-0.85x on the same base gives 3.2-3.4 years, so 2033. S1: the smallsat flies in 2031, so a large system follows after 2035. A clean-sheet program (5-13 years at 0.7-0.8x in S3) would land later; derivatives set the date. Band: the P7 default (Speculative) holds for S1. S2 Low and S3 Medium by 2035 (judgment): hot fire and flight tests are unchanged, and firms may not disclose what share AI produced. S4 equals S3: qualification, flight tests and disclosure bind, and integration robots add months at most. Bands are judgments.
capability-35-ai-native-large-system.strongest_case_small: Large systems carry more legacy process and liability, and firms may not publish what share AI produced. A launch stage is bound by hot fire and flight tests whoever designs it.
capability-35-ai-native-large-system.signpost: A launch firm or vehicle maker publishes AI-generated verification evidence for a new stage, vehicle or large spacecraft before flight, then reports flight success.
capability-35-ai-native-large-system.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension, scoped to stages, vehicles and large non-constellation spacecraft. S4 equals S3 because hot fire, flight tests and disclosure bind; robots on the build add months at most.

frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.title: Clay recognizes an AI answer to unforced Navier–Stokes
frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.description: The Clay Mathematics Institute states that an AI-produced proof settles the unforced 3D Navier–Stokes problem, either global smoothness (statements A/B) or blowup from smooth data with zero force, or changes its Millennium Problems listing to say so. Clay rules need publication in a qualifying outlet, two years, and general acceptance. Engineering effect: nil.
frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.status_oct2026: No unforced claim exists. Clay lists Navier–Stokes as unsolved, and its president called the evaluation of the forced claim 'deliberately unhurried'. OpenAI says it will not claim the prize for the forced result. Petrillo-Glimm (Sep 20, 2026) proposed a target for a programmatic unforced search.
frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.why: Chain: an unforced answer passes outside checks (frontier-ns-unforced: S1 2030, S2 2029, S3 2028), then refereed publication (about a year), then the two-year rule and general acceptance, then Clay's advisory board and a special committee (at least 6-12 months). That puts the earliest statement about four years after the check: 2032 in S3, 2033 in S2, 2034 in S1. The only precedent took about seven years from preprint to award (Perelman: 2002-03 to Mar 2010). The institutional clock runs at 1.0x in every scenario; only the start date differs. If Clay first accepts the forced result under (C) or (D), the prize problem is closed and a statement on the unforced case becomes discretionary, so frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling can pre-empt this node as well as speed it. Bands by 2035: Medium in S3 and S4, where about three years remain after eligibility; Low in S2, where the clock runs out only about 2033; Speculative in S1. Clay may still wait, or never rule without a claimant. This is the event readers will hear as 'AI solved a Millennium problem'. It changes no engine, heat shield or orbit (tl-position-2), and robots add nothing.
frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.strongest_case_small: Clay may never rule if no one claims the prize, and general acceptance of a long AI-produced proof can take many years. If Clay accepts the forced result first, the prize problem is closed. Even a ruling changes no CFD code, since codes already regularize.
frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.signpost: Refereed publication of an unforced Navier–Stokes proof (either answer) starts the two-year clock; then a Clay statement or a change to its Millennium Problems listing.
frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the Clay clock runs out about four years after the outside check, so the earliest year is 2032-34. A Clay ruling on the forced claim can close the prize first. The clock is institutional, so S4 equals S3.
frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.revision_note: E-math-frontier (2026-10-07): new node. Extends the famous-problem chain past frontier-ns-unforced; frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling keeps the forced claim. | R-math-frontier (2026-10-07): [skeptic] years S3 2031 -> 2032, S2 2032 -> 2033, S1 2033 -> 2034: Clay's board and committee add at least 6-12 months after eligibility, and the only precedent took about seven years; band_2031 Speculative in all scenarios; band_2035 S2 Medium -> Low, S1 Low -> Speculative; pre-emption by the forced ruling added. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Kept: about four years from the outside check (S3 Medium 2029) to a Clay statement puts S3/S4 Medium at 2034; S2 Low from 2033. Skeptic (seven-year precedent, pre-emption by the forced ruling) vs advocate (either answer counts) resolved at 2034. Bands unchanged.
frontier-35-clay-unforced-ns.gate_note: Clay's process binds; the unforced answer itself (cognitive) is the runner-up.

frontier-35-math-supply-chain.title: Certified math on demand reaches the supplier base
frontier-35-math-supply-chain.description: Tier-2 and tier-3 space suppliers (structures, propulsion components, avionics boxes, thermal hardware) routinely produce analysis with AI-derived proofs, guaranteed error bars or certified rare-event bounds and deliver it in data packages to primes and operators. This is the second wave after the leading firms (frontier-math-unbinds).
frontier-35-math-supply-chain.status_oct2026: Suppliers run commercial FEA and CFD tools with small specialist teams (general). Research-grade math models are internal to the labs. Export-control (ITAR/EAR) and defense cybersecurity rules limit which models may see supplier technical data (general).
frontier-35-math-supply-chain.why: Diffusion lags the leaders. Suppliers have small analysis teams, older toolchains, fixed-price contracts and export-control limits on which models may see their data. They adopt after primes and operators (frontier-math-unbinds: S2 2029, S3 2028) and after accredited models run on controlled networks (capability-controlled-data-access: 2028 in S2 and S3). A three-year lag gives S2 2032. S3 is 2031 because near-free cognition from about 2029 makes the service cheap for small firms. Plateau reaches the leaders' step only about 2033, so suppliers fall after 2035. Suppliers run commercial FE and CFD codes, so certified bounds also reach them as tool updates (struct-verified-fe-solvers: S2 2029; prop-cfd-auto-vv: S2 2028; both soft), after the usual version lag and tool validation. Primes speed adoption when they ask for certified bounds in supplier deliverables, which needs a shared rulebook (physclock-credibility-evidence-standard, soft); open-weight models at research level (soft) let small firms run them on their own networks. Bands by 2035: S3 and S4 are High because near-free cognition and certified commercial tools have had about four years to spread, and the node needs no certifier acceptance. S2 is Medium: three years after 2032 is short for many small firms, many build to print, and no contract data requirement is in motion. Effect (judgment): the same 8-14% of engineering hours as at the leaders, plus fewer late design changes from interface rework. Robots do no analysis, so S4 equals S3.
frontier-35-math-supply-chain.strongest_case_small: Many suppliers build to print, and the prime owns most analysis, so supplier math was never the bottleneck. Small firms adopt what customers demand, and liability keeps human sign-off.
frontier-35-math-supply-chain.signpost: A prime, NASA or Space Force contract data requirement asks suppliers for analysis with certified error bounds or machine-checked derivations; or an industry or agency survey finds most surveyed space suppliers delivering AI-produced analysis.
frontier-35-math-supply-chain.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the second wave after the leading firms lands about 2032 in the base case. Robots do no analysis, so S4 equals S3.
frontier-35-math-supply-chain.revision_note: E-math-frontier (2026-10-07): new node. Extends frontier-math-unbinds to the supply chain in 2032-35. | R-math-frontier (2026-10-07): [advocate, partly] commercial-solver channel added, with soft edges from struct-verified-fe-solvers and prop-cfd-auto-vv; S2 High and S1 Low rejected (three years is short for many small firms; S1 lands after 2035). [skeptic, rejected] S3 High kept: the node needs no certifier acceptance, so the regulatory cap does not apply, and certified bounds arrive inside the commercial tools suppliers already run. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Kept: suppliers lag leaders by about three years (S2 2032 earliest), so S2 Medium 2034; S3/S4 Medium 2032 and High 2035 as near-free cognition and certified commercial tools spread. Skeptic (build-to-print suppliers, later) vs advocate (tool updates carry bounds, earlier) resolved at the seed years. Bands unchanged.
frontier-35-math-supply-chain.gate_note: Supplier adoption binds; export-control limits on which models see supplier data (regulatory) are the runner-up.

frontier-35-certification-unbinds.title: A certifier audits AI analysis instead of redoing it
frontier-35-certification-unbinds.description: A certifying authority or mission-assurance office accepts AI-produced analysis with guaranteed bounds from verified numerics and independently checked derivations as certification evidence. Its specialists audit a sample of the key stress, thermal and GNC analyses instead of re-running all of them, so specialist re-analysis stops setting the pace of certification. The likely first case is uncrewed: NASA Launch Services certification of a launch vehicle for high-priority payloads (NPD 8610.7) or Space Force mission assurance for national security launches. A crewed delta certification comes later.
frontier-35-certification-unbinds.status_oct2026: NASA-STD-7009B (Mar 2024) requires a credibility assessment for models and simulations and has no route for AI-produced analysis. DO-333 covers formal methods in airborne software only (general). NASA launch-vehicle certification (NPD 8610.7) and Space Force mission assurance, where the Aerospace Corporation re-runs analyses, rely on independent specialist re-analysis (general). The NASA Engineering and Safety Center was set up after Columbia to give independent assessments (general). No authority has accepted AI-produced analysis as certification evidence.
frontier-35-certification-unbinds.why: The design-side outcome (frontier-math-unbinds) runs under each program's own sign-off. Certification is where scarce specialists still set the schedule, because certifiers re-run key analyses themselves. Dropping that step needs a rulebook for AI-made analysis (physclock-credibility-evidence-standard: S2 2029, S3 2028) and guaranteed bounds from verified numerics (infra-verified-numerics: S2 and S3 2028). Certifiers will likely re-run in full the first analyses that earn test credit (physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit: S2 2031, S3 2030, soft). The audit step then needs one delta certification, about 2-3 years. A full human-rating cycle takes about 6 years (Crew Dragon: 2014 to 2020), so the first case is uncrewed. Hence S2 2033 and S3 2032. Plateau gets the rulebook late, so the node falls after 2035. A software-proof precedent helps (infra-tool-qualification, soft), and so does crewed AI-proof credit (verif-hls-autonomy-certification, soft). Credit for Lean-checked derivations of analysis needs a qualified proof kernel, which no node models yet. Certifiers that re-run analyses with their own AI (physclock-regulator-ai-capacity, soft) shorten re-analysis earlier; this node marks the later step of dropping it. This node replaces specialist re-analysis. struct-35-test-standards-codify-ai-credit replaces tests, and verif-35-standards-proof-route covers software proofs. Bands: certifier acceptance with no named mechanism in motion caps 2035 at Medium (S3, S4). S2 is Low because only about two years remain after its earliest date. Institutional clocks set the date, so robots give no S4 credit. Effect: shorter review cycles for certified vehicles; tests and flights do not shorten (tl-position-4).
frontier-35-certification-unbinds.strongest_case_small: Certifiers answer for crew safety and may keep human re-derivation of critical analyses whatever the tools. Review time is mostly test evidence, boards and paperwork, so removing math checks saves little calendar time.
frontier-35-certification-unbinds.signpost: NASA Launch Services, Space Force mission assurance, the FAA or ESA accepts a certification package in which AI-produced analysis with guaranteed bounds replaces independent specialist re-analysis, with humans auditing a sample. A crewed delta certification that does the same is the second signpost.
frontier-35-certification-unbinds.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: certifiers move from re-running AI analysis to auditing it about two years after analysis first earns test credit, so 2032-33 in S2-S4, first on uncrewed vehicles. Institutional clocks bind, so S4 equals S3.

frontier-35-second-millennium.title: AI settles a Millennium problem other than Navier–Stokes
frontier-35-second-millennium.description: An AI-produced proof settles the Riemann hypothesis, the Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture or the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, either way, and passes outside checks (T4 Lean check or T2+ expert acceptance). Navier–Stokes and P vs NP have their own nodes. Engineering effect: nil.
frontier-35-second-millennium.status_oct2026: Open. Fortune (Oct 7, 2026) reported progress by OpenAI, short of solutions, on three other Millennium problems; no manuscript is public, so the report is T1 at best. The Riemann hypothesis is already stated in Lean's Mathlib, so a Lean proof could be checked quickly; the other three need library work before they can be stated in Lean (general).
frontier-35-second-millennium.premise_tier: T1 at best (press report of progress, no manuscript)
frontier-35-second-millennium.why: A scenario signpost with no hardware effect. Unforced Navier–Stokes has a forced precursor; these four problems have none, and Yang–Mills and Hodge also need posing and library work before a check. Judgment: several doublings beyond the unforced Navier–Stokes rung. S3 reaches near-free cognition about 2029, so a checked result is credible from 2030 and about as likely as not by 2035 (Medium). S2 gets cheap and abundant cognition only in 2033-35, so 2033 at the earliest and Low by 2035. S1 falls after 2035. Either answer counts. Reported progress is T1 at best, so no band goes above Medium. A move from Erdos-tier to Millennium-tier results outside fluids is the clearest public test of S3 against S2 in 2032-35. Robots add nothing, so S4 equals S3.
frontier-35-second-millennium.strongest_case_small: Even a proof of the Riemann hypothesis changes no engine, orbit or flight code. The problems may need ideas that scaling does not supply, as for P vs NP.
frontier-35-second-millennium.signpost: A lab claims one of the four problems with a Lean proof or a full manuscript, followed by a Comparator pass and statement audit, or by acceptance from specialists in the field.
frontier-35-second-millennium.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. A scenario signpost: Recursive cognition makes a Millennium result outside fluids about as likely as not by 2035, and the base case is Low. Robots add nothing, so S4 equals S3.
frontier-35-second-millennium.revision_note: R-math-frontier (2026-10-07): new node from the advocate review, added to branch members only. The proposed soft edge from frontier-ns-unforced was dropped, because fluid methods do not carry to these problems. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Kept: S3 near-free cognition about 2029 makes a checked result credible from 2030 and about as likely as not by 2035, so Medium 2033; S2 Low from 2033. Bands unchanged.
frontier-35-second-millennium.gate_note: The mathematics binds; posing and library work before a check (formalization) is the runner-up.

verif-35-mars-verified-landing.title: A Mars lander flies proof-checked landing and fault logic
verif-35-mars-verified-landing.description: A lander reaches the surface of Mars flying entry, descent and landing guidance and fault-management logic whose key properties are machine-checked: sensor gating, mode switches, engine and reboot logic, and guidance numerics, with assumptions red-teamed against Mars atmosphere and terrain models. The team says so publicly. Any Mars lander counts, from a 20 t Starship to a small commercial lander.
verif-35-mars-verified-landing.status_oct2026: No lander has reached Mars since 2021. Launch windows: late 2026, Dec 2028-Jan 2029, early 2031, about Apr 2033 and about mid-2035, so landings inside the horizon come in late 2029, late 2031 and late 2033. Landers already scheduled for 2028, such as ESA's Rosalind Franklin rover, fix their software before proof agents mature (general). Schiaparelli (2016) crashed when a saturated inertial unit led its software to compute a negative altitude.
verif-35-mars-verified-landing.why: Mars is where proof-checked autonomy matters most. One-way light time of 3-22 minutes rules out ground help during a descent of about 7 minutes, and Schiaparelli shows that one wrong assumption in fault logic loses a lander. The clock is the window. Chain (S2): toolchain 2028 and per-flight re-proof at the reusable launch operator 2029 -> that operator's first Mars landing, late 2031 from the early-2031 window, carries re-proved landing and fault logic, since its software changes between flights -> 2031 at the earliest. A new government lander needs a freeze 12-18 months before launch and lands in the 2033 window. S3 is the same year because windows and the operator's choices bind. S1: 2033. The 2035 window lands in 2036, past the horizon. Bands: this is a joint event. A Mars landing by 2035 is Medium (hyper-mars-heavy-landing), the likeliest carrier may not use or disclose proofs, and no funded non-Starship lander targets 2031 or 2033, so S2-S4 are Low by 2035 and Speculative by 2031. Mars truth data is scarce (about 10 successful landings ever), so the lunar-derived envelopes in verif-environment-assumption-models transfer only partly.
verif-35-mars-verified-landing.strongest_case_small: Mars landings stay rare through 2035, perhaps a handful, and most risk sits in entry physics, supersonic retropropulsion and hardware, which proofs do not touch. The lead candidate builds confidence through flight and may never say what it proved.
verif-35-mars-verified-landing.signpost: A Mars lander team, commercial or government, stating in a press kit, paper or review that its descent guidance and fault logic are machine-checked, for the 2031 or 2033 window.
verif-35-mars-verified-landing.note_2035: New node: the late-2031 and late-2033 Mars landings fall inside the horizon, but a landing, proof-checked logic and public disclosure must all happen, so it stays Low. S4 equals S3 because launch windows and landing physics bind, and robots add nothing to either.
verif-35-mars-verified-landing.revision_note: E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): added for the 2035 horizon. Hard edge from verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight; soft from hyper-mars-heavy-landing (any Mars lander counts), environment envelopes, optimizer certificates, certified EDL guidance and per-flight re-proof. | E-verified-autonomy resolver (2026-10-07): advocate's S2 2033 -> 2031 accepted: the likeliest carrier re-proves software between flights, so the new-program freeze does not bind (the reasoning B-round used for verif-rpo-assured-autonomy); soft edge from verif-launch-fsw-per-flight added. Skeptic's joint-event bands accepted: band_2031 S3-S4 Low -> Speculative, band_2035 S1 Low -> Speculative and S2-S4 Medium -> Low (Medium landing odds times adoption times disclosure gives about 0.1-0.3). S2 now equals S3. Thesis changed to Low. | R9-launch (2026-10-27): gate launch -> launch-internal (SpaceX's own manifest; Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 books Starlink, SpaceX's orbital compute, Moon and Mars cargo and NASA's lunar tanker flights in the internal account). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Low 2033 (the late-2031 landing carrying disclosed proof-checked logic is under 10%; the 2033 window passes it); stays Low by 2035 as a joint event.
verif-35-mars-verified-landing.gate_note: Mars windows bind; the carrier choosing to fly and disclose proof-checked logic (adoption) is the runner-up.

verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.title: Multicore space chip flies with proven worst-case timing
verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.description: A radiation-tolerant multicore processor or SoC flies on an operational mission with machine-checked proofs that flight software keeps its worst-case timing whatever runs on the other cores, including an onboard AI payload. This closes the gap left by today's verified stacks, where spatial isolation is proven and timing interference is only measured.
verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.status_oct2026: Multicore timing interference is measured and argued, and aviation accepts that evidence through FAA AC 20-193 and EASA AMC 20-193 (general). No flight processor has a proof of it. seL4 proves spatial isolation, and its time-protection work is research (general). verif-verified-onboard-stack and verif-onboard-ai-guardrails both name measured timing as their open gap.
verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.why: Orbital compute and onboard agents put AI payloads on the same processor as flight software, and this branch's verified-stack and guardrail nodes stop where timing is measured. Proving timing needs a processor designed for analyzable timing (partitioned caches, a predictable interconnect) plus RTL proofs, which hardware proof agents make cheap. Fabrication runs of 3-4 months, scarce heavy-ion beam time and 1-2 years of qualification do not compress, and after qualification, design-in and spacecraft integration add about a year before an operational flight. Chain (S2): hardware proof agents 2028 -> a timing-predictable design proved 2029-30 -> tape-out and radiation test 2030-31 -> qualification 2031-33 -> first operational flight 2034. S3 is a year earlier, 2033, because its AI-designed processors come a year sooner (capability-ai-eda-space-processor). S1 lands after 2035. Bands: Medium by 2035 in S3-S4, where near-free RTL proofs let any new space processor carry them and onboard agents create mixed-criticality demand. Low in S2, because most operators accept measured isolation or use separate processors.
verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.strongest_case_small: Operators can put flight software and AI on separate processors, which costs little mass at orbital-compute scale, and aviation already certifies multicore systems on measured evidence. A proven-timing processor may stay a niche part.
verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.signpost: A space processor vendor or agency program releasing a part with formal timing-isolation proofs; a flight announcement that cites them.
verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.note_2035: New node: a second-generation item that closes the timing gap the verified onboard stack leaves open, reachable in 2033-34. S4 equals S3 because fabs, beam time and qualification bind, and none is labor-bound.
verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.revision_note: E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): added for the 2035 horizon. Hard edges from verif-hardware-proof-agents and verif-verified-onboard-stack; soft from capability-ai-eda-space-processor and verif-onboard-ai-guardrails (demand). | E-verified-autonomy resolver (2026-10-07): skeptic's changes accepted: S2 2033 -> 2034 and S3-S4 2032 -> 2033 (the draft fused qualification and first operational flight into one year), band_2031 S3-S4 Low -> Speculative (the year is after 2031), band_2035 S2 Medium -> Low (thin demand: separate processors are cheap and AC 20-193 accepts measured evidence). Resolver: band_2035 S1 Low -> Speculative, since S1 has no chain inside the horizon. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S3-S4 Low 2033, Medium 2035 (seed 2034): the earliest year already uses the short end of fab, radiation-test and qualification lags, so a 30% chance needs a year of slip margin. S2 Low 2034. Skeptic (qualification slips 1-2 years) vs advocate (AI-designed processors come a year sooner in S3): Medium by 2035 kept, crossing moved to 2035.
verif-35-proven-timing-isolation.gate_note: Qualification and beam time bind; tape-out and fabrication runs (fabrication) are the runner-up.

verif-35-standards-proof-route.title: Flight-software standards write in credit for AI proofs
verif-35-standards-proof-route.description: A flight-software or assurance standard names AI-written, checker-verified proofs as an accepted verification method, so programs no longer argue the route plan by plan. Examples: a revision of NASA's NPR 7150.2 or NASA-STD-8739.8, an ECSS software standard, or an RTCA/EUROCAE update to DO-333.
verif-35-standards-proof-route.status_oct2026: DO-333 (2011) gives aviation credit for formal methods, and NPR 7150.2D (2022) and ECSS software standards permit them. No standard mentions AI-generated proofs. DO-178B came in 1992 and DO-178C in 2011. NPR 7150.2 revisions came in 2014, 2019 and 2022 (general). RCC 319 editions came in September 2014, July 2019 and June 2025 (RCC 319-25, Range Commanders Council, posted on the TRMC site).
verif-35-standards-proof-route.why: Plan-by-plan acceptance (infra-tool-qualification) sets precedent; a standard makes it the default and lets suppliers and small teams use the route without a bespoke argument. Standards bodies revise on 3-10 year cycles and usually codify practice after several programs have used it. Chain (S2): first plan acceptance 2030 -> completed certifications that bank the credit 2032-34 -> several programs on the route and the next revision of a NASA, ESA, RTCA or RCC document naming it 2034. S3 is a year earlier, 2033. S1 lands after 2035. Bands: S3-S4 Medium by 2035 because several bodies each revise inside the window; S2 Low because it reaches several programs only in 2033-34. No revision that addresses AI proofs is in motion today, so the cap holds at Medium.
verif-35-standards-proof-route.strongest_case_small: Standards may never single out AI. The checker-not-generator route already fits DO-333 and DO-330, so bodies can leave it to guidance material and individual plans, and this node would never be marked achieved even as practice changes.
verif-35-standards-proof-route.signpost: A draft revision of NPR 7150.2, NASA-STD-8739.8, an ECSS software standard or DO-333 that mentions machine-generated proofs; an RTCA or EUROCAE committee taking up the topic.
verif-35-standards-proof-route.note_2035: New node: codifying the route becomes reachable in 2033-34 once several programs have banked credit. S4 equals S3 because committees, comment periods and revision cycles are institutional clocks.
verif-35-standards-proof-route.revision_note: E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): added for the 2035 horizon. Hard edge from infra-tool-qualification; soft from the credibility-evidence standard, regulator AI capacity and the crewed certification precedent. | E-verified-autonomy resolver (2026-10-07): skeptic's changes accepted: S2 2033 -> 2034 and S3-S4 2032 -> 2033 (the node's own codify-after-several-programs logic and the 2-4-year certification lag in infra-tool-qualification), band_2035 S1 Low -> Speculative and S2 Medium -> Low; removed from the spine because it may never be marked achieved. RCC 319-25 (June 2025) checked and cited; NPR 7150.2 cadence added. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S3-S4 Medium 2034, a year after the earliest revision, because several bodies (NASA, ESA, RTCA, RCC) each revise inside the window after completed certifications in 2031-33. S2 Low 2034. Medium cap: no revision addressing AI proofs is in motion.
verif-35-standards-proof-route.gate_note: Standards revision cycles bind; several programs banking credit on the route (adoption) is the runner-up.

verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.title: Flight-software verification takes half the calendar time
verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.description: At a leading space firm, the calendar time to fully verify a safety-critical flight-software release, including proofs, hardware-in-the-loop runs and integrated vehicle regression, falls to half its 2026 level, and the firm, a customer or an agency review reports it. Proof work stops being the long pole by about 2029; this node needs the physical test slice to shrink as well.
verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.status_oct2026: Proof and unit verification are a large share of software cost, but hardware-in-the-loop rigs and integrated tests set release pace at most programs (general). astro-gnc-assurance-cost expects only a 20-30% cut in verification calendar time in S2 for that reason. Starliner's 2019 software errors were catchable by the end-to-end integrated test the program did not run (general).
verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.why: Once proofs are cheap, hardware-in-the-loop rigs and integrated vehicle tests set the verification calendar. Halving it needs that slice to shrink: more rigs (capital), AI-run sequencing (S3) and, in S4, general-purpose robots that reconfigure rigs, swap units and run integrated vehicle tests around the clock. Sketch (assumptions: rigs and integrated tests are about 80% of calendar time, and proofs cut the rest to 0.1-0.15 of 2026). S2: test compresses 1.2-1.4x by 2035, so the calendar ends near 0.6-0.7 of 2026 and never halves. S3: test at 0.60-0.69 of 2026 by 2035 gives 0.50-0.58, half only at the edge in 2035. S4 at robot-first firms: if half the test slice is robot-bound vehicle testing (2.1-2.8x by 2035 in embodied/research-space.json, less a quarter for adoption and requalification) and half is real-time HIL rig time at about 1.6x, the calendar reaches 0.48-0.54 in 2032 and 0.44-0.50 by 2035. Chain (S4): robot-run integration and test at a robot-first firm 2031 -> half the calendar at the optimistic edge 2032 -> one full release cycle and a report 2033. S3: AI-run rigs alone reach half only in 2035. Bands: S4 Medium by 2035 because its central case sits just under half but must be measured and reported; S3 Low because only its edge case reaches half.
verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.strongest_case_small: Leading firms already release flight software fast by flying often, so the change may not be measurable, and firms rarely publish verification calendars. Real-time HIL and soak runs do not shorten with robots, and requalifying robot-run test processes costs 6-24 months before any gain.
verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.signpost: A launch or spacecraft operator reporting release verification time, hardware-in-the-loop and integrated tests included, at half its earlier level; robot-run integration and test at a leading space firm.
verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.note_2035: The one place in this branch where S4 differs: robot-run vehicle tests at robot-first firms give S4 2033 and Medium against S3 2035 and Low, a larger credit than the usual 0.5-1.5 years because ground test is about 80% of the remaining calendar. It needs robo-24x7-integration-test (S4 2031), a requalified test process and one full release cycle before a firm can report.
verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.revision_note: E-verified-autonomy (2035 horizon, S4): added for the 2035 horizon. Hard edge from astro-gnc-assurance-cost; soft from AI-run test stands, per-flight re-proof and robo-24x7-integration-test. S4 credit under the four-condition rule. | E-verified-autonomy resolver (2026-10-07): years S2 2034 -> >2035, S3 2033 -> 2035, S4 2032 -> 2033; band_2035 S2 Low -> Speculative, S3 Medium -> Low, S4 Medium kept. Skeptic: the draft's own sketch left S3 near 0.55 by 2035 and S2 at 0.6-0.7, so neither halves at the draft's years; real-time HIL time is only partly robot-bound; the robo-requal-standard soft edge duplicated robo-24x7-integration-test's prerequisite chain and is dropped. Skeptic's S4 2034 and Low rejected: read at the same optimistic edge as S3, S4 crosses half in 2032 and reports in 2033, and its central case is under half by 2035. verif-35-verification-calendar-halved.gate_note: HIL rig and integrated-vehicle test time binds; buying more rigs (capital) is the runner-up.

comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.title: Satellites in service switch to post-quantum encryption
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.description: At least one operator of long-lived satellites (GEO, MEO or a government constellation) switches the key exchange and command authentication of several operational satellites from RSA or elliptic-curve algorithms to post-quantum or hybrid algorithms in orbit, using rekey and update protocols with machine-checked proofs. The satellites are operational, in revenue or mission service, and none is a demonstration spacecraft. Achieved means the operator discloses the switch and the proofs, or a government buyer confirms them.
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.status_oct2026: No operational fleet has switched in orbit. NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft, Nov 2024) deprecates 112-bit RSA and ECC by 2030 and disallows quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms by 2035. CNSA 2.0 requires new national-security acquisitions to comply from Jan 1 2027 and aims for quantum-resistant national-security systems by 2035 (general). Telecommand on pre-shared AES-256 keys is already quantum-safe. The Department of War's post-quantum strategy (Jun 23 2026) requires all its systems to support post-quantum crypto or be phased out by Dec 31 2030, and to use it by Dec 31 2031 unless otherwise noted (postquantum.com, Oct 2 2026). CNSA 2.0 phases out legacy equipment by 2033 (postquantum.com).
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.premise_tier: n/a (mandate deadlines; the AI-math share is the machine-checked update path)
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.why: The deadlines force a switch with or without AI. AI makes the switch on a 15-year asset safe to attempt: the rekey and update protocols carry machine-checked proofs, so a failed swap is unlikely to cost the command link. Only satellites that do public-key operations on board need it. Bent-pipe GEO payloads and AES-only telecommand do not. The main population is government satellites bought before CNSA 2.0 took effect in 2027 that stay in service past the Department of War's Dec 2031 use deadline, plus commercial GEO and MEO satellites with agile crypto that serve government users. Chain (S2): architecture 2028, flight demo 2029, switches made to meet the 2031 deadline, first disclosed or buyer-confirmed cutover 2032. S3 equals S2, because deadlines, contract lags and disclosure bind, and proofs are cheap in both by 2029. S1 2033. Disclosure is the main risk, which holds S2-S4 at Medium for 2035.
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.strongest_case_small: Most operators will replace satellites or rely on pre-shared symmetric keys and ground-side controls, so few in-orbit switches happen. Government programs that do switch will not disclose the details. The Department of War may grant exceptions for satellites near the end of their lives.
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.signpost: A GEO or government operator announcing a completed in-orbit post-quantum cutover with published proofs; CNSA 2.0 compliance reports for space systems; Department of War exception lists that name space systems.
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.note_2035: This is the 2032-35 end of the post-quantum chain. The Department of War's Dec 2031 use deadline pulls the first disclosed switch to 2032, and disclosure holds S2-S4 at Medium. S4 adds nothing because mandates, contract lags and operator choice bind.
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon. | E-networks resolver (2026-10-07): Years S1 2034 -> 2033, S2 2033 -> 2032, S3/S4 stay 2032, so S3 now equals S2 (skeptic: the gate is institutional and the overlay applies equally to S2-S4). Advocate's S3 2031 rejected. band_2035 S1 Speculative -> Low, S2 Low -> Medium (advocate: the DoW strategy's Dec 2031 use deadline, verified at postquantum.com, creates a real population of in-orbit switches, which answers the skeptic's thin-population point). Description now excludes demonstration spacecraft (skeptic). | E-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): title shortened from 'Satellites in orbit switch to post-quantum keys with proven update paths'. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2-S4 Medium 2033 (seed 2034): the Dec 2031 DoW use deadline forces switches in 2031-32 and CNSA 2.0 phases out legacy equipment by 2033, a second forcing date with compliance reporting as a disclosure path. Skeptic (government crypto operations are rarely disclosed, 2034-35) against advocate (a real population of in-service switches, 2032): 2033. Bands unchanged.
comms-35-in-orbit-pq-cutover.gate_note: The DoW Dec 2031 use deadline and CNSA 2.0 (regulatory) set the date; operators performing and disclosing the switch (adoption) is the runner-up.

comms-35-certified-shell-in-service.title: Constellation designed with certified tools enters service
comms-35-certified-shell-in-service.description: A new constellation shell or satellite generation whose orbits, beam plan, spectrum use and laser topology came from a design optimizer with certified interference and capacity bounds (comms-constellation-design-optimizer) is built, launched and in commercial service, and its coordination showings carry those bounds. Achieved means the operator states that a shell in service was designed this way, or its filings show it.
comms-35-certified-shell-in-service.status_oct2026: None. More than 10,000 commercial communications satellites operate in LEO and 50,000+ more are planned; design tools are in-house and uncertified. V3 Starlink satellites need Starship (33FG).
comms-35-certified-shell-in-service.why: Design tools act through new satellites. From a filing to a shell in service takes one satellite generation plus deployment: 18-36 months in 2026, 0.5-0.7x of that by 2031, plus launching hundreds of satellites. S2: optimizer used in a filing 2029, satellites built 2030-31, service 2032. S3: 2028 and 2031. S1: 2031 and 2034. Many filings are placeholders, but Part 100 schedules are machine-readable, so certified bounds in coordination showings are visible. That holds S2 at Speculative for 2031 and lets it reach High by 2035.
comms-35-certified-shell-in-service.strongest_case_small: Launch, manufacturing, spectrum rights and business plans shape constellations more than design software. Incumbents' in-house tools are good, and the certified bounds may change a design by a few percent.
comms-35-certified-shell-in-service.signpost: An operator or new entrant stating that a shell in service came from a design optimizer with certified bounds; coordination showings for a new shell that cite certified interference bounds.
comms-35-certified-shell-in-service.note_2035: Several new shells enter service after S2's 2032 date, and certified bounds in filings make the design method visible, so S2 reaches High with S3. S4 adds nothing because launch binds at the leading operators.
comms-35-certified-shell-in-service.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. comms-35-ntn-standard-ai-codes.title: AI-designed codes ship in a satellite link standard
comms-35-ntn-standard-ai-codes.description: An AI-designed short-block code, decoder or synchronization scheme with machine-checked finite-blocklength claims is part of a published 3GPP non-terrestrial-network release or a CCSDS standard, and ships in handsets, modems or ground terminals.
comms-35-ntn-standard-ai-codes.status_oct2026: No AI-designed code is in any 3GPP or CCSDS standard. LLM-guided search found seven record binary linear codes in Sep 2026 (arXiv 2609.37056). 3GPP's first normative 6G work is expected in Release 21, with commercial 6G around 2030 (general).
comms-35-ntn-standard-ai-codes.why: Short blocks are where coding gains remain. 0.5 dB on a handset uplink at the beam edge can decide whether a link closes, and telecommand and IoT links use short blocks too. The first 6G coding choices are made in Release 20-21 work around 2026-29, before AI code designs arrive in 2028 (S2), so the first realistic window is an enhancement release frozen around 2030-31 or a CCSDS revision. Chipsets and modems ship 1-2 years after a freeze. Committees do not speed up with cognition, so S3 equals S2. S2: contributions from 2028, freeze 2030-31, shipping 2033. S1: 2035. Core codes rarely change between releases (LTE kept turbo codes, NR kept LDPC and polar codes), so the likeliest entry is a control-channel, synchronization or CCSDS short-block code. Conservative committees, decoder complexity and patents hold S2 at Medium.
comms-35-ntn-standard-ai-codes.strongest_case_small: Most links already use standardized LDPC, turbo or polar codes within tenths of a dB of finite-blocklength bounds. 6G channel coding may be fixed before AI-designed proposals are ready, leaving the next window after 2035.
comms-35-ntn-standard-ai-codes.signpost: A 3GPP or CCSDS contribution with an AI-designed code that is accepted into a release; a chipset vendor shipping it.
comms-35-ntn-standard-ai-codes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: release and chipset cycles put the first shipping AI-designed codes in 2033. S4 adds nothing because committees and chipset cycles bind.

comms-35-leo-pnt-aviation-approval.title: Aviation approves low-orbit navigation with proven integrity
comms-35-leo-pnt-aviation-approval.description: An aviation authority (FAA or EASA) or an ICAO standard accepts a LEO navigation service, alone or combined with GNSS, for an operation that needs integrity, for example through an RTCA or EUROCAE avionics standard, resting on the provider's published integrity overbounds and fault statistics.
comms-35-leo-pnt-aviation-approval.status_oct2026: No aviation approval of any LEO navigation service. Xona announced on Oct 7 2026 that Pulsar is entering scaled production (Xona). Aviation GNSS integrity standards such as SBAS and ARAIM took about a decade each (general).
comms-35-leo-pnt-aviation-approval.why: Aviation needs integrity at about 1e-7 per approach (general), and overbounds for a new constellation need years of its own fault history. Chain (S2): service with published bounds 2029, three or more years of fault data, avionics standards drafted in parallel, approval 2035 at the earliest. S3 equals S2: fault history and committee calendars bind, and the institutional overlay is the same in every scenario. No named approval path exists for LEO navigation, so every scenario stays Speculative.
comms-35-leo-pnt-aviation-approval.strongest_case_small: Aviation integrity standards change over a decade. Spoofing pressure may push aviation toward hardened GNSS receivers and inertial sensors before it accepts a new satellite service.
comms-35-leo-pnt-aviation-approval.signpost: An RTCA or EUROCAE working group opening a standard for LEO navigation; ICAO navigation-systems panel work on LEO signals; a provider publishing several years of fault-rate data.
comms-35-leo-pnt-aviation-approval.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. Fault-history data and aviation committees bind, so the node sits at the edge of the horizon in every scenario and S4 adds nothing.

comms-35-joint-detection-ground-station.title: Deep-space laser ground station gets more bits per photon
comms-35-joint-detection-ground-station.description: An operational optical ground station receiving from a deep-space or far-cislunar laser terminal uses a joint-detection receiver and returns more bits per received photon than optimized pulse-position modulation with photon counting, under live conditions.
comms-35-joint-detection-ground-station.status_oct2026: None. NASA's DSOC returned 13.6 Tbit and ended on Sep 2 2025. Joint detection has been shown only in the lab (Green Machine, 2025). NASA awarded the Mars Telecommunications Network to Blue Origin on Sep 2 2026; it is expected at Mars by about 2030 (Wikipedia). Whether it carries a laser terminal is not public.
comms-35-joint-detection-ground-station.why: After a ground demo, a station upgrade takes about 2-3 years of engineering and funding, and it needs a laser terminal flying at deep-space range. The only committed Mars relay (MTN, about 2030) has not disclosed a laser terminal, so mission availability and budgets bind. S3: demo 2030, station 2033. S2: 2031 and 2034. S1: after 2035. Background light and optical loss shrink the gain, and the ground demo it depends on is Low by 2035, so every band stays Speculative.
comms-35-joint-detection-ground-station.strongest_case_small: PPM with superconducting detectors keeps improving and is within a few dB of practical limits (general). Agencies may prefer larger apertures, which are proven, over a new receiver.
comms-35-joint-detection-ground-station.signpost: NASA, ESA or JAXA funding a joint-detection receiver for an operational optical ground station; a deep-space mission with an optical terminal manifested for 2032-35. MTN or a later Mars or deep-space relay announcing a laser terminal.
comms-35-joint-detection-ground-station.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon, extending the receiver chain to operations. It stays Speculative because it needs a deep-space laser terminal that no committed mission has disclosed and a demo that is Low by 2035. S4 adds nothing because flight opportunities, budgets and background-light physics bind.
