comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.title: Independent suppliers ship 3,000 laser terminals a year
comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.description: Laser-terminal suppliers outside SpaceX, Amazon and China together deliver 3,000 or more space laser communication terminals in one year, so terminal supply no longer paces government, European or compute constellations.
comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.status_oct2026: Germany approved Rocket Lab's purchase of Mynaric for about $150 million on Mar 30 2026; Mynaric is a subcontractor on Rocket Lab's SDA satellites, and 33FG calls laser inter-satellite links a critical bottleneck for constellation operators (33FG). Mynaric had production delays and a restructuring in 2024-25, and SDA's Tranche 1 schedule slipped in part on optical terminal supply (general). SpaceX and Amazon build their own terminals. Merchant output for 2026 is not published; a few hundred to about 1,000 a year is a judgment.
comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.why: Space laser terminals are hand-aligned, bonded and tested optical assemblies, so skilled labor and test-chamber hours set output and cost. Demand outside the captive makers grows with SDA tranches, IRIS², Golden Dome and compute clusters. In S2, capital and specialized automation reach the threshold around 2035. S3's AI-run factories and test stands bring it to 2034. Terminal lines are high-mix and low-volume, which is where general-purpose robots add to that specialized automation. In S4 they reach aerospace suppliers after 2031 and pass 6-24 months of requalification, so robot-built terminals add volume from about 2033. That earns S4 one year and a band step. AI-designed photonics (comms-photonic-inverse-design) cut part count and alignment steps in every scenario. The 3,000 threshold is a judgment, about 3-6x estimated 2026 merchant output.
comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.strongest_case_small: Demand may bind first. If Golden Dome and compute clusters use RF links or captive terminals, merchant volume stays below 3,000 whatever robots do. Specialized alignment stations from telecom optics, already counted in S3, may remove most hand labor without general-purpose robots.
comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.signpost: A merchant supplier reporting annual output above 1,000 terminals; SDA or ESA stating that terminal supply no longer paces a tranche; robotic alignment or test cells qualified on a space terminal line.
comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.note_2035: New 2035-horizon node and the branch's one S4 credit. General-purpose robots reach aerospace suppliers after 2031 and pass requalification by about 2033, which earns S4 one year and a band step over S3.
comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.revision_note: E-networks resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the advocate (Mynaric sale verified at 33FG news 451). It is the branch's one gate that labor binds and meets all four S4 conditions at merchant suppliers after 2031. comms-35-merchant-laser-terminals.gate_note: Hand alignment, bonding and test-chamber hours (fabrication) bind; capital for specialized automation at merchant suppliers is the runner-up.

hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.title: Ship heat shield turned around in three days
hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.description: One Starship-class ship reaches 20 orbital flights and, at least once, flies twice within 72 hours, with heat-shield inspection and tile work done at the launch site. Achieved when flight records or the operator show both.
hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.status_oct2026: No ship has been caught or reflown: Flight 14 reached orbit on 28 Sep 2026 and splashed down. Musk expects the first ship and booster reflights at the end of 2026 or more likely early 2027. Mach33's base case has 18 flights per stack in 2030 and assumes later-generation stacks average 60 flights; Falcon 9 boosters that entered service in 2020 averaged 24 flights (Mach33, Sep 2026). Starfactory already uses specialized robots to install tiles and heat-shield pins (NASASpaceflight, Jan and Mar 2026).
hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.pathway: P7 (exogenous launch clock; AI-math effect through damage and inspection models, P1->P6)
hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.why: Reuse at the scale of the launch clock (hundreds of heavy flights a year by the mid-2030s, about $13/kg internal cost in Mach33's base case) rewards ships that turn around in days, and Mars-window and lunar tanker surges add demand. Chain (S2): five reflights with two-week heat-shield turnaround (hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield, 2030) -> reflight cleared from data (physclock-twin-reflight-clearance, 2030) -> inspect-by-exception from tile damage and fleet heating models (2029-31) -> pad-side refurbishment with under 1% of tiles replaced per flight -> a ship flies twice within 72 hours and reaches 20 flights, about 2034. A 72-hour turnaround leaves no time for teardown, so data-based clearance is a hard prerequisite. Falcon 9 took 8 years from first reflight (Mar 2017) to a 9-day record (Mar 2025), and its 2025 median was still 38 days. If a two-week ship record in 2030 falls 25-30% a year, 72 hours arrives about 2034-36. AI mathematics shortens the inspection list through damage and inspection models. S3 is a year ahead of S2 on the launch clock, so S3 has two years of slack by 2035 and is Medium at the low end; S2 has one year and is Low. S4 equals S3. A single 72-hour turnaround is a record that SpaceX can staff with people, and its tile and pin robots are already in S2 and S3. General-purpose robots matter for sustained fleet turnaround, which the trunk's cadence nodes also leave uncredited.
hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.strongest_case_small: The economics may never need a 72-hour ship turnaround, because a larger fleet flying every few weeks gives the same cadence, so SpaceX may not try. If the ceramic tile concept is a dead end for rapid reuse, a new heat-shield architecture resets the clock by years.
hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.signpost: Flight records showing one ship launched twice within a week, then within 72 hours; SpaceX statements on tiles replaced per flight and on robotic tile work at the pad.
hyper-35-ship-heatshield-72h.note_2035: This is the 2032-35 step of Starship heat-shield reuse. S3 and S4 are Medium with two years of slack and S2 is Low with one. S4 equals S3 because a one-off record can be staffed by people and the tile robots are already counted in S2 and S3.

hyper-35-ai-tps-primary-zone.title: AI-designed heat-shield material in regular service
hyper-35-ai-tps-primary-zone.description: An AI-designed TPS material, coating or ablator (as defined in materials-tps-new-material-flight) is the baseline material for a primary heat-shield zone (forebody, nose or windward acreage) of an operational reentry vehicle and has flown at least 3 missions in that role. Coupons and test tiles do not count.
hyper-35-ai-tps-primary-zone.status_oct2026: No AI-designed TPS material has flown, even as a coupon (general). Varda makes its C-PICA heat shields in-house and lost W-4 on reentry in May 2026; W-6 flew Sandia material samples and NASA Ames instrumented tiles. Starship Flight 10 (Aug 2025) flew metallic and actively cooled test tiles. New U.S. arc-jet capacity is being built (Kratos Project Helios, 20-25 MW, awarded Oct 2025).
hyper-35-ai-tps-primary-zone.why: Chain (S2): the first AI-designed coupon flies (materials-tps-new-material-flight, 2030) -> arc-jet qualification of the full material with its bond and attachment (1-2 years; the arc-jet queue binds) -> production scale-up and lot acceptance (about a year) -> baseline on a commercial capsule or a reusable vehicle's windward zone -> three missions, about 2034. Uncrewed commercial operators need no certifier, which lifts the band above the P7 Speculative default; crewed use would be capped at Medium. S3 is a year earlier because AI-run test stands (physclock-ai-run-test-stands, High in S3) shorten arc-jet qualification and lot acceptance; the coupon year is the same in S2 and S3. S4 equals S3: robots speed specimen preparation, and arc-jet runs double first in S4 (hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x, 2033), but that lands as qualification ends, and flight heritage at small operators binds, so the gain stays under half a year.
hyper-35-ai-tps-primary-zone.strongest_case_small: Operators rarely change primary heat-shield materials, and after the W-4 loss and Artemis I's char loss they favor flight heritage. Gains from a new material may be small next to manufacturing, bonding and attachment.
hyper-35-ai-tps-primary-zone.signpost: A capsule maker or reusable-vehicle operator names an AI-designed material as the baseline for a primary heat-shield zone; arc-jet qualification reports for such a material.
hyper-35-ai-tps-primary-zone.note_2035: This extends the AI-material chain from a coupon to regular service in 2033-35. S3 is Medium on AI-run test stands and S2 is Low with one year of slack. S4 equals S3: faster S4 arc jets arrive as qualification ends, and operators want flight heritage.
hyper-35-ai-tps-primary-zone.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.title: First aerocapture into orbit around another planet
hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.description: A funded spacecraft (science, relay or commercial) enters orbit around Mars, Venus or Titan with a single atmospheric pass as its planned orbit-insertion method. Earth demonstrations do not count.
hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.status_oct2026: Aerocapture has never flown. NASA ordered a $350k study of an Arc-based Earth aerocapture demonstration from Inversion (11 Sep 2026, to 30 Jun 2027). Uranus studies find MSL-heritage aeroshells adequate for aerocapture (NTRS 20240014677). Mars launch windows open about Apr 2033 and mid-2035 (arriving 2036). Venus windows come about every 19 months: late 2032 to early 2033 and about mid-2034 (general).
hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.why: Chain (S3): an Earth aerocapture demonstration (hyper-aerocapture-demo, 2030 at the earliest, Low by 2035) -> a small Venus or Mars mission adopts aerocapture and is funded (2031) -> a 3-4 year build (NASA small missions take 4-6 years from selection to launch, general) -> launch in the mid-2034 Venus window -> capture in late 2034 or early 2035. The Apr 2033 Mars window works only if the go-ahead comes before the demo flies, and the mid-2035 Mars window arrives in 2036. S2 is a year later. AI makes guidance, dispersion and rarefied-flow analysis cheap, so a small team can carry the analysis load; funding and the demo's success bind. The band is the demo's chance (Low) times the chance a funded adopter launches by mid-2034, under 10% in every scenario. S4 equals S3 because capital and launch windows bind.
hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.strongest_case_small: After a demo, a first planetary use still needs a mission whose design closes only with aerocapture, and with cheap launch most small missions can carry extra propellant instead.
hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.signpost: A Mars or Venus mission selection, or a commercial Mars relay, that baselines aerocapture for orbit insertion.
hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.note_2035: The first planetary use needs the Earth demo, a funded mission, a 3-4 year build and a window, so the mid-2034 Venus window is the only realistic slot inside 2035. Every scenario is Speculative by 2035, and S4 equals S3.
hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. Venus windows added to status; why chain rewritten. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Speculative through 2035 in every scenario. Bands unchanged.
hyper-35-planetary-aerocapture.gate_note: Funding binds; flight heritage from the Earth demo (qualification) is the runner-up.

hyper-35-mars-pinpoint-landing.title: Second heavy Mars lander lands within 1 km of the first
hyper-35-mars-pinpoint-landing.description: A second lander of 20 t or more, from the same launch window or a later one, lands intact on Mars within 1 km of an earlier lander, without disabling damage to it from plume or ejecta. This is the precision and keep-out an outpost cargo build-up needs.
hyper-35-mars-pinpoint-landing.status_oct2026: No 20 t-class Mars landing has been attempted. Landing ellipses for Curiosity and Perseverance were about 20 x 7 km and 8 x 7 km (general). Apollo 12 landed about 160 m from Surveyor 3, and its exhaust sandblasted the probe (general). In Feb 2026 SpaceX put Mars about 5-7 years out behind a Moon-first priority.
hyper-35-mars-pinpoint-landing.pathway: P7 (launch windows; AI-math effect through guidance and plume-surface models)
hyper-35-mars-pinpoint-landing.why: Chain: first heavy landing (hyper-mars-heavy-landing, 2031 window at the earliest) -> site data and terrain-relative navigation from that flight -> a second ship targets the same site in the Apr 2033 window and arrives late 2033. A same-window pair in 2031 is possible but unlikely: a 2031 landing most likely rests on one ship, and the five-ship fueling campaign (prop-35-mars-window-fueling) is dated to the 2033 window. Landing within 1 km is routine precision for propulsive landers; the hard part is the keep-out. Apollo 12 landed about 160 m from Surveyor 3 and its exhaust sandblasted the probe, and a Starship-class plume on unprepared regolith throws far more. AI mathematics helps through plume-surface models (prop-psi-models) and guidance with proven convergence; windows and SpaceX's priorities set the date. The band is the first landing's chance by 2035 (Medium) times the chance a second lander lands close without damage, so Low in S2-S4. S1 is Speculative because its plume-surface models are Low by 2035, so landers keep farther apart. S4 equals S3 because orbital mechanics binds.
hyper-35-mars-pinpoint-landing.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics barely changes the date; windows and SpaceX's priorities decide it. SpaceX may spread early landings across sites to scout, or keep landers several kilometres apart until a pad exists.
hyper-35-mars-pinpoint-landing.signpost: A SpaceX statement that a second Mars ship will target the first ship's site; published plume-ejecta keep-out distances for Starship-class landers on Mars.
hyper-35-mars-pinpoint-landing.note_2035: This is the 2033-window follow-on to the first heavy landing, and the plume-ejecta keep-out is what it tests. Windows bind, so every scenario shares the year and S4 equals S3.

hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.title: Crewed heat shield sized by probabilistic margins flies
hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.description: A crewed reentry vehicle certified by NASA or another space agency flies a heat shield whose thickness was set to a reliability target with joint probabilistic margins, including a flight-calibrated model-form term, in place of stacked aerothermal factors.
hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.status_oct2026: NASA practice stacks deterministic aerothermal factors and combines branches by root-sum-square (SRL design, IPPW 2026); the SRL alternative-margining study was preliminary, and SRL ended when Mars Sample Return received no FY2026 funding. Artemis I's char loss pushed NASA toward more margin; Artemis II flew a modified entry on the same shield design (10 Apr 2026).
hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.why: Chain (S2): probabilistic sizing adopted on uncrewed vehicles (2029) -> flight-calibrated model-form bounds (2030) -> a credibility standard that covers AI-built analysis (physclock-credibility-evidence-standard, 2029) -> an agency margin policy that allows reliability-based sizing for crew (2031-32) -> a heat-shield block change on a crewed capsule (Orion, Dragon or a national crew vehicle): redesign, arc-jet qualification and crew certification, 3 years or more -> flight, about 2035. Precedent: from Artemis I's char loss (Dec 2022) to a modified shield on Artemis III took about 5 years (general), and the char-loss investigation alone took 121 arc-jet tests over 8 campaigns. The certifier must accept the method, so the band is capped at Medium, and after Artemis I crewed programs favor margin. S3 is a year earlier because its model-form bounds land a year earlier; the institutional steps run at the same pace in S2-S4. S3 and S4 are Low by 2035 and S2 is Speculative. S1 lacks the calibrated bounds in time. S4 equals S3 because institutions bind.
hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.strongest_case_small: Crewed programs rarely trade heat-shield margin for mass, and a thinner crewed shield saves little that matters. Agencies may use the method for analysis while keeping stacked factors for sizing.
hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.signpost: A NASA EDL or TPS margin-policy revision that allows reliability-based sizing for crewed vehicles; a crewed heat-shield redesign that cites it.
hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.note_2035: This is where the margin chain meets crewed risk posture. Certifier acceptance and a crewed qualification of 3 years or more bind, so the first flight falls in 2034-35 at the earliest; S3 and S4 are Low by 2035, S2 is Speculative, and S4 equals S3.
hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon. Regulatory cap Medium; no named mechanism for crewed TPS margins is in motion, so 2035 stays capped. | E-entry resolver (2026-10-07): [skeptic] Hard edge from physclock-credibility-evidence-standard added (a crewed certifier accepts AI-built margins only through such a standard); soft edge removed. Years S2 2034 -> 2035, S3/S4 2033 -> 2034 (1-2 years from policy to a flown crewed shield was too short against the ~5-year Artemis precedent). band_2035 S2 Low -> Speculative. | E-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): title shortened from 'A crewed vehicle flies a heat shield sized by probabilistic margins'. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S3/S4 Low 2034 -> 2035: the 2034 floor needs every step on time, and the Artemis I precedent took about five years from finding to a modified shield. Skeptic (Speculative) and advocate (2034) weighed; band_2035 Low kept. Bands unchanged.
hyper-35-crewed-probabilistic-shield.gate_note: Certifier acceptance binds; a crewed heat-shield qualification of 3+ years (qualification) is the runner-up.

hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.title: Arc-jet test runs per year double
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.description: U.S. arc-jet facilities together complete at least twice as many heat-shield test runs a year as in 2026, from added facilities and from automated model change, instrumentation and turnaround between runs. Achieved when NASA, DoD test-resource reports or facility operators show the doubling.
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.status_oct2026: The Ames Arc Jet Complex is NASA's only ground facility for reentry TPS testing, built in the 1960s-70s, with flat maintenance funding; in 2026 the 30 kW mARC II needed a cooling-sleeve fix to extend run times. Kratos Project Helios (a 20-25 MW arc jet plus a 200 kW fiber laser, $68.3M, awarded 23 Oct 2025 under the Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program) adds capacity. Surveyed experts rank more arc jets as the top hypersonic-materials test need (ETI via Air & Space Forces).
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.pathway: P7 (test infrastructure; S4 lever is robot labor at the facilities)
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.premise_tier: n/a (infrastructure throughput anchor, not an AI-math implication)
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.why: Arc-jet time is the experiment gate for this branch. The S4 review splits arc-jet queue time into about 40% labor (model change, instrumentation, between-run turnaround, maintenance), 25% physics (run time, cooling, pump-down, electrode wear) and 35% capital, power and institution. Capital caps the number of facilities in every scenario; within each facility the labor share is what S4 compresses. Chain (S2): new capacity such as Helios enters service in the late 2020s -> AI scheduling and instant data reduction (physclock-ai-run-test-stands, Medium in S2) -> runs per year about 1.5-1.8x by 2035 (judgment), so doubling is Low and no earlier than 2035. S3 2034: AI-run stands are High, but they leave article setup to people, so S3 stays Low. S4 2033: general-purpose robots do bench and test work from 2030-31 (robo-lab-bench-useful, robo-24x7-integration-test) and help build new stands; automated model insertion and turnaround raise runs per day per facility about 1.3-1.8x (estimate), and leading facilities reach 0.41-0.47 of 2026 queue time by 2035. S4 is Medium by 2035. The S4 credit meets all four conditions: runs per year are throughput-bound, robots are useful there from 2030-31, there is no hard prerequisite, and S3's AI-run stands leave setup to people. Arc-heater power, electrode life and facility capital cap each run in every scenario, and S4 raises test demand too. S1 falls after 2035.
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.strongest_case_small: Arc-jet operations are high-voltage, hazardous work at government facilities that adopt new practice slowly, so robots may reach them late. Run counts are rarely published, so the doubling may be hard to see, and defense hypersonics may take most of the added runs.
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.signpost: Kratos Helios in service; an arc-jet operator reporting automated model insertion or runs per day; NASA or DoD test-capacity reports showing run counts or test hours.
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension and the branch's one S4 credit: S4 is a year ahead of S3 and Medium by 2035 because model change, instrumentation and turnaround are labor-bound steps that general robots take over from 2030-31. Arc-heater power, electrode life and facility capital still cap each run.
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.revision_note: E-entry resolver (2026-10-07): new node from the advocate review, tempered. The advocate's years (S2 2034, S3 2033, S4 2032) and band_2035 (Low/Medium/Medium/High) were moved one year later and one band lower in S3 and S4: the S4 review's typical-facility figure for 2035 (0.56-0.64 of 2026 queue time) does not reach a doubling without new capital, and arc-jet operators are government or typical firms, not robot-first. Tier 4 infrastructure in place of tier 1 (tier 1 holds mathematics). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S4 Medium 2034 -> 2035: the S4 review's typical-facility figure (0.56-0.64 of 2026 queue time) does not double runs without new capital, so doubling at a facility is 30% only at the horizon. Skeptic (Low) and advocate (2034) weighed; band_2035 Medium kept. Bands unchanged.
hyper-35-arcjet-throughput-2x.gate_note: Facility capital binds; labor-bound model change and turnaround between runs (experiment) is the runner-up.

hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.title: People return from orbit on a reusable ship
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.description: A crew of at least two launches to orbit and returns to Earth aboard the ship of a fully reusable heavy launcher (Starship-class), which comes through entry on its reusable heat shield and lands for reuse, on a licensed flight. Capsules, and lunar landers that never reenter Earth's atmosphere, do not count.
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.status_oct2026: No crew has flown on Starship. Flight 14 reached orbit on 28 Sep 2026 and splashed down; no ship has been caught or reflown. Starship has no launch escape system (general). Under NASA's HLS plan, crews transfer between Orion and Starship in lunar orbit, so no crew is planned to reenter Earth's atmosphere in a Starship (general). In Feb 2026 SpaceX shifted focus to a city on the Moon. The last crewed entries on a tiled reusable vehicle were Space Shuttle flights, which ended in 2011 after the 2003 Columbia loss (general).
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.pathway: P7 (exogenous launch clock; AI-math effect through tile damage models and reliability priors, P1->P6)
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.why: Without a launch escape system, the safety case is the vehicle's flight record. A zero-failure demonstration of 0.99 reliability at 90% confidence needs about 229 trials: 9.2 years at 25 flights a year, 2.3 years at 100 (S4 review). Chain (S2): 100+ heavy flights a year from 2030 (physclock-heavy-cadence-100) -> a long run of successful ship entries and landings by 2032-33 -> crew cabin, life support and an abort case -> an FAA license for a crewed flight -> first crewed orbital flight and landing, about 2034. Demand would come from SpaceX's Moon-first plan if it moves crews beyond the Orion-HLS handoff (judgment). AI mathematics enters through tile damage and fleet heating models, which make each entry better understood, and through model-based reliability priors (physclock-reliability-priors-credit), which can cut the flights needed. S3 is a year ahead on the launch clock and has two years of slack, so it is Medium by 2035; S2 has one year and is Low; S1 follows its later heat shield and cadence. A licensed crewed flight is capped at Medium. S4 equals S3: flight statistics and the operator's risk decision bind, and robots do not add flights.
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may keep crews on Dragon and Orion through 2035 and fly Starship crews only to the Moon, never through Earth entry. One ship loss in the run-up resets the record, and the tile concept carries the Columbia shadow.
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.signpost: A SpaceX crewed Starship flight plan with a date; a run of 100 or more consecutive successful ship entries and landings; an FAA license application for a crewed Starship flight.
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension: the first people through entry on a reusable tiled ship since the Shuttle. S3 and S4 are Medium and S2 is Low; S4 equals S3 because flight statistics and risk acceptance bind.
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.revision_note: E-entry resolver (2026-10-07): new node from the advocate review. Kept the advocate's years and bands (S1 Speculative, S2 Low, S3/S4 Medium) except S1 >2035 -> 2035, since the trunk dates S1's 100-flight cadence to 2030 as in S2. Capped at Medium as a licensed crewed flight. Soft edge from capability-35-heavy-cadence-300 left to the integrator (trunk node). | R9-launch (2026-10-27): gate launch -> launch-internal (SpaceX's own manifest; Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 books Starlink, SpaceX's orbital compute, Moon and Mars cargo and NASA's lunar tanker flights in the internal account). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Seed kept: S3 Medium 2034 (100+ flights a year from 2029 give ~229 entries by 2032, then crew systems and a licence). Skeptic (no abort system, 2035) and advocate (Moon-first demand, 2033) weighed. Bands unchanged.
hyper-35-crewed-ship-reentry.gate_note: The ship's flight record binds; an FAA crewed licence and risk acceptance (regulatory) is the runner-up.

auton-35-polar-water-pilot.title: First water mined from lunar polar ice
auton-35-polar-water-pilot.description: A pilot plant digs ice-bearing regolith in or beside a permanently shadowed crater at the lunar south pole and extracts at least 1 t of water in one campaign, measured and stored. It is the step between the first ice measurements and a lunar propellant supply.
auton-35-polar-water-pilot.status_oct2026: No ice extraction has been tried on the Moon. The form of polar ice is unknown: in lab tests excavation energy for ice-cemented simulant rises 52x as ice goes from 1 to 12 wt%, while pressure-sintered simulant gets easier to dig (Space and Planetary Resources, Sep 2026). NASA's IPEx is designed to dig about 20 t of regolith per mission. Ground truth from PROSPECT (2027), VIPER, LUPEX or Chang'e-8 is expected in 2027-29. Permanently shadowed regions sit near 40 K, so power must come by cable from a sunlit rim or from a reactor.
auton-35-polar-water-pilot.why: At 5 wt% ice, 1 t of water means digging and heating about 20 t of regolith, the scale IPEx was built for (general arithmetic). AI enters through the validated regolith model and model-based excavator design, which size the machine to the ice form found in 2028-29. Once a pilot runs, extraction takes days to weeks, so water comes in the landing year. Chain (S2): ground truth 2028 -> regolith model 2029 and excavator design 2030 -> pilot funded, built and qualified 2030-32 -> landed on a heavy cargo flight and 1 t extracted 2033. S3: model and design a year earlier and cadence 0.5-1 year faster -> 2032. S1: excavator design in 2032 plus the same three-year build-and-land lag -> 2035. The reactor option lands in 2033 at the earliest, so the pilot depends on a cable from a sunlit rim. No extraction payload is funded, and NASA ISRU payloads have taken about five years from selection to flight (PRIME-1, general). Power in the polar dark, funding and landing success remain, so S3 and S4 are Medium by 2035 and S1 and S2 are Low.
auton-35-polar-water-pilot.strongest_case_small: Early bases may skip ice and make oxygen from sunlit regolith, which needs no cold-trap operations. If the ice is vapor-deposited and hard, or patchy, a pilot may extract far less than 1 t per campaign.
auton-35-polar-water-pilot.signpost: NASA, SpaceX, Blue Origin or CNSA manifests an ice-extraction payload with a stated water target on a 2030-33 lander; a polar dataset fixes the ice form.
auton-35-polar-water-pilot.note_2035: New node: ice data from 2028-29 and routine heavy cargo put a first water pilot inside the 2035 horizon. S2 is Low because no extraction payload is funded and one would need funding by about 2030. S4 equals S3 because power in permanently shadowed craters and funding bind, and few general-purpose robots will work at 40 K by 2035.
auton-35-polar-water-pilot.revision_note: E-moon-mars (2035 horizon, S4): added. Hard edges from auton-icy-regolith-ground-truth and auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing; soft from the regolith and excavation models, base power and robo-lunar-construction. S4 = S3 (power and funding bind). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): S1 2034 -> 2035 and band_2035 S2 Medium -> Low (skeptic): the S1 chain now uses the same three-year lag as S2 and S3, and S2 would need a payload funded about 2029-30 with power by cable from a sunlit rim. Advocate's one-year-earlier years rejected: the extra landing-to-extraction year is removed from the chain, but funding, build and qualification of a first-of-kind plant still take about three years after the excavator design. Soft edge from robo-lunar-construction removed (later in every scenario). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S3 Medium 2035. Skeptic: no extraction payload is funded and ISRU payloads take about five years to fly, so under 30% by 2035. Advocate: SpaceX's Moon priority, so 2033. Resolved 2035, keeping Medium by 2035 only just. Bands at 2031 and 2035 unchanged.
auton-35-polar-water-pilot.gate_note: Funding binds; delivering power by cable into a 40 K crater and building a first-of-kind plant (fabrication) are the runner-up.

auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.title: Lunar oxygen fuels landers at 10 t a year
auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.description: A second-generation lunar plant makes oxygen at an annualized 10 t a year or more, from regolith or from polar ice, and at least 1 t of it is liquefied and transferred into a lander or depot as propellant. Oxygen is about 78% of methalox propellant mass, so this is the first step toward lunar-made propellant.
auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.status_oct2026: No lunar plant exists. A 2025 systems study sizes a 10 t/yr molten regolith electrolysis plant at about 1.1 kg/h and under 30 kW. The best ground run made 0.07 kg/h for 9 h (the KSC and Lunar Resources LR-1 rig, late 2024). A Starship return would need about 65 kg/h of oxygen. NASA's Lunar Reactor-1 (100 kWe) targets launch readiness in late 2029, and the model dates a 100 kWe reactor on the Moon to 2033 (struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe).
auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.why: A 10 t/yr plant runs about 8,800 h a year at 1.1 kg/h, so anode life, a feed of tens of tonnes of regolith a year and power through the lunar night set the pace. It follows the 1 t/yr pilot by 2-3 years: one cycle to learn from pilot data and land a larger unit. AI reactor models and anode discovery shorten the design half of that cycle. Chain (S3): pilot 2031 -> second unit designed 2032 -> landed and at rate 2034. S2: pilot 2032 -> 2035. S1: pilot 2034 -> beyond 2035. S4 equals S3. The plant is designed, built and qualified on Earth, where robots reach suppliers after 2031 and each new process needs 6-24 months of requalification. On the Moon one excavator covers the regolith feed. Landing, funding and a buyer bind, so S2-S4 are Low by 2035.
auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.strongest_case_small: No buyer needs lunar oxygen while Starship brings oxygen from Earth at falling cost. A plant at this scale may run as a demonstration, and liquefaction and storage add power and mass that a pilot never tested.
auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.signpost: A funded second-generation ISRU plant with a 10 t/yr target and a named delivery date; a lunar pilot that runs more than 3,000 h in a year.
auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.note_2035: New node: the lunar oxygen spine reaches propellant scale inside the horizon in S2-S4, first in 2034 in S3 and S4, and is Low by 2035. S4 equals S3 because plant build, anode life, power and a buyer bind.
auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.revision_note: E-moon-mars (2035 horizon, S4): added. Hard edge from auton-lunar-oxygen-ops; soft from the ice pilot, anodes, ROMs, fission power, cryogenic models and robo-lunar-construction. S4 credit: one year and one band (labor-bound scale-up, robots useful off Earth from 2032, prerequisite 2031, general-purpose robots beyond S3's specialized excavators). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): S4 2033 -> 2034 and band_2035 S4 Medium -> Low (both reviewers). The credit fails condition 1 (a buyer and plant funding bind; one excavator covers the feed) and condition 2 (robots reach suppliers after 2031, and a 2033 landing freezes its design about 2031, before pilot run data and before robot processes are requalified). The robots branch dates outpost-scale lunar robot work to S4 2033, after the draft's 'about 2032'. Description now requires at least 1 t liquefied and transferred; status names the LR-1 rig and NASA's Lunar Reactor-1 separately. Soft input from the new cargo-cadence node. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Low from the earliest year (S3 2034, S2 2035); stays Low by 2035. Bands at 2031 and 2035 unchanged.
auton-35-lunar-oxygen-propellant.gate_note: Plant funding and a buyer bind; anode life and run hours (experiment) are the runner-up.

auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.title: A hundred robots work on the Moon at once
auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.description: At least 100 robots of 20 kg or more (rovers, excavators, manipulators or humanoid-class machines) do excavation, hauling, construction or maintenance on the lunar surface at the same time, survive the lunar night, and are supervised by a ground team of fewer than 50 people using AI planning and machine-checked plans.
auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.status_oct2026: Fewer than ten robots have ever worked on the Moon at once (general), and most lasted one lunar day. CADRE (late 2026) will test a three-rover team. NASA's Moon Base plan foresees up to 30 CLPS landings from 2027, and NASA moved to raise the CLPS contract ceiling to $4.2B in May 2026 (SpaceNews via 33FG). Perseverance flew its first AI-planned drives in Dec 2025.
auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.why: Two curves meet here. AI planning with machine-checked plans cuts operator time per robot severalfold by 2029 (S2), and 100 robots of 20-100 kg weigh 2-10 t, a fraction of one heavy cargo landing. What remains is the supply of lunar-rated robots, night survival and base power. Chain (S3): heavy cargo 2028 and ridge solar from Moon Base Phase 2 (2030) -> robots from several programs accumulate -> 100 at once in 2032. S2: 2033. S1: 2035. In S1-S3 lunar robots stay bespoke and programs fly a few per landing, so S2 and S3 are Low by 2035 and S1 is Speculative. S4 keeps the S3 year, because robots landing before 2032 fly on hardware frozen in 2027-28. By 2035 S4 rises to Medium: robot variants of Earth designs reach lunar hardware after 2031, and the S4 robot path puts hundreds of robots off Earth by 2035 if cargo reaches ten landings a year. Lunar units still need new actuators, lubricants, seals, thermal control and electronics for vacuum, dust and about -170 to +120 C, so S4 stays below High.
auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.strongest_case_small: Lunar robots stay bespoke, short-lived and expensive. Programs may fly a few large machines instead of many small ones, and the count says little about useful work.
auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.signpost: A Moon Base or commercial operator reports 25 or more robots active at once through a lunar night; a humanoid-class robot flown to the Moon.
auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.note_2035: New node: the productivity chain reaches fleet scale inside the horizon. S4 keeps the S3 year (2032) and rises from Low to Medium by 2035, because the count of lunar-rated robots binds and robot variants of Earth designs supply it after 2031. Landed mass and night power keep S4 below High.
auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.revision_note: E-moon-mars (2035 horizon, S4): added. Hard edges from auton-surface-productivity and auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing; soft from verified lunar autonomy, planning ceilings, base power and robo-fleet-10m, robo-mtbi-1000h, robo-foundation-models-field, robo-lunar-construction. S4 credit: one band by 2035 (robot supply is throughput-bound and relieved by S4). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic accepted in part. Years 2034/2032/2031/2031 -> 2035/2033/2032/2032 and band_2031 S3 and S4 Low -> Speculative: fewer than ten robots have ever worked on the Moon at once, and robots landing in 2030-31 fly on hardware frozen in 2027-28. Description now requires robots of 20 kg or more doing real work. auton-moon-base-infrastructure moved from soft to hard (night survival for 100 robots needs base power). S4 band_2035 High -> Medium, matching robo-lunar-construction (S4 Medium). Resolver: S2 and S3 Medium -> Low and S1 Low -> Speculative. The S4 analysis puts off-Earth general-purpose robots at tens in 2031 and hundreds by 2035 on the S4 base path, and only with ten cargo landings a year. S1-S3 run the slower robot path and robo-lunar-construction is Low in S3, so bespoke fleets in S1-S3 rarely reach 100. Binding gate stays fabrication: the metric is the robot count, and landed mass for 100 robots is a fraction of one landing. Soft edge from robo-lunar-construction removed (it lands later in every scenario); soft inputs from robo-aerospace-tolerance-work (advocate) and the new cargo-cadence node. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Low from 2033 in S3-S4 and 2034 in S2 (a year after the earliest year). S4 Medium 2035. Skeptic: lunar units need new actuators, seals and night survival, so Low. Advocate: the S4 path puts hundreds of robots off Earth by 2035, so 2034. Resolved 2035. Bands at 2031 and 2035 unchanged.
auton-35-lunar-robot-fleet.gate_note: The supply of lunar-rated robots binds; programs funding robots and base power (capital) are the runner-up.

auton-35-lunar-long-stay.title: Crews stay on the Moon for 90 days or more
auton-35-lunar-long-stay.description: A crew of two or more lives at a lunar surface base for 90 days or longer in one stay, and the base runs itself between crews. It marks the start of long-duration presence (Moon Base Phase 3).
auton-35-lunar-long-stay.status_oct2026: The longest lunar surface stay is about 75 hours (Apollo 17, 1972; general). Artemis II flew in Apr 2026, and the first Artemis landing is planned for 2028, with crewed landings about every six months at first. Reporting dates Moon Base Phase 3, long-duration presence, to 2032 onward. NASA was reported near bulk launch buys for its roughly $30B Moon Base (Bloomberg via 33FG, Oct 6 2026). China plans a crewed landing by 2030 and a research station in the 2030s (general).
auton-35-lunar-long-stay.why: A 90-day stay needs a pressurized habitat with power through three lunar nights, life support with spares, local medical and fault response, and a rescue option. It also needs a ride home that waits 90 days on the surface with its propellant kept cold, or a second crewed vehicle. AI contributes through crew-side diagnosis, sparing models and a base that maintains itself between stays. Chain (S2): Phase 2 elements and crew-optional operations 2031 -> a pressurized habitat and night power in place 2032-33 -> first 90-day stay 2033. S3: 2032. S1: 2035. Appropriations, human rating and landing safety do not compress, and both hard parents are Medium by 2035, so S2-S4 are Low and S1 is Speculative.
auton-35-lunar-long-stay.strongest_case_small: Government flagships slip 2-7 years. A budget fight, a landing accident or a radiation policy can hold stays to weeks until well past 2035.
auton-35-lunar-long-stay.signpost: NASA or a partner contracts a surface habitat with a named 2031-33 delivery; a crew stays more than 30 days on the Moon.
auton-35-lunar-long-stay.note_2035: New node: Moon Base Phase 3 puts long stays inside the 2035 horizon, but a pressurized habitat, night power and a ride home must all arrive in time, so S2-S4 are Low. S4 equals S3 because appropriations, human rating and landing safety bind.
auton-35-lunar-long-stay.revision_note: E-moon-mars (2035 horizon, S4): added. Hard edges from auton-moon-base-infrastructure and auton-crew-optional-lunar-ops; soft from crew-side diagnosis, life-support reliability and closure, radiation risk, lunar oxygen, landing pads and fission power. S4 = S3 (institution- and appropriations-bound). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): band_2035 S1 Low -> Speculative and S2-S4 Medium -> Low (skeptic). The stay needs both Medium hard parents, a habitat beyond Phase 2's semi-habitable element, night power with fission Low by 2035, and a ride home; Artemis-era stays are planned at about a week. Soft inputs from prop-cfm-models (cold ascent propellant) and the cargo-cadence node. The advocate's soft edge from robo-lunar-construction is not added: it lands later than this node in every scenario. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Low a year after the earliest year (S2 2034, S3 2033): Artemis stays are planned at about a week, and a 90-day stay needs a habitat and night power first. Bands at 2031 and 2035 unchanged.
auton-35-lunar-long-stay.gate_note: Appropriations and a habitat bind; human rating, life support and a ride home (qualification) are the runner-up.

auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.title: Crops grown through repeated harvests on the Moon
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.description: A pressurized plant module at a lunar base completes at least three successive harvests of a food crop under model-based stability control, tended by crew or robots. It is the first bioregenerative food and air step beyond seed sprouting.
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.status_oct2026: Chang'e-4 sprouted a cotton seed on the Moon in 2019, and it died within days (general). NASA's LEAF plant experiment is planned for an early Artemis landing (general). China's Lunar Palace 1 ran a 370-day crewed closed test on the ground in 2017-18. MELiSSA is working toward full loop closure in its pilot plant (ICES 2025).
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); family 149 enters only through the conditional stability-theory accelerator
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.why: Crop cycles of 60-120 days make three harvests take 6-12 months, and lighting a module through 14-day nights takes hundreds of watts per square meter of growing area (general). A ground-validated controlled loop comes first. Chain (S3): closed ground test 2030 and ridge solar from Moon Base Phase 2 (2030) -> module landed 2032 -> three harvests 2033. S2: 2034. S1: its ground test lands in 2034, so beyond 2035. Funding and biology set the clock, so every scenario is Low by 2035 and S1 is Speculative.
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.strongest_case_small: Physico-chemical life support and food shipped from Earth stay cheaper at base scale through 2035, so plant modules remain small experiments.
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.signpost: A lunar greenhouse payload with a multi-harvest goal on a Moon Base or Chinese research-station manifest.
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.note_2035: New node: it extends the bioregenerative chain from ground tests to the Moon inside the horizon. S4 equals S3 because crop cycles and funding bind.
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.revision_note: E-moon-mars (2035 horizon, S4): added. Hard edges from auton-blss-closed-test and auton-moon-base-infrastructure; soft from stability theory, long crew stays and fission power. S4 = S3 (biology clock and funding). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): Text only: base power is ridge solar from Moon Base Phase 2, since the 100 kWe reactor is 2033 in every scenario (advocate). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Low a year after the earliest year (S3 2034, S2 2035): a module must land and then grow three harvests. Bands at 2031 and 2035 unchanged.
auton-35-lunar-crop-harvests.gate_note: Funding binds; three 60-120 day crop cycles (experiment) are the runner-up.

auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.title: Robots prepare a Mars landing site and power
auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.description: Robots delivered by a 20 t-class Mars landing deploy at least 100 kW of power, survey and dig for ice, and prepare a site for later ships, working through at least one Mars season under Earth supervision with a one-way light time of 3-22 minutes.
auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.status_oct2026: No robot has deployed power or prepared a site on Mars. SpaceX put Mars work on hold in Feb 2026 to prioritize the Moon and skipped the late-2026 window. Windows inside the horizon: Dec 2028-Jan 2029, early 2031 and about Apr 2033, with landings in late 2029, late 2031 and late 2033. A Starship-scale propellant plant needs megawatt-class power.
auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.why: Lunar robot operations train the methods, and AI planning with machine-checked plans lets a small team supervise across the light-time delay. Mars adds a 26-month gap between deliveries. Chain (S2 and S3): a 20 t-class landing in late 2031 carries robots and arrays -> 100 kW deployed and a site surveyed during 2032. S1: weaker autonomy and the 2033 window -> 2034. Each window allows one try and a new vehicle class lands well below certainty, so S2-S4 are Low by 2035 and S1 is Speculative.
auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may use the 2031 and 2033 windows for landing tests only and send no working robots, and power hardware that survives Mars dust storms may not be ready.
auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.signpost: A Mars cargo manifest for the 2031 or 2033 window that lists robots and surface power.
auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.note_2035: New node: the late-2031 and late-2033 Mars landings fall inside the horizon, and a propellant plant needs robots to set up power first. S4 equals S3 because Mars windows bind, and general-purpose robots add no windows.
auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.revision_note: E-moon-mars (2035 horizon, S4): added. Hard edge from hyper-mars-heavy-landing and hard edge into auton-mars-propellant-plant (a plant cannot run before robots deploy its power); soft from the lunar robot fleet, surface productivity, verified autonomy, excavation design and the Mars ISRU demo. S4 = S3 (launch windows). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): Soft edge from robo-lunar-construction removed (skeptic): it lands later than this node in every scenario and crosses to another planet. Years and bands unchanged. | R9-launch (2026-10-27): gate launch -> launch-internal (SpaceX's own manifest; Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 books Starlink, SpaceX's orbital compute, Moon and Mars cargo and NASA's lunar tanker flights in the internal account). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Low from 2034, not 2033: the early-2031 landing is itself a long shot (Mars heavy landing Low), so 10% comes with the late-2033 landing and work in 2034. Bands at 2031 and 2035 unchanged.
auton-35-mars-robot-site-prep.gate_note: Mars windows on SpaceX's manifest bind; SpaceX's priority and funding for Mars cargo (capital) are the runner-up.

auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.title: Ten heavy cargo landings on the Moon in one year
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.description: Ten or more cargo landings of at least 10 t each reach the lunar surface in one calendar year, from Starship, Blue Moon or other heavy landers. It is the landed-mass rate behind lunar outpost work after 2031.
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.status_oct2026: No heavy cargo has landed on the Moon. Starship reached orbit on Sep 28, 2026, and ship-to-ship propellant transfer is expected in early 2027. In Feb 2026 SpaceX made a lunar city its priority. NASA's Moon Base plan (Mar 2026) foresees up to 30 CLPS landings, NASA moved to raise the CLPS ceiling to $4.2B (May 2026, SpaceNews via 33FG), and it was reported near bulk launch buys for the roughly $30B Moon Base (Bloomberg via 33FG, Oct 6, 2026).
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.why: This node is an exogenous anchor with no AI-math pathway. Each Starship lunar cargo landing needs on the order of ten tanker launches or more (public estimates vary; general), so ten landings need 100 or more heavy launches in a year. The launch clock passes 100 heavy launches a year about 2030 (S3 2029) and reaches hundreds by the mid-2030s, so demand and lander production decide. Chain (S3): first heavy cargo 2028 -> two to four a year in 2030-31 -> ten in 2032. S2: 2033. S1: 2034. The budgets of one or two customers and landing failures keep S2-S4 at Medium by 2035.
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.strongest_case_small: NASA's budget buys only a few heavy landings a year, and SpaceX may hold its own lunar flights until propellant transfer and landing are routine. One landing failure can pause a fleet for months.
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.signpost: A contract or company plan for five or more heavy lunar cargo landings in one year; two heavy cargo landings within six months.
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.note_2035: New node: it makes explicit the landed-mass rate behind the 2033-35 lunar outcomes and the S4 analysis's off-Earth robot count. S4 equals S3 because launch binds and robots add at most about 1.4x to launch campaigns.
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.revision_note: R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): added from the acceleration advocate. Both reviewers found that the 10+ cargo landings a year behind the reviewed lunar S4 credits had no node. Hard edges from auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing and physclock-heavy-cadence-100; soft from the refueling economy, cheap internal launch cost and robot launch refurbishment (robo-earth-pads-plants dropped: S4 2035 is after this node). Soft edges out to the 10 t/yr oxygen plant, the robot fleet, long stays and robo-lunar-construction. No S4 credit. | R9-launch (2026-10-27): gate launch -> launch-internal (SpaceX's own manifest; Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 books Starlink, SpaceX's orbital compute, Moon and Mars cargo and NASA's lunar tanker flights in the internal account). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Medium 2035, S3 2034. Skeptic: ten landings need 100+ tankers and one or two customers' budgets, so 2035. Advocate: SpaceX's self-growing city plan, so 2033. Resolved two years after the earliest year. Bands at 2031 and 2035 unchanged.
auton-35-lunar-cargo-cadence.gate_note: Launch and refuelling cadence bind; customer budgets and lander production (capital) are the runner-up.

prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.title: An engine built around an AI-designed alloy flies
prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.description: A new rocket engine or major engine version flies with hot-section parts (preburner, turbine, chamber or nozzle) made from an alloy proposed by an AI design loop, and the alloy is what lets it run a hotter preburner or turbine, or a higher chamber pressure, than its heritage alloys allow. A drop-in part at the old operating point does not count; that is materials-ai-alloy-flight.
prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.status_oct2026: No engine has been designed around an AI-designed alloy (general). Oxygen-rich staged-combustion engines already depend on purpose-built alloys, such as SpaceX's in-house SX500 superalloy for Raptor and NASA's GRCop family for chambers (general). NASA's GRX-810 targets service above about 1,100 C and has not flown in an engine.
prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.why: The first AI-alloy flight (2030 in S2 and S3) is a substitution at the old operating point. The payoff comes when an engine version is designed around the new alloy's margin. A major engine version takes about 3 years, about 2-2.5 years by 2035 in S2-S3 (gate table 0.7-0.8x), and the alloy also needs production powder lots and in-house allowables from several heats. A reusable engine spends minutes at temperature per flight, so measured fatigue, short-time creep and oxidation data on the flown alloy back the design margin; long-life models help. Chain (S2): alloy flight 2030 -> version designed around the alloy 2031 -> hot-fire campaign and first flight 2033. S3: 2032. S1: alloy flight 2032 -> 2035 at the earliest. Oxygen-rich preburners and turbines are limited by their alloys' temperature (general), so the gain is performance or life. S2 is Low by 2035: it needs the alloy flight (Medium by 2035), a full engine version after it, and an engine maker willing to say the gain came from an AI-designed alloy. S3 is Medium because its alloy flight is High. Robots speed the engine-version hot-fire campaign at leading firms, but the alloy flight and attribution bind, so S4 equals S3.
prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.strongest_case_small: Engine makers already design proprietary alloys without AI (SX500), so attribution is hard to see. A hotter preburner buys a few percent of specific impulse or thrust-to-weight, and reuse economics turn on reliability more than on peak performance.
prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.signpost: An engine maker states that a new engine version's preburner temperature, turbine inlet temperature or chamber pressure rose because of an AI-designed alloy, with hot-fire data.
prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the performance step after the first AI-alloy flight, 2032-33 in S2-S3. The 2032-35 gate is the engine-version hot-fire campaign. Robots speed that campaign at leading firms, but the alloy flight and attribution bind, so S4 equals S3.
prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the alloy chain past materials-ai-alloy-flight. | E-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): materials-creep-oxidation-life-models hard -> soft (advocate, accepted): at minutes per flight, measured data on the flown alloy cover a rocket duty cycle. S2 Low kept, advocate's S2 Medium rejected: the node needs the alloy flight, now Medium in S2 by 2035, plus a three-year engine version, so it sits below it. S1 >2035 -> 2035 (advocate, cascade). Soft edges from robo-24x7-integration-test and robo-aerospace-tolerance-work (advocate): they land before this node in S4; no band change. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Lows a year after the earliest years (S2 2034, S3 2033): the node needs the alloy flight plus a 2-3-year engine version. S3 Medium 2035: the alloy flight is 30% likely by 2031 and not every flight leads to a version. Skeptic (Low) and advocate (2033) weighed; band_2035 Medium kept at the edge. Bands unchanged.
prop-35-alloy-enabled-engine.gate_note: The engine-version hot-fire campaign binds; production powder lots and multi-heat allowables (fabrication) are the runner-up.

prop-35-four-year-engine.title: A new large engine flies four years after program start
prop-35-four-year-engine.description: A clean-sheet liquid rocket engine of at least 1 MN (about 225,000 lbf) thrust flies on an orbital-class launch within four years of its program start, as disclosed by the developer. Program start is the earliest of the developer's disclosed start date, its first public announcement and its first funded contract. Derivatives of an existing engine family do not count.
prop-35-four-year-engine.status_oct2026: Clean-sheet engines take 6-13 years (model gate table). BE-4 went from program start in 2011 to first flight in Jan 2024 (general). Raptor work began about 2012; it first flew on a hop in 2019 and on an orbital-class flight in 2023 (general). LEAP 71's Noyron took two 20 kN engines from specification to first flame in under three weeks (Dec 2025), but large engines are paced by hot-fire failure discovery. SpaceX's McGregor site has 15 engine test stands (S-1/A).
prop-35-four-year-engine.premise_tier: n/a (capability and physical-gate premise; no catalog family)
prop-35-four-year-engine.why: Design labor is already near zero for small engines. Large engines are paced by turbopump and combustion failures that appear only in hot fire, each costing a redesign, a rebuild and a re-test. The stability tool is required, as for engine-development compression, because instability drives most of those loops; turbopump tools help. The gate table puts a new engine at 0.7-0.8x of its 6-13 years in S3 by 2031 and about 10% faster by 2035, so four years needs a best-case program that starts with S3 tools about 2029 (2033, Low). S2 compresses less (about 0.7-0.85x by 2035), so only a program started about 2031 that avoids a major test-stand loss fits (2035, Low). This is the one node in the branch where robots earn S4 credit, as a band step. The rate at which a firm finds failures is set by how many development engines it can build and how fast it turns its stands around, which is throughput. A robot-first firm builds development engines in parallel and runs its existing stands around the clock; the gate table gives a leading firm 0.45-0.51x by 2035 against about 0.63-0.72x in S3. Development engines are test articles, so flight-process requalification does not gate them. The credit applies to programs whose hot-fire phase falls in 2031-35, after robots are useful at leading firms (2030-31) and once 24/7 robot test is likely (High by 2035), and it lifts S4 from Low to Medium by 2035. The year stays 2033: a 2032 flight needs a 2028 start, and most of its hot fire would come before 24/7 robot test is likely (Low in 2031).
prop-35-four-year-engine.strongest_case_small: Fast firms already iterate on cheap printed hardware, so the four-year mark may be set by funding and test-stand losses (BE-4 stand explosions in 2015 and 2023, general), whatever the tools or robots. Few clean-sheet engines of this size start in any five-year period, so the chance rests on two or three programs.
prop-35-four-year-engine.signpost: A developer announces a clean-sheet 1 MN-class engine program in 2028-31 and reports full-duration hot fire within two years; disclosed robot counts at engine factories and test stands.
prop-35-four-year-engine.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. Robots lift S4 from Low to Medium by 2035: a robot-first firm that starts a program in 2030-31 builds development engines in parallel and turns its stands around 24/7 through its hot-fire phase. The year stays 2033 because a program flying in 2032 would do most of its hot fire before robot test is likely.
prop-35-four-year-engine.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; carries the S4 analysis's year-scale engine-development credit (2032-34), which prop-engine-dev-compression's test-count criterion does not measure. | E-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): S4 band step kept (draft) against the skeptic, and the advocate's S4 2032 rejected. Condition 1: the rate of finding failures is throughput (development engines built, stand turnaround). That is the mechanism the S4 gate table credits at leading firms (0.45-0.51x by 2035) and the S4 analysis's year-scale engine credit for 2032-34. Condition 2 holds only for programs with hot fire in 2031-35, which is why the band moves and the year does not (robo-24x7-integration-test is Low in S4 2031). Leading firms already have several large stands (SpaceX's McGregor site has 15), so no new stands are needed; development engines are test articles outside flight requalification. Hard edge from prop-stability-design-tool (skeptic, accepted; no year moves). Program start defined so the four-year clock cannot be gamed (skeptic). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S3/S4 Low 2033 -> 2034: a four-year program flying in 2033 would start in 2029 before the stability tool exists. S4 Medium 2035 (was 2034): a robot-first program started 2031 flies at the horizon. Skeptic (BE-4 took 13 years) and advocate (robot-first 2030 start, 2034) weighed. Bands unchanged.
prop-35-four-year-engine.gate_note: Hot-fire failure loops bind; how many development engines a firm can build (fabrication) is the runner-up.

prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.title: Engines fly 50 missions without overhaul
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.description: Fleet-leader main engines on a heavy reusable launcher fly 50 or more missions each without removal for overhaul, and the operator's scheduled overhaul interval reaches 50 flights, with inspection intervals and retirement limits set by calibrated life models and fleet data, as disclosed by the operator.
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.status_oct2026: A Falcon 9 booster flew its 33rd mission on Feb 21, 2026 (33FG), with Merlin engines refurbished between campaigns (general). Raptor 3 first flew in May 2026 and the Raptor 3 fleet had logged more than 40,000 s of runtime by Apr 2026 (newspaceeconomy). Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026) reached orbit with V3 and expended both stages as planned, so V3 reuse had not begun (33FG). Mach33's base case has Starship flights per stack, a flight-weighted average lifetime, rising from 3.3 (2027) to 18 (2030).
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise on an exogenous launch clock)
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.why: Each life data point costs a flight, so this node rides the launch exponential. Mach33's base case blends early stacks (2.5 flights) with later-generation stacks assumed to reach 60 flights, an average of 18 flights per stack in 2030. That lifetime is an assumption, so the launch clock the model adopts already expects stacks of 50+ flights. A later-generation stack entering service in 2028 at about 8-12 flights a year (judgment) passes 50 flights in 2032-34. Model-based reuse life (prop-reuse-extended, 2029 in S2 and S3) lets the operator stretch intervals step by step without a teardown at each step. Chain (S2): model-based intervals 2029 -> 100+ heavy flights a year 2030 -> fleet leaders at 8-12 flights a year -> 50 flights without overhaul 2033. S3: 2032, with cadence a year earlier. S1: 2034, on the same launch clock with slower, more conservative life models. It stays Medium because the operator must also set a 50-flight overhaul interval and disclose it, and one engine-caused failure resets the practice. Robotic inspection and refurbishment shorten turnaround, worth about half a year within 2032 at a robot-first operator, but pads and flights bind more than labor, so S4 equals S3.
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.strongest_case_small: Operators may stretch life empirically just as fast, and engine design (Raptor 3 was built for long life) matters more than models. The gains are internal and may not be disclosed.
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.signpost: An operator discloses engine flight counts above 50 without removal, or NASA or a defense customer accepts a mission on engines past a model-set life limit.
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the operating maturity of model-based reuse, reached 2032-34 as heavy cadence passes hundreds of flights a year. S4 gains about half a year inside 2032 from robotic refurbishment; flights bind, so its year and band equal S3.
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the reuse chain past prop-reuse-extended. | E-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): Description tightened to fleet leaders plus a 50-flight overhaul interval (skeptic, accepted): read as every engine on a 33-engine booster, it would be a far harder reliability claim. Why corrected (advocate, accepted; checked in 33FG): Mach33's 18 flights per stack is a flight-weighted lifetime that assumes 60-flight later-generation stacks, not a flight rate. Status adds Flight 14 (both stages expended) and the Falcon 9 33-flight record. Soft edge from capability-35-heavy-cadence-300 (advocate). Advocate's S3/S4 High rejected: the stricter description needs an operator-set interval and disclosure, and the 60-flight stack lifetime is a model assumption. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): S2 Medium 2034, S3 2033: a stack entering service in 2028 at 8-12 flights a year passes 50 in 2032-34, a year earlier in S3 on the launch clock. Bands unchanged.
prop-35-engine-50-flight-life.gate_note: Engine life data bind; the heavy-flight cadence that accumulates cycles (launch-internal) is the runner-up.

prop-35-depot-market.title: Propellant sold in orbit to outside customers
prop-35-depot-market.description: A depot operator delivers cryogenic propellant in orbit to at least one customer outside its own company, priced per delivered tonne, with the delivered mass measured to an agreed accuracy (custody transfer).
prop-35-depot-market.status_oct2026: No propellant has been sold in orbit (general). Eta Space targets a commercial LOX depot, Cryo-Dock, by 2030 (satnews, May 2026), informed by the LOXSAT demonstration. SpaceX's refueling is internal to its own lunar-lander contract.
prop-35-depot-market.why: Selling propellant needs routine transfers (prop-cislunar-propellant-economy: 2030 in S2), a customer and a measured delivered mass. Gauging with proven error bounds (prop-mass-gauging) and validated boil-off models make custody transfer contractible: at 1% gauging error, a 100 t delivery carries a 1 t dispute (illustrative). Customers would be third-party landers, NASA vehicles outside the lunar-lander contract and other operators' Mars missions; Cryo-Dock aims at LOX. Chain (S2): routine transfers 2030 -> an interface standard and a first contract 2031-32 -> first metered sale 2033. S3: 2032. S1: 2034. Low in every scenario: a vertically integrated SpaceX may never sell propellant, third-party depots need their own launches and customers, and AI mathematics moves the launch clock by months. Launches and customers bind, so S4 equals S3.
prop-35-depot-market.strongest_case_small: The stake of better models is small (about 0-1 tanker of margin per campaign), and the market may not exist: SpaceX fuels its own ships, and others may not build compatible vehicles before 2035.
prop-35-depot-market.signpost: A signed contract for propellant delivered in orbit to an outside customer, or Cryo-Dock receiving and dispensing propellant.
prop-35-depot-market.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the commercial end of the refueling chain, 2032-34. Customers and vertical integration bind in every scenario, so all are Low, and S4 equals S3.
prop-35-depot-market.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; gives prop-mass-gauging a downstream use (custody transfer). | E-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): band_2035 S3/S4 Medium -> Low (skeptic, accepted): the gate is capital and customers, and the reasons for S2 Low do not depend on scenario; a year of earlier cadence does not create a buyer. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Seed years kept: Low 2033 in S2-S4 (a year of earlier cadence does not create a buyer), 2034 in S1. Bands unchanged.
prop-35-depot-market.gate_note: Customers and capital bind; launches for third-party depots (launch-external) are the runner-up.

prop-35-mars-window-fueling.title: Tankers fuel five Mars ships for one window
prop-35-mars-window-fueling.description: In the months before one Mars launch window, tankers fill five or more Mars-bound Starships in Earth orbit, and the ships depart in that window. The ships may carry cargo or crew.
prop-35-mars-window-fueling.status_oct2026: The late-2026 Mars window is being skipped (model). Later windows open about Dec 2028-Jan 2029, early 2031, Apr 2033 and mid 2035 (model). NASA's OIG (Mar 2026) says a lunar-lander refueling needs more than 10 tankers; a Mars ship needs a comparable full refill. In Feb 2026 SpaceX put the Moon first, with Mars work to begin in 5-7 years (model). Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026) reached orbit and expended both stages as planned (33FG). On Aug 25 2026 SpaceX and Louisiana announced a launch campus at Pecan Island with five complexes of two pads each, on-site propellant production, construction from 2027 and first launches as soon as 2029 (33FG).
prop-35-mars-window-fueling.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
prop-35-mars-window-fueling.why: Not mainly an AI-math implication: windows, launch cadence and ship readiness set the date. Five ships need roughly 40-75 tanker flights (illustrative, at 100-150 t per tanker). Fuelled ships can wait only weeks in orbit, so the tankers fly in the 2-3 months before departure, a surge at an annualized rate of about 160-450 heavy flights. Pads and propellant plants for 300+ heavy flights a year (capability-35-heavy-cadence-300) make that surge routine; below that, most of the fleet must turn to Mars for a quarter. Boil-off margin sets the tanker count and the departure order; validated boil-off and transfer models (prop-cfm-models) trim that margin by a few tanker flights per campaign at most. Chain (S3): routine transfers 2029 and 300+ heavy flights a year 2032 -> Apr 2033 window. S2: routine transfers 2030 and 300+ heavy flights 2033 -> Apr 2033 window at the earliest. S1: 300+ heavy flights 2034 -> mid-2035 window. The early-2031 window is out of reach in every scenario: even S3 flies well under 300 heavy flights a year then, lunar campaigns compete for them, and SpaceX put the Moon first in Feb 2026. Medium by 2035 in S2-S4: two windows remain and the mid-2035 surge needs less than 300 flights a year sustained, but SpaceX's Mars plans have slipped before, and a missed window costs 26 months. Orbital mechanics fix the window, so S4 equals S3.
prop-35-mars-window-fueling.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics is off the critical path, which runs through cadence, ship reliability and funding. SpaceX may fly fewer, larger campaigns or skip windows.
prop-35-mars-window-fueling.signpost: SpaceX manifests five or more ships for the Apr 2033 window; a surge of tanker flights in the quarter before a window.
prop-35-mars-window-fueling.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the Mars-window end of the refueling chain. The Apr 2033 window is the earliest in S2-S4, after 300+ heavy flights a year; Plateau waits for the mid-2035 window. Orbital mechanics and cadence fix the dates, so S4 equals S3.
prop-35-mars-window-fueling.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the refueling chain past prop-cislunar-propellant-economy. | E-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): S3/S4 2031 -> 2033 and band_2031 Low -> Speculative (skeptic, accepted): 40-75 tanker flights in the 2-3 months before a window need a surge at an annualized 160-450 heavy flights, S3 reaches 300+ a year only in 2032, lunar campaigns compete for flights, and SpaceX put the Moon first in Feb 2026. prop-35-lunar-lander-reuse.title: One lunar lander makes three landings, refueled in space
prop-35-lunar-lander-reuse.description: One lunar lander is refueled beyond low Earth orbit (in lunar orbit, near-rectilinear halo orbit or on the surface) and makes at least three landings on the Moon, reusing its engines and tanks between them.
prop-35-lunar-lander-reuse.status_oct2026: No lander has been refueled or reused (general). NASA's 2023 Sustaining Lunar Development award went to Blue Origin's Blue Moon MK2, designed to be reusable and refueled in lunar orbit by a Cislunar Transporter (general). In Feb 2026 SpaceX put the Moon first (model).
prop-35-lunar-lander-reuse.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
prop-35-lunar-lander-reuse.why: Lander reuse with refueling in space turns cheap launch into cheap landed mass on the Moon. Blue Moon MK2 is designed for it (general), and SpaceX's Moon-first plan needs many landings. Chain (S2): routine transfers 2030 and heavy cargo landings 2029 -> tanker or depot operations in lunar orbit 2031-32 -> a lander's third landing 2033. S3: 2032, with cadence a year earlier. S1: 2034. Validated boil-off, relight-transient and engine life models trim margins; launches and funding set the date. Medium by 2035 in S2-S4 because two programs aim at it; Low in S1. Robot-built pads (robo-lunar-construction, S4 2033) limit plume damage on repeat landings, but three landings can use an unprepared site, so S4 equals S3.
prop-35-lunar-lander-reuse.strongest_case_small: Expendable or single-use landers may stay cheaper while Earth-launched propellant is cheap, and lunar-orbit tanker logistics may slip with every lander program.
prop-35-lunar-lander-reuse.signpost: A lander refueled in lunar orbit lands a second time; a tanker or depot flight to lunar orbit is manifested.

struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.title: Megawatt-class compute satellites fly
struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.description: A compute satellite with at least 1 MW of solar power flies and operates in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit. That is nearly seven times AI1's 150 kW peak (four times a later 250 kW generation), with roughly 4,000-6,000 m2 of array and a high-voltage power bus.
struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.status_oct2026: Starmind's design point rose from 150 kW peak (Jun 2026) to 250 kW peak (Aug 2026); Musk said on Oct 1 2026 that each spacecraft carries over 250 kW of solar and the rack runs near 250 kW average. SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response bounds each satellite under 4,000 kg, 200 m2 of radiator and 1,500 m2 of solar. Starcloud-3 (~200 kW) is designed for Starship. 33FG estimates that holding a 256-expert model inside one 72-GPU satellite costs up to 44% of serving output (Jul 2026). No flight-dated compute satellite above about 250 kW was found as of Oct 2026.
struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.why: Not an AI-math implication in its timing: satellite size is a SpaceX design choice on the hardware clock, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Cheap launch removes the reason to keep satellites small, and a larger satellite holds more GPUs inside one coherent domain, which cuts the penalty of splitting a model across satellites (up to 44% of serving output for one 72-GPU satellite, 33FG). At 1 MW a 250 V bus would carry 4,000 A, so the design pulls in 300-800 V buses (materials-wbg-rad-hard-power, struct-hv-power-bus-stability) and 4,000-6,000 m2 deployable arrays whose shape and loads must be predicted (struct-deployment-mechanics). That array is 1.6-2.4 times the ISS total (about 2,500 m2) on one free-flyer. These are the AI-math inputs, all soft. A 1 MW satellite falls outside the filed per-satellite envelope (4,000 kg, 200 m2 radiator, 1,500 m2 solar) by about 3-4 times, so it needs an FCC modification; the Gen2 amendment took about 16 months to a partial grant. Starlink's major size steps took 3-4 years each (V1 2019, V2 mini 2023, V3 2026). Chain (S2): first Starmind flights 2028 -> yearly generations from 2030 -> a MW-class design after two generations of telemetry -> FCC modification and array qualification -> first flight 2033. S3 is a year earlier through faster generations. Bands (judgment): Medium by 2035 in S2-S4 because SpaceX's stated architecture is ten-satellite formation clusters of 150-250 kW satellites (AI1 at 150 kW peak, then a later generation) and no filing covers MW-class satellites; S1 Low.
struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may keep satellites near 250 kW and scale by numbers and formation flying, as Starlink did. Software that shrinks the single-satellite penalty would remove the main reason to go bigger.
struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.signpost: A Starmind version or competing design above 500 kW announced with a flight date; a SiC or GaN power stage above 300 V named on a compute satellite.
struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S2 is 2033 and S3 and S4 2032 because a 1 MW satellite needs an FCC modification and 4,000-6,000 m2 of deployable array. S4 equals S3 because array deployment, power-part qualification and the FCC modification bind, and none is labor.
struct-35-mw-class-compute-satellite.revision_note: E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): new node. Extends the hardware chain past the first 100-kW-class flights; gives the deployment, bus-stability and SiC nodes a 2032-35 outcome. Review: Skeptic: years S2 2032 -> 2033, S3/S4 2031 -> 2032, band_2031 S3/S4 Low -> Speculative (FCC envelope gate, array size, Starlink step history); status updated with Musk Oct 1 2026. Advocate's High by 2035 rejected (single-trend extrapolation reaches 1 MW only about 2033; SpaceX states a cluster architecture; no MW-class filing) and the robo-24x7-integration-test soft edge not added (robo-aerospace-tolerance-work already carries the link; the gates are not labor). | R9-orbital-compute (2026-10-27): sized against AI1 (150 kW peak) with the 250 kW unit named as a later generation (review OC-2). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Medium a year after the earliest year (S2 2034, S3/S4 2033). Skeptic (FCC modification of about 16 months, Starlink size steps took 3-4 years) vs advocate (the design point already rose from 150 to 250 kW in two months; Starcloud-3 is about 200 kW): one year after the earliest year, not two.
