struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute.title: 10 GW of compute operating in orbit
struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute.description: Orbital data centers with at least 10 GW of combined power operate in orbit: about 67,000 AI1-class satellites at 150 kW peak, or fewer larger later generations. At AI1 density (about 14,000 t per GW) that is about 140,000 t, or about 100,000 t at the S-1's 100 kW/t: about 1,100-2,350 Starship flights at 60-90 t to dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit.
struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute.status_oct2026: Orbital compute is at kilowatt scale. Musk has suggested Starship could support about 10 GW a year of space compute in the 2030s and projected 300-500 GW a year later (Nov 2025); he names chip and packaging supply as the main limit. SpaceXAi's S-1 (May 2026) describes Terafab, a captive chip fab in Grimes County, Texas, with Tesla and Intel on Intel 14A; land clearing began in Aug 2026. Beijing Astro-Future has proposed 16 GW of dawn-dusk orbital data centers. Anthropic and SpaceX said in May 2026 that they are interested in jointly developing multiple GW of orbital compute. Approved Starship site caps total about 145 launches a year (Starbase 25, LC-39A 44, SLC-37 76). Mach33's Launch Keystone reference case (Sep 2026) launches 38,600 t of SpaceX's own compute in 2030 and 108,000 t in 2032, passing 10 GW during 2032 at today's mass per GW (calculation). That needs about 700-1,100 compute flights in 2032 alone, about three times the 300 heavy flights a year the model's trunk first reaches in 2032-33. Mach33 is a single commercial forecaster (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous anchor on launch, satellite production, chip supply and capital, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. At AI1 density (about 14,000 t per GW; Mach33's reconstruction, 150 kW peak, 2.1 t) 10 GW is about 140,000 t, or about 100,000 t at the S-1's 100 kW/t: about 1,100-2,350 Starship flights at 60-90 t to dawn-dusk SSO. Only the Florida pads reach these orbits; Starbase cannot fly south. At a third to a half of 300 flights a year and 60-90 t per flight to SSO, compute gets about 0.4-1.4 GW a year at AI1 density and 0.6-2.0 GW at S-1 density. Chain (S3): 1 GW in 2031 -> 300+ heavy flights a year from 2032 (capability-35-heavy-cadence-300) -> cadence keeps growing by about 100 flights a year -> compute takes about half -> Starship V4 lifts about 150 t to dawn-dusk orbit and new satellites reach 100 kW/t -> 3-4 GW a year by 2034-35 -> 10 GW in 2035. Every link is an upside case. S2 runs a year behind on cadence and reaches 10 GW only after 2035. A rough simulation on the trunk's launch clock (calculation, ranges as above) puts a central case near 5-6 GW at end-2035 in S3 and 4-5 GW in S2. Chips and packaging co-bind: about 2.9 million GPU packages at 250 kW per 72-GPU satellite (a later generation), more at AI1's 150 kW. Capital is large but reachable: Mach33's base case puts orbital capex at $46B per GW, falling toward $24B over a decade, so 10 GW is roughly $240-460B (a single commercial forecaster's model). Mach33's own paths run far ahead: the AI Compute Keystone installs about 9 GW by 2032 and 29 GW by 2035 in its base case (1.8 GW in 2035 in the cadence-bound lens), on a launch clock several times faster than the model's trunk. AI math is second-order: hotter chips, lighter radiators and right-sized radiation mitigation cut launched mass by a few percent to about 10%. S4 gets no credit. Robot-built pads and plants arrive only about 2035 in Embodied (Low), too late to add launch capacity before end-2035.2-2 GW by end-2035 (calculation); that leaves S4 at Low, and airspace, approvals, chips and capital do not compress. Satellite and array lines already run ahead of flights. Bands (judgment): S3 and S4 Low by 2035; S2 and S1 Speculative, after 2035.
struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics could vanish from the chain without moving this node by more than months: launch cadence, chip supply and capital set the date. If terrestrial power and permits ease, orbital compute may stall well below 10 GW.
struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute.signpost: Heavy flights above 300 a year with compute taking about half, by 2033; Starship V4 flying about 200 t; SpaceX reporting several GW deployed by end-2033; Starmind satellites flying Terafab chips.
struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. Launch binds: on the trunk's clock compute gets under 2.5 GW a year until cadence grows well past 300 flights a year, so 10 GW is Low by 2035 in S3 and S4 and comes after 2035 in S2. Robot-built pads add flights in 2034-35, too few to change the band, so S4 equals S3.

Review: Skeptic: years S2 2035 -> >2035, S3/S4 2034 -> 2035; band_2035 S2 Low -> Speculative, S3/S4 Medium -> Low (the draft chain claimed 2-3 GW a year from 100-150 compute flights, which delivers 0.6-2.3 GW); hard edge from capability-35-heavy-cadence-300 replaces the soft one; chip co-binding and the dawn-dusk payload penalty added. struct-35-orbital-training-run.title: A large AI model is trained in orbit
struct-35-orbital-training-run.description: An AI lab releases or deploys a model whose main training run, at least 1e26 FLOP, ran mainly on orbital compute.
struct-35-orbital-training-run.status_oct2026: Starcloud trained a small language model on one H100 in orbit within 38 days of its Nov 2025 launch. Anthropic and SpaceX said in May 2026 that they are interested in multiple GW of orbital compute, citing ground constraints on training and inference. 33FG argues that high orbits suit asynchronous training and low orbits suit inference (Dec 2025). No multi-satellite training run has been reported.
struct-35-orbital-training-run.why: Training uses the most power and tolerates latency, so it fits orbit well, and Anthropic named it among its reasons. It is also where radiation errors cost most: a silent error can corrupt weeks of work. That is where validated error rates (materials-see-system-models) and proven fault-tolerance bounds (materials-verified-fault-tolerance) earn their keep. A 1e26 FLOP run needs on the order of 100 NVL72-class satellites for about a month (calculation at about 40% utilization, assumption), about 25 MW, a few percent of a fleet near 1 GW. It spans several ten-satellite clusters (struct-formation-compute-clusters) joined by laser links and low-communication training methods. SpaceXAi runs both the fleet and an AI lab, and an announced run in orbit helps sell orbital compute. Chain (S3): clusters 2029 -> several hundred MW in orbit in 2031 -> the operator's own lab runs a 100-satellite job and releases the model in 2031. S2 is a year later, when its fleet nears 1 GW. Bands (judgment): High by 2035 in S3 and S4, where 1 GW is High; Medium in S2, where the fleet itself is less certain and labs may not say where a model trained; S1 Low.
struct-35-orbital-training-run.strongest_case_small: Labs may keep their largest runs on the ground, where interconnect is denser and failed parts are easy to swap, and use orbit for inference. That limits frontier-scale runs; a 1e26 run needs only a few percent of the fleet. Even then AI mathematics moves the date by months, since fleet size and links bind.
struct-35-orbital-training-run.signpost: A lab states that a released model's main training run ran in orbit; a training job spanning 50 or more compute satellites reported by 2032.
struct-35-orbital-training-run.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. A 1e26 FLOP run needs about 100 satellites, a few percent of a 1 GW fleet, and the operator runs its own lab, so S3 and S4 are High by 2035 and S2 Medium. S4 equals S3 because the S3 year is 2031.
struct-35-orbital-training-run.revision_note: E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): new node. Gives the radiation side lane (error models -> proven fault tolerance) a 2031-35 outcome. Review: Advocate (partly accepted): years S2 2033 -> 2032, S3/S4 2032 -> 2031, band_2031 S3/S4 Speculative -> Low, band_2035 S3/S4 Medium -> High (the 1e26 threshold is a few percent of the fleet and the operator runs a lab). Advocate's S2 High rejected: S2 holds 1 GW at Medium, so the fleet that would host the run is less certain. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Re-checked against the AI1 re-base that raised 1 GW to Medium by 2031 in S2: S2 Medium in 2033 (seed 2034) and S3/S4 High in 2034 (seed 2035), since a 1e26 FLOP run needs only about 25 MW. Skeptic (inference pays better, multi-satellite training unproven) vs advocate (SpaceXAi runs both fleet and lab): S2 stays Medium, not High, by 2035.

struct-35-beyond-dawn-dusk-compute.title: 100 MW of orbital compute outside dawn-dusk orbits
struct-35-beyond-dawn-dusk-compute.description: At least 100 MW of compute operates in orbits other than dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, such as inclined low orbits, medium Earth orbit or high Earth orbit.
struct-35-beyond-dawn-dusk-compute.status_oct2026: Starmind, Starcloud and Suncatcher designs use dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, which gives near-continuous sunlight, needs only ~100 um of coverglass and keeps array loss under 1% a year (33FG, Dec 2025). 33FG estimates the dawn-dusk band is about 1% of usable low-orbit volume; in medium Earth orbit, belt exposure drives coverglass to ~700 um and array loss to ~3% a year.
struct-35-beyond-dawn-dusk-compute.why: Dawn-dusk orbits give near-continuous sun and mild radiation, so early fleets stay there. Two forces could move 100 MW elsewhere: crowding of the dawn-dusk band, which 33FG puts at about 1% of usable low-orbit volume, as fleets pass several GW; and operators choosing high orbits for asynchronous training (33FG). Inclined low orbits put batteries through about 5,500 eclipse cycles a year; higher orbits raise array loss from under 1% to about 3% a year and raise chip error rates. Here the branch's AI-math side lanes pay off: validated workload-level error rates (materials-see-system-models), proven fault-tolerance bounds (materials-verified-fault-tolerance) and model-based battery qualification (materials-battery-life-qual) let operators size shielding, batteries and mitigation before flight data exist. A tranche outside dawn-dusk orbit needs a new FCC filing or modification, since SpaceX's Jan 2026 application covers 500-2,000 km sun-synchronous orbits only. Chain (S2): dawn-dusk fleets pass several GW in 2034 -> a first tranche in another orbit, authorized and flown in 2035. S3 and S4 are a year earlier. Bands (judgment): Low by 2035 in S2-S4 because larger satellites let dawn-dusk shells hold more power and no operator has filed for another orbit; S1 Speculative. Basis (R9): early fleets are AI1-class satellites (150 kW peak, 120 kW average, about 2.1 t) in dawn-dusk SSO, the orbit the AI1 reconstruction and the 16 Oct orbit ruling use.
struct-35-beyond-dawn-dusk-compute.strongest_case_small: Larger satellites let dawn-dusk shells hold well over 10 GW, and operators may fly, measure and iterate in a new orbit instead of relying on models; AI mathematics then changes little.
struct-35-beyond-dawn-dusk-compute.signpost: An FCC or ITU filing for compute satellites in inclined low, medium or high Earth orbit; published error and degradation statistics from a compute satellite outside dawn-dusk orbit.
struct-35-beyond-dawn-dusk-compute.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S2 is 2035 and S3 and S4 2034 because crowding needs fleets of several GW and a new filing. S4 equals S3 because licensing, launch and the cost of batteries and shielding bind.
struct-35-beyond-dawn-dusk-compute.revision_note: E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): new node. Gives the radiation and battery lanes a 2034-35 outcome. struct-35-test-standards-codify-ai-credi.title: Test standards write in credit for AI analysis
struct-35-test-standards-codify-ai-credi.description: A base revision of a structural or environmental test standard (NASA-STD-5001, GSFC-STD-7000 GEVS, SMC-S-016, ECSS-E-ST-10-03 or ECSS-E-ST-32-10) states when credibility-graded, AI-produced analysis may reduce or replace a qualification test, and with what factors and evidence. Credit then no longer needs a program-by-program waiver or tailoring.
struct-35-test-standards-codify-ai-credi.status_oct2026: No structural or environmental test standard mentions AI-produced analysis. NASA-STD-5001B (2014) allows no-test options for some metallic structures at higher factors, and GEVS (GSFC-STD-7000B, 2021) allows protoflight and qualification by similarity. Base revisions come every 8-10 years: GEVS 2013 and 2021, ECSS-E-ST-10-03 2012 and 2022, NASA-STD-7009 2008, 2016 and 2024 (physclock-credibility-evidence-standard).
struct-35-test-standards-codify-ai-credi.why: Standards codify practice after precedents. Chain (S2): rulebook 2029 -> first structural credit 2030 -> environmental credit on derivatives 2031 -> a base revision that cites those cases 2033. S3 is a year earlier because its precedents are. Codification turns one-off credit into default practice for government buys, where most of the remaining savings sit, since commercial operators already set their own tests. Capped at Medium because a standards body must accept it and no revision is committed to address AI analysis. S2 is Low because about one base revision falls inside its window after its precedents.

struct-35-qual-campaigns-30pct-shorter.title: Qualification campaigns 30% shorter at leading firms
struct-35-qual-campaigns-30pct-shorter.description: At leading space firms, qualification campaigns for spacecraft and launch-vehicle subsystems on programs started in 2031 or later run at least 30% shorter than the pre-2027 environmental qualification baseline of roughly 6-18 months. The cut comes from analysis credit, fewer re-tests, autonomous stands and round-the-clock integration and test. Leading firms set their own test programs, so industry-wide shortening and government credit speed it up but do not gate it. It is the second step after physclock-qual-cycle-compressed (15%, typical programs).
struct-35-qual-campaigns-30pct-shorter.status_oct2026: Environmental test campaigns take 6-18 months. GEVS sets at least 4 thermal-vacuum cycles at spacecraft level and 8 at component level, with plateaus of at least 12 hours (NASA TFAWS 2026, via embodied/research-space.json). Labor (fixtures, instrumentation, axis changes, teardown, troubleshooting) is about 35-45% of campaign time (embodied/s4-embodied.md gate table).
struct-35-qual-campaigns-30pct-shorter.why: The gate table puts environmental qualification at 0.7-0.8x of today in S3 2031, about 0.63-0.72x in S3 2035 and 0.71-0.83x in S2 2035, and at 0.58-0.67x for typical and 0.43-0.50x for leading S4 firms in 2035. Labor is about 45% of a campaign (labor, physics, materials and institutions 45/25/10/20), so robot-run setup, instrumentation and teardown cut it, while thermal-vacuum plateaus and cycles stay fixed. Parallel robot-tended rigs also shorten component reliability trials (0.3-0.5x), which counts here when it shortens a campaign. Robot labor gains alone give about 25% (45% at 2.3x), so the cut also needs a firm that accepts analysis in place of tests; that is the hard edge from physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual. Programs must start in 2031 or later and report, so the earliest evidence is 2033 in S3 and S4; S2 reaches 30% only at leading firms at the top of its range, about 2035. S4 gets a band and no year. Robots in cleanrooms and test chambers need contamination and ESD qualification on top of process requalification (6-24 months per process), and the first programs on a new robot line absorb that dip. S4 credit meets all four conditions: the gate at the achieving firm is labor and queue, robots do tolerance work at leading firms from 2030-31, no hard prerequisite lands later, and general-purpose robots add to S3's specialized stands.
struct-35-qual-campaigns-30pct-shorter.strongest_case_small: Firms spend saved time on more testing, and workmanship screening and thermal time constants set a floor. Robots on flight hardware need process requalification at each supplier, so early adopters slow down first. Leading firms rarely publish campaign durations.
struct-35-qual-campaigns-30pct-shorter.signpost: A leading firm or GAO reports qualification phases at least 30% shorter than the firm's pre-2027 programs on programs started in 2031 or later, citing robot-run integration and test or analysis credit.
struct-35-qual-campaigns-30pct-shorter.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon and the branch's clearest S4 effect. A 30% cut sits below even typical S4 programs (33-42% shorter by 2035), so it is High in S4 against Medium in S3, where leading firms sit at the top of a 28-37% typical range and disclosure is the risk. The year stays 2033 in both because the first programs on new robot lines absorb requalification. Thermal-vacuum dwells and cycles are unchanged in every scenario.
struct-35-qual-campaigns-30pct-shorter.gate_note: Test physics and robot-line requalification (qualification) bind; firms accepting analysis in place of tests (adoption) is the runner-up.

science-35-answer-first-missions.description: A science mission selected after 2028 puts onboard science products with certified error bounds into its requirements, so its downlink and ground segment are sized for answers. Raw data become the exception, kept for calibration and audits. A constellation, an Explorer-class or larger mission, or a deep-space probe counts, from any space agency or nonprofit. A commercial imaging service that ships its own analytics does not count: that is a business choice already under way.
science-35-answer-first-missions.status_oct2026: No science mission is designed this way. Onboard autonomy flies as an add-on (EO-1 from 2004 and AEGIS on Mars rovers, general; Phi-sat-2 since 2024, ESA), and requirements still assume raw or losslessly compressed downlink (general).
science-35-answer-first-missions.why: Second-generation step after the first mission accepts onboard products (science-onboard-science-inference, 2029 in S2 and S3). Chain: first accepted use 2029 -> a proposal team baselines it for a 2029-30 opportunity -> selection 2030 -> build and launch about 2033. Explorer-class missions take 5-6 years from selection to launch (science-bhex-flight), so 2033 needs a Scout, cubesat constellation or similar fast mission. S3 equals S2 because the onboard-inference input is 2029 in both and selection cycles bind. S3 is Medium by 2035 and S2 Low: S3's input is High by 2031, so more teams baseline onboard products at the 2029-31 opportunities, and ESA, CNSA, JAXA and nonprofit missions add chances outside NASA's scarce selections under the FY2027 request. S1's input lands in 2031, so its mission flies after 2035. No S4 credit: selection binds. Bands are judgments.
science-35-answer-first-missions.strongest_case_small: Optical links may raise downlink faster than onboard inference saves it, and science teams prize raw data for re-analysis, so missions may keep raw downlink as the baseline.
science-35-answer-first-missions.signpost: An Explorer, Discovery, ESA M-class or commercial science proposal with onboard products in its top-level requirements; a smallsat science constellation that tasks itself from onboard products.
science-35-answer-first-missions.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension: a mission selected about 2030 flies in 2033-36 with onboard products in its requirements. Selection binds, so S4 equals S3.

science-35-second-private-observatory.title: A second privately funded space telescope returns data
science-35-second-private-observatory.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
science-35-second-private-observatory.description: A philanthropically or commercially funded space telescope of 1 m aperture class or larger, other than Lazuli and started after it, returns science data.
science-35-second-private-observatory.status_oct2026: Lazuli (3 m, Schmidt Sciences) is the only private 1 m-class space telescope announced; its team calls a July 2028 launch 'admittedly aggressive' (Sky & Telescope, Jan 14 2026). Blue Skies Space delivered first data from its 13 cm Mauve on Jul 6 2026 (bssl.space). No second funder is known (general).
science-35-second-private-observatory.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous anchor for the private lane after 2031. Chain (S3): Lazuli returns data 2029-31 -> a second funder commits about 2030, as customer launch falls under $1,000/kg (S3 2030) -> a 2.5-3 year build with AI-run test stands -> data 2033. S2 is a year later through slower test campaigns and launch prices, and S1 later again. The funder's decision binds first, then mirror, detector and integration work. S4 gets no year: a build that ends in 2032-33 runs while robots are only starting flight-hardware work at leading firms (2030-31), requalification takes 6-24 months per process, and mirrors and detectors come from suppliers, who get robots after 2031. The S4 gate table gives leading firms about 15% on environmental qualification by 2031, which saves 2-4 months on a 3-year build. Low by 2035 in S2-S4 because no second funder is named and the first telescope has not flown. Bands are judgments.
science-35-second-private-observatory.strongest_case_small: Lazuli may be a one-off from one donor. If it slips or fails, no second funder follows by 2035.
science-35-second-private-observatory.signpost: Announcement of a second philanthropic or commercial 1 m-class space telescope; its build contractor and whether robots run its integration and test.
science-35-second-private-observatory.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension: the private lane may add a second telescope in 2033-35. S4 equals S3: the build ends before robots reach optics and detector suppliers, so they trim months, not a year.

Binding gate set to capital, since funding comes first. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Unchanged from the seed: Low from 2034 in S2 and 2033 in S3-S4; no second funder is named. Bands unchanged.

science-35-earth-twin-rv.title: Earth-mass planet found in a Sun-like star's habitable zone
science-35-earth-twin-rv.description: A planet under 2 Earth masses in the habitable zone of a nearby G or K dwarf is detected by radial velocity at 3 sigma or better, and the detection survives independent re-analysis.
science-35-earth-twin-rv.status_oct2026: The Terra Hunting Experiment's HARPS3 is being commissioned on the robotic Isaac Newton Telescope for a 10-year survey aimed at Earth-mass planets, with first science light expected in summer 2026 (ING instrument page). An Earth twin moves its star by about 9 cm/s, and stellar activity is about ten times larger (general). PLATO is scheduled to launch in March 2027 (DLR, Jul 20 2026). Earlier claims of Earth-mass planets around nearby stars have been withdrawn after re-analysis (general).
science-35-earth-twin-rv.why: Separating stellar activity from a 9-30 cm/s planet signal is a statistics and stellar-physics modelling problem, so cheap cognition attacks it directly. Chain (S3): nightly HARPS3 data from late 2026 -> activity models good to about 10 cm/s around 2030, once cognition is near-free -> six to seven observing seasons give a claim in 2033 -> independent re-analysis within months (science-claims-audit). S2 is a year later, and S1 needs most of the 10-year survey. K dwarfs help, because their habitable-zone planets give 20-30 cm/s. Low by 2035 in S2-S4: granulation and supergranulation set noise floors that only more nights reduce, weather and seasons fix the cadence, and Earth-mass claims have a record of failing re-analysis. A detection would shape the Habitable Worlds Observatory's target list. S4 equals S3: telescope time and seasons bind, and the telescope already runs robotically. Bands are judgments.
science-35-earth-twin-rv.strongest_case_small: Stellar noise at habitable-zone periods may not average down within a decade, and the survey may simply not hold a detectable Earth twin among about 40 stars.
science-35-earth-twin-rv.signpost: Terra Hunting Experiment or ESPRESSO papers reporting activity-corrected residuals near 10 cm/s; a habitable-zone Earth-mass claim and its independent re-analysis.
science-35-earth-twin-rv.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension: a 10-year survey started in 2026 could yield a habitable-zone Earth-mass planet in 2033-35 if activity modelling reaches about 10 cm/s. Seasons and telescope time bind, so S4 equals S3.
science-35-earth-twin-rv.revision_note: E-science resolver (2026-10-07): new node from the advocate, facts verified (ING instrument page; DLR on PLATO). Advocate's S3/S4 Medium lowered to Low: stellar noise floors, observing seasons and the record of withdrawn Earth-mass claims bind alongside modelling. Tier set to 3 (physics result from data), as for science-dark-energy-verdict. | E-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): title shortened from 'An Earth-mass planet found in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star'. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Unchanged from the seed: Low from 2034 in S2 and 2033 in S3-S4. Bands unchanged.

astro-35-cm-debris-custody.title: Debris tracked down to about 2 cm in the busiest shells
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.description: A shared, screening-grade catalog keeps custody of most objects larger than about 2 cm that cross the main constellation shells (450-600 km), roughly 50,000-100,000 objects (illustrative: a breakup-model size slope near d^-1.7, and small debris peaks at 750-1,000 km), with covariances good enough for conjunction screening. Operators can then screen against much of the 1-10 cm population that no catalog covers today.
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.status_oct2026: ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report counts about 1.2 million objects of 1-10 cm, nearly all untracked, against more than 40,000 catalogued objects. LeoLabs' sub-10 cm RANGER radar is in development. Space Fence (operational 2020, general) has not visibly grown the public catalog several-fold. Star trackers on constellations see roughly 10 cm and larger at useful ranges (general estimate). LeoLabs said in Oct 2019 that its Kiwi Space Radar was designed to track about 250,000 additional objects down to 2 cm (LeoLabs press release), and by late 2025 it ran 11 radars at seven sites (Wikipedia). Seven years on, no 2 cm catalog exists. The gate is revisit, sensitivity at slant range and sharing; single-site detection already exists.
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.pathway: P1 (association and orbit determination at 10^5-10^6 scale); sensor build-out and data sharing are not AI-math-driven
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.why: This is the second step on the sensor gate that limits LEO safety. Detection down to 2 cm exists at single sites. Custody needs enough 2 cm-capable sites for daily revisit and enough sensitivity at slant range. Below about 3 cm, S-band radar returns fall roughly with the sixth power of object size (Rayleigh scattering, general), so each step down in size costs much more power-aperture. AI applied math supplies the cognitive share: associating faint, sparse tracks and fitting orbits with honest covariances for tens of thousands of objects. Chain (S3): 5 cm catalog 2030 -> money for more 2 cm-capable sites through a commercial raise or a defense contract 2030-31 -> sites built in about 1-2 years each, 2031-33 -> association and covariance validation 2033 -> screening use 2034. S2 is a year later. Government radars take longer (Space Fence took about six years from contract to operation, and its second site was never built, general), so the commercial route sets the earliest year. S1 starts from its 2032 catalog and lands after 2035. Sensors compress about 1.0-1.3x and data sharing 1.0x, so S3 stays Low by 2035.
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.strongest_case_small: Radar power-aperture, money and willingness to share bind, and mathematics moves none of them. Operators can cut exposure to small debris by flying lower, where it decays within a few years, without tracking it at all.
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.signpost: A radar demonstrating custody of 2-3 cm objects in LEO (for example LeoLabs RANGER at full capability); a catalog with screening-grade covariances covering most 2-10 cm objects that cross 450-600 km.
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.note_2035: Inside the horizon only in S2-S4, and only at the end of the window. Hosted cameras on constellations are a second route (astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing). S4 adds nothing: radar arrays are factory electronics with months of site work, and capital and data sharing bind.
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon. | E-safe-orbits resolver (2026-10-07): years and bands kept. The skeptic's later dates rest on government radar precedent, and the commercial route with existing 2 cm detection is faster. The advocate's earlier dates ignore that no 2 cm catalog appeared in the seven years after Kiwi. Population cut to roughly 50,000-100,000 (both reviewers). Status adds Kiwi and the LeoLabs network; chain rewritten. Soft edge from robo-construction-trades dropped (both reviewers). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Seed kept: Low from S2 2035 and S3 2034, never Medium; S1 beyond 2035.
astro-35-cm-debris-custody.gate_note: Revisit and sensitivity at slant range (data) bind; money for more 2 cm-capable sites (capital) is the runner-up.

astro-35-adr-recurring-service.title: Debris removal becomes a recurring paid service
astro-35-adr-recurring-service.description: At least three defunct satellites or spent stages are removed in one calendar year, at least one of them paid under a commercial contract or a regulatory obligation. The servicers are built in series. Technology demonstrations do not count toward the three.
astro-35-adr-recurring-service.status_oct2026: No recurring removal service exists. Starfish Space holds a $52.5M Space Force contract, awarded through the Space Development Agency in Jan 2026, for an end-of-life disposal mission for Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture satellites, launch targeted 2027, with options for more (Wikipedia). It raised more than $100M in Apr 2026 to scale Otter production and has more than $90M of government backlog (SpaceNews via 33FG). Airbus ordered more than 100 Astroscale docking plates in Mar 2025 (Wikipedia). ADRAS-J2 is planned for 2027, ClearSpace-1 for 2028 on Vega-C, and ELSA-M for Eutelsat, ESA and UKSA no earlier than 2028 (Wikipedia).
astro-35-adr-recurring-service.pathway: P7 (exogenous; AI math enters through safety-case and autonomy tools)
astro-35-adr-recurring-service.why: The first removal (2028 in every scenario) shows capture works. A recurring service also needs servicers built in series and a payer, and both exist in early form: Starfish builds Otters as a product line, and the Space Development Agency pays to dispose of its own satellites. Chain: paid SDA disposal and ADRAS-J2 2027-28 -> SDA options and other contracts exercised 2028 -> servicers from series production fly 2029-30 -> three removals in one year about 2030 at the earliest. Removal missions slip (ClearSpace-1 by two years so far), so the bands carry that risk. AI math trims each mission's test campaign and safety review through certified capture envelopes and assured autonomy. It creates no demand. Demand comes from owners removing their own failed satellites, disposal rules, liability or a capacity regime. Years and bands are the same in every scenario because payers and first flights set the pace.
astro-35-adr-recurring-service.strongest_case_small: Removal may stay a few contracts a year from a handful of government payers, because no rule obliges commercial operators to pay. Below about 600 km, drag clears failed satellites within years, and Cycle 26 drag peaks in the mid-2030s, so paid removal there has little case. Demand sits at 1,000-1,200 km (SDA, OneWeb), where failed satellites stay up for centuries (general).
astro-35-adr-recurring-service.signpost: The Starfish SDA disposal flown and an option exercised; ELSA-M results; a constellation operator or insurer paying to remove its own failed satellite; a government contract for several removals with one servicer design.
astro-35-adr-recurring-service.note_2035: Paid disposal exists from 2026 and servicers are built as a product line, so three removals in one year by 2035 is about even odds in every scenario. Slips of two years or more are common, which holds it at Medium. S4 adds nothing because payers and first flights set the date before robots reach servicer makers.
astro-35-adr-recurring-service.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. Robot soft edges moved to astro-35-adr-at-scale. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): All scenarios Medium 2032 (seed 2033): three removals in one year is possible from 2030, and the typical two-year slip of removal missions puts 30% at 2032; about even odds by 2035. Skeptic (payers beyond SDA are thin) against advocate (SDA options and Starfish series production): 2032. Bands unchanged.

astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination.title: Chinese and Western fleets coordinate maneuvers by machine
astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination.description: At least one Western megaconstellation (for example Starlink) and at least one Chinese megaconstellation (Guowang or Qianfan) exchange ephemerides and maneuver intent machine to machine under an agreed protocol, and resolve close approaches without ad hoc human contact.
astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination.status_oct2026: No US-China ephemeris or maneuver-intent exchange exists. On Dec 9, 2025 a payload from a Chinese Kinetica-1 launch passed close to Starlink-6079 (reported about 200 m, unverified) with no coordination. Guowang and Qianfan are each planned above 10,000 satellites, and China filed for about 200,000 satellites at the ITU in Dec 2025.
astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination.pathway: P2 (verified protocol); the agreement itself is political
astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination.why: Chinese megaconstellations are the largest group of satellites outside Western coordination. Verified protocols (astro-coordination-protocols) and Western machine-to-machine coordination (astro-autonomous-ca-at-scale) make the technical bridge cheap. The gate is a government decision on both sides. Chain (S2): Western protocol operational 2031 -> technical talks and a pilot exchange 2032 -> agreed machine-readable exchange 2033 at the earliest. Politics runs at 1.0x in every scenario, so S3 and S4 match S2. S1 trails its 2033 Western rollout.
astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination.strongest_case_small: US-China relations, export rules and military sensitivities may block any exchange whatever the math shows. Conjunction warnings already reach Chinese operators through existing channels (general), and both sides may judge that enough. The Wolf Amendment in each appropriations act bars NASA and OSTP from bilateral work with China, so a government route runs through Commerce or DoD. The FY2027 request cuts the Office of Space Commerce, which runs TraCSS, from $52.5M to $11M.
astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination.signpost: A published agreement between SpaceX and a Chinese operator, or between the US and Chinese governments, on ephemeris and maneuver-intent exchange; Chinese operators joining TraCSS or another shared screening service.
astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination.note_2035: A new 2035-horizon node. S4 adds nothing because a political agreement sets the date.

astro-35-l5-storm-arrival-forecast.title: Solar-storm arrival forecast within 6 hours, using Vigil
astro-35-l5-storm-arrival-forecast.description: The best routinely run CME arrival-time forecast reaches a mean absolute error of 6 h or less over at least 40 impacting CMEs, using real-time side-view coronagraph and heliospheric-imager data from ESA's Vigil, with calibrated probability windows.
astro-35-l5-storm-arrival-forecast.status_oct2026: The best routinely run ensemble (Ensemble WSA-Enlil+Cone) has a mean absolute error of 10.3 h, and all CCMC scoreboard submissions together 13.2 h (Kay et al. 2024). Vigil carries NOAA's CCOR coronagraph, a heliospheric imager and a photospheric magnetic imager; it is planned to launch in Q3 2031 on Ariane 6, start quasi-nominal operations about 30 degrees from Earth and reach L5 after a cruise of about 3 years (Wikipedia).
astro-35-l5-storm-arrival-forecast.why: Side views constrain CME speed and direction, which with the background solar wind dominate arrival error (Kay et al. 2024). With Vigil data from about 2033, assimilative ensembles built on the 8 h systems can run in real time. Validation runs on an event-count clock: with an error standard deviation near 15-17 h, about 40 impacting CMEs are needed, roughly two years as Cycle 26 rises. Chain (S2-S4): Vigil quasi-nominal data 2033 -> real-time ensembles with side-view imaging 2033 -> 40 events by 2035. The 6 h target is a judgment (illustrative). S1 reaches the 8 h step only in 2033 and lands after 2035. Events count from Vigil's quasi-nominal start at 30 degrees, about early 2033. Vigil flies as a secondary passenger on an Ariane 6 dual launch (Wikipedia), and a launch slip of about a year moves the node beyond 2035. S3 cannot beat the event count: at about 20-25 impacting CMEs a year early in the rise, 40 events arrive about early 2035, and S2 has cheap cognition by 2033 as well.
astro-35-l5-storm-arrival-forecast.strongest_case_small: Earlier side views from STEREO barely moved the error, and background solar-wind modeling may limit skill more than viewing angle. A one-year Vigil slip pushes the test beyond 2035.
astro-35-l5-storm-arrival-forecast.signpost: Vigil launch on schedule (Q3 2031) and its first real-time heliospheric-imager products; a scoreboard model posting a mean absolute error below 7 h over 40 impacting CMEs.
astro-35-l5-storm-arrival-forecast.note_2035: A new 2035-horizon node that lands only at the end of the window, in S2-S4. S4 adds nothing because launch and event-count clocks bind.

Advocate's S3/S4 2034 rejected: the event count binds, and the same argument would move S2. | E-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): title shortened from 'Storm arrival forecasts within about 6 hours using Vigil's side views'. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Seed kept: Low 2035 in S2-S4 only, never Medium; a year of Vigil slip moves the node beyond 2035.
astro-35-l5-storm-arrival-forecast.gate_note: The event-count clock with Vigil side views (data) binds; Vigil's launch date (launch-external) is the runner-up.

astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.title: Lunar navigation with proven error bounds in routine use
astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.description: A lunar navigation service (ESA Moonlight, a LunaNet provider or a commercial relay) broadcasts with integrity monitoring whose protection levels carry machine-checked bounds, and at least three missions, including surface-base operations, use it as a primary navigation source.
astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.status_oct2026: ESA Moonlight plans initial navigation services at end-2028, interoperability tests in 2029 and full operations in 2030; the Lunar Pathfinder relay is planned to begin operations in 2026 (ESA, Oct 2024). LuGRE obtained a GNSS fix on the lunar surface on Mar 3, 2025. NASA paused Gateway in its current form in Mar 2026 and redirected resources to a lunar surface base (NASA via 33FG). No lunar navigation service publishes integrity bounds yet.
astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.why: Surface-base operations need navigation integrity like aviation GNSS has. Moonlight reaches full operations about 2030, and certified filters (2028 in S2) plus a flown monitor (2029) make an integrity-bounded service a software step. Chain (S2): flight demo 2029 -> integrity monitor in a provider's ground and user segments 2030-31 -> three missions using it as a primary source, one at the surface base, 2032. S3 cannot beat the lunar manifest, so it matches S2. S1 follows its 2031 demo by three years. Moonlight full operations in 2030 is an ESA plan; a slip moves this node year for year. The 2035 band is the joint odds of three things: the surface base (a hard prerequisite), Moonlight on schedule, and a provider adopting machine-checked bounds.
astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.strongest_case_small: Accuracy is set by signals, clocks and geometry. Providers can publish integrity from conventional overbounding without machine-checked proofs, and missions may keep their own optical navigation as the primary source.
astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.signpost: Moonlight or LunaNet service documents specifying formally verified protection levels; a lunar lander or surface-base operation naming the service as its primary navigation source.
astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.note_2035: By 2035 the node rides on the surface base: Medium in S3 and S4, where the base is likely, and Low in S2 and S1, where it is less so. Uncrewed users need no certifier, so the regulatory cap does not set the band. S4 adds users. Launches set the date, so it adds no years.
astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon. | E-safe-orbits resolver (2026-10-07): hard edge from auton-moon-base-infrastructure (skeptic): the definition requires surface-base operations; it moves no year. band_2031 S2-S4 Low -> Speculative (skeptic; the year is 2032). band_2035 S2 Medium -> Low (resolver: the node's odds follow the base, which is less likely in S2). Advocate's High by 2035 and robo-lunar-construction soft edge rejected. | R9-launch (2026-10-27): gate launch -> launch-external (an outside customer buys the flight). Hard prerequisite physclock-customer-launch-access added: customers wait for capacity to reopen (v1.3 reference 2031, tested 2029 to 2033). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Seed kept: S3/S4 Low 2032, Medium 2034 (joint odds of the surface base, Moonlight on schedule and a provider adopting bounds); S2 Low 2033 only. Bands unchanged.
astro-35-lunar-nav-certified-service.gate_note: Lunar launches through customer access (launch-external) bind; a provider adopting machine-checked bounds and three missions using it (adoption) is the runner-up.

astro-35-adr-at-scale.title: Ten or more dead satellites removed in one year
astro-35-adr-at-scale.description: Servicers remove at least 10 defunct satellites or spent stages from orbit in one calendar year, under paid contracts or regulatory obligations. Technology demonstrations do not count.
astro-35-adr-at-scale.status_oct2026: No servicer has yet removed a satellite. Starfish Space raised more than $100M in Apr 2026 to scale Otter production and has more than $90M of government backlog (SpaceNews via 33FG). Airbus ordered more than 100 Astroscale docking plates in Mar 2025 (Wikipedia), so future clients can be prepared for capture.
astro-35-adr-at-scale.pathway: P7 (exogenous; AI math enters through safety-case and autonomy tools)
astro-35-adr-at-scale.why: Removal at this rate is what would start to bend the debris curve at 1,000-1,200 km. Failed satellites there (SDA, OneWeb, later Guowang) stay up for centuries, so owners must pay to clear them. Chain (S2): three removals in one year 2030 -> owners and regulators turn single contracts into fleet disposal programs 2031-32 -> multi-client servicers built in series 2032-34 -> ten removals in one year about 2035. S3 is a year earlier because its servicer design, test and safety-case cycles run faster. The count is set by payers and their budgets. Cheaper servicers buy a few more removals at the margin.
astro-35-adr-at-scale.strongest_case_small: Payers may stay a few governments with small budgets. Many of the most dangerous derelicts are Soviet and Russian upper stages near 800-1,000 km, and removing them needs Russian consent (general). Operators may meet disposal rules through better reliability and their own deorbit systems, which leaves few clients.
astro-35-adr-at-scale.signpost: A fleet disposal program (for example SDA options covering a whole tranche, or Eutelsat paying to clear failed OneWeb satellites); a servicer that removes more than one client per mission; insurers pricing removal into constellation cover.
astro-35-adr-at-scale.note_2035: S4 equals S3. Labor is about 20% of servicer build (S4 space research), and build is only part of a removal's cost with launch, operations and insurance, so robot-built servicers cut cost per removal by well under 10% (illustrative). Servicer makers are small firms that get robots after 2031 and must requalify each process (6-24 months). Capture arms are specialized machines already counted in S2 and S3. Payers set the count.
astro-35-adr-at-scale.revision_note: E-safe-orbits resolver (2026-10-07): new node from the acceleration advocate. Its S4 credit (S4 2033, Medium by 2035) is rejected: the four-condition rule fails on condition 1, because payers set the count and labor is a small share of cost per removal. S4 = S3. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Seed kept: Low from S2 2035 and S3 2034, never Medium; S4 equals S3 (labor is a small share of cost per removal).
astro-35-adr-at-scale.gate_note: Payers and their budgets (capital) bind; multi-client servicers built in series (fabrication) are the runner-up.

astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.title: Constellation cameras detect debris down to about 2 cm
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.description: Dedicated small cameras hosted on at least one megaconstellation detect debris down to about 2 cm at ranges up to a few tens of km, and the detections feed a shared screening catalog. Star trackers flown for attitude control do not count.
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.status_oct2026: SpaceX Stargaze (Jan 2026) uses about 30,000 star trackers to track the trackable population with minutes of latency, but star trackers see roughly 10 cm and larger at useful ranges (general estimate). No operator has announced a dedicated debris camera payload.
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.pathway: P1 (too-short-arc orbit determination and association at millions of detections a day)
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.why: Short range removes the radar's power-aperture problem. A 10 cm object is about magnitude 7-8 at 100 km (astro-constellation-hosted-ssa). A 2 cm object has 1/25 the area, so it is about magnitude 8-9 at 25 km (illustrative), within reach of a 5-10 cm camera with fast readout. The hard part is mathematics. Each detection is a streak lasting a fraction of a second at degrees per second, so orbits come from associating millions of too-short arcs a day across thousands of hosts. That work is near-free in S3 from 2029. Chain (S3): hosted tracking with honest error bars 2028 -> camera added to a satellite generation 2030-31 (generations refresh about yearly) -> association pipeline validated and feeding a catalog 2032. S2 is a year later. S1 trails on the association work and lands after 2035.
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.strongest_case_small: Targets must be sunlit against a dark background, and relative speeds up to about 15 km/s smear the signal, which cuts the duty cycle. No operator has announced such a payload, and an operator flying at 480 km, where cm-class debris decays within a few years, may see little reason to fly one.
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.signpost: A megaconstellation operator announcing a dedicated debris camera payload; published detections of sub-5 cm objects from a hosted camera; a shared catalog citing hosted-camera tracks.
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.note_2035: The bands stay Low because no operator has announced such a payload and streak detection at these rates is unproven in orbit. S4 adds nothing because host satellites come from specialized constellation lines already counted in S2 and S3.
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.revision_note: E-safe-orbits resolver (2026-10-07): new node from the acceleration advocate, a non-radar route to cm-class custody. Years kept (S2 2033, S3 2032). band_2035 S3 and S4 cut from Medium to Low: no announced payload, and the physics is unproven in orbit. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Seed kept: Low 2033 in S2-S4 (no payload announced, so the S3 earliest year 2032 is under 10%), never Medium; S1 beyond 2035.
astro-35-hosted-cm-debris-sensing.gate_note: An operator choosing to fly debris cameras (adoption) binds; associating millions of too-short arcs a day (cognitive) is the runner-up.

plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.title: Full-thruster plasma simulation fast enough for design work
plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.description: Full-device 3D kinetic simulation of a 5 kW-class Hall thruster at real mass ratio, with neutrals and wall emission, runs in hours on a leadership-class machine or in about a day on a commercial cluster. A design loop can then afford hundreds of kinetic evaluations, so thruster design no longer has to wait for a universal transport closure.
plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.status_oct2026: No facility-scale kinetic simulation of a Hall thruster exists at feasible cost (Whittaker, Marks, Gorodetsky, AIAA 2026). The tree's estimate for a 1 ms full-device run is about 1e18-1e19 particle pushes, weeks to months on a full exascale machine today (plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale).
plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.why: Days per run (plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale, S2 2028) still rules out design loops. Hours per run needs another 10-50x. The parent already uses the main algorithm families (sparse-grid, low-rank, asymptotic-preserving, learned subgrid models) to reach days, so a second 3-10x from them is the optimistic case and needs S3's recursive algorithm work from 2029. Hardware for memory-bound particle-in-cell codes gains about 3-5x over 2028-33 (judgment). Large AI clusters add capacity, but by 2028 leadership-class machines are built from the same accelerators (general), so they do not add a separate factor. Chain (S3): hero runs 2028 -> four years of recursive algorithm work and newer hardware -> design-loop speed 2033. S2: 2034. S1 does not get there by 2035. With hours-long runs, designers can optimize on kinetic physics directly and use the closure (plasma-hall-anomalous-closure) as a check. Medium in S3 because gains may stall and surrogates may make the full loop unnecessary. Algorithms and compute bind, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.strongest_case_small: Some cost may be irreducible: electron-cyclotron drift waves must be resolved over a millisecond of xenon transit, and algorithm gains could stall near 10x. Surrogates trained on a few hero runs may give designers the same answer more cheaply.
plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.signpost: A paper or company reports a design optimization that ran at least 100 full-device kinetic simulations of a Hall thruster, each at real mass ratio and real geometry.
plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the step after hero runs, 2033 in S3 and 2034 in S2. It gives predictive design a second route that does not wait for a universal transport closure, and gives the closure and erosion models many more training cases. Algorithms and compute bind, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.revision_note: E-plasma-nuclear (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the kinetic-simulation chain past plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale. | Resolver (2026-10-07): S3/S4 2032 -> 2033 and the algorithm credit cut to a second 3-10x (skeptic: the parent already spends these algorithm families). Advocate's hardware point partly accepted (3-5x for memory-bound PIC; AI clusters are not a separate factor once leadership machines use the same accelerators); its S2 2033, S2 Medium and S3 High rejected. Skeptic's S2 2035 and S3 Low rejected. Soft edges added to plasma-ep-predictive-design, plasma-hall-anomalous-closure and plasma-ep-life-by-analysis (advocate). | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Unchanged: S3/S4 Medium 2034, a year after the earliest year; S2 Low from 2034. Skeptic (gains may stall, surrogates may make it unnecessary) vs advocate (recursive algorithm work from 2029): Medium kept in S3.
plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop.gate_note: Algorithm gains (cognitive) bind; hardware for memory-bound particle-in-cell codes (fabrication) is the runner-up.

plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.title: AI-designed thrusters fly across a whole constellation
plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.description: An electric thruster designed mainly by an AI optimization loop (as defined in plasma-ai-designed-thruster-flight) flies on at least 1,000 satellites of one constellation, with fleet performance inside the pre-flight predicted band and the design attribution public.
plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.status_oct2026: Starlink flies thousands of Hall thrusters (krypton, then argon) designed by conventional iteration (general). No AI-designed thruster has flown (plasma-ai-designed-thruster-flight).
plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.why: Constellation operators refresh satellite generations about yearly from 2029-31 (physclock-satellite-gen-cadence) and build thrusters in house, so a design that proves itself in one flight can enter the next generation. Chain (S2): first AI-designed thruster flight 2031 -> adopted in the next satellite generation 2032 -> 1,000 units flown 2033. S3: 2032. S1: first flight 2033 -> 2035, at the horizon, so Speculative. The band is held down by disclosure, because operators may not say how a thruster was designed. Satellite generations and launch set the pace, and thruster production is not the bottleneck, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.strongest_case_small: Constellation thrusters are cheap and mature, and their economics turn on propellant, power-processing mass and production rate. A few points of efficiency may not justify changing a working design, and an in-house design loop may never be described in public.
plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.signpost: A constellation operator states that a new satellite generation flies a thruster designed mainly by an AI loop, with fleet performance data.
plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: fleet adoption after the first flight, 2032 in S3 and 2033 in S2. Satellite generations and launch set the pace, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.revision_note: E-plasma-nuclear (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends plasma-ai-designed-thruster-flight to fleet use. | Resolver (2026-10-07): Advocate's S2 Low -> Medium and S3/S4 Medium -> High rejected: one constellation must fly 1,000 units of one AI-designed thruster and say so, and the leading in-house maker does not publish design methods. Unchanged. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Unchanged: S3/S4 Medium 2034, two years after the earliest year; S2 Low from 2033. Disclosure holds the band down.
plasma-35-ai-thruster-constellation.gate_note: Operators adopting and disclosing AI-designed thrusters (adoption) bind; satellite generations and their launches (launch-internal) are the runner-up.

plasma-35-abep-service.title: Air-breathing electric propulsion in operational service
plasma-35-abep-service.description: At least one operational satellite (commercial or government; technology demonstrations do not count) holds a mission orbit below 250 km for at least a year, using air-breathing electric propulsion for drag makeup.
plasma-35-abep-service.status_oct2026: Laboratory demonstrations only (general). Albedo's Clarity-1 flew at 350-380 km on xenon ion propulsion for nine months (Albedo, Jan 2026). No air-breathing thruster has flown (plasma-abep-demo).
plasma-35-abep-service.why: A demo (S2 2031, S3 2030) proves intake and discharge physics. An operational unit also needs endurance data, a product design and a customer who values orbits below 250 km, where stored propellant runs out. Chain (S3): demo 2030 -> one to two years of on-orbit endurance, including atomic-oxygen erosion, and a funded product -> first operational satellite 2033 -> a year in service 2034. S2: 2035. S1: demo 2033 -> after 2035. An operational unit must also be sized for the solar cycle 26 maximum, expected around 2035 (general), when density at 200-250 km is several times higher; a demo near the 2030-31 minimum does not test that. Low at best because the business case competes with conventional electric propulsion at 300-380 km and with cheap replacement launches. Launch, customers and endurance data bind, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-abep-service.strongest_case_small: Cheap launch makes short-lived low-orbit satellites easy to replace, and conventional electric propulsion already holds 300-380 km. Intake efficiency and atomic-oxygen erosion may keep air-breathing propulsion a niche.
plasma-35-abep-service.signpost: A low-orbit operator orders an air-breathing propulsion system for an operational satellite, or an in-orbit demo reports more than six months of drag makeup.
plasma-35-abep-service.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: service after the first demo, 2034 in S3 and 2035 in S2. Launch, customers and endurance data bind, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-abep-service.revision_note: E-plasma-nuclear (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends plasma-abep-demo to operational service. | Resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic accepted: S3/S4 2033 -> 2034, S2 2034 -> 2035, band_2035 S2 Low -> Speculative (zero slack); solar-cycle sizing added to why. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Unchanged: Low from 2034 in S3/S4 only.
plasma-35-abep-service.gate_note: A customer for orbits below 250 km (adoption) binds; on-orbit endurance data including atomic-oxygen erosion (experiment) is the runner-up.

plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.title: A reactor-powered electric spacecraft thrusts for a year
plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.description: A spacecraft powered by a space fission reactor (Space Reactor-1 Freedom or a successor) runs its electric thrusters on reactor power for a cumulative year in space. These are the first nuclear-electric propulsion operations.
plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.status_oct2026: SR-1 Freedom (over 20 kWe, HALEU fuel, Gateway PPE bus with three 12 kW AEPS and four 6 kW Hall thrusters) targets a Dec 2028 launch at a $2.1B estimate (Sep 2026), with $10M recommended by the House Appropriations Committee (May 2026). No U.S. reactor has flown since SNAP-10A (1965).
plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.why: SR-1 must launch toward Mars in a Mars window. At about 20 kWe its thrust is about 1 N or less, roughly 1e-4 m/s2 on a several-tonne craft, so spiralling out from low orbit would take about two years (general arithmetic). A launch in the early-2031 window, the earliest year of physclock-reactor-in-space in every scenario, gives a cumulative year of thrust in 2032, and only if FY2027 or FY2028 funds SR-1 in full. The next window, about Apr 2033, gives 2034. A mid-2035 launch finishes after 2035. A lunar reactor does no thrusting. The AEPS thrusters on the PPE bus finish their wear test in Sep 2029 (plasma-aeps-life-qual), so thruster life is not the gate. Low in every scenario because the reactor launch is Low by 2035 and only the 2031 and 2033 windows count. Appropriations and launch windows bind, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.strongest_case_small: Every U.S. space reactor program since 1965 has been cancelled, and SR-1 is underfunded against its Dec 2028 date. If SR-1 misses the Apr 2033 window, a year of nuclear-electric thrust waits past 2035.
plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.signpost: SR-1 Freedom receives a full FY2027 or FY2028 appropriation and a firm launch date; a ground criticality test of its reactor.
plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the propulsion payoff of SR-1, 2032 at the earliest in every scenario. Only the early-2031 and Apr 2033 Mars windows give a full year of thrust by 2035. Appropriations and launch windows bind, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.revision_note: E-plasma-nuclear (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends physclock-reactor-in-space to nuclear-electric operations; side chain. | Resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic's window logic accepted (why rewritten; a lunar reactor does no thrusting). S1 2033 -> 2032; the skeptic's 2034 is rejected because physclock-reactor-in-space now has the early-2031 window as its earliest year in every scenario. Advocate's S2-S4 Medium rejected: it rested on a Medium reactor band, now Low. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Low from 2034 (seed 2033): a year of thrust by 2032 needs the early-2031 window, which the reactor launch itself reaches only at about 10%, so 10% is first passed via the Apr 2033 window in 2034. Never Medium.
plasma-35-nep-year-of-thrust.gate_note: Appropriations for SR-1 (capital) bind; Mars launch windows (launch-external) are the runner-up.

plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.title: Fusion-drive ground prototype makes fusion and thrust
plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.description: A ground prototype built to a closed fusion-propulsion design (plasma-fusion-propulsion-design-closure), using the magnet, heating and nozzle layout of that design at no less than one-tenth of its design heating power, produces measured fusion reactions while exhausting plasma through its magnetic nozzle, with thrust measured. Breakeven is not required. A fusor, or a device without a nozzle, does not count.
plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.status_oct2026: Direct Fusion Drive is a concept tested at small scale at PPPL (PFRC). Pulsar Fusion's Sunbird exhaust (no fusion) is targeted for an in-orbit demonstration in 2027 (pulsarfusion.com). No fusion-propulsion prototype has produced fusion.
plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.why: Chain (S3): design closure 2030 -> funding 2031 -> 4-6 years to build and commission a new device, as for SPARC (about six years from construction to its 2027 first-plasma target, after slips) and Helion's Polaris (about four to five years with large private funding; general) -> 2035 at the earliest. S2: closure 2031 -> after 2035. S1: closure 2034 -> after 2035. Deuterium fuel is enough to show fusion products, so He-3 supply does not gate this step. Speculative because fusion-propulsion funding is small and compact field-reversed devices have not reached fusion-relevant conditions. Funding runs on investor and appropriations clocks that do not differ by scenario, and experiments bind, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.strongest_case_small: Fusion-propulsion firms are small and thinly funded, and a flight-like mass budget is far harder than a lab device. A credible design does not by itself bring the money to build one.
plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.signpost: NASA, DARPA, ESA or private investors fund a fusion-propulsion prototype build; a PFRC-class experiment reports deuterium fusion neutrons.
plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the ground step between a closed design and flight, 2035 at the earliest in S3 and after 2035 in S2. Building a new fusion device takes 4-6 years after funding in every scenario, so it is Speculative. Experiments and funding bind, so S4 equals S3.
plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.revision_note: E-plasma-nuclear (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the fusion-propulsion chain between design closure and flight; spine. | Resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic accepted in full: S3/S4 2034 -> 2035, S2 2035 -> >2035, band_2035 S3/S4 Low -> Speculative; description made checkable (one-tenth of the design's heating power with its magnet, heating and nozzle layout, replacing 'flight-like mass per unit of power', which has no meaning below breakeven). Both reviewers: the link to plasma-fusion-propulsion-flight is now a hard edge. | R9-odds (2026-10-27): Unchanged: after 2035 everywhere (Speculative even in S3's 2035 earliest year).
plasma-35-fusion-drive-ground-test.gate_note: Building and commissioning a new device (experiment) binds; fusion-propulsion funding (capital) is the runner-up.

physclock-customer-launch-access.title: Outside customers can book launch again after the rideshare closure
physclock-customer-launch-access.description: SpaceX reopens capacity to outside customers beyond the 2028-29 manifest: Starship spare capacity offered for sale, and rideshare and dedicated slots bookable again for missions that want to fly after early 2029. Until then an outside operator, lunar-mission team or constellation without an existing contract buys from other launchers or waits.
physclock-customer-launch-access.status_oct2026: As of late June 2026, at least nine SpaceX partners and customers told SpaceNews that new Transporter and Bandwagon bookings beyond late 2028 or early 2029 are closed (SpaceNews, via Mach33's launch research handoff; TODO(source): link the SpaceNews item). Bandwagon-5 flew in Oct 2026. Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 opens Starship spare capacity to customers in 2031 in its reference case and tests 2029 to 2033; opening in 2029 gives a 2030 spot price of $921/kg, opening in 2033 keeps 2031 at $6,236/kg. Starship carries 1,644 customer tonnes in 2029 and 9,820 in 2031 in the reference case (Mach33, 10 Sep 2026). A dedicated Falcon 9 costs about $5,300/kg today.
physclock-customer-launch-access.gate_note: SpaceX's decision to release spare capacity binds; internal demand (Starlink, own orbital compute, lunar tankers) is the runner-up because it absorbs the flights that would be sold.
physclock-customer-launch-access.pathway: P7 (exogenous; AI math enters only through competitors' engineering)
physclock-customer-launch-access.launch_source: Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 (wave 44 internal path, 23 Sep 2026; wave 38b customer path, 10 Sep 2026)
physclock-customer-launch-access.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous launch anchor. Mach33's Launch Keystone thesis is that an activity becomes viable for a provider using spare capacity on its own rocket before it becomes viable for a customer buying a flight. v1.3 opens Starship spare capacity to customers in 2031 in its reference case and varies the year from 2029 to 2033, so the odds cross Medium in 2031 and High in 2033, the end of the tested range. The earliest year needs 100+ heavy flights a year first (physclock-heavy-cadence-100: S2 2030, S3 2029), because spare capacity exists only once cadence outruns Starlink and SpaceX's own compute. S3 and S4 open a year earlier on that cadence, not because of mathematics; S1 follows a year later because a plateau weakens the cadence case. Competing reusable fleets (physclock-reusable-competition) accelerate release rather than gate it. Wave 45 (v1.4) moves the price hinge to 2030; the model stays pinned to v1.3. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (Mach33 discloses SpaceX equity holdings).
physclock-customer-launch-access.strongest_case_small: Other launchers (Rocket Lab, Blue Origin, Arianespace, Chinese providers) sell capacity today, so a determined customer never fully loses access; the closure bites hardest on rideshare-priced small missions.
physclock-customer-launch-access.signpost: A published Starship rideshare or customer price list; Transporter or Bandwagon slots offered for 2030 or later; the number of non-SpaceX payloads on Starship in 2029-30.
physclock-customer-launch-access.note_2035: Medium by 2031 and High by 2033 in S2 to S4, following the v1.3 opening year and its tested range; S1 a year later. S4 equals S3 because cadence and allocation bind.
physclock-customer-launch-access.revision_note: R9-launch (2026-10-27): new node for the launch-internal / launch-external split (review LK-2, PRD WS2). Dated against Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 (wave 44 internal path, 23 Sep 2026; wave 38b customer path, 10 Sep 2026).

comms-d2c-v2-service.title: Second-generation direct-to-cell service (V2 D2C) in commercial use
comms-d2c-v2-service.description: SpaceX's V2 direct-to-cell satellites, the filed next generation after the V1 D2C payloads flying today on the V2 Mini bus, carry a '5G-like' service with about 100 times V1's data density to unmodified or lightly modified phones, on the EchoStar 2 GHz MSS band among others, sold through partner operators (naming per Mach33's Connectivity Keystone).
comms-d2c-v2-service.status_oct2026: V1 D2C flies today: about 650 D2C-enabled satellites on the V2 Mini bus carry texting, IoT and light data; 22M monthly Starlink Mobile users through 36 operators (Aug 2026) against 7.4M monthly unique devices in the S-1 (Mach33, State of Connectivity, 14 Oct 2026). V2 D2C is framed for 2027 to 2028, with the EchoStar 2 GHz band roadmap aiming at video, voice and cellular broadband at up to 150 Mbps per user (Mach33 news, 2026). Spectrum in Oct 2026: the FCC approved SpaceX's purchase of three AWS-3 licenses (21 Oct); SpaceX agreed to buy up to 14 MHz of 800 MHz (8 Oct); ANATEL granted 15+15 MHz of 2 GHz S-band in Brazil (9 Oct); CTIA and carriers urged the FCC to drop 2.5 and 3.45 GHz from the satellite-to-phone plan (22 Oct).
comms-d2c-v2-service.gate_note: Handset silicon and operator go-to-market bind (Mach33's named gating items); spectrum approvals are the runner-up.
comms-d2c-v2-service.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous connectivity anchor, dated from the public 2027 to 2028 window for V2 D2C (TODO(source): replace with the Connectivity Keystone's dates and odds when released; Mach33 post 154 says the model is not yet out). The tree's 1.5-3x slip calibration on announced SpaceX schedules puts the earliest year at 2028, Medium from 2029 and High from 2031. Mach33 names handset silicon and go-to-market as the gating items, so the binding gate is adoption; spectrum (EchoStar 2 GHz, AWS-3, 800 MHz) is the runner-up and is largely in hand by Oct 2026. AI math enters only through certified coexistence scheduling (comms-d2d-coexistence-scheduling), an accelerator. All scenarios share the date because the gates are handsets, operators and spectrum.
comms-d2c-v2-service.strongest_case_small: V1 already reaches 22M monthly users; V2's gain is data density, which demand and handset support may not use for years.
comms-d2c-v2-service.signpost: A V2 D2C launch; a partner operator selling a data plan above 10 Mbps per user over satellite; 2 GHz MSS handset chipsets shipping.
comms-d2c-v2-service.note_2035: High from 2031 in every scenario. S4 equals S3 because handsets, operators and spectrum bind.
comms-d2c-v2-service.revision_note: R9-d2c (2026-10-27): new node (review CK-1). Dated from the public 2027 to 2028 V2 D2C window pending the Connectivity Keystone (TODO(source)).

comms-d2c-v3.title: Third-generation direct-to-cell satellites (V3 D2C) in service
comms-d2c-v3.description: V3 D2C satellites, launched on Starship after the V3 Starlink ramp, enter commercial service with an order of magnitude more direct-to-cell speed and two orders more capacity than today's V1 payloads (Mach33, Oct 2025).
comms-d2c-v3.status_oct2026: Not yet. Starship's first orbital flight (Flight 14, 28 Sep 2026) deployed 26 V3 Starlink satellites; Mach33's base case puts V3 at about 1 Tbps per satellite, ten times a V2 Mini (State of Connectivity, 14 Oct 2026). SpaceX is seeking 80,000 US cell sites (22 Oct 2026); Verizon's CEO says SpaceX needs 4 to 6 years and $300B to $500B for a US network (26 Oct 2026).
comms-d2c-v3.gate_note: V3 D2C rides Starship on SpaceX's own manifest, so internal launch cadence binds; spectrum for broadband to phones is the runner-up.
comms-d2c-v3.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous connectivity anchor dated after the V3 Starlink ramp (TODO(source): replace with the Connectivity Keystone's dates and odds when released). V3 satellites need Starship, and a D2C variant follows V2 D2C in service and 100+ heavy flights a year (physclock-heavy-cadence-100: S2 2030, S3 2029), so the earliest year is 2030 in S2, Medium from 2031 and High from 2033. Internal launch binds; spectrum for broadband to phones (2 GHz, AWS-3, 800 MHz, and the contested 2.5 and 3.45 GHz bands) is the runner-up. AI math enters only through coexistence scheduling, an accelerator.
comms-d2c-v3.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may fold D2C into later broadband satellites rather than fly a distinct V3 D2C generation, which would blur the milestone without changing capacity.
comms-d2c-v3.signpost: A filing or launch of V3-class D2C satellites; Starship flights carrying D2C payloads; US cell-site agreements.
comms-d2c-v3.note_2035: High from 2033 in S2 to S4 (2034 in S1). S4 equals S3 because launch and spectrum bind.
comms-d2c-v3.revision_note: R9-d2c (2026-10-27): new node (review CK-1). Dated after the V3 Starlink ramp pending the Connectivity Keystone (TODO(source)).

comms-starlink-mobile.title: Starlink Mobile serves 100 million phones a month
comms-starlink-mobile.description: Starlink Mobile, SpaceX's direct-to-cell brand since MWC Barcelona (Mar 2026), reaches at least 100 million monthly users through partner operators, with broadband-class data (video and voice) available, not only texting.
comms-starlink-mobile.status_oct2026: 22M monthly Starlink Mobile users through 36 operators (Aug 2026), against 7.4M monthly unique devices in the S-1 (Mach33, 14 Oct 2026); 13M users in 12 countries at an ITU session (Feb 2026); VEON passed 11M users in under a year (Oct 2026); Starlink Mobile went live nationwide in Brazil with Vivo (26 Oct 2026). Mach33 'Starlink Mobile: Bundling Unit Economics' covers the pricing.
comms-starlink-mobile.gate_note: Operator bundling and handset support bind the user count; spectrum approvals are the runner-up.
comms-starlink-mobile.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous adoption outcome. Users roughly doubled from 13M (Feb 2026) to 22M monthly (Aug 2026) through 36 operators; with V2 D2C's broadband-class service from 2028, a further 4.5x to 100M is credible from 2029 and Medium from 2030 (judgment). High from 2033, after V3 D2C lifts capacity two orders of magnitude. TODO(source): replace with the Connectivity Keystone's user path when released; post 154 says direct-to-device enters its model alongside other uses of the fleet. All scenarios share the date because operators, handsets and spectrum bind.
comms-starlink-mobile.strongest_case_small: Most of these users are occasional texters in coverage gaps; monthly users can grow fast without much traffic or revenue.
comms-starlink-mobile.signpost: Reported monthly users above 50M; a major US or European operator selling satellite data as a standard plan feature.
comms-starlink-mobile.note_2035: High from 2033 in every scenario. S4 equals S3 because adoption binds.
